de.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Old French de Middle French de French de Inherited from Middle French de, from Old French de, from Lati…

dame.e: Inherited from Old French dame, from Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina.

je.e: From Middle French je, from Old French je, from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆.

est.e: Inherited from Old French, from Old English ēast.

être.e: From Middle French and Old French estre and ester, respectively from Early Medieval Latin essere (< esse "be") and Latin stāre (“stand”). Conjugations reflect both but more so the former.

pas.e: Inherited from Old French pas, from Latin passus. e. “not at all” – originally used with certain verbs of motion.

le.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-der. Proto-Italic *olnos Old Latin olle Latin ille Old French le Middle French le French le From Middle French le, from Old French le, from Latin illum, by dropping il- and -m.

que.e: Inherited from Latin quid, usurping some of the roles of Latin quod.

la.e: From Middle French la, from Old French la, from Latin illam, which is the accusative singular feminine of ille.
c: « Elle aime la musique. » « Moi aussi. »

vous.e: Inherited from Middle French vous, from Old French vos, vous, from Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs.

tu.e: From Old French tu, from Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognates with the exact same usage are the Italian tu, as well as du in German or ты in Russian.

taire.e: , or from the future forms), itself from Latin tacēre, from Proto-Italic *takēō.

un.e: Inherited from Middle French un, from Old French un, from Latin ūnum, accusative singular of ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.

à.e: Inherited from Old French a, a merge of Latin ad and ab.
c: On a un compte à régler.

et.e: Inherited from Middle French et, from Old French et, from Latin et. Often written as e in Old French, the spelling with t was re-established in the 12ᵗʰ century based on the Latin spelling.
c: J'ai un chien noir et blanc.
Bir siyah ve beyaz köpeğim var.

il.e: From Middle French il, from Old French il, from Late Latin illī.

c: Alors il y a un problème...
On a un compte à régler.

elle.e: Inherited from Old French ele, from Latin illa, feminine of ille.

ne.e: From Middle French, from Old French nen (preceding vowel sounds) or ne (preceding consonant sounds), from Latin nōn (“not”).

c: Je prépare le déjeuner tous les jours.
Ben her gün öğle yemeği yaparım.
La police vous fera trouver les balles.

en.e: From Middle French en, from Old French en, from Latin in, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”).
c: Elle ne veut pas en parler.
O, o konu hakkında konuşmak istemiyor.

on.e: Inherited from Old French hom, om (nominative form), from Latin homō (“human being”) (compare homme from the Old French oblique form home, from the Latin accusative form hominem).

ça.e: Syncopic contraction of cela (“that”), from ce + -là. Compare French ceci (“this”).

une.e: Inherited from Old French une, from Latin ūna, feminine of ūnus.

pour.e: Inherited from Middle French pour, from Old French por, pur, from Late Latin pōr, from Latin prō.
c: C'est trop beau pour être vrai.
O, gerçek olamayacak kadar çok iyi.

avoir.e: Inherited from Middle French avoir, from Old French avoir, aveir, aver, from Latin habēre (“have, hold, possess”), probably from a Proto-Italic *habēō or *haβēō, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰh₁bʰ- (“t…

c: Loin des yeux, loin du cœur.
Gözden ırak olan, gönülden ırak olur.

qui.e: Inherited from Middle French qui, from Old French qui, from Latin quī.

mais.e: Inherited from Old French mes, mais, from Latin magis.
c: Désolé, mais je dois travailler ce soir.
Je ne suis pas médecin, mais professeur.
Ben bir doktor değilim fakat bir öğretmenim.

mai.e: Inherited from Old French mai, from Latin Maius.
c: Son anniversaire est le cinq mai.

dans.e: Inherited from Old French denz, from Vulgar Latin dē intus, from Latin dē + intus, meaning "from inside" or "from within".
c: Je suis tout seul dans ce pays étranger.
Comment trouves-tu de la nourriture dans l'espace ?

dan.e: Borrowed from Japanese 段 (dan), from Chinese 段 (duàn).

nous.e: Inherited from Middle French nous, from Old French nous, nos, from Latin nōs, from Proto-Italic *nōs. ), this use was perceived as peasant-like and thus often mocked since the 15th century (for example by Molière).

me.e: From Middle French me, from Old French me, from Latin mē (accusative of ego), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁me- (“me”).

bien.e: Inherited from Middle French bien, from Old French bien, from Latin bene (“well”).

si.e: From Old French se, from Latin si (“if”).
c: Si je pouvais être comme ça...

du.e: Inherited from Old French del. The expected modern form would be *deau or *deu, but it underwent stronger contraction, due to its unstressed use. Akin to Galician do, Portuguese do, Sicilian dû, Italian and Spanish del.

y.e: From i grec (“Greek i”), referring to the letter upsilon (Υ), originally borrowed from the Greek alphabet, as opposed to "Latin i" (I).

non.e: From Old French non, from Latin nōn.

avec.e: Inherited from Middle French avec, avecques (“with”), from Old French avoc, avoec, avuec (“with”), from an assumed Vulgar Latin *aboc, *abhoc, *apud hŏque, from Latin apud (“with, near, close to”) + hoc (“this”) + -que.

tout.e: Inherited from Middle French tout, from Old French tot, from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration (likely via expressive gemination) of Latin tōtus.

plus.e: Inherited from Middle French plus, from Old French plus, from Latin plus.

plaire.e: Inherited from Middle French plaire, from Old French plaire, from plaisir, from Latin placēre.

mon.e: Inherited from Middle French mon, from Old French mun, mon, meon, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin mum, a reduced variant of Latin meum, accusative masculine and neuter singular of meus.

te.e: From Middle French te, from Old French te, from Latin tē, (accusative of tū), from Proto-Indo-European *twé, *te, accusative of *túh₂ (“you”).

fait.e: Inherited from Middle French fait, from Old French fet, from Latin factum.

faire.e: From Middle French faire, from Old French faire, from Latin facere. ) originated in the Latin form fēcī, with metaphony (*/ˈfed͡zi/ > */ˈfit͡s/).

moi.e: Inherited from Middle French moy, from Old French mei, moi, mi (“me”), tonic form of me, from Latin mē (“me”), from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)me-, *(h₁)me-n- (“me”). More at me.

oui.e: First attested in 1380, from Old French oïl (1100), from Vulgar Latin *hoc ille or by surface analysis a compound of Old French o (affirmative particle) and il (“he”). ”). See the Old French term for details.

aller.e: From Middle French aller, from Old French aler, from Early Medieval Latin alāre, of uncertain origin. Forms beginning with v- come from Latin vado; forms beginning with ir- come from Latin eo.
c: Gidiş dönüş mü? Sadece tek yön.

ils.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin illī, which sounded il in Old French, to which a plural -s was added.

sur.e: Inherited from Middle French sur, from Old French sur, seur, sor, soure, souvre, sovre (“on, upon, over”), from Latin super (“over, on, above”). Doublet of super, a borrowing.
c: Je n'ai pas d'argent sur moi.
J'étais sur le point de quitter ma maison.

quoi.e: From Latin quid; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís. Cognate to English what, which differs due to changing under Grimm’s law.

se.e: From Middle French se, from Old French se, from Latin sē. See also soi.

comme.e: From Middle French comme, from Old French come, from Late Latin quōmodo et.

savoir.e: Inherited from Old French savoir/eir, from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Latin sapĕre.

vouloir.e: Inherited from Old French voloir, voleir, from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

ici.e: From Old French ci (“here”), from Late Latin ecce hīc, with /i-/ added by analogy with Old French iluec (“there, in that place”), from Latin illoc.

toi.e: Inherited from Middle French toi, tei, from Old French tei, te, from Latin tē.

dit.e: From Old French dit, from Latin dictus.

dire.e: Inherited from Middle French dire, from Old French dire, from Latin dīcō, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).

c: Cette robe lui va vraiment bien.

votre.e: Inherited from Middle French vostre, from Old French vostre, from Latin voster (alongside the 'proper' vester).

pourquoi.e: From Middle French parquoy, from Old French por quoi.

où.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *kʷuðei Old Latin cubī Latin ubi Old French ou Middle French où French où Inherited from Middle French où, from Old French ou, from Latin ubi (“where”).

là.e: Inherited from Middle French la, from Old French la, from Latin illāc. The grave accent on the a was added to disambiguate with la (“the”). Compare Spanish allá, Portuguese lá, from Latin ad + illāc.

rien.e: Inherited from Middle French rien, from Old French rien, from Latin rem (“thing”). Compare Catalan res (“nothing”) or Galician ren (“nothing”).

quand.e: From Middle French quand, from Old French quant, from Latin quandō (“when”).

pouvoir.e: Inherited from Middle French povoir, from Old French povoir, pooir, from earlier Old French poeir, podeir, from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.
c: İsteğin olduğu yerde, bir yol vardır.

son.e: Inherited from Old French son, suen, suon, from Latin sonus (the current form may be remade after or influenced by sonner).

alors.e: ), from Old French a + lors. Compare Italian allora, Spanish alora, Occitan alara and Catalan aleshores.

ton.e: Inherited from Old French ton, tos, from Latin tuus.

comment.e: Inherited from Old French coment (“how”). Analyzable as comme + -ment.

par.e: Inherited from Middle French par, from Old French par, from Latin per.
c: J'ai été surpris par la nouvelle.

ou.e: Inherited from Old French ou, from Latin aut.
c: Tek ya da çift kişilik oda?
À la bouteille ou au verre ?

chose.e: Inherited from Middle French chose, from Old French chose, from Latin causa. Compare Italian cosa, Portuguese coisa, Spanish cosa among many others. Compare cause, a borrowed doublet.

merci.e: From Middle French merci, mercy, from Old French merci, from Latin mercēdem (“wages, fee, price”).

juste.e: Inherited from Old French juste, in this form probably borrowed from Latin iūstus, jūstus, from Proto-Italic *jowestos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.

très.e: Inherited from Middle French trés, from Old French trés, inherited from Latin trāns, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“through, throughout, over”). Doublet of trans-, trans, and tré-.

jamais.e: Inherited from Old French ja mais (“any more”, only in reference to the future), the two components deriving from Latin iam and magis. Compare Spanish jamás, Italian giammai, Occitan jamai and Portuguese jamais.
c: Geç olması hiç olmamasından daha iyidir.

été.e: Inherited from Old French esté, from Latin aestātem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“burn; fire”).
c: Son sac a été volé hier.

aussi.e: Inherited from Middle French aussi, from Old French ossi, ausi, alsi (“as, in the same way as”), from Vulgar Latin *ale si (“other so, else so”), from Latin alid, aliud (“other, another, any other, else”) + sīc (“so, th…
c: « Elle aime la musique. » « Moi aussi. »
Je n'ai jamais été aussi heureux.
Daha önce hiç bu kadar mutlu olmamıştım.

vraiment.e: Inherited from Middle French vrayement, from Old French veraiement. By surface analysis, vrai + -ment. Compare Italian veramente.

voir.e: Inherited from Middle French veoir, from Old French veoir, veir, from earlier vedeir, from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-.

même.e: Inherited from Middle French mesme, from Old French mesme, earlier medesme or medisme and meïsme, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from Latin -met + ipse + -issimus.

sa.e: From Old French sa, from Latin sua feminine form of suus.
c: À chaque homme sa façon de penser.
Çok sayıda insan çok sayıda akıl.
Elle est aussi belle que sa mère.

maintenir.e: Inherited from Old French maintenir, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). Equivalent to main + tenir.
c: Le beau temps va se maintenir.

tous.e: Inherited from Middle French tous < Old French toz. By surface analysis, tout + -s.

deux.e: Inherited from Middle French deux, from Old French deus, from Latin duōs, masculine accusative plural of duo, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁.

c: Şu ayakkabılar için ödeme yaptınız mı?

ta.e: From Old French ta, from Latin tua, feminine of tuus.

autre.e: Inherited from Middle French aultre, from Old French autre, from Latin alterum.

peu.e: Inherited from Old French poi, from Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare Catalan poc, Italian poco, Portuguese pouco, Spanish poco.

temps.e: Inherited from Old French temps and its variants, from Latin tempus.

toujours.e: From Middle French tousjours, from Old French toz jorz, tuzjurz (“without ceasing”, literally “all days”). By surface analysis, tous + jours (compare Dutch altijd (“always”), Danish altid (“always”)).

encore.e: Probably from Old French ancor, from Late Latin in hanc hōram (“until this hour”). Compare Catalan and Occitan encara, Italian ancora. Sense 5 is a semantic loan from German noch (adverb).

notre.e: Inherited from Old French nostre, from Latin noster.

mes.e: From Old French mes, from Latin meōs, meī and meās, meae.

besoin.e: Inherited from Middle French, Old French besoing; can be seen as a masculine variant of besogne, from Old French besonge, from Old Frankish *bisunnija, from *sunnijōn (“to look after”) (whence soigner), possibly through…

falloir.e: Inherited from Old French faloir, from an earlier falleir, from a changing of Old French faillir after its third person singular, faut, earlier falt (from Latin fallit), based off the model of valoir.

devoir.e: Inherited from Middle French debvoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (to owe; ought, must).

vie.e: Inherited from Old French vie, from older Old French viḍe, from Vulgar Latin vītam, from the accusative of Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā.

peut-être.e: From peut (“(it) can”, “(it) may”) + être (“be”). Equivalent to Catalan potser, English maybe, Sicilian po siri ~ po (gghi)èssiri.

fois.e: Inherited from Middle French foys, from Old French foiz, from earlier feiz, from Latin vicem. The reason for the development of an initial /f/, instead of the expected /v/, is not entirely clear.

foi.e: Inherited from Middle French foy, from Old French foi, fei, feid, from Latin fidem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“to command, to persuade, to trust”).

vu.e: Past participle of voir. Inherited from Old French veü, from earlier vedüt, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *vidūtus in place of Latin vīsus. Compare Italian veduto, Romanian văzut.

donc.e: Inherited from Old French dunc, from Vulgar Latin dunc, from a crossing of Latin tunc with dum. Compare Italian dunque, Occitan donc and Catalan doncs.

sans.e: Inherited from Old French sans, senz, sens, from Latin sine conflated with absentia in the sense "without". Cognates include Spanish sin, Portuguese sem, Italian senza, Catalan sens, sense.
c: Ma vie est vide sans lui.

monde.e: ), itself inherited from Latin mundus. The alteration was likely driven by the desire to distinguish from unrelated mont (“mountain”).

c: C'est parce que tu es une fille.
Parce que je veux devenir professeur d'anglais.
Bir İngilizce öğretmeni olmak istememin nedeni odur.

avant.e: Inherited from Middle French avant, from Old French avant (“before, prior in time, forward”), from Late Latin ab ante (“before, in front of”), from Latin ab (“from”) + ante (“before”).
c: Görev başka her şeyden önce gelmeli.

sûr.e: Inherited from Middle French sceur, from Old French seür, inherited from Latin sēcūrus.

trop.e: Inherited from Middle French trop, from Old French trop (“unreasonably excessive”), from Frankish *þorp (“a cluster, agglomeration", also "collection of houses, village”), from Proto-Germanic *þurpą (“village”), from Pr…

parler.e: Inherited from Middle French parler, from Old French parler, from Early Medieval Latin parabolāre (“to express”), from Latin parabola (“parable, comparison”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ).

personne.e: Inherited from Middle French personne, from Old French persone, presonne, from Latin persona, of unknown, perhaps Etruscan, origin.

père.e: Inherited from Middle French pere, from Old French pedre, pedra, pere, from Latin patrem, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.

croire.e: Inherited from Old French creire, croire, from Latin crēdere. Cognates with Norman creire, Gallo craire, Picard croère, Bourguignon croire, Franco-Provençal crêre, Occitan creire, créser, Corsican credè.

après.e: Inherited from Middle French aprés, from Old French aprés, from Late Latin ad pressum, from Latin ad + pressum. Compare obsolete Spanish aprés.
c: Entrez dans la pièce après moi.

dieu.e: Inherited from Middle French dieu, from Old French deu, from Latin deus, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós.

ouais.e: From oui via dialectal variants; also possibly from oyez.

c: John écrit à ses parents une fois par mois.
John ayda bir ailesine mektup yazar.
Je n'ai pas eu de ses nouvelles depuis cinq ans.
Ben beş yıl boyunca ondan bir haber almadım.

penser.e: Inherited from Middle French penser, from Old French penser, from Latin pēnsāre, whence also the doublet peser, as well as panser, originally an alternative spelling which acquired a special sense.

états-unis.e: From États (“states”) + unis (“united”), calque of English United States.
c: Elle a eu une vie heureuse.

aimer.e: From Middle French aymer, from Old French amer, from Latin amō (“to love”).

leur.e: Inherited from Middle French leur, from Old French lor, from Latin illōrum, genitive masculine plural of ille.
c: Ils ont appelé leur enfant Jane.

homme.e: Inherited from Middle French homme, from Old French home, hom, hume, homme, etc, from Latin hominem (with the loss of the -in- syllable, via syncope and then assimilation of -mn- to -mm-), from Old Latin hemō, from Prot…

venir.e: Inherited from Middle French venir, from Old French venir, from Latin venīre.

vrai.e: Inherited from Old French verai, from Early Medieval Latin vērāgus, from Latin vērāx.

femme.e: Inherited from Middle French femme, from Old French fame, feme, fenme, femme, from Latin femina; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-éh₂ (“(the one) nursing, breastfeeding”), derivation of the verbal root *…
c: Sa mère est une femme magnifique.

an.e: From Old French, from Latin annus, from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”).

mal.e: From Old French mal, from Latin malus, possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mel- (“bad, wrong”). Near cognates include Portuguese mal, Italian male and Spanish malo.

chez.e: Inherited from Middle French chez, from Old French chies, from Latin casa (“house”). Doublet of case.

déjà.e: From Middle French desia, from Old French des ja corresponding to dès + jà.

depuis.e: Inherited from Middle French depuis, from Old French depuis, from Late Latin dē post and influenced by Old French puis or a later variant, *dē postius.

beaucoup.e: Inherited from Old French biau cop, first attested circa 1210. Equivalent to beau (“nice, beautiful”) + coup (“hit, strike”).

mort.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French mort, from Vulgar Latin *mortu, from Latin mortuus.

mourir.e: Inherited from Middle French mourir, from Old French morir, from Latin morīrī, variant of morī.

mieux.e: Inherited from Middle French mieulx, from Old French mielz, mialz, miels, from Latin melius.

mère.e: Inherited from Middle French mere, from Old French medre, mere, from Latin mātrem, from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.

fille.e: * (daughter): From Middle French fille, from Old French fille, from Latin fīlia.

tes.e: Inherited from Old French tes, from Latin tuōs, tuī and tuas, tuae.

gens.e: From an earlier gents, from the plural of Old French gent, genz, from gentem, accusative of gēns.
c: J'oublie toujours les noms des gens.
Les gens ont peur de la guerre.

quel.e: Inherited from Middle French quel, from Old French quel, from Latin quālis.

c: Ca semble trop beau pour être vrai.
O gerçek olamayacak kadar çok iyi görünüyor.
Le calcium est un élément chimique dont le symbole est Ca.
Kalsiyum, sembolü Ca olan kimyasal bir elementtir.

voilà.e: Literally, “look there”. ”), second-person singular imperative of voir (“to see, to look”) and là (“there”).

petit.e: Inherited from Old French petit, from Vulgar Latin pittitus (775; compare Latin pitinnus, pitulus). Compare Spanish pequeño.
c: Bu kitap ne kadar da küçük !

maison.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French maisun, meson, inherited from Latin mānsiōnem (“abode, home, dwelling”), from maneō (“remain, stay”) (whence also French manoir). Doublet of mansion, a borrowing.

soit.e: From Latin sĭt, third-person singular present subjunctive of sum.
c: Penses-tu que ce soit une mauvaise chose ?
Onun kötü bir şey olduğunu düşünüyor musun?
En effet, il semble que ce soit une erreur.

cela.e: By surface analysis, ce + là. See also -là.

c: Il a travaillé toute la journée.

soir.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-rós Proto-Italic *sēros Latin sērus Proto-Indo-European *-éad Proto-Italic *-ōd Latin -ō Latin sērō Old French seir Old French soir French soir Inherited f…

passer.e: Inherited from Middle French passer, from Old French passer, from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).
c: Ne laisse pas passer cette chance !

prendre.e: Inherited from Middle French prendre, from Old French prendre, prandre, from Latin prēndere, alternative form of prehendere (“to seize”), from prae- (“before”) + *hendō (“to take, seize”) (not attested without prefix),…

jour.e: From Middle French jour, from Old French jor(n), from Late Latin diurnum. Doublet of diurne, a borrowing.
c: Je vais rester ici plusieurs jours.

monsieur.e: From mon (“my”) + sieur, from the oblique case of Old French sire (the nominative case giving rise to messire), ultimately from Latin senior (whence also seigneur).

salut.e: Inherited from Old French salut, salu, from Latin salūtem, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).

cet.e: From Middle French cest, from Old French cist~cest, from Vulgar Latin *ecce iste, from Latin ecce + iste.

nom.e: Inherited from Old French nom (whence Norman nom), from Latin nōmen (whence Italian and Portuguese nome; Spanish nombre), from Proto-Italic *nomən, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (whence Ancient Greek ὄνομα (ónoma),…

argent.e: Inherited from Middle French argent m, from Old French argent m, from Latin argentum n, according to the TLFi etymological dictionary, a borrowing).

bonjour.e: Inherited from Middle French bonjour, from Old French bon jor (literally “good day”). By surface analysis, bon (“good”) + jour (“day”).

nuit.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts Latin nox Old French noit Middle French nuyt French nuit Inherited from Middle French nuyt, from Old French noit, from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽…
c: Bonne nuit. Fais de beaux rêves.

nuire.e: Inherited from Old French nuire, from Vulgar Latin *nocĕre, from Latin nocēre (whence Old French nuisir).
c: Cela pourrait nuire à notre entreprise.
Il l'a fait sans intention de nuire.

raison.e: Inherited from Old French reson, raison, inherited from Latin ratiōnem. Compare the borrowed doublet ration.

moins.e: Inherited from Middle French moins, from Old French meins, from Latin minus.
c: Daha ucuz bir odanız var mı?

arriver.e: Inherited from Middle French arriver, from Old French ariver, from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre. Synchronically a- + rive + -er.

maman.e: Inherited from Middle French memmen, from baby talk, possibly influenced by Latin mamma.

reste.e: Inherited from Middle French reste, from Old French reste, equivalent to the stem of rester.

rester.e: From Middle French rester, from Old French rester, from Latin restāre. According to the Trésor informatisé, the Old French is a borrowing from Latin.
c: Je vais rester dans cette ville.

seul.e: Inherited from Latin sōlus. Doublet of solo, which is a borrowing from Italian.

aider.e: Inherited from Middle French ayder, from Old French aidier, from Latin adiutāre (“to help, assist”). Cognate with Catalan aidar, Spanish ayudar, Romanian ajuta, Italian aiutare, Portuguese and Catalan ajudar.

air.e: Inherited from Old French air, aire, from Latin āēr.

entre.e: Inherited from Middle French entre, from Old French entre, inherited from Latin inter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”). Doublet of inter-, a borrowing.
c: Je dois choisir entre les deux.
Ben ikisinin arasında seçim yapmak zorundayım.

papa.e: From Middle French papa, child-speak, syllable-repetitive; compare maman.

problème.e: Inherited from Middle French probleme, a borrowing from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”).

ah.e: Inherited from Old French a! (“oh! ah! ”), of expressive origin.

peur.e: Inherited from Middle French peur, from Old French peor, poür, from Latin pavōrem (“fear, fright”). Compare Catalan por and Italian paura.

regarder.e: From Middle French, from Old French reguarder, corresponding to French re- + garder.

gars.e: Inherited from Old French gars, the nominative singular of garçon m, from Early Medieval Latin garciō m.

trouver.e: Uncertain. Probably inherited from Old French trover, truver, from Vulgar Latin *tropāre (“to compose a poem”, > “to invent” > “to find”), from Latin tropus m (“figurative use of a word”); compare English trope.
c: On peut toujours trouver du temps.

fils.e: Inherited from Old French fils, fiz, fil, from Latin filius (“son”). Cognate to Spanish hijo, Portuguese filho, , Italian figlio and Romanian fiu, among others.

fil.e: From Old French fil, from Latin fīlum.

attendre.e: Inherited from Old French atendre, from Latin attendere.

trois.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *tréyes Proto-Italic *trejes Proto-Italic *trēs Latin trēs Old French trois Middle French troys French trois Inherited from Old French trois, treis, from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic…

assez.e: Inherited from Middle French assez, from Old French asez, from Late Latin ad satis, from Latin ad + satis. Cognate with Franco-Provençal asséds, Occitan assatz, Italian assai, Portuguese assaz, and Spanish asaz.

famille.e: Inherited from Middle French famille, borrowed from Latin familia.

dû.e: Old French deü, from Vulgar Latin *dēbūtus, past participle of Latin dēbēre. Cognate to Italian dovuto. Compare dette (“debt”), from the Classical Latin past participle dēbita n pl.

c: Bob peut répondre à toutes les questions.
Je pourrais répondre à toutes les questions.

travail.e: Inherited from Middle French travail (“suffering, pain”), from Old French travail (“suffering, pain”), deverbal of travailler, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre, from Late Latin tripālium (“torture device made of three stak…

pris.e: Inherited from Old French pris, from Latin prēnsus, variant of prehensus.

tête.e: Inherited from Middle French teste, from Old French teste, from Latin testa (“pot, jug, brick”). Replaced French chef (from Latin caput), which is still used in some expressions.

appeler.e: Borrowed from Latin appellāre (“to address, to call by name”).

partir.e: Inherited from Middle French partir, from Old French partir, from Latin partīre.

vite.e: From Old French viste, of disputed origin:. * According to Littré, from Italian visto (“seen”), from Vulgar Latin *visitus, from Latin vidēre.

arrêter.e: Inherited from Middle French arrester (“to stop”), from Old French arester (“to stay, stop”), from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“stop, remain behind, stay back”). Compare English arrest.

voiture.e: Inherited from Old French voiture, from Latin vectūra.

enfant.e: Inherited from Middle French enfant, from Old French enfant, from Latin īnfantem.
c: Chaque enfant a reçu un cadeau.

tuer.e: Inherited from Middle French tuer, from Old French tuer (“kill, extinguish”), from Latin tūtārī (“avert, ward off”). Compare Occitan tuar.

merde.e: Inherited from Middle French merde, from Old French merde, from Latin merda.

c: Elle a été malade pendant longtemps.

pendre.e: Inherited from Old French pendre, from Late Latin pendĕre (conjugation confused with or altered by pendere (“to suspend, hang”)) for Latin pendēre, present active infinitive pendeō, from Proto-Italic *pendēō, from Proto…

idée.e: Borrowed from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”).

chance.e: From Old French cheance (“accident, chance, luck”), inherited from Vulgar Latin *cadentia (“falling”). Doublet of cadence, a borrowing from Italian.

part.e: From Old French part, from Latin partem, accusative of pars, from Proto-Italic *partis.
c: Je ne veux aller nulle part.

elles.e: Inherited from Old French eles, from Latin illās, accusative feminine plural of ille.

grand.e: Inherited from Middle French grand, from Old French grant, from Latin grandem.

aujourd'hui.e: Inherited from Middle French auiourd'huy; univerbation of au + jour + de + hui, literally “on the day of today”; since hui comes from Latin hodie.

ami.e: Inherited from Middle French amy, ami, from Old French ami, amic, from Latin amīcus (“(male) friend”). Compare Catalan amic, Italian amico, Portuguese amigo, Romanian amic, Sardinian amícu, Spanish amigo. Doublet of igo.

demain.e: Inherited from Old French demain, from Late Latin dē māne (“early in the morning”), from Latin dē + māne, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to mature, ripen”).

tard.e: Inherited from Old French tard, tart, from Latin tarde.

puis.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *postius, a comparative of Latin post (“after”). Compare Portuguese pois, Spanish pues, Italian poi, and Romanian apoi (archaic păi).

truc.e: From Middle French truc, from Old French trut, borrowed from Old Occitan truc, deverbal from trucar, from Vulgar Latin *trūdicāre.

c: Ne kadar tatlı bir kız çocuğu!

tant.e: Inherited from Old French tant, from Latin tantum.
c: Je veux tant connaître votre pays.
Ülkeniz hakkında çok şey bilmenizi istiyorum.

combien.e: Inherited from Old French combien, from comme + bien.

mec.e: From mac, a shortening of maquereau (“pimp”), from Dutch makelaar (“broker”).

sens.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sent-der. Proto-Italic *sentiō Latin sentiō Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Italic *-tus Latin -tus Latin sēnsusbor. Proto-Germanic *sinnaz Frankish *sinnbor.

sentir.e: Inherited from Old French sentir, from Latin sentīre, from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”).

porte.e: Inherited from Old French porte, from Latin porta, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to pass through”). Compare English portal.

porter.e: Inherited from Old French porter, from Latin portāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go, traverse”).

sortir.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin sortīrī, probably influenced by surrectus (through a Vulgar Latin form *surctus and its derivatives, possibly through a verb *surrectīre, surctīre).

super.e: Borrowed from Latin super. Doublet of the inherited sur. See also hyper, borrowed from Ancient Greek.

heure.e: From Middle French heure, from Old French houre, from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “time, season, year”), from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”).

contre.e: Inherited from Middle French contre, from Old French contre, from Latin contra.

coup.e: Inherited from Old French colp, cop, from Late Latin colpus, syncopated form of Latin colaphus, from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos).

comprendre.e: Inherited from Middle French comprendre, from Old French, from Latin comprehendere.

c: Ben o şarkıyı daha önce duydum.

entendre.e: Inherited from Middle French entendre, from Old French entendre, from Latin intendere (“to turn one’s attention, to strain”).

ensemble.e: From Old French ensemble, from Latin īnsimul, a variant of simul See also Italian insieme, Catalan ensems.
c: Birlikte öğle yemeği yemek ister misin?

nouveau.e: Inherited from Middle French nouveau, from Old French novel, from Latin novellus.

amour.e: Inherited from Middle French amour, from Old French amor, from Latin amor. The regular phonetic development would be ameur, attested in Old French (compare Picard anmeur).

importer.e: Borrowed from Latin importāre. The second sense is a semantic loan from Italian importare.

sang.e: Inherited from Old French sanc, from Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Latin sanguinem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”).

cas.e: Inherited from Old French cas, borrowed from Latin cāsus.

sous.e: From Middle French soubs, from Old French soz, from Latin subtus.
c: Rien de nouveau sous le soleil.
Hiçbir şey güneşin altında yeni değildir.

sou.e: Inherited from Old French, inherited from Late Latin soldus, from Latin solidus. Doublet of solide. See also the form sol, which kept the historical spelling from Old French, even if it came to be pronounced like sou.

finir.e: Inherited from Middle French finir, from Old French fenir (altered by association with fin), from Latin fīnīre.
c: Elle a dû finir ce travail hier.

question.e: ), borrowed from Latin quaestiō. At first a learned word, therefore retaining preconsonantal -s- (compare related quête).

histoire.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *weyd- Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Indo-European *wéydtōr Proto-Hellenic *wístōr Ancient Greek ῐ̔́στωρ (hĭ́stōr) Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *-eyéti Proto-Indo-Eu…

aide.e: Inherited from Middle French ayde, from Old French aide, aie, from aidier (modern Old French aider (“to help”)). The medial -d- would've been regularly lost, but was reinserted on the basis of the verb.

dernier.e: From a contraction of earlier derrenier, a derivation of Old French derrain (through analogy with premier), itself derived from Vulgar Latin *dēretrānus, from Latin dē + retrō + -ānus.
c: Il faisait chaud la nuit dernière.
J'étais à Londres le mois dernier.

demande.e: Inherited from Old French demande, from the verb demander.

demander.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē- Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂-der.

chercher.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-der. Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos)bor.

genre.e: From Old French gen(d)re, borrowed from Latin genere. Noun sense 6 is a semantic loan from English gender.

seulement.e: From Middle French seullement, from Old French solement, from Early Medieval Latin sōlā mente. Synchronically derivable from seule + -ment.

police.e: Borrowed from Late Latin polītīa (“state, government”), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía).

car.e: From Old French quer (“as, since, because, for”), from Latin quārē (“how; why”). Compare Catalan car.
c: Je vais bien car je suis vivant.
Je le fais car j'en ai envie.

mois.e: Inherited from Middle French moys, from Old French mois, from earlier meis, from Latin mēnsis. Compare Catalan mes, Italian mese, Occitan mes, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais, Spanish mes.
c: Je serai là tout le mois.
Je suis enceinte de quatre mois.

frère.e: Inherited from Old French frere, from older fredre, fradre, from Latin frātrem, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.
c: Je suis fier de mon frère.

laisser.e: Inherited from Middle French laisser, from Old French lesser, lessier, laissier (“to let, let go, leave”), from Latin laxāre (“to relax, loosen”); possibly partly from or influenced by Old High German lāzan (“to let, le…

aucun.e: From Old French alcun, from Vulgar Latin *alicunus, from Latin aliquī + unus. Cognate with Italian alcuno, Spanish alguno, Galician algún, Portuguese algum.

mettre.e: Inherited from Middle French mettre, from Old French metre, from Latin mittere, probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with Occitan metre.
c: Il a mis un pantalon propre.

chaque.e: From Middle French chasque, a backformation from chascun, from Old French chascun (whence modern chacun).

ville.e: Inherited from Middle French ville, from Old French ville, vile, inherited from Latin vīlla (“country house”). Doublet of villa.

longtemps.e: From long + temps, from Old French lonc tans. Ultimately inherited from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos, which is also where the English long time came from.
c: Elle a été malade pendant longtemps.

bébé.e: Nickname given to Nicolas Ferry, renowned throughout Europe as the court dwarf of the Polish King Stanisław Leszczyński.

place.e: Inherited from Old French place, from Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa).

c: Puis-je placer ça sur ton bras ?
Je n'ai aucun intérêt à placer mon argent dans tes rêves.

revoir.e: From re- + voir, or from Latin revidere.

putain.e: Inherited from Old French putain, originally the oblique case of pute (“dirty woman”) formed with the suffix -ain, from Vulgar Latin pūtta, from Latin pūta (“girl”). Compare with salope, Italian puttana, Spanish puta.

compris.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin comprēnsus, variant of comprehēnsus.

ni.e: From Middle French ny, from Old French ne, from Latin nec. Compare Italian né, Catalan and Spanish ni, Portuguese nem.
c: Ça n'a ni queue ni tête.
O herhangi bir anlam ifade etmiyor.

donner.e: Inherited from Middle French donner, from Old French doner, from Latin dōnāre.

endroit.e: Inherited from Middle French endroict, from Old French endroit, endreit, from Latin in directum. Equivalent to en + droit. Compare Occitan endrech, Catalan indret.
c: Tout le monde aime cet endroit.

corps.e: Inherited from Middle French cors, from Old French cors, inherited from Latin corpus (“body”). The p was added back to reflect the Latin etymology. Doublet of corpus.
c: Tout mon corps me fait mal.

façon.e: Inherited from Middle French façon, from Old French façon, from Latin factiōnem. Compare faction, a borrowed doublet.

c: Elle lui a donné une montre.

voici.e: Literally, “look here”. ”), second-person singular imperative of voir (“to see, to look”) and ci (“here”).

train.e: Inherited from Middle French train, from Old French train, from the verb trahiner (“to pull, drag”) (whence traîner).
c: Désolé. Le train était en retard.

dont.e: Inherited from Middle French dont, from Old French dunt, from Vulgar Latin/Latin dē unde (“from where”). Compare Spanish donde (“where”).
c: Histoires dont vous êtes le héros.
Voici la ville dont je te parlais.

écouter.e: Inherited from Middle French escouter, from Old French escouter, from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre. Doublet of ausculter, a borrowing from Latin.

c: Garde un œil sur les filles.

type.e: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos).

perdre.e: Inherited from Middle French perdre, from Old French perdre, from Latin perdere.

premier.e: Inherited from Middle French premier, from Old French premier, from Latin prīmārius. Doublet of primaire.
c: Cette université était mon premier choix.
À première vue, la question semble simple.
Je me souviens de la première fois.

côté.e: Inherited from Middle French costé, from Old French costé, from Latin costātus. Compare Spanish costado, Catalan costat.

point.e: Inherited from Middle French poinct (with orthography modified to reflect the Latin etymology), from Old French point, from Latin pūnctum.
c: Elle ne croit point en Dieu.
Ce n'est pas mon point fort.

tellement.e: From Middle French tellement, telement, from Old French telement. By surface analysis, tel + -ment. Compare Italian talmente.

main.e: Inherited from Middle French main, Old French main, mein, man, from Latin manus (“hand”), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to b…
c: Elle écrit de la main gauche.

tenir.e: Inherited from Middle French tenir, from Old French tenir, from Early Medieval Latin tenīre, from Classical Latin tenēre.

vieux.e: From Middle French vieulx, from Old French viel, from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.

matin.e: Inherited from Latin mātūtīnus (“of the morning”), from Matuta, Roman goddess of morning.
c: Demain, allons au marché du matin.
Il faisait moins dix ce matin.
Bu sabah sıfırın altında on dereceydi.

suite.e: Inherited from Old French suite, from earlier siute, from Vulgar Latin *sequita, (instead of classical secūta), as the feminine past participle of *sequere, from Latin sequi.

vers.e: From Latin versus (past participle of vertere). Cognate to Italian verso (preposition). Doublet of versus.

ver.e: Inherited from Old French ver, verm (“worm”), from Latin vermem (“worm”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.

minute.e: Inherited from Old French minute, borrowed from Latin minūta. Compare menu, an inherited doublet.

devant.e: From de + avant. False cognate of Indonesian and Malay depan despite similarity of both words in definition and pronunciation.

enfin.e: Univerbation of en + fin. Literally, “in the end”.

cause.e: Inherited from Old French cause, borrowed from Classical Latin causa. Compare chose, an inherited doublet.
c: Je me sens triste à cause de ça.
Ben bu konu hakkında üzgün hissediyorum.
Nous ne pouvons pas dormir à cause du bruit.

nouvelle.e: Inherited from Middle French nouvelle, from Old French novele, from Vulgar Latin *novella, substantivized neuter plural form of Latin novellus (“new, novel”). Compare Italian novella. Doublet of novelle.
c: Onun yeni elbisesini fark ettin mi?
Il a acheté une nouvelle voiture.

chambre.e: Inherited from Old French chambre, cambre, from Latin cambra, Medieval spelling of Latin camera (“room”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “something with an arched cover: a covered wagon, a covered boat, a vaulted ch…
c: Tek ya da çift kişilik oda?

droit.e: Inherited from Old French droit (spelled dreit in Early Old French, such as the Oaths of Strasbourg), inherited from Late Latin drictus, syncopated form of Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direct.

eau.e: Inherited from Middle French eau, eaue, from Old French ewe, euwe, egua (“water”), from Latin aqua (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water, flowing water”), related to Frankish *ahu ~ ahwā (“stream, water”…

compte.e: Inherited from Middle French compte, from Old French conte (with ⟨mp⟩ added back to reflect Latin computus). Cf. also the form conte.

compter.e: Inherited from Middle French compter, conter, from Old French compter, conter, cunter, from Latin computāre. Doublet of conter and computer.

terre.e: Inherited from Middle French terre, from Old French terre, from Latin terra (“earth”), from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”).

beau.e: Inherited from Middle French beau, from Old French biau, bel, from Latin bellus.

espérer.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *spéh₁s Proto-Italic *spēs Old Latin spēs Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-E…

loin.e: Inherited from Latin longē, from the adjective longus (“long, far-off”). Compare Catalan lluny, archaic Spanish lueñe.

mari.e: Inherited from Old French mari, from Latin marītus.

fin.e: From Middle French fin, from Old French fin, from Latin finis.
c: Toutes les choses ont une fin.
Sais-tu quel âge a Mme Nakano ?
Bayan Nakano'nun kaç yaşında olduğunu biliyor musun?
Appelez-moi Mme Suzuki, s'il vous plaît.

madame.e: From Old French ma dame (“my lady”), equivalent to ma + dame.

gros.e: Inherited from Old French gros, from Latin grossus.

boulot.e: Deverbal of boulotter, similar semantic development as in -role

plutôt.e: From Middle French plustost, see plus + tôt. Compare Italian piuttosto and Catalan més aviat. Compare the etymology of English rather.
c: Cela sera plutôt difficile pour lui.

chéri.e: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish شرع (şerʿ, şeriʿ), from Arabic شَرْع (šarʕ).

prêt.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i?

bureau.e: Inherited from Old French burel, diminutive of *bure (compare Middle French bure (“coarse woolen cloth”), French bourre (“hair, fluff”)), from Late Latin burra (“wool, fluff, shaggy cloth, coarse fabric”); akin to Ancie…

hier.e: Inherited from Old French ier, from Latin heri.

jouer.e: Inherited from Old French joer, from Latin iocārī.
c: Jouer aux cartes est un passe-temps.

celui.e: From icelui, from ici (“here”) + lui (“him”) or from Vulgar Latin *ecce illui, (genitive-)dative masculine singular of *ecce ille (influenced by Latin cui 'to whom'; cf. French lui), from Latin ecce + ille.
c: Ce livre est plus vieux que celui-là.

jeune.e: Inherited from Middle French jeune, from Old French juene, juefne, from Vulgar Latin *iŏvenem, from Latin iuvenem.

dehors.e: Inherited from Middle French dehors, defors, from Old French defors, from Vulgar Latin dē forīs, from Latin dē + forīs (“outdoors”).

a-t-il.e: a (“has”) + -t- (a restoration of the Latin 3rd-person-singular -t) + il (“he”).

confiance.e: Borrowed from Latin cōnfīdentia, altered after the noun fiance. Doublet of confidence.

année.e: Inherited from Old French anee. By surface analysis, an + -ée; an (“year”) from Latin annus (“year”). Perhaps alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *annāta, from Latin annāre; compare Italian annata.
c: Je vis ici depuis dix années.
Noël tombe un dimanche cette année.
Noel, bu yıl pazara denk geliyor.

vérité.e: Inherited from Middle French verité, from Old French verité, borrowed from Latin vēritātem. An inherited/popular Old French form verté also once existed. Compare English verity.

école.e: Inherited from Middle French eschole, from Old French escole, an early borrowing or semi-learned word taken from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).

chef.e: Inherited from Middle French chief, from Old French chief, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *kaput-. Doublet of cap.

c: Vous faites erreur à ce propos.
Je dirai quelque chose à ce propos.
Ben onun hakkında bir şey söyleyeceğim.

semaine.e: Inherited from Middle French sepmaine, from Old French semaine, from Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), derived from septimus (“seventh”).

vivre.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃- Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti Proto-Italic *gʷīwō Latin vivō Old French vivre Middle French…
c: Je ne veux pas vivre seul.

feu.e: Inherited from Old French fu, from Latin focus (“hearth”), which in Late and Vulgar Latin replaced the Classical Latin ignis (“fire”). Not related to English fire or German Feuer.

journée.e: From Old French jornee, from Vulgar Latin *diurnāta.

téléphone.e: From télé- + -phone from Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, “afar”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice, sound”).

c: Biri nerede bir telefon konuşması yapabilir?

près.e: Inherited from Old French prés (“closely”), from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”) and pressus (“concise”), from premō (“to press, push, condense”).
c: Bill vit près de la mer.

meilleur.e: Inherited from Middle French meilleur, from Old French meillor, from Latin meliōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *mélyōs, from *mel- (“strong, big”).

dessus.e: Inherited from Latin dēsūrsum, from dē and sūrsum.

prier.e: From Old French proiier, preier, from Latin precārī.

équipe.e: Inherited from Middle French equippe, from Middle French equipper, esquiper. More at French équiper.

vas-y.e: Second-person singular informal imperative of y aller.

manger.e: Inherited from Middle French manger, from Old French mengier, from Late Latin manducāre (“chew, devour”).

dur.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin dūrus.

guerre.e: Inherited from Middle French guerre, from Old French guerre, from Early Medieval Latin werra, borrowed from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”). Compare English war.

marcher.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French marchier, from Frankish *markōn, from Proto-Germanic *markōną. Compare also marquer.

sécurité.e: Borrowed from Latin secūritātem. Doublet of sûreté.

garçon.e: Inherited from Middle French garçon, from Old French garçon, garçun m (“servant, boy”), from Early Medieval Latin garciōnem, accusative of garciō m (“mercenary, servant, boy”), from Frankish *wrakkjō (“servant, boy”), f…

essayer.e: Inherited from Middle French essayer, essaier, from Old French essaiier, essayer, essaier, from essay, essai (“attempt; assay; experiment”) + -er (“infinitive-forming suffix”), from Late Latin exagium (“weight; weighing…

c: Onun tam olarak niyet ettiği oydu.

fort.e: Inherited from Old French fort, from Latin fortem (“strong”), from Old Latin forctis, fortis.

presque.e: Univerbation of près + que. Akin to Italian pressoché.

plein.e: Inherited from Old French plein, from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

derrière.e: Inherited from Old French deriere, from Late Latin dē retrō, from Latin dē + retrō. Cognate with Italian dietro.

c: Eh ben voyons ! Et puis quoi encore ?
İyi, görelim! Ve sonra, ne var?
T'es pas enceinte, non ? Bon ben arrête de boire !
Hamile değil misin? Peki, o zaman içki içmeyi kes!
Je vais la demander en mariage.

parent.e: Inherited from Middle French parent, from Old French parent, from Latin parentem.

capitaine.e: Inherited from Middle French capitaine, from Old French capitaine, borrowed from Late Latin capitaneus, from Latin caput. Compare the inherited Old French chevetaine (whence English chieftain). Doublet of cheftaine.

fou.e: Inherited from Middle French fol, from Old French fol, from Latin follem. Cognate with English fool.

tomber.e: ), or alternatively more likely from Frankish *tumbōn, tūmōn (“to rotate, reel, sway”), from Proto-Germanic *tūmōną (“to turn, rotate”), of uncertain origin. More at tumb. Displaced the native choir, inherited from cadō.

souvenir.e: Inherited from Middle French soubvenir, from Old French sovenir, from Latin subvenīre (“come to mind, occur to”), from sub + veniō. Doublet of subvenir.

envie.e: Inherited from Old French enveie (with /ei̯/ modified to /i/ to match the verb envier), from Latin invidia.

fête.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁stosder. Proto-Italic *θēstos Proto-Italic *fēstosder.

fêter.e: Inherited from Old French fester. By surface analysis, fête + -er.
c: Il n'y avait rien à fêter.

jeu.e: Inherited from Old French geu, gieu, giu, from Latin iocus, jocus.

pays.e: Inherited from Middle French pays, from Old French pais, from Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”), derived from Latin pāgus (“countryside; district”). See related terms. Cognates include Italian paese.
c: Chaque pays a sa propre histoire.

garde.e: Inherited from Old French guarde, from the verb guarder (or less likely directly from Frankish *warda), from Frankish *wardōn (“to protect”). Compare Italian guardia, Spanish guarda. Cognate with English ward.

garder.e: Inherited from Middle French garder, from Old French guarder, from Early Medieval Latin wardāre. Cognate to English ward.
c: Lütfen bunu bir sır olarak sakla.

cours.e: Inherited from Old French cours, inherited from Latin cursus. Doublet of course and cursus. Compare Italian corso.

cour.e: Inherited from Middle French court, from Old French cort, from Latin cortem, shortening of cohors. Doublet of cohorte and court (“tennis court”).
c: Bienvenue dans la cour des grands.

bientôt.e: Inherited from Old French bientost. By surface analysis, bien (“very”) + tôt (“early”).

numéro.e: Borrowed from Italian numero. Doublet of nombre.

cinq.e: From Middle French cinq, from Old French cinc, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, dissimilation of Classical Latin quīnque (“five”), from Proto-Italic *kʷenkʷe, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe, cognate with Portuguese and Spani…
c: Cinq est plus petit que huit.

parfait.e: Calque of Latin perfectus based on French par- + fait, inherited from Latin per- and factus respectively.

ainsi.e: Inherited from Middle French ainsi, from Old French ensi, ainsins, probably from Latin ad (“to”) + in (“in”) + sīc (“thus”).

c: Gidiş dönüş mü? Sadece tek yön.

sembler.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sem- Proto-Indo-European *sem-h₂-lo- Proto-Italic *semalis Latin similis Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Pr…

autant.e: From Vulgar Latin *al tantu, earlier *aliud tantum (compare with aliud), corresponding to Classical Latin alterum tantum.
c: O, seni benim sevdiğim kadar çok seviyor.

peine.e: Inherited from Old French peine, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Cognate with Spanish pena, Italian pena, Portuguese pena. False friend of Spanish peine (“comb”).

plan.e: From earlier plant, derived from the verb planter, or from Latin planus. Doublet of plant or plain, depending on which etymology is right.

c: Bir süre sakin ol ve konsantre ol.

prison.e: Inherited from Old French prison, inherited from Latin prehēnsiōnem, from prehendō. Doublet of préhension.
c: Il a été envoyé en prison.

arme.e: Inherited from Middle French arme, from Old French arme, from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).

mauvais.e: ), from Latin malus (“bad”) + fātum (“fate”). Cognate with Italian malvagio, and with Spanish and Portuguese malvado, all of them through Old Occitan malvatz.

mot.e: Inherited from Middle French mot, from Old French mot, from Late Latin muttum (“sound”), from muttīre (“mutter, make a mu-noise”), of onomatopoeic origin.

travailler.e: Inherited from Middle French travailler, from Old French travailler (“to toil, suffer, torment”), from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“to torture”), derived from Late Latin tripālium (“torture instrument”), from Latin tripāl…

quatre.e: Inherited from Old French quatre, qatre, catre, from Latin quattuor, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Compare Catalan quatre, Italian quattro, Portuguese quatro, Spanish cuatro.

choix.e: Inherited from Middle French choix, from Old French chois, deverbal from choisir, coisir (“to differentiate, see distinctly”), from Frankish *keusan (see contemporary Dutch kiezen), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *keusa…

abord.e: ], from aborder, from Old French aborder (“to hit a ship in order to board it”), from bord (“side of a ship, edge”), from Frankish *bord (“side of a ship or vessel”), from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“edge, border, side”), f…

faute.e: Inherited from Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin *fallita, feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō. Compare Catalan, Spanish, and Portuguese falta. Doublet of faillite.

facile.e: ), a borrowing from Latin facilis (“easy”), likely under influence of Italian facile.

bas.e: Inherited from Old French bas, from Late Latin bassus.

changer.e: From Old French changier. Cognate with Norman changi, Walloon candjî.

plaisir.e: Inherited from Middle French plaisir, from Old French plaisir, from Latin placēre. Compare Occitan plaser, Catalan plaer.

propre.e: Inherited from Old French propre, borrowed from Latin proprius.

tour.e: Inherited from Old French tor, from Latin turrem, from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis), τύρσις (túrsis).

ensuite.e: Univerbation of en + suite. Compare Spanish enseguida.

agent.e: Inherited from Middle French agent, from Latin agentem.

lit.e: Inherited from Old French lit, from Latin lectus.

lire.e: Inherited from Old French lire, from Latin legere, from Proto-Italic *legō, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-.

adorer.e: Inherited from Old French adorer, borrowed from Latin adōrāre.

amie.e: Inherited from Middle French amye, from Old French amie (“lover”), from Latin amīca (“(female) friend”).

rendre.e: Inherited from Old French rendre, from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere.

allons-y.e: First-person plural imperative of y aller.

route.e: From Old French rote, from Latin rupta [via].

lieu.e: Inherited from Middle French lieu, from Old French leu, from Latin locum, from Old Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”).

commencer.e: Inherited from Middle French commencer, from Old French comencier, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre.

service.e: Inherited from Old French servise, borrowed from Latin servitium (compare Portuguese serviço, Italian servizio, Norman sèrvice, Spanish servicio), from servus.

drôle.e: Inherited from Middle French drolle (“a merry fellow, pleasant rascal”) from Old French drolle (“one who lives luxuriously”), from Middle Dutch drol (“fat little man, goblin”), itself from Old Norse troll, from Proto-Ge…

pire.e: Inherited from Middle French pire, from Old French pire, from Latin peior, from Proto-Indo-European *ped-yōs (“to the ground, downward”). Related to pis.

état.e: Inherited from Old French estat, borrowed from Latin status (whence also the past participle été).
c: Mon père est dans un bon état depuis son opération.
Elle était dans un état pitoyable.

ceci.e: Equivalent to ce + ci. See also -ci.

sorte.e: Inherited from Old French sorte, borrowed from Latin sortem. Doublet of the inherited sort.

oublier.e: Inherited from Old French oblier, from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre, frequentative of Latin oblīvīscor (via its past participle oblītus).

tôt.e: From Old French tost, from Vulgar Latin tostum, from the neuter of Latin tostus (“toasted”), later meaning "hotly, promptly" in Vulgar Latin.

inquiet.e: ), a borrowing from Latin inquiētus. ). By surface analysis, in- + quiet.

payer.e: Inherited from Middle French payer, from Old French paiier, paier, from Latin pacāre (“pacify”).

cœur.e: Inherited from Middle French coeur, from Old French cuer, from Proto-Romance *corem m, from Latin cor n (“heart”).

dès.e: Inherited from Late Latin dē ex.
c: Onu mümkün olduğunca kısa sürede yap.

revenir.e: Inherited from Middle French revenir, from Old French revenir, from Latin revenīre (“come back, return”).

chien.e: Inherited from Middle French chien, from Old French chien, from Latin canis, canem (“dog”).

café.e: Borrowed from Italian caffè, first appearing as the form caveé, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve) (Turkish kahve), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa, “coffee”). Doublet of caoua.

calme.e: Inherited from Middle French calme, probably borrowed from Italian calma, from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma) (or alternatively through the intermediate of an Iberian language as opposed to Italian).

calmer.e: From calme + -er, or possibly from Italian calmare.

montrer.e: Inherited from Middle French monstrer, from Old French monstrer, semi-learned form of older moustrer, mostrer, from Latin mōnstrāre, whence also English demonstrate.
c: Elle lui a montré la photo.

ferme.e: Inherited from Middle French ferme, from Old French ferm, ferme (“solid”), from Latin firmus (“solid, secure”), from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”…

fermer.e: Inherited from Old French fermer (“to close”), Latin firmāre (“make firm, confirm”).

musique.e: Inherited from Old French musique, borrowed from Latin mūsica, borrowed from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “art of the Muses”), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).

courant.e: Inherited from Middle French courant, from Old French courant, from Latin currēns, ~rentis. By surface analysis, courir + -ant.

courir.e: Inherited from Old French courre, corre (modified under the influence of -ir verbs), from Latin currere (“to run”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).

sauf.e: From Old French salv, salf, inherited from Latin salvus. Cognate to Italian and Spanish salvo.

moyen.e: Inherited from Middle French moyen, from Old French moien, earlier meien, inherited from Latin mediānus. Doublet of médian, a borrowing, and also of misaine.
c: Il doit y avoir un moyen.
Il a trouvé un moyen, n'est-ce pas ?

avis.e: Inherited from Old French avis, from vis, from Latin visus.

sauver.e: Inherited from Middle French saulver, from Old French sauver, salver, from Gallo-Romance salvar, from Late Latin salvāre (“to save”), from Latin salvus.

hôpital.e: ), a borrowing from Late Latin hospitāle (“hospital, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”). Doublet of hôtel.

meurtre.e: From Middle French meurtre (“murder”) from Old French murtre, mordre (“murder”) (compare Medieval Latin murdrum (“murder”)), both from Frankish *murþar (“murder”) from Proto-Germanic *murþrą (“murder, killing, death”),…

sérieux.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sēriōsus, from Classical Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”).

seconde.e: The first sense is a borrowing from Latin (minuta) secunda.

second.e: Inherited from Old French secunt, second, segont, borrowed as a semi-learned term from Latin secundus (“second”); related to sequi (“follow”). Doublet of son (“bran”), which was inherited.
c: Tourne au second feu à gauche !
Je suis le second de trois enfants.

esprit.e: Inherited from Middle French esperit, from Old French, borrowed from Latin spiritus through Ecclesiastical Latin and Christian religious texts.
c: J'ai fermé mon esprit à ce problème.
C'est un honneur de vous rencontrer, Mademoiselle.

marché.e: Inherited from Old French marchié, marchiet, from Latin mercātus. Doublet of mercato.

haut.e: Inherited from Middle French hault, from Old French haut, halt (“high, tall, elevated”), a conflation of Frankish *hauh, *hōh (“high, tall, elevated”) and Latin altus (“high, raised, profound”).

salle.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sel-der. Proto-Germanic *saliz Frankish *salider. Old French saleder.
c: Il était seul dans la salle.

malade.e: Inherited from Middle French malade, from Old French malade, from Latin male habitus (“ill-kept, not in good condition”).

gentil.e: Inherited from Old French gentil, borrowed from Latin gentīlis, from gēns (“Roman clan”).

six.e: Inherited from Middle French six, from Old French sis, six, from Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

simple.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin simplex.
c: Tek ya da çift kişilik oda?
Gidiş dönüş mü? Sadece tek yön.

john.e: Borrowed from English John. Doublet of Jean.

c: Cette voiture est celle de Brian.

appris.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin apprēnsus, variant of apprehensus.

apprendre.e: Inherited from Middle French apprendre, from Old French aprendre, aprandre, inherited from Latin apprendere, contracted form of apprehendere. Doublet of appréhender, which was borrowed.

seigneur.e: Inherited from Middle French seigneur, from Old French seignor (oblique form), from Latin seniōrem (compare sire, derived from the nominative form). Doublet of senior.
c: Le dimanche est le Jour du Seigneur.

dîner.e: Inherited from Old French disner, from Vulgar Latin *disiūnāre, from disieiūnāre, disjejūnāre (“to break the fast”), from dis- + Late Latin iēiūnāre (“to fast”), from Latin ieiūnus. Doublet of déjeuner.

supposer.e: Inherited from Middle French supposer, from Old French supposer, borrowed from Latin suppōnere, altered based on French poser.

chemin.e: Inherited from Middle French chemin, from Old French chemin, from Early Medieval Latin cammīnus, borrowed from Gaulish *kamman, or from Latin -īnus.
c: Il a peut-être perdu son chemin.

partout.e: Univerbation of par + tout. Akin to Catalan pertot. Compare Italian dappertutto and Spanish por todas partes for similar constructions.

bras.e: Inherited from Middle French bras, from Old French bras, from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn).

cul.e: Inherited from Middle French cul, from Old French cul, from Latin cūlus.

c: Gelecek sefer daha iyi bir iş çıkar.

prochain.e: Inherited from Old French prochain, from Vulgar Latin *propeānus, derived from Latin prope (“near”). Cognate with Sardinian probianu.

visage.e: Inherited from Old French visage, from vis (from Latin visus) + -age, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *visāticum.

c: Daha iyi bir fikrin var mı?

face.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French face, from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face, shape”). Doublet of faciès.

c: Hoş bir akşam için teşekkür ederim.
Il sera là toute la soirée.

roi.e: Inherited from Middle French roy, from Old French roi, rei, from Latin rēgem.

surtout.e: From sur + tout. Akin to Italian soprattutto and Spanish sobre todo.
c: Sa maladie était surtout dans sa tête.

écrit.e: (past participle) From Middle French escrit, from Old French escrit, from Latin scriptus.

écrire.e: Inherited from Middle French escrire, from Old French escrire, escrivre, from Latin scrībere.

livre.e: Inherited from Middle French livre, from Old French livre, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin librum. The strictly inherited form would be *loivre. Doublet of liber.

livrer.e: Inherited from Old French livrer, inherited from Latin līberāre. Doublet of libérer.
c: Je peux livrer cela à Tom.

message.e: Inherited from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”).

valoir.e: Inherited from Middle French valoir, from Old French valoir, valeir, from Latin valēre, from Proto-Italic *walēō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl̥h₁éh₁yeti, from *h₂welh₁- (“to rule, be strong”).
c: Geç olması hiç olmamasından daha iyidir.
Mieux vaut ne pas y aller.

boire.e: Inherited from Middle French boire, from Old French boivre, beivre, from Latin bibere, from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti.

bois.e: Inherited from Middle French boys, from Old French bois, from Early Medieval Latin boscus (“grove”), borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

sinon.e: Contraction of Middle French si non. Compare Catalan sinó, Portuguese senão, and Romanesco "sinnò".
c: Plus vite, sinon tu seras en retard.
Allons-y maintenant. Sinon, nous serons en retard.
Şimdi gidelim. Aksi halde, geç kalacağız.

erreur.e: From Old French, borrowed from Latin errōrem.
c: Il a fait une erreur grave.
La personne que nous avons vue ce matin était Mr. Green.
Bu sabah gördüğümüz adam Bay Green'di.
Mr Brun parle très bien le japonais.
Bay Brown Japonca'yı çok iyi konuşur.

rendez-vous.e: Nominalization of the second person plural imperative form of se rendre; see rendez and vous

joue.e: From Old French joe, from Vulgar Latin *ga(v)ota.

pauvre.e: Inherited from Middle French pauvre, relatinisation of earlier povre, from Old French povre, inherited from Latin pauper, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”).

devenir.e: Inherited from Old French devenir, from Latin dēvenīre, from dē + veniō.

sud.e: Inherited from Middle French sud, su, from Old French su(d), borrowed from Old English sūþ (“south”), which see.

rencontrer.e: From Old French encontrer prefixed with re-, from Late Latin *incontrare.

sort.e: Inherited from Old French sort, from Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Cf. also the borrowed doublet sorte.

occuper.e: Inherited from Middle French occuper, from Latin occupāre.

souvent.e: Inherited from Old French suvent, sovent, from Latin subinde, morphologically sub + inde. The original meaning of subinde was “immediately after”, which then evolved to “repeatedly” and then to “often”.

pièce.e: Inherited from Middle French piece, from Old French piece, from Late Latin pettia, from Gaulish *pettya, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis.
c: Cette pièce est agréable pour travailler.

recevoir.e: Inherited from Middle French recevoir, from Old French recevoir, from Vulgar Latin *recipēre, from Latin recipiō. Cognate with English receive through borrowing, see there for more.

grave.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷreh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-us Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us Proto-Italic *gʷraus Latin gravis Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-In…

mets.e: Inherited from Old French més, from Latin missum. The form was later influenced by the underlying mettre.

honneur.e: Inherited from Middle French honneur, from Old French enor, eneur, onor, honor, from Latin honor, honōrem.

dormir.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *drem- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti Proto-Italic *dormiō Latin dormīre Old French dormir Middle French dormir French dormir Inherited from Middle French d…

faux.e: Inherited from Middle French faulx, from Old French fauz, faus, fals, from Latin falsus.

c: Mesdames et messieurs, bienvenue à bord.
Bayanlar ve baylar, gemiye hoş geldiniz.

groupe.e: From Italian gruppo, itself derived from Vulgar Latin *cruppus.
c: J'aime faire partie de ce groupe.
Bu grubun parçası olmak hoşuma gidiyor.
J'aimerais faire partie de ton groupe.

rêver.e: Inherited from Middle French resver, from Old French resver (“to consider, reflect, be delirious”), of uncertain origin.

es: pensar en la inmortalidad del cangrejo

carte.e: Learned borrowing from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Cognate with French charte.

manque.e: Inherited from Middle French manque (first attested in 1594), from Old Italian manco (“lack”).

manquer.e: Borrowed from Italian mancare, derived from manco (“maimed”).
s: In the sense expressing that something almost happened
faillir is generally more common in modern French

envoyer.e: Inherited from Old French enveier, from Late Latin inviāre, from Latin via (“road, path”). Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Occitan, and Catalan enviar, Italian inviare.

début.e: Inherited from Middle French début, deverbal of desbuter (“to move, begin”) (whence débuter).
c: Je le savais depuis le début.

content.e: Inherited from Middle French content, from Old French, borrowed from Latin contentus.

secret.e: Inherited from Middle French secret, from Old French secret, borrowed from Latin sēcrētus.

cher.e: Inherited from Middle French cher, from Old French cher, chier, from Latin cārum (“dear, valuable”), from Proto-Italic *kāros, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros, from *keh₂- (“to desire, to wish”).

effet.e: From Old French effect, from Latin effectus.

sac.e: Inherited from Old French sac, from Latin saccus, from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, bag; sackcloth”), ultimately from Semitic.

acheter.e: Inherited from Old French acheter, from Vulgar Latin *accaptāre, from Latin acceptāre. Doublet of accepter.

voix.e: Inherited from Middle French voix, from Old French voiz, from Latin vōcem, accusative of vōx (“voice”), from Proto-Italic *wōks, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs.

c: Parmi eux certains sont mes amis.
Certains d'entre eux sont en bonne santé mais pas les autres.
Onlardan bazıları sağlıklı ama diğerleri değil.

certain.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *krey- Proto-Italic *kritos Latin certus Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Latin *certānus Old French certain French certain Inherited from O…

noël.e: Inherited from Middle French Noël, from Old French Noel, Naël, inherited from Vulgar Latin *notālis, from Latin nātālis [diēs Dominī] (“birthday of the Lord”) with dissimilation of the first -a- to -o-. Doublet of natal.

gagner.e: Inherited from Middle French gaigner, from Old French gaigner, gaaignier, itself inherited from Vulgar Latin *wadaniāre, ultimately from Frankish *waiþanōn.

grâce.e: Inherited from Old French grace, from an early borrowing from Latin grātia, from grātus (“as a favour”). The lengthening of the vowel, which is indicated with the circumflex, is irregular.

maître.e: Inherited from Middle French maistre, from Old French maistre, from Latin magistrum. Doublet of maestro, borrowed from Italian, magister, borrowed from Latin, and master, borrowed from English.

prix.e: Inherited from Old French pris, from Latin pretium (“price, reward”), from Proto-Indo-European *préti (“back”). Compare précieux.

général.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁os Proto-Italic *genos Latin genus, generis Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisde…
c: Il rentre chez lui tard en général.
En général je suis d'accord avec elle.

âge.e: Inherited from Middle French âge, from Old French aage, eage, edage, from Vulgar Latin *aetāticum. The Old French forms displaced eé, the direct reflex of Latin aetātem.

long.e: Inherited from Old French long, from longe, longue, feminine of lonc, lunc, from Latin longus. Cognate with English long, origin of German Chaiselongue.

rue.e: Inherited from Old French rue, developed figuratively from Latin ruga.
c: Ne joue pas dans la rue.

tirer.e: From Middle French tirer, from Old French tirer, from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.
c: Arrête de me tirer les cheveux !
Elle garde toujours ses cheveux propres.
O, her zaman saçını temiz tutar.
Tu devrais te couper les cheveux.

cheveu.e: Inherited from Middle French cheveu, from Old French cheveu, from Latin capillus. See there for more details.
c: Attends une minute ! À qui est ce cheveu ?!
Bir dakika bekle! Bu kimin saçı?!

noir.e: Inherited from Middle French noir, from Old French noir, neir, from Latin nigrum. Doublet of nègre.

promettre.e: Inherited from Old French prometre, an early borrowing from Latin promittere, adapted to or based on French mettre.
c: O onunla evlenmek için söz verdi.
O, onunla evlenmek için söz verdi.

patron.e: From Old French patron (“patron, protector”), from Latin patrōnus, from pater (“father”).

avocat.e: ), a borrowing from Latin advocātus. Doublet of avoué, which may be inherited or an earlier borrowing.

force.e: Inherited from Old French force, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”).

forcer.e: Inherited from Old French forcier, from Vulgar Latin *fortiāre, a verb based on Late Latin fortia, a noun based on Latin fortis (“strong”).

dix.e: Inherited from Old French dis, from Latin decem, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥. For the pronunciation compare six.

bout.e: From Middle French, from Old French bout (“a blow”), derivative of bouter (“to strike”), of Germanic origin. More at bouter.

bouillir.e: Inherited from Middle French bouillir, from Old French boillir (“to boil, burst”), inherited from Latin bullīre (“to bubble”), derived from Latin bulla (“bubble, bud, button”).

ordre.e: Inherited from Old French ordre, ordene, borrowed from Latin ōrdinem (accusative of ōrdo). Doublet of the inherited orne, now a regional term with a specialized agricultural sense.

armer.e: Inherited from Old French armer, from Latin armāre. By surface analysis, arme + -er.

cru.e: Inherited from Middle French crud, from Old French cru, creu, from Latin crūdus (English crude).

Mutlu olmak için milyonlara ihtiyacın yok.

million.e: Inherited from Middle French million, from Italian milione.

J'ai un million de questions à poser.

voyage.e: Inherited from Old French voiage, viage, veiage, from Latin viāticum. Doublet of viatique.

utiliser.e: From Italian utilizzare. By surface analysis, utile + -iser.

dos.e: Inherited from Old French dos, from Latin dorsum (through Vulgar Latin dossum). Compare Romansh dies, Catalan dors, Italian dosso, and Romanian dos.

paix.e: Inherited from Old French pais, paiz, from Latin pāx (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to join, to attach”).

battre.e: Inherited from Middle French battre, from Old French batre, from Latin battere, from earlier battuere.

décider.e: Inherited from Middle French décider, borrowed from Latin decidere.

Ne yapacağına karar vermek size kalmış.

pars.e: Borrowed from Classical Persian پَارْس (pārs), from Middle Persian 𐭯𐭠𐭫𐭮𐭩 (Pārs), from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠pārsa⁠/).

avion.e: Coined by French inventor and engineer Clément Ader for a patent application. From earlier Avion (1875), from Latin avis (“bird”) + -on, replacing earlier aéroplane after WWI.

bordel.e: Etymology tree Medieval Latin bordellum Old French bordel Middle French bordel French bordel Inherited from Middle French bordel, from Old French bordel, from Medieval Latin bordellum (“brothel, small hut”).

table.e: Inherited from Old French table, from Latin tabula (“tablet”). Doublet of tôle and taule.

rouge.e: Inherited from Middle French rouge, from Old French roge, rouge, from Latin rubeus.

système.e: Inherited from Middle French systeme (first attested 1552), from Late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “organised whole, body”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

médecin.e: Inherited from Middle French medecin, a back-formation from Old French medeciner (“to treat medically”). Replaced Old French mire, mege, meide, meie, etc. inherited from Latin medicus.

bateau.e: From Old French batel, Anglo-Norman bat, from Old English bāt (English boat) + suffix from Latin -ellus. It displaced the native word nef, which comes from Latin navis.
c: On peut encore voir le bateau.
Tu peux y aller en bateau.

stupide.e: Borrowed from Latin stupidus (“struck senseless, amazed”), from stupeō (“be amazed or confounded, be struck senseless”).

faim.e: Inherited from Old French faim, fain, from Latin famēs (“hunger”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, Portuguese fome, Italian fame and Romanian foame.

autour.e: From au + tour, replacing Old French entor (compare alentour).
c: La Terre tourne autour du Soleil.

fond.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin fundus. Doublet of fonds.

fondre.e: Inherited from Old French fondre, from Latin fundere (“to melt”), from Proto-Italic *hundō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd-.
c: La glace est en train de fondre.

surprise.e: From the feminine of surpris, past participle of the verb surprendre.

ligne.e: Inherited from Old French ligne, from Latin līnea.

colère.e: Old borrowing from Late Latin cholera, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra), from χολή (kholḗ). Doublet of choléra.

clair.e: Inherited from Middle French cler, from Old French cler, from Latin clārus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call”, “to shout”).

balle.e: Inherited from Middle French balle, from northern Italian balla. Doublet of balle (“bundle”).

or.e: From Middle French or, from Old French or, from Latin aurum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂é-h₂us-o- (“glow”), from *h₂ews- (“to dawn, become light, become red”).

hors.e: Inherited from Middle French fors, from Old French fors, from Latin forīs, or more likely derived from dehors (in Middle and Old French defors).

risque.e: Inherited from Middle French risque (first attested in 1578), borrowed from Old Italian risco (modern Italian rischio).
