terminer.e: Inherited from Old French terminer, borrowed from Latin termināre.

mission.e: Inherited from Old French mission, borrowed from Latin missiōnem.

joli.e: Inherited from Middle French joly (“considerable, ingenious, agreeable, pretty”), from Old French joli, jolif (“pretty, smart, joyful, merry”), possibly from Old Norse jól (midwinter festival), from Proto-Germanic *jehw…

cadeau.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan capdel (“ornament”), from Latin capitellum. Doublet of cadet, caudillo, and chapiteau.

voler.e: Inherited from Old French voler, from Latin volāre. Displaced Old French rober (unrelated to Modern French rober (“to wrap a cigar in a sheet of tobacco”)).

plusieurs.e: Inherited from Old French plusors, from Vulgar Latin *plūsiōres, alteration of Late Latin plūriōres (by influence from plūs), from Latin plūres.

gauche.e: From gauchir (“to bend, dodge, warp”), a conflation of Old French gauchier (“to tread”) (from Frankish *walkijan, *walkan, cognate with English walk) + Old French guenchir (“to deviate”) (from Frankish *wenkijan (“to sw…

neuf.e: Inherited from Middle French neuf, from Old French nuef, from Latin novem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.

ouvrir.e: Inherited from Middle French ouvrir, from Old French ovrir, obrir, from Vulgar Latin *operīre, alteration of Classical Latin aperīre (“to open”). See also Italian oprire; Catalan obrir.

allez-y.e: Second-person plural and formal imperative of y aller.

suivre.e: Inherited from Middle French suyvre, from Old French sivre, siure, segre, from Vulgar Latin *sequere of deponent Latin sequī.

réponse.e: From the feminine of répons, or from Old French response, from respons (also the past participle of respondre), a semi-learned word from Latin respōnsum. Cf. the verb répondre.

lumière.e: Inherited from Middle French lumiere, from Old French lumiere, from Late Latin lūmināria, plural of neuter lūmināre reinterpreted as a feminine noun, ultimately from Latin lūmen. Doublet of luminaire.
c: Il a vu une lumière au loin.
J'aime lire un livre à la lumière du jour.

pied.e: Inherited from Middle French pied, from Old French pié, from Latin pedem. The -d was added to the spelling in Middle French after the Latin form. Doublet of foot.

espèce.e: Borrowed from Latin speciēs. Doublet of épice, an older borrowing.

pareil.e: Inherited from Middle French pareil, from Old French, from Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Compare Occitan parelh, Spanish parejo.

soleil.e: Inherited from Middle French soleil, from Old French soleil, from Vulgar Latin *sōliculus, diminutive of Latin sōl (“sun”), from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.

cuisiner.e: Inherited from Late Latin cocīnāre, from Latin coquīnāre. By surface analysis, cuisine + -er.

Bu gemiye kimin ad koyduğunu merak ediyorum.

enfer.e: Inherited from Old French enfer, from Latin īnfernus.

vendre.e: Inherited from Old French vendre, from Latin vēndere.

responsable.e: Inherited from Middle French responsable, corresponding to response (Modern French réponse) + -able.

nul.e: Inherited from Middle French nul, from Old French nul, from Latin nūllus.

signe.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French signe, a borrowing from Latin signum. Doublet of seing, which was inherited through Vulgar Latin.

signer.e: From a modification, based on signe, of Old French seignier, itself from Latin signāre.

lieutenant.e: Univerbation of lieu tenant, literally “placeholder”, from tenir lieu (“to hold the place of someone, to act as a substitute for someone”).
c: Il fut rétrogradé au rang de lieutenant.
Lieutenant, ma patience est plus courte que mon épée.
Teğmen, benim sabrım kılıcımdan daha kısadır.

étrange.e: From Middle French estrange, from Old French estrange, from Latin extrāneus.

diable.e: Inherited from Middle French diable, from Old French diable, deable, a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin or Late Latin diabolus, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

c: Ce soir nous allons à l'église.

emmener.e: Attested in Old French as enmener. By surface analysis, en- + mener.

honte.e: Inherited from Middle French honte, from Old French hunte (“dishonour”), from Early Medieval Latin haunta, borrowed from Frankish *haunitha (“disdain, scorn, ridicule”), from Proto-Germanic *hauniþō (“humiliation”), fro…

bouche.e: Inherited from Middle French bouche, from Old French boche, buche, from Latin bucca. Doublet of bouque.

boucher.e: From Old French bouchier, from bouc (“goat”), of Germanic origin.
c: Nous devons trouver quelque chose pour boucher ce trou.
Bu deliği tıkamak için bir şey bulmalıyız.

préférer.e: Inherited from Middle French preferer, from Old French preferer, borrowed from Latin praeferre.
c: Onu tek başıma yapmayı tercih ederim.

coupable.e: Inherited from Old French coupable, from Ecclesiastical Latin culpābilis (“culpable”), derived from culpa.

rire.e: Inherited from Middle French rire, from Old French rire, from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre. The past participle's root-final S was lost.

soin.e: Inherited from Middle French soin, from Old French soing (“care”), from Frankish *sunnija (“worry, care, concern”), from Proto-Germanic *sunjō, *sunþijō (“truth, care, responsibility”), derived from Proto-Indo-European…

milieu.e: Inherited from Middle French milieu, meilleu, mileu, from Old French milliu, meillieu, mileu, formed from mi- + lieu. Analyzable as mi- (“mid-”) + lieu (“place”).
c: Celle du milieu est la mienne.

appartement.e: Borrowed from Italian appartamento, from Spanish apartamiento.

cerveau.e: Inherited from Middle French cerveau, cervel, from Old French cervel, from Latin cerebellum, diminutive of cerebrum, from Proto-Italic *kerazrom, from a Proto-Indo-European form *ḱerh₂-s-ro, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“head…

paris.e: Inherited from Old French Paris, from Late Latin name of an earlier settlement, Lūtētia Parīsiōrum (“Lutetia of the Parisii”), from Latin Parīsiī, a Gaulish tribe.

blague.e: 18th century, from Dutch balg. The sense “joke” (ca. 1800) from the notion of something puffed up, hence vain, fanciful.

choisir.e: Inherited from Middle French choisir, from Old French choisir, coisir (“to differentiate, see distinctly”), from Frankish *kauʀijan (“to choose”) or Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (kausjan), both from Proto-Germanic *kauzijaną,…

c: Elle était belle à son époque.

voie.e: Inherited from Old French voie, veie, inherited from Latin via. Doublet of via. Unrelated to voir and voirie, despite influencing the latter.
c: Il faut que je la voie !

allée.e: Inherited from Old French alee, allee.

intérêt.e: From Medieval Latin interesse, from Latin interesse, from inter- + esse.
c: Il agit dans son propre intérêt.

cheval.e: Inherited from Middle French cheval, from Old French cheval, from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin.

combattre.e: Etymology tree Vulgar Latin combatto Old French combatre French combattre Inherited from Middle French combatre, from Old French combatre, from Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin cum + battuō, from Gaulish.
c: Combattre le mal par le mal.
Je n'en peux plus de combattre.
Ce mot n'existe pas en français.

tel.e: Inherited from Middle French tel, from Old French tel, tal, from Latin tālis. Compare Spanish tal.
c: As-tu déjà entendu une telle chose ?
Hiç böyle bir şey duydun mu?

trou.e: From Early Medieval Latin traugus, a "barbarous" Latin word first attested in the Ripuarian Law, probably related to torus (“round hill”). Thought to be of Celtic, specifically Gaulish, origin.

public.e: Borrowed from Latin pūblicus. The noun is from the adjective.
c: O, herkesin önünde konuşmaktan nefret eder.
Ne le descends pas en public.
Herkesin önünde onun hakkında kötü konuşma!

cacher.e: Inherited from Old French cachier, from Vulgar Latin *coacticāre, from Latin coactāre.

amoureux.e: Inherited from Middle French amoureux, from Old French amoreus, amereus, from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, derived from Latin amōrem (“love”, noun). Compare English amorous, borrowed from Middle French.

drogue.e: First attested in Middle French circa 1462, probably from Middle Dutch droge (modern Dutch droog).

commandant.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm Proto-Italic *kom Proto-Italic *kom- Latin con- Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂-der.
c: Qui est le commandant de ce navire ?
Les soldats obéirent à leur commandant sans poser de questions.
Paul leur a acheté un cadeau.

nord.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *nér Proto-Indo-European *-teros Proto-Indo-European *nŕ̥t(e)ros Proto-Germanic *nurþraz Proto-West Germanic *norþr Old English norþbor.

c: Le gouvernement devait des millions de dollars.

adresse.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Proto-Italic *ad- Latin ad- Old French a- Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ ▲ Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu.

adresser.e: Inherited from Old French adrecier (“to straighten, address”), from a- (Latin ad (“to”)) + drecier, drecer (compare with modern French dresser) < Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre, from Latin dīrēctus (“straight or right”), from…
c: À qui dois-je adresser la lettre ?
Elle est partie sans m'adresser un regard.

journal.e: Inherited from Old French journal (“daily”), from Latin diurnālis, from diurnus (“of the day”), from diēs (“day”).
c: Il tient un journal en anglais.

dingue.e: Probably derived from dinguer (“fall, strike”) or divaguer (“wander, blather”).

récupérer.e: Borrowed from Latin recuperāre. Doublet of recouvrer, which was inherited.

base.e: Inherited from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).
c: Ça se base sur des faits.
Je parle sur la base d'expérience.

peau.e: Inherited from Middle French peau, from Old French pel, from Latin pellem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).

servir.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ser- Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *serwos Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *serweyéti Proto-Italic *serwijeti Proto-Italic *serwijit Proto-Italic *serwi…

peuple.e: ), from Latin populus, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”). Doublet of people and pueblo.

exemple.e: Borrowed from Latin exemplum. Displaced Old French essainple.

ficher.e: Inherited from Middle French ficher, from Old French fichier, from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“fasten, fix”). The "give a damn" sense is a minced oath of foutre (“to fuck”).
c: Nous devons ficher le camp d'ici.
Il y avait un max de monde à cette soirée.

blesser.e: Inherited from Middle French blesser, from Old French blecier (“to injure, hurt”), from Frankish *blaitijan.

société.e: Inherited from Middle French societé, from Old French societé, borrowed from Latin societātem (“society”), from socius. Compare the inherited Old French doublet soisté.
c: La société a abandonné ce projet.

tort.e: Inherited from Old French tort, from Latin tortum, substantive use of tortus, the past participle of torqueō (“twist, turn”).

sept.e: Inherited from Middle French sept, from Old French set, from Latin septem (“seven”), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

ouvert.e: Inherited from Middle French ouvert, from Old French overt, from Vulgar Latin *opertus, from Latin apertus. Doublet of apert.

héros.e: 14th century, borrowed from Latin hērōs, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs). The aspiration is secondary and originated in the desire to avoid les héros sounding like les zéros. The related words remain unaspirated.

mentir.e: Inherited from Middle French mentir, from Old French mentir, from Latin mentīrī.

c: Bill vit près de la mer.

jeter.e: Inherited from Old French jeter, from Late Latin iectāre, from Latin iactāre.

bière.e: ), a borrowing from Middle Dutch bier and/or Middle High German bier, both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *beuzą. See beer for more. Displaced cervoise.
c: Bir bira için hayatımı feda ederim.

asseoir.e: Inherited from Middle French asseoir, from Old French asseoir, from Vulgar Latin *assedēre, re-formed from Latin assidēre, on the basis of sedeō.

robe.e: Inherited from Old French, from Proto-Germanic *raubō (“booty”), later "stolen clothing".

prévoir.e: Inherited from Middle French prevoir, from Old French preveoir, borrowed from Latin praevidere.
c: Nul ne peut prévoir ce qui va arriver.

répondre.e: Inherited from Middle French respondre, from Old French respondre, from Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre.
c: « Le téléphone sonne. » « Je vais répondre. »

pute.e: From Old French pute (nominative singular of putain) – perhaps from:.

c: La fille est entrée dans la pièce.
Personne ne se tient devant l'entrée.

horrible.e: Inherited from Old French horrible, orrible, orible, borrowed from Latin horribilis.

vin.e: Inherited from Middle French vin, from Old French vin, from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.

dommage.e: Inherited from Old French damage, inherited from Vulgar Latin *damnāticum, from Latin damnum, or from Old French dam + the suffix -age, probably becoming dommage under the influence of Old French dongier (“danger”).

colonel.e: From Italian colonnello. Compare Middle French coronel, borrowed earlier from the same source. See English colonel for more.
c: Il tient le rang de colonel.
Il fut élevé au rang de colonel il y a deux ans.
İki yıl önce albay rütbesine yükseltildi.

règle.e: ), borrowed from Latin regula. Displaced the earlier borrowing Old French riule, reule (whence English rule). Compare also the inherited Old French reille (whence English rail).
c: Explique-moi la règle, je te prie.

nez.e: Inherited from Middle French nez, from Old French nés, from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Compare Italian naso.

justice.e: Inherited from Old French justise, justice, borrowed from Latin jūstitia. Doublet of justesse.

fbi.e: Borrowed from English FBI (“Federal Bureau of Investigation”).
c: C'est une personne importante au FBI.

découvert.e: Inherited from Old French descovert, from Late Latin discoopertus, from Latin dis- + coopertus.

découvrir.e: Inherited from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō.
c: C'est ce que je voulais découvrir.
Il le savait depuis le départ.

bruit.e: Inherited from Old French bruit, used as a noun of the past participle form of bruire (“to roar”), from a Proto-Romance alteration (by association with braire (“to bray; to cry out, shout out”)) of Latin rugītus (“braye…

secours.e: Inherited from Old French secors, socors, from Vulgar Latin *succursum, from Latin succursus. Compare Italian soccorso, Portuguese socorro and Spanish socorro.

vérifier.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin vērificāre, from Latin vērus (“true”) + faciō (“to do, to make”).
c: Je ne sais pas. Laisse-moi vérifier !

enceinte.e: Inherited from Old French enceinte, from Latin incīncta, feminine past participle of incingō. Compare Italian incinta, Spanish and Catalan encinta.

témoin.e: Inherited from Middle French tesmoing, from Old French tesmoin, from Latin testimōnium.

directeur.e: Learned borrowing from Latin dīrēctor. By surface analysis, directer + -eur.

c: Ben gitmek zorunda olduğum için üzgünüm.

excuser.e: Inherited from Middle French excuser, from Old French escuser, borrowed from Latin excūsāre.

environ.e: Inherited from Old French environ (“around”), from en (“in”) + viron (“a turn”), from virer (“to turn, veer”), whence also French virer.

terrible.e: Inherited from Middle French terrible, from Old French terrible, from Latin terribilis.

danse.e: Deverbal from danser (“to dance”). Doublet of dance.

danser.e: From Old French dancier, from Vulgar Latin *dantiāre. Displaced the older Old French baller.

position.e: Inherited from Old French posicion, borrowed from Latin positiōnem.

humain.e: From Middle French, from Old French humain, umain, from Latin humanus (“of or belonging to a man, human, humane”), from homo (“man, human”).
c: Malgré cela, vous êtes un être humain.
Öyle olsa bile, sen bir insansın.
Görünüşe göre, Tom yarın burada olacak.

avenir.e: From the expression temps à venir ("time (that is) to come"). Cf. also Old French avenir.

bête.e: Inherited from Middle French beste, from Old French beste, probably partially borrowed from Classical Latin bēstia (“beast”), or less likely from an alternative Vulgar Latin bēsta (“animal”).

bravo.e: Borrowed from Italian bravo. Doublet of brave.
c: Bravo, Tom ! C'est toi le meilleur !

approcher.e: Inherited from Old French aprochier, from Late Latin appropiāre, a verb based on Latin prope (“near”).
c: Le président est difficile à approcher.

nourriture.e: Inherited from Old French norriture, from Latin nūtrītūra (“act of feeding or nourishing”) and remade after the verb nourrir.
c: La nourriture n'est pas encore prête.
Comment trouves-tu de la nourriture dans l'espace ?

fric.e: Unknown. Possibly an apocopic form of fricot (“feast”), with influence of fricoter.

plupart.e: From Middle French, from Old French pluspart (“the greater/greatest part of something”). By surface analysis, plus + part.
c: La plupart des gens pensent ça.
La plupart des jeunes ont un téléphone portable.
Çoğu genç bir cep telefonuna sahip.

lycée.e: From Latin lyceum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion) (the name of a gymnasium, or athletic training facility, near Athens where Aristotle established his school), from Λύκειος (Lúkeios, of uncertain meaning; possibly…

tas.e: ], from Old French tas (“heap, mass”), from Frankish *tas (“mass”), from Proto-Germanic *tassaz (“heap, mow”), from Proto-Indo-European *dāy- (“to divide, split, section, part, separate”).
c: Ça m'est arrivé des tas de fois.

empêcher.e: Inherited from Old French empeechier, inherited from Latin impedicāre. Cognate with English impeach. Doublet of empiéger.
c: Je ne peux pas m'en empêcher.
Je ne pouvais m'empêcher de rire.
Le sexe est important pour moi.

niveau.e: Inherited from Old French nivel, livel, from Vulgar Latin *libellus m, from Latin lībella f. Cognate with English level, Spanish nivel, and Portuguese nível.
c: Le niveau de la mer monte.
À quel niveau peut-on le croire ?
Ne dereceye kadar biz ona güvenebiliriz?

banque.e: From Middle French banque, from Italian banca (“counter, moneychanger's table”), from Old High German bank, banch, banc (“counter, bench”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench, counter”).

c: Personne ne peut éviter la mort.

lune.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *lewk- Proto-Indo-European *-sneh₂ Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂ Proto-Italic *louksnā Latin lūna Old French lune Middle French lune French lune Inherited from Middle French lune, fro…
c: Je ne demande pas la lune.

pitié.e: Inherited from Old French pité, pitet, inherited from Latin pietātem. Doublet of piété.

liberté.e: Inherited from Old French liberté, itself borrowed from Latin lībertātem.

c: Cette expérience compte beaucoup dans sa vie.
Bu tecrübe onun yaşamında çok önemli sayılır.

procès.e: Borrowed from Latin prōcessus. Doublet of processus.

radio.e: An abbreviation of words like radiotélégramme, radiotélégraphiste, radiodiffusion, etc. Compare English radio.

hum.e: Expressive onomatopoeia; possible descent in ancient Latin or Frankish interjections.
c: Hum ! Je ne veux pas parler de ce sujet maintenant !
Hmm! Şimdi bu konuda konuşmak istemiyorum.

thé.e: Borrowed from Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (tê). Compare Spanish té. Doublet of chai.

mur.e: Inherited from Middle French mur, from Old French mur, from Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Italic *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).
c: La carte est sur le mur.

pose.e: Deverbal from poser. Compare Italian posa. Also related with pause.

c: Tom ikinci bir şansı hak ediyor.

bande.e: From Middle French bande, from Old French bande, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bindā (“join, link”), cognate with English bind.

bander.e: Inherited from Middle French bander, from Old French bander, bender, from Frankish *bandijan, from Proto-Germanic *bandijaną. Cognate with English bend.

copain.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm Proto-Italic *kom Proto-Italic *kom- Latin con- Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-der.? Latin pānis Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.?

baiser.e: Inherited from Middle French baiser, from Old French baisier, from Latin bāsiāre (“to kiss”). As far as the verb is concerned, the meaning “fuck” arose via euphemism and has become the dominant sense.

anglais.e: Etymology tree Old French anglois Middle French anglois French anglais Inherited from Middle French anglois, from Old French anglois. By surface analysis, Angle (“Angle”) + -ais (“-ese”).

c: Il ne reste plus de papier toilette.
Il chante des chansons de Simon and Garfunkel.
O, Simon ve Garfungel şarkılarını söyler.

déranger.e: Attested in Old French desrengier. By surface analysis, dé- + ranger.

rôle.e: Inherited from Middle French rolle, from Old French role.

censé.e: Past participle of Middle French censer (verb), from Latin cēnseō.

james.e: From Old French James, from Vulgar Latin Iacomus, spoken and altered pronunciation of Latin Iacobus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos), from Ἰακώβ (Iakṓb), from Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (Yaʿăqōḇ).
c: Henry James était américain de naissance.

reine.e: Inherited from Old French reïne, reyne, royne, from Latin rēgīna.

église.e: Inherited from Middle French eglise, from Old French eglise, esglise, from Vulgar Latin *eclesia, from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “gathering”).
c: Il y avait une église ici.

vide.e: From Old French vuit, from Vulgar Latin *vocitum. The modern French form is due to generalisation of the feminine (Old French vuide) and assimilation vui- → vi-.

vider.e: From Middle French vuider, from Old French vuidier, from Vulgar Latin *vocitāre, from Vulgar Latin *vocitum, ultimately connected to Latin vacuus.
c: J'avais besoin de vider mon sac.
J'ai besoin de me vider la tête.

obtenir.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French obtenir, borrowed from Latin obtinēre, with conjugation based on tenir.
c: Nous devons obtenir autant d'informations que possible.
Mümkün olduğu kadar çok bilgi almalıyız.
Tu peux obtenir un prêt d'une banque.

connerie.e: From con + -erie; both semantically and lexically, a nearly exact parallel of English cuntery.

ennui.e: Inherited from Old French enui, probably from the verb enuier.

personnel.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin persōnālis. By surface analysis, personne + -el.

conduire.e: Inherited from Old French conduire, cunduire, from Latin condūcere (“to lead, bring or draw together”), from con- + dūcō (“to lead”).

c: Le sol doit être très propre.
Pourquoi mon code ne fonctionne-t-il pas ?
Je n'arrive pas à me souvenir du code secret.

huit.e: Inherited from Middle French huyct, from Old French uit, from Latin octō, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.

spécial.e: Borrowed from Latin speciālis; compare Old French especial.

vidéo.e: From Latin videō with technical senses borrowed from English video.

vêtement.e: Inherited from Old French vestement, from Latin vestīmentum.

défense.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Late Latin dēfēnsa, from Latin dēfendō.

alex.e: Short form of Alexandre and Alexis or Alexandra, ultimately from Ancient Greek.

grand-mère.e: Inherited from Middle French grand mere, grant mere.

bombe.e: Borrowed from Italian bomba, from Latin bombus (“a boom”).

tante.e: Inherited from Middle French tante, alteration of ante, from Old French ante, from Latin amita ("father's sister"). The initial t- is probably due to childish reduplication.

paraître.e: Inherited from Middle French paroistre, from Old French paroistre, pareistre, from Vulgar Latin *pārēscere, from Latin pārēre.

magasin.e: Etymology tree Arabic خَزَنَ (ḵazana)der. Arabic مَخْزَن (maḵzan) Arabic مَخَازِن (maḵāzin)bor. Italian magazzinobor.?

marier.e: Inherited from Middle French marier, from Old French marier, from Latin marītāre.

chère.e: Inherited from Old French chiere, from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cara (“face”), from Ancient Greek κάρα (kára). Compare Spanish cara.

proche.e: Inherited from Old French proche, derived from prochain.

douleur.e: Inherited from Old French dolor, from Latin dolor (“pain”), from doleō + -or.

presser.e: From Latin pressāre, present active infinitive of pressō, frequentative of premō.
c: Je n'aurais pas dû me presser.
Nous n'avions pas à nous presser.

merveilleux.e: From Middle French merveilleux, from Old French merveillos, merveillus, equivalent to merveille + -eux.

ravir.e: Inherited from Old French ravir, from Vulgar Latin *rapīre, from Latin rapiō, from Proto-Italic *rapjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁r̥p-i-, from *h₁rep- (“to snatch”).
c: Ce chapeau me va à ravir.
Cette robe lui allait à ravir.
En fait, il va en Amérique.
Nitekim, o Amerika Birleşik Devletlerine gidiyor.

fenêtre.e: Etymology tree Etruscan *𐌚𐌍𐌄𐌔𐌕𐌓𐌀 (*fnestra)bor.? Latin fenestra Old French fenestre Middle French fenestre French fenêtre Inherited from Middle French fenestre, from Old French fenestre, from Latin fenestra.

mien.e: Inherited from Middle French mien, from Old French meon, from Latin meum, the neuter of meus.

terrain.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ters- Proto-Indo-European *tersos Proto-Italic *terzos Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *terzeznos Latin terrēnum Vulgar Latin *terranum Old French terrain Fr…
c: Bu arazi parçası hiçbir şeye değmez.

sergent.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French sergeant, sergent, serjant, sergient, sergant (“sergeant, servant”), from Medieval Latin or Late Latin servientem (“a servant, vassal, soldier, apparitor”), from Classical L…

quartier.e: From quart + -ier, possibly Medieval Latin quarterium, compare also Latin quartārium; cognate with Italian quartiere.

planète.e: From Latin planēta, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “to wander”).

rapide.e: Borrowed from Latin rapidus. Compare the inherited Old French rade.

c: Lorsque je suis avec toi, je suis heureux.
Seninle birlikte olmak beni mutlu ediyor.
Ma mère est morte lorsque j'étais enfant.

assurer.e: Inherited from Middle French asseurer, from Old French asseürer, from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrāre, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe”). By surface analysis, a- + sûr + -er.
c: Assure-toi de ne pas trop manger.

mignon.e: Inherited from Middle French mignon, from Old French mignon (“dainty, pleasing, gentle, kind”), from Frankish *minnju (“love, friendship, affection, memory”), from Proto-Germanic *minjō (“affectionate thought, care”), f…

tourner.e: Inherited from Middle French tourner, from Old French torner, from Latin tornāre (“turn”).

bob.e: From the English personal name Bob, used to designate light infantrymen, and probably introduced into French during the First World War.

présenter.e: Borrowed from Latin praesentāre (“show, present”). Morphologically présent + -er.

mériter.e: From mérite, or borrowed from Latin meritāre, from meritus. Replaced inherited Old French merir, from merere.

machine.e: Inherited from Middle French machine, borrowed from Latin machina (“a machine, engine, contrivance, device, stratagem, trick”), itself a borrowing from Doric Ancient Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́).
c: Bu makinede garip bir şey var.

programme.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

honnête.e: Inherited from Middle French honneste, from Old French honeste, a borrowing from Latin honestus, from honor.

connard.e: Two possibilities : * From con + -ard, formed around the 20th century but based on earlier cornard. * Inherited from Middle French conart, inherited from Old French conart.

occasion.e: Borrowed from Latin occāsiōnem (accusative of occāsiō). Compare the inherited Old French ochoison, achaison (the latter being influenced by Latin accūsātiō).

prouver.e: Inherited from Old French prover, from Latin probāre.

glace.e: Inherited from Middle French glace, from Old French glace (“ice", also "glass, mirror, radiance”), from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs (“ice”).

parier.e: From a combination of Old French perier (“to be part of a pair, be equal, associate with”) (from per (“pair”)) and Old French pairier (“to mate, couple”) (from paire), remodelled after Latin pariare (“to make equal, be…

camion.e: Unknown origin, however, most likely early 19th century.

fier.e: Inherited from Old French fer, from Latin ferus.

c: Elle avait quelque chose à discuter avec lui.

spectacle.e: From Latin spectaculum, from spectare (“to look”).

rose.e: Inherited from Middle French rose, from Old French rose, borrowed from Latin rosa (the expected form if it was inherited would be *reuse).

vis.e: Inherited from Old French vis, from Latin vītis (“vine”).

parole.e: Inherited from Middle French parole, from Old French parole, inherited from Vulgar Latin *paraula, from Late Latin, from Latin parabola (“comparison; (later) speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ).

apprécier.e: Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin appretiāre (“to appraise”), from Latin pretium. Cf. also the Old French aprisier.

réalité.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reālitās, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”). Morphologically, from réel + -ité.

savon.e: Inherited from Middle French savon, from Old French savon (“soap”), from Latin sāpōnem (“soap”), from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ (“soap”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out, drip, strain, trickle”).

respect.e: Borrowed from Latin respectus. Doublet of répit.

remettre.e: Inherited from Old French remetre, inherited from Latin remittō. By surface analysis, re- + mettre.

détruire.e: Inherited from Middle French destruire, from Old French destruire, from Vulgar Latin *destrugere, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

c: Ha ha ha ! Tu veux tuer toutes les mouches ?
Ha ha ha! Tüm sinekleri öldürmek mi istiyorsun?
Ha ! ha ! ha ! un écureuil ivre ! ce sera bien drôle.
Ha! ha! ha! Sarhoş bir sincap! bu çok komik olacak.

officier.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin officiō (infinitive officiāre).

bill.e: Borrowed from English bill; doublet of bulle (“bubble”).

solution.e: Inherited from Old French solucion, from Latin solūtiōnem, from the verb solvō.

information.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin īnfōrmātiōnem.

monstre.e: Inherited from Middle French monstre, from Old French monstre, borrowed from Latin mōnstrum.

ordinateur.e: Borrowed from Latin ōrdinātōrem (“one who orders”), from ōrdinō (“to order, organize”).

nature.e: Inherited from Middle French nature, Old French nature, borrowed from Latin nātūra.

énergie.e: Learned borrowing from Latin energīa, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia).

pierre.e: Inherited from Middle French pierre, from Old French pierre, from Latin petra.

sarah.e: A spelling variant of the biblical given name Sara.
c: Sarah paralarının geri verilmesini talep etti.

espace.e: Inherited from Middle French espace, from Old French espace, borrowed from Latin spatium.

c: Je veux que mes enfants soient en sécurité.
La faim est l'un des plus sérieux problèmes qui soient.

portable.e: Borrowed from Latin portābilis. By surface analysis, porter + -able.

préparer.e: Inherited from Middle French preparer, from Old French, borrowed from Latin praeparāre.

court.e: Inherited from Old French curt, from Latin curtus.

envers.e: Nominalisation of the Old French adjective envers, inherited from Latin inversus. Doublet of inverse.
c: Il est toujours gentil envers les animaux.
O her zaman hayvanlara karşı naziktir.

bain.e: Inherited from Latin baneum, variant of balneum. Doublet of bagne.

charge.e: Inherited from Middle French charge, from Old French charge, carge, equivalent to a deverbal from charger.

charger.e: Inherited from Old French chargier, from Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus (“four-wheeled baggage wagon”). Compare Spanish cargar.

c: Harry était en retard en cours hier à cause de son accident.
Harry geçirdiği kazadan dolayı dün derse geç kaldı.

ennemi.e: Inherited from Old French enemi, anemi, from earlier inimi, inimic, from Latin inimīcus.

énorme.e: Inherited from Middle French enorme, borrowed from Latin ēnormis.

grand-père.e: Inherited from Middle French grand père, grant pere, grant père.

test.e: From Old French test, from Latin testum. The orthography of this form reflects semi-learned influence; compare the doublet têt.

réfléchir.e: Borrowed from Latin reflectere and adapted to French fléchir.

chanter.e: Inherited from Middle French chanter, from Old French chanter, from Latin cantāre.

lâche.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg- Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg-s-ós Latin laxus Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-…

lâcher.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg- Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg-s-ós Latin laxus Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-…

épouser.e: Inherited from Middle French espouser, from Old French espouser, from Latin spōnsāre.

fleur.e: Inherited from Old French flur, flour, flor, from Latin flōrem (“flower; the finest part of something”), from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃-s (“flower, blossom”), from *bʰleh₃- (“to bloom”).

riche.e: Inherited from Middle French riche (“rich”), from Old French riche (“rich, wealthy”), from Frankish *rīkī (“rich”), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“rich, powerful”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to straighten, dire…

ancien.e: Inherited from Middle French ancien, from Old French anciien, from Vulgar Latin *anteānus.

stop.e: 1792. Borrowed from English stop. The sense "hitchhiking" is a pseudo-anglicism.

accepter.e: From Middle French accepter, from Old French accepter, borrowed from Latin acceptāre. Doublet of acheter.

sauter.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin saltāre. Cognate with Spanish saltar.

c: Elle fut malade durant une semaine.
Il a parlé une heure durant.

durer.e: Inherited from Old French durer, from Latin dūrāre.

inviter.e: Borrowed from Latin invītāre. Compare convier and Old French envier.
c: Beni davet ettiğiniz için çok teşekkür ederim.

politique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin polīticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós).

dent.e: Inherited from Middle French dent f, with change of gender from Old French dent m, from Latin dentem m, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts.

patient.e: Inherited from Middle French patient, from Old French patient, borrowed from Latin patientem.

repas.e: From Old French repast, from the verb repaistre, from Latin repascere.
c: Bu yemek üç kişi için yeterlidir.

jambe.e: Inherited from Old French jambe, from Late Latin gamba.
c: Je me suis cassé la jambe.
Il a changé de sujet de conversation.

tô.e: Borrowed from Bambara to or Dyula too.

mémoire.e: From Middle French memoire, from Old French memoire, from Latin memoria.

c: Tu es un tueur en série.
C'est la première d'une longue série !

contraire.e: Borrowed from Latin contrārius. See contre and -aire.

vent.e: Inherited from Middle French vent, from Old French vent, from Latin ventus, from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts < *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
c: Il y avait beaucoup de vent.
Il y a un peu de vent.

taille.e: Inherited from Old French taille, deverbal of Old French taillier (“to cut”). Compare Italian taglia, Catalan talla.

chat.e: Inherited from Middle French chat, from Old French chat, from Late Latin cattus.

contrat.e: Inherited from Old French contract, borrowed from Latin contractus (noun), from contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”) [from con- (“with, together”) + trahere (“to draw, to pull”)] + -tu…

couteau.e: Inherited from Old French coutel, from Latin cultellus, diminutive of culter (“knife, plough blade”); cognate with Italian coltello. Not related to couper.

double.e: Inherited from Old French doble, from Latin duplus.
c: Tek ya da çift kişilik oda?

doubler.e: Inherited from Old French dobler, from Late Latin dūplāre, from Latin dūplus. Compare Spanish doblar, Catalan doblar, Portuguese dobrar, Italian doppiare.
c: On ne pouvait pas le doubler.
Tu ne peux pas doubler le camion maintenant.

carrière.e: Inherited from Middle French carriere. Borrowed from Old Occitan carreira or Italian carriera, itself from Old Occitan, from Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Compare the inherited doublet charrière.

descendre.e: Inherited from Middle French descendre, from Old French descendre, borrowed from Latin descendere.

université.e: Inherited from Old French universitei, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin universitātem.

sentiment.e: Inherited from Old French sentement, from Latin sentimentum.

papier.e: From Old French papier, from Old Catalan paper.
c: Cette boîte est faite en papier.
Herhangi bir değişiklik fark ettiniz mi?

vécu.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French vescu, derived from the preterite vesqui, itself from a metathesis of Latin vixi, likely influenced by nasqui (“I was born”).

courage.e: Inherited from Middle French corage, from Old French corage, from Vulgar Latin *corāticum, from Latin cor. Cognate with Catalan coratge, Italian coraggio, Occitan coratge, Spanish coraje.

beauté.e: Inherited from Middle French beauté, from Old French biauté, from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fair”).

c: Est-ce que monsieur Richard est à la maison ?
O, zengin bir adam için çalıştı.

étant.e: Inherited from Latin stantem, from stō, stāre (the source of all forms of être in ét-).
c: Étant fatigué il est allé au lit.
Même étant malade, il est venu travailler.
O, hasta olmasına rağmen işe geldi.

couple.e: Inherited from Old French couple, from Vulgar Latin *cōpla, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copule.
c: Bu çiftin yedi tane çocuğu var.
Pour conduire, il faut un permis.
Bir araba sürmek için, bir ehliyete ihtiyacın var.

permettre.e: Inherited from Middle French permettre, borrowed from Latin permittere, based on French mettre.
c: Je ne peux pas me permettre de payer autant.
O kadar çok ödemeyi göze alamam.
Je ne peux pas vous permettre de faire ça.

différence.e: From Old French difference, borrowed from Latin differentia.

course.e: From Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”), with influence of Italian corsa.

c: Il nous faut nous dégager d'ici.
Je me demande si ça va se dégager demain.
Havanın yarın açıp açmayacağını merak ediyorum.

mille.e: Inherited from Middle French mille, from Old French mile, from Latin mīlle (“thousand”) (plural mīlia), from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂ (“one thousand”).
c: Chaque personne a payé mille dollars.

accès.e: From Latin accessus (“approach”), from accēdō (“approach, accede”).
c: La porte donne accès au jardin.
Il avait des accès de mauvaise conscience.

cible.e: Attested from 1671, originally as sible. Originally Swiss French, borrowed from Alemannic German Schiibe or rather the diminutive Schiibli; compare German Scheibe.

joyeux.e: From joie + -eux. cf. also Late Latin gaudiōsus.

bonheur.e: Inherited from Middle French bon-heur; univerbation of bon heur, literally “goodhap, good fortune”. Compare Occitan bonur.

action.e: From Old French acciun, aucion, etymologically reconstructed in Middle French to resemble the Latin actiōnem.
c: Il fait une bonne action par jour.
Günde bir kez nazik bir harekette bulunur.

restaurant.e: From the present participle of restaurer. Corresponds to Latin restaurāns, restaurantem.

restaurer.e: Borrowed from Latin rēstaurāre via Old French restorer. The sequence -au- replaced the -o- to reflect the original Latin spelling.

crise.e: Borrowed from Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίσις (krísis).
c: La crise a directement touché notre pays.
Les gens disent que la crise est passée.

piste.e: Borrowed from Italian pista, variant of pesta (“footprint”).
c: Vous êtes sur la bonne piste.

puisque.e: Univerbation of puis + que. Compare Italian poiché.
c: Puisque tu es ici, autant commencer.

coupe.e: Inherited from Old French cope, cupe, from Late Latin cuppa, from Latin cūpa. Doublet of cuve. The sports sense is a semantic loan from English cup.

couper.e: Inherited from Old French coper, colper (“to cut off”), probably, derived from cop (“blow”), colp (modern coup), with its meaning coming from the idea of cutting off with a blow.
c: Tu devrais te couper les cheveux.
Il s'est fait couper les cheveux.

prince.e: Inherited from Middle French prince, from Old French prince, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin prīnceps.

marrer.e: Probably borrowed from Spanish marear (“to get dizzy”), with semantic shift "to get dizzy" > "to be bored" > "to be amused" (via antiphrasis).

refuser.e: Inherited from Old French refuser, from Vulgar Latin *refūsāre, a blend of Latin refūtāre and recūsāre.
c: Onun teklifini geri çevirmek zorunda kaldım.

casser.e: Inherited from Old French quasser, from Latin quassāre, influenced by Late Latin cassāre (“to annul”).

lors.e: Inherited from Middle French lors, from Old French lors, lores, from earlier lur, lor, from Vulgar Latin illā hōrā, from Latin ille + hōrā.
c: Elle était dès lors hors de danger.
Elle a une maladie du cœur.

week-end.e: Borrowed from English week-end (now more commonly weekend).

alcool.e: Etymology tree Akkadian 𒎎𒋆𒁉𒍣𒁕 (guḫlum)bor. Aramaic כוחלא (kuḥlā)bor. Arabic كُحْل (kuḥl) Andalusian Arabic كُحُول (kuḥūl)bor. Medieval Latin alcohollbor.

quitte.e: ), borrowed from Latin quiētus (pronounced in Medieval Latin as quíetus > quitus). Doublet of inherited coi and the later borrowing quiet.

claire.e: From Latin Clara, with transparent meaning in modern French (claire).

londres.e: Inherited from Middle French Londres, from Old French Londres, ultimately from Latin Londinium. However, it is not a natural evolution from Latin to French, as Londinium would render *Londin, *Londein.

île.e: Originally written isle; from Middle French isle, from Old French isle, from Vulgar Latin *īsula, from Classical Latin īnsula.
c: Là est l'île de mes rêves !
Cette île est un paradis pour les enfants.
Bu ada çocuklar için bir cennet.

caméra.e: Borrowed from English camera, itself from New Latin camera obscura (“dark chamber”), from Latin camera (“chamber, bedchamber”). Doublet of chambre, which was inherited from Latin.

pleurer.e: Inherited from Middle French pleurer, from Old French plourer, plorer, from Latin plōrāre (“cry out”). Cognate with Catalan plorar, Spanish llorar.

régler.e: From règle + -er, or borrowed from Latin rēgulāre. See also réguler.

entier.e: Inherited from Old French entier, inherited from Latin integrum (although modified with the -ier suffix analogically). Compare the borrowed doublet intègre.

animal.e: Borrowed from Latin animal. Compare the archaic inherited doublet aumaille and its variant armaille, both from the Latin neuter plural animālia.

image.e: Inherited from Old French image, borrowed from Latin imaginem (“a copy, likeness, image”).

étage.e: From Old French estage: ester + -age (see also stage), or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *stāticum, from Latin stāre.
c: Mon appartement est au troisième étage.
Notre appartement est au deuxième étage.

soldat.e: Inherited from Middle French soldat, borrowed from Italian soldato, past participle of soldare, from soldo (“money, military pay”). Replaced soudard.

amuser.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Proto-Italic *ad- Latin ad- Old French a- Medieval Latin musumder.?

langue.e: Inherited from Middle French langue, from Old French langue, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”).
c: Personne ne parle plus cette langue.
Artık hiç kimse bu dili konuşmuyor.
Dans quelle direction est la plage ?

frais.e: Inherited from Middle French frais, from Old French freis, from Vulgar Latin *friscum. Related to English fresh. Doublet of fresque.

c: Tu as appris l'anglais avec Miss Long n'est-ce pas ?
İngilizceyi Bayan Long'tan öğrendin, değil mi?

couleur.e: Inherited from Middle French couleur, from Old French color, from Latin colōrem m.

frapper.e: Inherited from Middle French frapper, from Old French fraper, frapper (“to deliver a blow to someone, hit, strike”), from Frankish *hrapōn (“to snatch, scuffle”), from Proto-Germanic *hrapōną, *hrapjaną (“to touch, scra…

rater.e: Emerged in the early 1700s, likely originally in reference to a firearm misfiring, from the expression (1651) prendre un rat (“to misfire”, literally “to get a rat”), from rat (“rat”). More at rat.

épouse.e: Inherited from Old French espose, from Latin spōnsa.

jésus.e: From Latin Iēsūs, from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs), from Hebrew ישוע (y'hoshúa).

faible.e: Inherited from Middle French foible, from Old French feble, foible, from Vulgar Latin *febilis, dissimilated form of Latin flēbilis. Doublet of flébile, a borrowing. Compare English feeble.

c: Je suis venu tôt afin d'avoir une bonne place.
İyi bir yer almak için erken geldim.
Laisse-moi l'écrire afin que je ne l'oublie pas.

bleu.e: Inherited from Middle French bleu, from Old French blöe, bleve, blef, bleu (“blue”), from Late Latin blāvus, from Frankish *blāu (“blue”), from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰléh₁-, *bʰlh₁-…

pont.e: Inherited from Old French pont, from Latin pontem.
c: Ce pont est à New York.
Ce pont est fait de bois.

gay.e: Borrowed from English gay, itself a borrowing from French gai. Doublet of gai.

attraper.e: From Middle French attraper, from Old French atraper (compare also Old French antraper), equivalent to a- + trapper.

poisson.e: Inherited from Middle French poisson, from Old French poisson, peisson, from an older form peis with suffix -on, from Latin piscem, see below. Alternatively, but less likely, through a Vulgar Latin *pisciō, pisciōnem.

date.e: Inherited from Old French date, a borrowing from Late Latin data, from the feminine of Latin datus.

intention.e: Inherited from Middle French entention, from Old French entencion, borrowed from Latin intentiōnem. Respelled intention in Middle French to more closely match the Classical Latin form.
c: Onun tam olarak niyet ettiği oydu.

procureur.e: Etymology tree French procurer Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French procureur From procurer + -eur.
c: Mon avocat est en train de parler au procureur.
Le procureur me posa une question insidieuse.
Savcı bana cevabı yönlendiren bir soru sordu.

goût.e: Inherited from Middle French goust, from Old French goust, from Latin gustus, from Proto-Italic *gustus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.

c: Le shérif vous attend dans son bureau.
Il y a un nouveau shérif en ville.

sourire.e: Inherited from Middle French soubrire (silent b), from Old French sorrirre, from Vulgar Latin *subrīdĕre, from Latin subrīdēre.

lait.e: Inherited from Old French lait, from Late Latin lactem, from Latin lac, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵlákts. Compare Occitan lach, lait.

chasse.e: Inherited from Middle French chasse, from Old French chace, deverbal of chacier.

chasser.e: Inherited from Old French chacier, from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus. Doublet of catch.

signal.e: Re-latinization of Old French segnal, from Medieval Latin signale, from Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum.
c: Il nous a donné le signal pour commencer.
O, bize başlamak için sinyal verdi.
Il a répondu au signal que je lui ai donné.

français.e: Altered from Middle French françois, from Old French françois, franceis, from France + -ois, corresponding to Early Medieval Latin francēnsis, from Late Latin Francus (“a Frank”). By surface analysis, France + -ais.

chier.e: Inherited from Middle French chier, from Old French, inherited from Latin cacāre. Doublet of caguer.

doigt.e: Inherited from Middle French doigt, doit, from Old French doit, doi, from Latin digitus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deyǵ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”).
c: Je me suis coupé le doigt.
Daniel est le fils unique de Jacob.

adieu.e: Shortened form of Old French a Dieu vos comant, from Medieval Latin ad Deum, equivalent to Old French à dieu vous commant (“I commend (entrust) you to God”).

costume.e: PIE word *ḱóm PIE word *swé Borrowed from Italian costume, from Latin cōnsuētūdinem (“custom, habit”). Doublet of consuétude and coutume.

entreprise.e: Feminine past participle of entreprendre (“undertake”). Compare Italian impresa for a similar construction.

utile.e: Inherited from Middle French utile, borrowed from Latin ūtilis.

lien.e: Inherited from Middle French lien, from Old French lien, liem, from Latin ligāmen (“bond”), from ligō.

appartenir.e: Inherited from Old French apartenir, borrowed from Late Latin appertinēre (“belong to”), from Latin pertineō. Cf. also Old French partenir.

amener.e: Inherited from Old French amener, from a- + mener (“to lead”), ultimately from Latin minārī (“to threaten”) (infinitive minārī).

c: Quels sont tes amis les plus proches ?

enfoiré.e: Past participle of the archaic verb enfoirer (“to cover with excrement”)

discours.e: Inherited from Middle French discours, borrowed (with influence from cours) from Late Latin discursus (“the act of running about”) (from Latin discurrō (“run about”), from dis- (“apart”) + currō (“run”)).

robert.e: From Édouard Robert, name of the creator of a type of baby bottle.
c: Je suis un ami de Robert.

art.e: From Latin artem, accusative singular of ars.

c: Ce salaud pense que tout le monde devrait le vénérer.
Bu piç, herkesin ona ibadet etmesi gerektiğini düşünüyor.

bouteille.e: From Old French boteille, from Late Latin butticula.
c: À la bouteille ou au verre ?
Ses çok hızlı şekilde hareket eder.

bref.e: From Old French brief, from Latin brevis. A folk etymology derives it as an acronym of Bon, Revenons-En aux Faits, but this is completely inaccurate.

c: Ils ont fait appel de la décision du tribunal.
Il y a beaucoup de pièces.

obliger.e: Inherited from Middle French obliger, from Old French obligier, borrowed from Latin obligāre.
c: Rien ne pourra m'obliger à abandonner.
Hiçbir şey ondan vazgeçmem için beni zorlayamaz.

formidable.e: Learned borrowing from Latin formīdābilis (“formidable, terrible”), from formīdō (“fear, dread”).

pause.e: From Middle French pause (14th c. in the musical sense), from Latin pausa.

campagne.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan campanha or Old Northern French campaigne, corresponding to Old French champa(i)gne. Doublet of Champagne and champagne.

c: Mark Zuckerberg m'a volé mon idée !
Mark Twain était un romancier américain.

morceau.e: Inherited from Middle French morceau, from Old French morsel (whence also English morsel), from Early Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, past part…

os.e: Inherited from Middle French os, from Old French os, from Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst.
c: Elle a donné un os au chien.

nombre.e: Inherited from Middle French nombre, from Old French nombre, nonbre, from Latin numerus. Doublet of numéro.
c: Nous avons choisi le nombre au hasard.

intelligent.e: Learned borrowing from Latin intelligēns (“discerning”), present active participle of intellegō (“understand, comprehend”), itself from inter (“between”) + legō (“choose, pick out, read”).

gâteau.e: Inherited from Middle French gasteau, from Old French gastel, from Frankish *wastil, from Proto-Germanic *wastilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to eat; consume”).

dépendre.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēpendĕre, from Classical Latin dēpendēre. By surface analysis, dé- + pendre.

cou.e: From Latin collum. Doublet of col. Cognate with Italian collo, Galician and Portuguese colo, Spanish cuello.

reprendre.e: Inherited from Old French reprendre, from Latin reprendere, contracted variant of reprehendere.

joie.e: Inherited from Old French joie, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin *gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium.

star.e: Borrowed from English star. Doublet of aster.
c: Tom est la star de l'émission.

regard.e: Inherited from Middle French regard, from Old French regard, from reguarder.

menace.e: Inherited from Old French manace, from Latin minācia (“threat”), a noun based on mināx (“threatening”).

menacer.e: Inherited from Old French menacier, manecier, from Vulgar Latin *mināciāre, from Latin minācia (“threat”). Equivalent to menace + -er.

malgré.e: Inherited from Middle French maugré, maulgré (literally “bad will”), from Old French malgré, from mal + gré. Cognate with Italian malgrado and Catalan malgrat.

appareil.e: From appareiller (in Old French apareil). Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *apparic(u)lum; cf. apparātus (whence apparat).

adam.e: Borrowed from Hebrew אָדָם (adam, “earth, man, soil, light brown”).

ange.e: Inherited from Old French ange, angle, from Late Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos). Doublet of angélus.

résultat.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin resultātum, the substantivized neuter singular of resultātus (perfect passive participle of resultō). By surface analysis, résulter + -at.

naître.e: Inherited from Middle French naistre, from Old French naistre, from Latin nascere.

pain.e: Inherited from Middle French pain, from Old French pain, from Latin pānem.

en: fly by the seat of one's pants

leçon.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French leçon, from Latin lēctiōnem; according to the Trésor de la Langue Française, the Old French was an (early) borrowing from the Latin, making it a semi-learned term.

paquet.e: From Middle French paquet, from Middle Dutch pac (modern Dutch pak), from Old Dutch *pakko, from Frankish *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.

immeuble.e: Inherited from Old French immeuble/immoble, borrowed from Latin immōbilis (“that which is immovable”) but adapted to the ending of meuble (“furniture”), inherited from the Latin antonym mōbilis (“that which is movable”).

chinois.e: From Chine (“China”) + -ois (“-ese”). Sense 3 of the noun comes from the strainer's resemblance to a traditional Asian conical hat.

aveugle.e: Inherited from Middle French aveugle from Old French avogle, from Late Latin ab oculīs (“without eyes”, literally “away from the eyes”), possibly a calque of Ancient Greek ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων (apò ommátōn) or more likely from G…

oiseau.e: Inherited from Middle French oyseau, from Old French oisel c.

propriétaire.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin proprietārius.

anna.e: A Latinate variant of French Anne, from Ἄννα (Ánna), equal to the Hebrew female name חַנָּה (ḥannâ) of Old Testament, meaning "grace, gracious". Cognate with English Anna.

c: J'appelle de la part de Monsieur Simon.
Tu es Simon, fils de Jean.

al.e: Created in 2015 by Alpheratz, based on Old French al, a variant of the pronoun el.
c: Le Maroc s'appelle « Al-Maghrib » en arabe.

lis.e: Inherited from Middle French lis, from Old French lis, generalised from the nominative singular and accusative plural of earlier lil, from Latin lilium. ), but fleur de lis was formerly also pronounced with /li/.

station.e: Inherited from Old French estation, estacion, borrowed from Latin stātiōnem.
c: Je descends à la prochaine station.

mandat.e: Borrowed from Latin mandātum, from mandō (“put in one's hands, command”), from Proto-Indo-European *man- (“hand”) + *dʰeh₁- (“put”).

assassin.e: From either Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, “hashish users”) or أَسَاسِيُّون (ʔasāsiyyūn).
c: Les parents de Tom sont tous les deux des assassins.
Tom'un hem annesi hem de babası katildir.

thomas.e: Ultimately borrowed from Latin Thōmās m. Inherited from Middle French Thomas m, inherited from Old French Tumas m, Latin Thōmās m. Compare Occitan Tomàs m.

c: Biz kutlama yapmak için dışarı çıkıyoruz.

bague.e: Inherited from Middle French bague, possibly a borrowing from Middle Dutch bage, bagge (“ring”), of obscure origin, but likely from Old Frisian bāg, bāch (“ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *baug, ultimately from Proto-G…

tente.e: Inherited from Old French tente, possibly from Vulgar Latin *tenta, from the feminine of tentus, perfect passive participle of tendō, or alternatively from Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin tenda, itself possibly a con…

tenter.e: Inherited from Middle French tenter, from Old French tempter, from Latin temptāre.

ventre.e: Inherited from Middle French ventre, from Old French ventre, from Latin ventrem, from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-.

genou.e: Inherited from Old French genouz, genoilz plural of genoil, from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.
c: Je me suis blessé au genou.

terme.e: Inherited from Old French terme, inherited from Latin terminus, from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”). Doublet of terminus.
c: Le mois approche de son terme.
Le contrat arrive à terme sous peu.

vert.e: Inherited from Middle French verd, vert, from Old French vert, from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Compare Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish verde.

hâte.e: Inherited from Middle French haste, from Old French haste, from Frankish *hai(f)st (compare Old High German heisti).

réveiller.e: From r- + éveiller, or from Old French resveillier.
c: Elles ont oublié de me réveiller.

commander.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm Proto-Italic *kom Proto-Italic *kom- Latin con- Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂-der.

commun.e: Inherited from Old French comun, from Latin commūnis.

souris.e: Inherited from Middle French souris, from Old French soris, soriz, from Vulgar Latin *sōrīcem, alteration of the Classical Latin sōricem (“shrew”). The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.

diriger.e: Inherited from Middle French diriger, from Latin dīrigere (“to direct”), simplified into a first conjugation French verb.
c: De quel côté devrions-nous nous diriger ?
Pourriez-vous me diriger dans la bonne direction ?

sport.e: Earlier 19th century, borrowed from English sport. At first also pronounced with a final /t/.

virer.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *virāre, probably from Latin vibrāre (in which case it is a doublet of vibrer) or possibly from an alteration of gȳrō. Compare Italian virare, Spanish virar.

fiston.e: From fils (“son”) + -on with influence of rejeton (“offshot, kid”).
c: Je suis fier de toi, fiston.

étoile.e: From Middle French estoile, from Old French estoile, esteile, from Late Latin stēla, from Latin stēlla. Doublet of Estelle.
c: Il a découvert une nouvelle étoile.
Aucune étoile ne pouvait être vue dans le ciel.
J'aimerais trouver un médecin parlant français.
Fransızca konuşan bir doktor bulmak istiyorum.
Pouvez-vous me présenter à un avocat parlant français ?
Beni Fransızca konuşabilen bir avukatla tanıştırır mısın?

pluie.e: From Middle French pluye, from Old French pluie, from Vulgar Latin *plo(v)ia.
c: Après la pluie, le beau temps.
Il est sorti sous la pluie.

ombre.e: Inherited from Old French onbre, ombre, from Latin umbra, probably from Old Latin *omra, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mr-u-, *h₂mrup-.

rome.e: Inherited from Old French Rome, from Latin Rōma.

épisode.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπεισόδιον (epeisódion).
c: Tu veux regarder un autre épisode ?
Başka bir bölüm izlemek ister misin?

talent.e: Borrowed from Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance; a particular weight, especially of gold; sum of money; a talent”).

chocolat.e: Borrowed from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl, of uncertain origin; see that entry for more information.

angleterre.e: Inherited from Middle French Angleterre, Engleterre, from Old French Engleterre, calque of Old English Engla land.

site.e: From Latin situs. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English site, a clipping of website.
c: Ce site internet est très utile.

neige.e: ), deverbal from neiger (“to snow”). Displaced related Old French noif, from Latin nix, nivem.
c: Ça ressemble à de la neige.

chemise.e: Inherited from Old French chemise, from Late Latin camisia, from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi (“shirt”).

emploi.e: Deverbal from employer. Akin to Italian impiego, Occitan emplec, and Spanish empleo.

c: Je te suis reconnaissant pour ce que tu as fait précédemment.
Daha önce yaptığın şeyi takdir ediyorum.

surveiller.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Italic *super Latin super Latin super- Old French sur- Proto-Indo-European *weǵ-der.

c: Je tiens à ma vie privée.
Elle a vécu ici sa vie entière.
O tüm hayatı boyunca burada yaşadı.

facilement.e: Inherited from Old French facilement. By surface analysis, facile + -ment.
c: Il a facilement gagné la course.

voleur.e: Etymology tree French voler Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French voleur From voler (“to steal”) + -eur.

véritable.e: Inherited from Middle French veritable, from Old French veritable. By surface analysis, vérité + -able.

chaise.e: Originally, simply a variant of chaire. From Middle French chaire, inherited from Latin cathedra (“seat”), a borrowing from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).

accuser.e: Inherited from Middle French accuser, from Old French acuser, accuser, borrowed from Latin accūsāre.
c: Es-tu en train de m'accuser de quelque chose ?

zéro.e: Borrowed from Italian zero, alteration of zefiro, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صفر. Doublet of chiffre.

clairement.e: Inherited from Middle French clerement, clérement, clèrement, from Old French clerement. By surface analysis, clair + -ment.

mouvement.e: From mouvoir + -ment, (found in Old French as movement); cf. also Medieval Latin mōvimentum (probably partly based on the Old French), from Latin moveō.
c: Ce fut un assez bon mouvement.

sommeil.e: Inherited from Old French sumeil, from Vulgar Latin *somniclum < *somniculum, from Latin somnus (“sleep”) + -culus (diminutive suffix), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.

survivre.e: Inherited from Old French survivre, from Latin supervīvō, from super + vīvō. Equivalent to sur- + vivre.
c: Je ne pouvais pas survivre sans Tom.
Tes « o » ressemblent à des « a ».
La formule chimique de l'eau est H₂O.

traduction.e: Learned borrowing from Latin trāductiō (“transferring, translation”, literally “leading across”), from trādūcō (“to lead across”), from trāns (“across”) + dūcō (“to lead”).

repos.e: Inherited from Old French repos. Compare Catalan repòs, Italian riposo, Spanish reposo, Portuguese repouso, Romanian repaus.

siège.e: From Old French siege, sege, seige, from Vulgar Latin *sedicum, from sediculum, diminutive of Latin sedem. Alternatively, derived from a lost verb Old French *siegier (cf.

puissance.e: Inherited from Middle French puissance, derived from Old French puissant.

c: Tom était mon compagnon de cellule.
Tom et John sont compagnons de cellule.

engager.e: From Middle French engager, from Old French engagier (“to pawn, make a pledge, plight”), from en- (“in, under”) + gage, guage (“pledge”), from Late Latin wadium (“pledge”), from Frankish *wadi ~ waddj- (“pledge”), from…

adorable.e: From Latin adorābilis. By surface analysis, adorer + -able.

violence.e: Inherited from Old French violence, from Latin violentia, from the adjective violentus, see violent.

ours.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos Proto-Italic *orsos Latin ursus Old French urs Middle French ours French ours Inherited from Middle French ours, from Old French urs, from Latin ursus, from Proto-Italic *ors…

gorge.e: Inherited from Old French gorge, from Late Latin gurga, related to Latin gurges (“eddy, whirlpool; gulf; sea”).
c: Tom a mal à la gorge.

examen.e: Learned borrowing from Latin exāmen. Doublet of essaim.

major.e: From Middle French major, from Spanish mayor, from Latin maior. Doublet of maire, majeur, and mayeur.
c: Un major est au-dessus d'un capitaine.

distance.e: From Middle French distance, from Old French destance, destaunce, distaunce (“debate; difference, distinction; discord, quarrel; dispute; space between two points; time interval”), borrowed from Latin distantia (“differ…

titre.e: Inherited from Old French title, a semi-learned term borrowed from Latin titulus.
c: Quel est le titre du livre ?
À la fin seulement on comprend le titre.

lundi.e: Inherited from Old French lundi, from Latin *Lūnae diēs, variant of diēs Lūnae (“day of the moon”).

choc.e: Etymology tree Proto-West Germanic *skokkōnder. Old French choquer Proto-West Germanic *skokkōnder. Picard chuquier /çukerbor. Middle French chocquer French choquerdeverb.

théâtre.e: Borrowed from Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see, to watch, to observe”).

rivière.e: From Middle French riviere, from Old French riviere, from Early Medieval Latin rīpāria.
c: Il est tombé dans la rivière.
Le courant de cette rivière est rapide.
Allo, est-ce le service du personnel ?

logique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin logica, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ), ellipsis of λογικὴ τέχνη (logikḕ tékhnē, “the art of reasoning”).

alice.e: Inherited from Old French Alis, Alice, from Old High German Adalheid.

miracle.e: Inherited from Old French miracle, borrowed from Latin mīrāculum. Compare the inherited Old French mirail (“mirror”).

montagne.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *men- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *móntis Proto-Italic *monts Latin mont- Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Proto-Indo-Euro…
c: Je pense partir à la montagne.
Je préfère la montagne à la mer.
Tom vit à Chicago depuis un an.

auprès.e: Univerbation of au + près. Compare au loin.

c: Tom avait le sourire aux lèvres.
Vous avez de très belles lèvres.

lèvre.e: Inherited from Middle French lévre, from Old French levre, earlier lavras (plural) (ca. 980), from Vulgar Latin labra, originally a neuter plural of Latin labrum, from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang down, droop”).
c: Une moustache pousse sur la lèvre supérieure.

plat.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- Proto-Indo-European *-us Proto-Indo-European *pléth₂us Proto-Hellenic *plətús Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús)bor.

mine.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)mēy(H)- Proto-Indo-European *mēy(H)nis Proto-Celtic *meinis Gaulish *meinabor.

pistolet.e: From pistole + -et. Ultimately from Czech píšťala (“whistle”).

c: Le divorce est un droit humain.

forêt.e: Inherited from Middle French forest, from Old French forest, from Early Medieval Latin forestis.
c: Marie est seule dans la forêt.

respirer.e: Inherited from Middle French respirer, from Old French respirer, borrowed from Latin respīrāre.

fortune.e: Inherited from Middle French fortune, from Old French fortune, borrowed from Latin fortūna.

mener.e: Etymology tree Latin mīna Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu.
c: Mon rêve est de mener une vie tranquille à la campagne.
Hayalim kırsalda sakin bir hayat yaşamak.

maria.e: From Vulgate Latin Maria, from Ancient Greek Μαρία (María), Μαριάμ (Mariám), from Aramaic מרים (Maryām), corresponding to the Hebrew מרים (Miryām). A Latinate variant of the vernacular French Marie.

responsabilité.e: Modelled after or borrowed from English responsibility, corresponding to responsable + -ité.

c: Annie est brune et Madeleine blonde.
Les roses se fanèrent et Annie pleura beaucoup.
Güller soldu ve Ania çok ağladı.

épée.e: Inherited from Middle French espee, from Old French espee, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē). Doublet of spathe, a borrowing from Latin, and espade, a borrowing from Occitan.

c: Le cabinet du médecin se trouve au premier étage.
Tous les membres du cabinet étaient présents.

alerte.e: From Old French a l'herte (“on the watch, on guard”), from Italian all'erta (“to the height”), from erta (“lookout, tower”).
c: En cas d'urgence, alerte la police.
C'est sans doute une fausse alerte.

libérer.e: Borrowed from Latin līberāre (“to set free”). Doublet of livrer, which was inherited. Unrelated to French délibérer.

commis.e: From the past tense of commettre

commettre.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin committere.

vision.e: Inherited from Middle French vision, from Old French vision, a learned borrowing from Latin vīsiō, from vīsus + -tiō.

mesure.e: Inherited from Old French mesure, from Latin mēnsūra (“measure”).
c: Je pourrais être en mesure d'aider.

mesurer.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- Proto-Italic *mētis Latin mētior Proto-Indo-European *-tew-? Proto-Indo-European *-r-eh₂?
c: Je ne peux pas me mesurer.
Je ne pouvais me mesurer à lui.

arthur.e: Equivalent to English Arthur, used in France since the Middle Ages.
c: Guenièvre était la femme du roi Arthur.

louis.e: Inherited from Middle French Loïs, Loïc, from Old French Looïs, Luis, Lodevis, Lodhwig, from Latin Ludovicus < Clodovicus, from Frankish *Hlūdawīg, from Proto-Germanic *hlūdaz (“loud, famous”) + *wīgą (“battle”).

secrétaire.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin secrētārius, from Latin secrētus.

fuite.e: Remodeled, on the model of suite, from Old French fuie, from Vulgar Latin *fūgita, feminine past participle of *fūgīre, from Latin fugere. Doublet of fuie.

amitié.e: Inherited from Old French amistiet, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”).
c: Je ne mérite pas ton amitié.
Bugün uzun bir gün olacak gibi görünüyor.

annoncer.e: Inherited from Old French anoncier, from Latin adnūntiāre.
c: J'irai lui annoncer la bonne nouvelle.

pousser.e: Inherited from Old French, inherited from Latin pulsāre, from pulsus (“a push”) (and frequentative of pellō). Compare the prefixed verb expulser, a borrowing from Latin.
c: Rien ne semble pousser sur ce sol.
Bu toprakta bir şey yetişmez gibi görünüyor.
Pourrais-tu pousser la porte pour l'ouvrir ?

william.e: Borrowed from English William, though ultimately of Anglo-Norman origin. Doublet of Guillaume.
c: William a immédiatement commencé à pleurer.

nombreux.e: From nombre + -eux, or from Latin numerōsus.
c: Elle devait parler devant un public nombreux.
Büyük bir dinleyici kitlesi önünde konuşmak zorunda kaldı.
Bob a de nombreux livres dans sa chambre.
Bob'ın odasında bir sürü kitap var.

briser.e: Inherited from Middle French briser, from Old French brisier (“to break to pieces by a shock or violent blow, bust”), from Late Latin brisāre, of uncertain further origin.

cardiaque.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek καρδιακός (kardiakós), from καρδία (kardía, “heart”) (which is related to Latin cor, cordis, whence cœur).

minuit.e: Inherited from Middle French mynuyt, from Old French mie nuit, from mie, feminine singular of mi (“half, half way”) + nuit (“night”). Equivalent to mi- + nuit.

humeur.e: Inherited from Old French humor, humour, borrowed from Latin hūmōrem. Doublet of humour.
c: O kötü bir ruh hali içinde.
Kötü bir ruh hali içinde misin?

los.e: Inherited from Old French los, from Latin laus, probably via the nominative singular form.
c: J'ai une tante qui habite à Los Angeles.
Los Angeles'ta yaşayan bir teyzem var.
Nous avons volé non-stop d'Osaka à Los Angeles.

sein.e: Inherited from Old French sein, from Latin sinus, from Proto-Italic *sinus, from Proto-Indo-European *sinos. Doublet of sinus. Compare Italian seno, Romanian sân, Romansh sain, Portuguese seio, Spanish seno.
c: Elle a un cancer du sein.

crier.e: Inherited from Middle French crier, from Old French cri(d)er, from Vulgar Latin *crītāre.

c: Je veux le top du top.
Jouer au Go est ma seule distraction.

romantique.e: Etymology tree Latin Rōma Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Latin Rōmānus Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icus Latin rōmānicus Latin -ē Vulgar Latin rōmān…

lac.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *lókus Proto-Italic *lakus Latin lacuslbor.?

vente.e: From vendita, the feminine of Latin vēnditus (“sold”), past participle of vēndō (“to sell”).

vache.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French vache, from Latin vacca.

étude.e: From Old French estude, borrowed from Latin studium.
c: Pour le moment, ce projet est toujours à l'étude.

modèle.e: Inherited from Middle French modelle, from Old Italian modello, from Vulgar Latin *modellus, diminutive form of modulus (“measure, standard”), diminutive of modus (“measure”).

version.e: Inherited from Middle French version, from Medieval Latin versiōnem (“turning, rendition”), from Latin vertō (“turn”).
c: Laisse-moi te donner ma version de l'histoire.
Sana hikayenin benimle ilgili kısmını anlatayım.
Şu andan itibaren daha dikkatli olun.

plaisanter.e: First attested in Middle French, from plaisant + -er. Gradually replaced Old French gaber.

concert.e: Borrowed from Italian concerto, deverbal from concertare.

blessure.e: First attested in Old French as blesseüre, corresponding to blesser + -ure.

c: Je n'ai jamais vu pareil tir.

chauffeur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱleh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *ḱl̥h₁éh₁yeti Proto-Italic *kalēō Latin caleō Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁k- Proto-Indo-European *-yét…

puissant.e: Old present participle of the verb pouvoir (formed with the stem puis-; compare the modern form pouvant), from Old French puissant, pussant.
c: L'amour est plus puissant que la mort.

moteur.e: Borrowed from Latin mōtor. Displaced Old French mouveur.

city.e: Unadapted borrowing from English the City, ellipsis of City of London.
c: L'année dernière je vivais à Sanda City.
Atlantic City est célèbre pour sa promenade.
Atlantic City ahşap yürüyüş yoluyla ünlüdür.

coûter.e: Inherited from Middle French couster, from Old French coster, inherited from Latin cōnstāre. See also constat, constater.
c: Ça va me coûter mon poste.
L'accident a failli lui coûter la vie.
Je ne peux pas reculer maintenant.

dessous.e: From Latin dē (“from”) + subtus (“beneath”), corresponding to de (“from”) + sous (“beneath”) in French. Compare Italian di sotto, Romanian dedesubt.

souffler.e: Inherited from Old French sofler, from Latin sufflāre.
c: J'ai senti le vent souffler sur mon visage.
Peut-être pourrais-tu souffler un mot en ma faveur.
Belki bana destek çıkacak bir şeyler söyleyebilirsin.

construire.e: Inherited from Old French construir, borrowed from Latin cōnstruere.
c: Je me fais construire une nouvelle maison.
J'espère construire une nouvelle maison l'année prochaine.
Gelecek yıl yeni bir ev yapmayı ümid ediyorum.

démon.e: Borrowed from Latin daemon, from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn).
c: Le démon le plus dangereux, c'est le fric.

cesser.e: Inherited from Middle French cesser, from Old French cesser, borrowed from Latin cessāre.

c: Il est arrivé à la gare.
Demande-lui le chemin pour la gare.

garer.e: Inherited from Middle French garrer, guerrer, from Old French garer, warer, varer, of Germanic origin, from Old Frankish *warōn (“to guard, keep watch”) and/or Old Norse vara (“to warn, protect”); both ultimately from P…

bosse.e: Inherited from Middle French bosse, from Old French boce (“protrusion, outgrowth, lump”), from Frankish *bottja. Compare Occitan bòssa, Italian boccia and bozza; cf. also Romanian bot.
c: Il a une bosse sur la tête.
Il n'y a que moi qui bosse, ici !

bosser.e: First attested in 1878. Probably from bosse + -er (see below) with some sort of semantic shift.
c: Tu trouves que c'est normal de passer sa vie à bosser ?
Birinin hayatını çalışarak geçirmesinin normal olduğunu düşünüyor musun?

fer.e: Inherited from Middle French fer, from Old French fer, from Latin ferrum.

c: Mary a donné un coup de pied dans les couilles de Tom.

couille.e: Inherited from Middle French couille, from Old French coille, from Vulgar Latin *cōlea n pl, from Latin cōleus m sg.
c: Il y a une couille dans le potage.

quiconque.e: Inherited from Old French kiqunques, composed of qui (“who”) + qu(i) + onques (“ever”). The adverbial /-s/ may have later been removed by influence of Latin quīcumque, which has the same meaning.

soutien.e: Deverbal from soutenir. (soutien-gorge): Compare typologically Russian подтя́жки (podtjážki) (distantly cognate vie Proto-Indo-European *ten-).

usine.e: From Middle French oeuchine, œussine, oucine, huisine, ozine, uisine, usine, from Old French oechine, oechevine, ouchine, wisine, huysine, from Latin officīna. Doublet of officine.

château.e: Inherited from Middle French chasteau, château, chastel, from Old French chastel, from Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum.

garage.e: Etymology tree Middle French garrer French garer Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos Proto-Italic *-ātos Latin -ātus Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto…

délicieux.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin deliciōsus.

c: Elle lui a posé des questions.
Elle lui a posé quelques questions.

voisin.e: Inherited from Old French voisin, veisin, from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.
c: Tom est le voisin de Marie.

sage.e: Inherited from Middle French sage, from Old French sage, ultimately from the Classical Latin adjective sagāx.

crédit.e: Borrowed from Italian credito, from Latin crēditum.
c: Ben kredi ile ödeme yapabilir miyim?

ambulance.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₂énts? Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰíder. Proto-Italic *amβi- Latin ambi- Proto-Indo-European *h₂elh₂-der.

puce.e: Inherited from Old French puce, pulce, from Latin pūlicem, the accusative form of pūlex, from Proto-Indo-European *plus- (“flea”).
c: Allons au marché aux puces, demain !

canon.e: Inherited from Old French canon, corresponding to Italian cannone (from which borrowed most of the weaponry senses).

liquide.e: Inherited from Old French liquide, from Latin liquidus.

c: Pouvez-vous liquider vos emprunts sous un an ?

deviner.e: Inherited from Late Latin dēvināre, from Latin dīvīnāre.

particulier.e: Inherited from Middle French particulier, from Old French particulier, borrowed from Latin particularis.
c: Je ne suis personne de particulier.
Je ne vois rien de particulier.
Je le vis traverser la route.
Je l'ai vu traverser la route.

criminel.e: Inherited from Old French criminal, borrowed from Late Latin or Juridical Latin criminālis, from Latin crīmen.

c: À ce moment-là, cependant, c'était trop tard.
Ancak, o zamana kadar, çok geçti.

sombre.e: Inherited from Old French sombre, likely from Latin sub umbra (“in/under the shade”); compare Spanish and Portuguese sombra (“shade, shadow”).

sombrer.e: From a Middle French soussombrer, from alteration of soussoubrer, with influence from sombre, and the first part perhaps being interpreted as a prefix.
c: J'ai vu le navire sombrer en mer.
Je travaille pour une agence de voyage.
Ben bir seyahat acentesi için çalışıyorum.
Où se trouve l'agence de voyage la plus proche ?

gouverneur.e: Inherited from Middle French gouverneur, from Old French gouvreneur, from Latin gubernātōrem, from Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman, pilot, guide”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, to drive, to guide…

c: Ne comprends pas mes paroles de travers !

résoudre.e: From Middle French résouldre, from Old French resoldre, inherited from Latin resolvere.
