Nous lui avons laissé la décision finale.

culture.e: Borrowed from Latin cultūra (“cultivation; culture”), from cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“till, cultivate, worship”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”).

c: Les femmes n'ont pas de pénis.

décevoir.e: From Old French deceveir, decevoir (“to deceive”), from Latin decipere.
c: Sizi hayal kırıklığına uğrattığım için üzgün olmalıyım.
La production de la voiture commença en 1980.

bible.e: From Latin biblia, from Ancient Greek τά βιβλία (tá biblía, literally “the books”).

gant.e: Inherited from Old French guant, from Frankish *want (compare Middle Dutch want, Old High German wantus), from Proto-Germanic *wantuz (“glove”). Cognate with Italian guanto, Spanish guante, and Catalan guant.
c: Ça te va comme un gant !
J'ai perdu mon gant droit quelque part.
Beth est une fille bizarre qui aime les serpents.
Beth, yılanları seven garip bir kızdır.

nina.e: Associated with Ninette and Ninon, French pet forms of Jeannine, Jeanne.
c: Je n'arrive jamais à avoir Nina au bout du fil.

rumeur.e: Inherited from Old French rumeur, rimur, from Latin rūmōrem.

indice.e: Borrowed from Latin indicium, from indicō (“point out, indicate, show”).

ministère.e: Learned borrowing from Latin ministerium, from minister (whence French ministre). See also métier.
c: Le ministère de la Santé met en garde.
Le dossier a été adressé au ministère.

témoignage.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French tesmoignage, from tesmoigner (“to witness”).
c: Nous aimerions vous remettre ceci en témoignage de notre reconnaissance.
Bunu size minnettarlığımızın göstergesi olarak vermek isteriz.

effrayer.e: Inherited from Middle French effreer, from Old French esfreer, esfreder (whence also English affray), from a Vulgar Latin *exfridāre, itself of Germanic origin (with the prefix ex- added), from a Frankish *friþu (“secur…
c: Tu es en train d'effrayer les enfants.
Il n'y a pas de quoi s'effrayer.

fouiller.e: From Old French, from Vulgar Latin *fodiclāre < *fodiculāre, from Latin fodicāre, from fodere. Compare fouir.
c: Tom a commencé à fouiller la maison.
Diane est aussi ta demi-sœur, George.
Diane de üvey kız kardeşin, George.

actrice.e: Inherited from Middle French actrice, borrowed from Latin āctrīcem.

pisser.e: Inherited from Old French pissier, from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, of originally Germanic origin or more likely of echoic origin. Cognates include Catalan pixar, Italian pisciare, Romanian pișa.

entrepôt.e: Deverbal from entreposer (“to store goods in a warehouse”), with the ending influenced by dépôt (“store, warehouse, depot”).
c: Il travaille comme gardien dans un entrepôt.
Bir depoda güvenlik görevlisi olarak çalışıyor.

conclure.e: Inherited from Old French conclure, borrowed from Latin conclūdere.
c: Je dois conclure ce marché dans la semaine.
Bir hafta içinde bu anlaşmayı bitirmek zorundayım.

salade.e: From Northern Italian salada, salata (compare insalata), from Vulgar Latin *salāta, from *salō, from Latin saliō, from sal (“salt”).

indique.e: Inherited from Middle French indique, from Latin indicus.

c: Je vais vous indiquer la sortie.

matinée.e: Inherited from Middle French matinee f, from Old French matinee f, ultimately from Latin mātūtīnus (“of the morning”), from Mātūta f (“goddess of morning”).
c: Elle était là toute la matinée.

flotte.e: First attested in Old French as flote, from Proto-Germanic *flutô (“a float; raft; boat; ship”) through Norman or Frankish *flote

flotter.e: Inherited from Middle French flotter, from Old French floter (“to float”), from Frankish *flotōn (“to float, swim”), from Proto-Germanic *flutōną (“to float, swim”), from Proto-Indo-European *plew-, *plōw- (“to flow, sw…
c: Le magicien a fait flotter la jeune femme dans l'air.

rage.e: Inherited from Middle French rage, from Old French rage, from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs.
c: Tom est devenu fou de rage.

amiral.e: , from Medieval Latin amiralis, from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander”) + -alis (“-al”).
c: Nous avons détruit le vaisseau amiral de l'ennemi !

frigo.e: Clipping of frigorifique, frigorifié, or réfrigérateur.

christ.e: Inherited from Middle French Christ, borrowed from Latin Christus, from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós), proper noun use of χριστός (khristós, “the anointed one”), a calque of Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšīaḥ, “anointed”) or th…

c: Il me faut un avocat sachant parler français.
Fransızca konuşabilen bir avukata ihtiyacım var.
Ne sachant que faire, j'ai appelé la police.
Ne yapacağımı bilmediğim için polisi aradım.
Il est nécessaire d'éviter le stress.
Tom n'est pas capable de gérer le stress.

guide.e: From Old French guide, borrowed from Old Occitan guida, from the verb guidar, ultimately of Germanic origin, possibly through Medieval Latin; compare Frankish *wītan.
c: Ben sizin için bir kılavuz olarak hareket edeceğim.

chic.e: Probably from German Schick (“elegant appearance; tasteful presentation”). The word is akin to Dutch schielijk (“hasty”), schikken (“to arrange”), Old English sċēon (“to happen”).

comte.e: Inherited from Old French comte, conte, from Latin comitem.
c: Auguste Comte est considéré comme le père de la sociologie.
Auguste Comte, sosyolojinin babası olarak görülür.

fauteuil.e: Inherited from Middle French faulxdestueil, fauldesteul, fausdestueil, from Old French faudestuel, faldestoel, borrowed from Frankish *faldistōl (“folding seat”). Cognate with English foldstool, faldstool.
c: Je devrais retourner à mon fauteuil.

noble.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French noble, borrowed from Latin nōbilis according to the TLFi dictionary.
c: Le néon est un gaz noble.

auteur.e: Inherited from Middle French autheur, from Old French autor, from Latin auctor, from augeō + -tor.

c: Il vit séparé de sa femme.
Je me suis séparé de Tom.

botte.e: Inherited from Old French bote, from Frankish *butt, from Proto-Germanic *buttaz. See English boot.

espion.e: Inherited from Middle French *espion (attested only in the verb espionner), from Old French espion, spion (“one assigned to observe or spy”).

violent.e: Inherited from Old French violent, borrowed from Latin violentus.

violer.e: Borrowed from Latin violāre (“to treat with violence; to maltreat; to violate, to defile, to profane”).

c: Je pense que nous devrions repartir.
Tu dois maintenant travailler, tu dois repartir vers ta machine.
Artık çalışmalısın, makinene geri gitmen gerekir.
M. Spencer travaille dans un magasin.

serment.e: Inherited from Middle French serement (1415, Charles d'Orléans), from Old French sairement (twelfth century), from earlier sagrament (842, Serments de Strasbourg), from Latin sacramentum. Doublet of sacrement.
c: J'aimerais te rappeler que tu es sous serment.

promotion.e: Borrowed from Latin prōmōtiōnem, from prōmoveō (whence French promouvoir).

division.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin divisiōnem, noun of process form from perfect passive participle divisus (“divided”), from dīvidō (“divide”).
c: Il y a plus de filles que de garçons dans cette division.
Bu bölümde erkeklerden çok kızlar var.
Cette calculatrice ne permet pas d'effectuer des divisions.
Bu hesap makinesi bölme işlemi yapmaya imkan tanımıyor.

foie.e: Inherited from Old French foie, feie, from Late Latin fīcātum (“liver (as food)”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver, foie gras”).
c: L'alcool peut détruire le foie de l'homme.
Alkol bir insanın karaciğerini yok edebilir.
Benim karaciğerim ağır biçimde hasar görmüştür.

robot.e: Borrowed from Czech robot, from robota (“drudgery, servitude”), from Old Czech robota, from Proto-Slavic *orbota, from *orbiti + *-ota.

collection.e: Learned borrowing from Latin collēctiō. Cf. also Old French quieuçon, which may be inherited from the same source, and the modern cueillaison, which was probably formed analogically.
c: Cette collection est ouverte au public.
Il est fier de sa collection.

option.e: Borrowed from Latin optiōnem (“choice; option; act of choosing”), from optō (“to choose, select”).

communication.e: Inherited from Old French communicacion, borrowed from Latin commūnicātiō (“sharing, communication”). By surface analysis, communiquer + -ation.
c: Que signifie pour vous la communication ?
Sizin için iletişim ne ifade ediyor?
La langue est un moyen de communication.

rigole.e: Inherited from Old French regol, from Middle Dutch regel (“row”), from Latin rēgula (“straight line”). Doublet of rail, règle, reille, and rille.

rigoler.e: rire (“to laugh”) + Old French galer (“to have fun, enjoy oneself”), of Frankish origin.

vague.e: Inherited from Middle French vague, from Old French vague (“movement on the surface of a liquid, ripple”), from Old Norse vágr (“sea”), from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz (“wave, storm”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to dr…

laboratoire.e: From Latin labōrō (“to labor”) (supine stem labōrāt-) + -oire (suffix forming masculine nouns).
c: Je travaille dans un laboratoire d'hôpital.

soutenir.e: Inherited from Middle French soustenir, from Old French sustenir, soustenir, from Vulgar Latin *sustenīre, from Latin sustinēre. Asynchronically analyzable as sou- + tenir.
c: Il a fait un discours pour soutenir le projet.
Planı desteklemek için bir konuşma yaptı.
Il a naturellement une bonne mémoire.
O doğuştan iyi bir hafızasıya sahip.
Mike a quelques amis en Floride.
Combien la Floride compte-t-elle de comtés ?

charme.e: Inherited from Old French charme (“chant, magic spell”), from Latin carminem (“song, recitement, incantation”).
c: Ça fait partie de son charme.

clan.e: Borrowed from English clan, from Scottish Gaelic clann (“progeny, race”), from Old Irish cland, from Old Welsh plant, from Latin planta (“shoot, offspring”), and therefore a doublet of plante.
c: Son mari est un membre du clan Oda.
Onun kocası Oda ailesinin bir üyesidir.

livraison.e: From livrer + -aison, or possibly corresponding to Latin līberātiōnem. Doublet of libération, a borrowing from Latin.
c: Teslimat için bir ücret alıyor musunuz?

efficace.e: Borrowed from Latin efficācem (“efficacious, effectual, powerful, efficient”).

c: Nous sommes revenus dans le salon.

diplôme.e: Learned borrowing from Latin diplōma, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma).

c: De retour dans votre pays, veuillez consulter un médecin interne.
Ülkenize döndüğünüzde, bir iç hastalıkları doktorundan tavsiye alınız.

ennuyeux.e: Inherited from Old French enuieus, corresponding to ennui + -eux. Compare Occitan enugiu.

électricité.e: Borrowed from English electricity. By surface analysis, électrique + -ité.

baby.e: Borrowed from English baby, from Middle English baby.
c: Nous devons trouver une nouvelle baby-sitter.
Yeni bir bebek bakıcısı bulmamız gerekiyor.
Nous entrons dans une nouvelle phase de la guerre.
À quelle heure dois-je me faire enregistrer ?
À partir de quelle heure peut-on s'enregistrer ?

révolution.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin revolūtiō, from Latin revolvō.
c: La révolution a ses propres lois.
La révolution fut le début d'une nouvelle ère.

barbe.e: Inherited from Middle French barbe, from Old French barbe, from Latin barba, from earlier *farba, from Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂ (“beard”).

commerce.e: Inherited from Middle French commerce, borrowed from Latin commercium (“commerce, trade”), from com- (“together”) + merx (“good, wares, merchandise”).
c: Il fait commerce de voitures d'occasion.
O, ikinci el araba ticareti yapar.
Je travaille pour une entreprise de commerce.
Ben bir ticaret firması için çalışıyorum.

formation.e: Inherited from Old French formacion, borrowed from Latin fōrmātiōnem. Cf. also the archaic formaison.

habiller.e: Inherited from Old French abiller, from a- + bille + -er. The orthography with -h-, starting around the 15th century, is likely due to influence from or semantic association with the etymologically unrelated habit.

fichu.e: Past participle of ficher (various senses). Also a minced oath for foutu.

c: J'ai besoin de renseignements sur eux.
On a besoin de quelques renseignements sur la ville.
Kentle ilgili biraz bilgiye ihtiyacımız var.
Elle travaille pour le compte du Renseignement Français.
On a reçu un renseignement anonyme.
Ne dis pas de bêtises, Tom.
Les garçons aiment bien faire des bêtises.

commissariat.e: From commissaire + -at. Compare Medieval Latin commissāriātus [1352].

tuyau.e: Inherited from Middle French tuyau, from Old French tuel, tuial, tudel (“tube, pipe”), from Frankish *thūta (“pipe”), from Proto-Germanic *þeutǭ (“pipe, channel, flow”), from *þeutaną (“to howl, roar, resound”), from Pr…

convenir.e: Inherited from Latin convenire. Spelt covenir in Old French, etymologically reconstructed in Middle French to closer match the original Latin spelling.
c: Ça ne peut pas convenir à tout le monde.

total.e: ), a borrowing from Medieval Latin tōtālis.
c: Il y avait 30 membres au total.

éteint.e: Inherited from Old French esteint, from Latin extinctus.

éteindre.e: Inherited from Middle French esteindre, from Old French estaindre, from Latin extinguere.

c: Reste à l'écart de cet endroit !
Cette ville compte un million d'habitants.
Bu şehrin bir milyon sakini var.

comté.e: Inherited from Middle French comté m, conté m, from Old French conté m or f. Doublet of comtat. Compare Medieval Latin comitātus. By surface analysis, comte (“count”) + -é (“-ate”).
c: Elle a rencontré un garçon à la foire du comté.

bol.e: First attested in the 18th century. Borrowed from English bowl. For the semantic development of etymology 1 sense 2 compare pot (“jar; (colloquial) luck”). Possibly a doublet of boule.
c: Est-ce que tu as un bol plus grand ?
Daha büyük bir kâseniz var mı?
Tom est sorti pour prendre un bol d'air.
Tom temiz hava almak için dışarı çıktı.

dette.e: Inherited from Middle French debte (with silent b), from Old French dete, from earlier *depte, from Latin dēbita, plural of dēbitum. Doublet of débit.
c: À combien se monte ma dette ?
Des amis m'ont invité à diner.
Bazı arkadaşlar beni akşam yemeğine davet etti.
J'ai accepté de diner avec Tom.
Tom'la akşam yemeği yemeyi kabul ettim.

interrompre.e: From Middle French interrompre, partial relatinization of Old French entrerompre, itself a calque of Latin interrumpere.

plastique.e: From Middle French plastique, borrowed from Latin plasticus. Doublet of plastic.

minable.e: From the sense "likely to be destroyed by a mine," from miner + -able.
c: Nous avons finalement mangé dans ce restaurant minable.
Sonunda, biz, o eski püskü lokantada yemek yemeyi sona erdirdik.

léger.e: Inherited from Old French legier, from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from *levius + -ārius, the former element representing an alteration of Latin levis (“lightweight”). Compare Catalan lleuger, Occitan leugièr.

cité.e: Inherited from Middle French cité, from Old French citet, from older ciptet, from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”).
c: Tom a seulement cité Mary deux fois.
Tom sadece iki kez Mary'ye bahsetti.
Tom a été cité à comparaître.
Je ne vais pas citer de noms.

las.e: Inherited from Old French las, from Latin lassus.
c: Je suis trop las pour conduire. Pourrais-tu le faire ?
Araba süremeyecek kadar çok yorgunum. Siz sürer misiniz?

russie.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Russia. By surface analysis, russe + -ie.

c: Elle a appelé tandis que j'étais sorti.
J'ai rencontré Bob et Marie tandis que j'attendais Kate.
Kate'i beklerken Bob ve Mary ile karşılaştım.

espagnol.e: From Spanish español or from Middle French espaignol, from Old French espagneul or espaigneul, borrowed from Old Occitan espaignol, espainol, from a Vulgar Latin *Hispaniolus, from Latin Hispānus, from Hispania.

pilule.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pilula, apparently first attested in the fourteenth century, in turn inherited from the Classical Latin, attested in the medical sense in Pliny.

c: Aïe ! Je me suis mordu la langue.

sain.e: Inherited from Old French sain, from Latin sānus, from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vigorous”).

évidence.e: Etymology tree Latin evidens Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -ia Latin evidentialbor. French évidence Learned borrowing from Latin ēvidentia.

fidèle.e: Borrowed from Latin fidēlis (“loyal”), replaced the inherited Old French fedel, fëel (cf. French féal).
c: Je pense que Tom est fidèle.

cimetière.e: From Old French cimitiere, a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion, “sleeping chamber”).
c: Il fut enterré dans ce cimetière.

couler.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin cōlāre (“filter, strain, purify”).

fâcher.e: Inherited from Middle French fascher, from Old French faschier. Probably from Vulgar Latin *fasticāre, from an alteration of Late Latin fastidiāre < Classical Latin fastīdīre.
c: Je ne veux pas te fâcher.
Ça ne sert à rien de se fâcher contre lui.
Le plan fut mis à exécution.
Vous devez mettre votre plan à exécution.
Elle m'a surpris en train de regarder du porno.
Tom a omis quelques éléments de la liste.
Mélanger tous les éléments pour faire une seule pièce.
Tek parça yapmak için tüm parçaları birleştirin.
Tu n'es pas dans ton élément, ici.
C'est un élément nécessaire de l'équipement.

rang.e: Inherited from Middle French ranc, from Old French renc, reng, ranc, rang, from Frankish *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring, circle”). Cognate with Dutch ring, German Ring, English ring.
c: Il tient le rang de colonel.
Je vais vous dénoncer aux autorités.

fierté.e: From fier + -té, corresponding to Latin feritātem.
c: Ce fut le moment de plus grande fierté de ma vie.

diamant.e: Inherited from Middle French diamant, from Old French diamant, from Late Latin diamas, probably from metathesis of adimas (whence aimant), from Latin adamās, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas).

processus.e: Unadapted borrowing from Latin prōcessus (“process, progression”). Doublet of procès, another borrowing.
c: Le processus peut prendre des années.

caution.e: Inherited from Old French caution, borrowed from Latin cautiōnem, from cautus, past participle of caveō, cavēre (“be on one's guard”).
c: La défense a demandé une mise en liberté sous caution.

lecture.e: Borrowed from Late Latin lēctūra, feminine of Classical Latin lēctūrus.

rond.e: Inherited from Old French reont, from Late Latin retundus, dissimilated variant of Latin rotundus. Doublet of rotonde.
c: Arrête de tourner en rond et va droit au but.
Boşa uğraşmayı bırak ve sadede gel.

écraser.e: From Middle French ecraser (“to squash”), from Middle English crasen (“to break, shatter”), from Old Norse *krasa (“to shatter”), ultimately imitative. More at craze.
c: Tom a failli se faire écraser.

caractère.e: Learned borrowing from Latin character, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “type, nature, character”).

intelligence.e: Learned borrowing from Latin intelligentia (“discernment, intelligence”).
c: Elle a un haut niveau d'intelligence.
Onun yüksek bir zeka derecesi var.
La foi est la mort de l'intelligence.
Je vais avoir besoin de renfort.

douze.e: Inherited from Old French doze, from Latin duodecim.

plaindre.e: Inherited from Middle French plaindre, pleindre, from Old French plaindre, pleindre, from Latin plangere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂k-.

exprimer.e: Learned borrowing from Latin exprimere. Compare the inherited doublet épreindre.
c: O yüksek sesle konuştuğu için mahcup oldu.

religion.e: Inherited from Middle French religion, from Old French religion, borrowed from Latin religiōnem.

c: J'ai abandonné tout espoir de survie.
Je sens quelque chose de pourri.

pourrir.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *puH-der. Latin puter Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Italic *-ējō Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁tiinflu.
c: Cette pomme a commencé à pourrir.
Les fruits tendent à pourrir tout de suite.

esclave.e: ), a borrowing from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”). Doublet of slave.

septembre.e: Borrowed from Latin Septembrem. Compare Old French setembre, sietembre.
c: C'est déjà septembre mais il fait très chaud.
Şu anda eylül ayındayız ama hava çok sıcak.

tradition.e: Inherited from Middle French tradition, from Old French, borrowed from Latin trāditiōnem, from the verb trādere. Compare trahison.

jusque.e: Inherited from Old French jusque, from Latin inde + ūsque.
c: Il a marché jusque chez lui.

stratégie.e: Inherited from Old French strategie, from Latin strategia, a borrowing from Ancient Greek στρατηγία (stratēgía, “office of general, command, generalship”), from στρατηγός (stratēgós, “the leader or commander of an army,…

chasseur.e: From chasser + -eur; found in Old French as chaceür, chaceor. Compare Italian cacciatore, Spanish cazador.
c: Le roi était un grand chasseur.

guitare.e: Inherited from Middle French guitare, from Old Spanish guitarra, from Arabic قِيثَارَة (qīṯāra), from Aramaic קיתרא, from Ancient Greek κῐθᾰ́ρᾱ (kĭthắrā). Doublet of cithare and cistre.

louer.e: Inherited from Old French loer, from Latin locāre.

attacher.e: Inherited from Old French atachier, variant of estachier (“bind”), derived from estache (“stick”). Cognate with Old Occitan estacha, Italian stacca, Spanish estaca; from Gothic *stakka. Doublet of attaquer.

nue.e: Inherited from Middle French nue, from Old French nue, from Vulgar Latin *nūba, from Latin nūbēs. Compare Occitan niu; Portuguese nuvem; Spanish and Italian nube.

améliorer.e: Inherited from Old French ameillorer, from a prefixed version of Late Latin meliōrāre, a verb based on Latin meliārī (“better”).

amant.e: Borrowed from Latin amantem, present participle of amō. Compare aimant, the present participle of aimer.

escalier.e: Inherited from Middle French escallier, borrowed (through written form) from Occitan escalier, from Late Latin scālārium (attested in some inscriptions), neuter nominalization of *scālārius (“pertaining to a flight of s…

chirurgien.e: Inherited from Middle French chirurgien, from Old French cirurgiien (see also Old French surgien, inherited through Vulgar Latin), or simply formed from the root of chirurgie, borrowed from Latin chīrūrgia, from chīrūrg…

c: Je suis en classe de quatrième.

accent.e: Inherited from Middle French accent, from Old French acent, accent, borrowed from Latin accentus (“accent, tone, accentuation”).

personnalité.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin persōnālitās.

commandement.e: First attested in the eleventh century as Old French comandement. By surface analysis, commander (“to order”) + -ment.
c: Aimer Dieu et ses voisins sont les deux grands commandements.
Tanrıyı ve komşuları sevmek iki büyük emirdir.

lampe.e: Inherited from Middle French lampe, from Old French lampe, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “lamp, flambeau”).

crever.e: From Old French crever, inherited from Latin crepāre (“to rattle, creak, crack”). The informal sense of 'die' is shared with the Italian cognate crepare and Romanian crăpa.

ken.e: Clipping of kéni, the verlan form of niquer.

c: Il est revenu de son voyage en Asie centrale.
Oscar était le chien de ma mère.

goûter.e: Inherited from Middle French gouster, from Old French goster, inherited from Latin gustāre. Compare the borrowed prefixed verb déguster.

nerf.e: Inherited from Middle French nerf, from Old French nerf, inherited from Latin nervus.
c: Je suis à bout de nerfs.
Tom est à bout de nerfs.
Toute sa vie, Tom n'a jamais su se dépasser.
Tom hayatı boyunca beklenenin altında kaldı.
Tom a été sauvé par un passant.
Tom yoldan geçen biri tarafından kurtarıldı.
Il me fit signe de la tête en passant.
C'est une perte totale de temps.
C'était une totale perte de temps.
C'est ainsi que le font les pros.

dessin.e: Deverbal from desseigner, dessigner, dessiner (influenced by Italian disegno). Doublet of dessein and design.

généreux.e: Inherited from Middle French genereux, from Latin generōsus.

c: C'est vendredi ! Le moment de se bourrer la gueule.
Pourquoi ne sortons-nous pas nous bourrer la gueule ?

manuel.e: Etymology tree Biblical Hebrew עִמָּנוּ (ʕimmɔnū) Biblical Hebrew אֵל (ʔel) Biblical Hebrew עִמָּנוּאֵלbor. Spanish Emanuelaph. Spanish Manuelbor. ▲ Biblical Hebrew עִמָּנוּאֵל (ʕimmɔnūʔel)bor. Portuguese Emanuelaph.

officiel.e: From Old French, from Latin officiālis.
c: Le dîner officiel a eu lieu à la Maison Blanche.
Resmi akşam yemeği Beyaz Sarayda gerçekleşti.

reconnaissance.e: From reconnaiss- (present participle stem of reconnaître, cf. reconnaissant) + -ance. Compare also Medieval Latin recognōscentia (“a recognizing, acknowledgement”), Italian riconoscenza.
c: Tout le monde veut de la reconnaissance.
Voici un présent pour vous, comme marque de notre reconnaissance.
Takdirimizin bir belirtisi olarak işte senin için bir hediye.

boisson.e: Inherited from Late Latin bibitiōnem, from Latin bibitus, from bibere (“to drink”).

appétit.e: Inherited from Middle French appetit, from Old French apetit, loaned from Latin appetītus.

câble.e: e. Old Norman or Picard) variant of chable, cheable, chaable, from Vulgar Latin *caplum, contracted form of Late Latin capulum, from Latin capiō.
c: Câble-moi immédiatement, au cas où il y aurait un accident.
Kaza olması durumunda bana hemen telgraf çek.

phrase.e: From Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”), from φράζω (phrázō, “to tell, express”).
c: Cette phrase ne veut rien dire.
Bu cümle herhangi bir anlama gelmiyor.
As-tu un réveil dans ta chambre ?
Odanda bir çalar saatin var mı?

avérer.e: From Old French averer, from Early Medieval Latin advērō, derived from Latin vērus (“true”).
c: Trouver un appartement peut s'avérer difficile.
Bir apartman dairesi bulmak zor olabilir.

champs.e: (Champs-sur-Marne): From Middle French Champs. Attested on the Cassini map (1740s) and official until 1962.

dose.e: From Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis). Doublet of dot.
c: Assurez-vous de prendre une dose trois fois par jour.
Lütfen günde üç kez bir doz aldığından emin ol.

coma.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek κόμη (kómē)bor. Latin cōmalbor. French coma Learned borrowing from Latin cōma, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κῶμα (kôma).

social.e: From Latin sociālis (“of or belonging to a companion, companionship or association, social”), from socius (“a companion, ally”).
c: Je ne suis pas assez social.
Il fait attention à ses manières.

mortel.e: From Old French mortel, from Latin mortālis.

c: Je ne suis pas une gamine.
Cette gamine veut une bonne gifle.
Şu kız iyi bir tokat istiyor!
Dan a plaidé coupable d'homicide involontaire.
Dan ikinci derece cinayetten suçlu bulundu.

suer.e: Inherited from Old French suer, from Latin sūdāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.
c: Mes mains se sont mises à suer.
Tom et Sue se connaissent depuis 1985.
Tom ve Sue 1985 ten beri birbirlerini tanıyorlar.
Même en regardant bien on ne voit rien.
Dikkatlice baktığında bile hiçbir şey görmüyorlar.
On dirait que c'est facile, en te regardant.

riz.e: Inherited from Middle French riz, ris, from Old French ris, from Old Italian riso, risi, from Byzantine Greek ὄρυζα (óruza), ὄρυζον (óruzon).

zut.e: From 1813. Origin disputed:. * Combination of zest and flûte ; * Formed from a linking z and ut/hut, attested 1791: :* Allons, allons, hut! pas de ça:Le Véritable P.
c: Zut ! J'ai oublié mon appareil photo !
Zut, j'ai encore raté le train !
Lanet olsun, ben yine treni kaçırdım!

accueillir.e: Inherited from Old French acoillir, from Vulgar Latin *accolligere, from Latin ad- + colligere. Cognate with Catalan acollir, Italian accogliere, Occitan aculhir, Portuguese acolher, Spanish acoger.

ongle.e: Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *ungla, syncopated form of Latin ungula, from unguis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃negʰ-.

portrait.e: From Middle French portraict, pourtraict, nominal use of the past participle of portraire (“portray”), from Latin prōtrahō (< prō- + trahō).
c: C'est un beau portrait de famille.

désastre.e: From dés- + astre, a calque of Italian disastro (literally “bad star”).

métal.e: Borrowed from Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”), of unknown origin.

c: Tom n'écoute que du heavy metal.

jennifer.e: From English Jennifer in the 20th century.

traverse.e: From Vulgar Latin traversa, feminine of traversus.

italie.e: From Latin Italia via Ancient Greek Ῑ̓ταλίᾱ (Ītalíā), from Oscan 𐌅𐌝𐌕𐌄𐌋𐌉𐌞 (víteliú, “land of bulls”), a name for the southwestern tip of the boot of Italy; usually assumed to be a cognate of vitulus (“calf”).

degré.e: Inherited from Old French degré, from Latin gradus, with the prefix de- (probably to avoid a conflation with gré).
c: Quel degré de danger présente la situation ?

masse.e: From Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “bread”).
c: Ce mec est complètement à la masse, quel dingue !
Bu adam, kafayı tamamen tırlatmış. Allah'ın delisi!

masser.e: Probably borrowed around the end of the 18th century from Arabic مَسَّ (massa, “feel, touch”). An alternative possibility is that it was borrowed from Portuguese amassar.
c: Viens par ici. Je vais te masser le dos.

drapeau.e: From Old French drapel. By surface analysis, drap (“cloth”) + -eau (diminutive suffix).

traîne.e: Deverbal from traîner. See also train.
c: Je ne traîne pas avec lui.
Ne me laisse pas à la traîne !
Il lui a baisé la main.

noix.e: Inherited from Old French nois, from Latin nux.

cabane.e: ), from Old Occitan cabana, from Late Latin capanna, which see. Doublet of cabine. Perhaps also related with cahute.
c: Avant, il y avait une cabane par ici.
On a mis le feu à la cabane.

lion.e: Inherited from Middle French lyon, from Old French lion, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin leōnem, from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn).

c: Il est difficile de convaincre Jonathan.

budget.e: English budget, from Old French bougette. Doublet of bougette.
c: C'est un film à petit budget.

malédiction.e: Borrowed from Latin maledictiōnem. See mal and bénédiction. Supplanted the inherited Old French form maleiçon. Compare also maudition.

lot.e: Inherited from Middle French lot, from Old French loz, los, from Frankish *lot, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą. Cognate with English lot.

méthode.e: Inherited from Middle French method, borrowed from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos, “pursuit of knowledge, investigation, mode of prosecuting such inquiry, system”), from μετά (metá, “after”) + ὁδός…

avenue.e: From Old French avenue, feminine past participle of avenir (“approach”), from Latin advenīre (“come to”), from ad (“to”) + veniō, venīre (“come”).
c: Mon bureau fait face à la Cinquième Avenue.
Ofisim Fifth Avenue ile karşı karşıya.

autopsie.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek αὐτοψία (autopsía, “seeing with one's own eyes”). By surface analysis, auto- + -opsie.

puer.e: Inherited from Old French puir (with a change in conjugation), from Vulgar Latin *putīre, from Classical Latin pūtēre (also with a change in conjugation), present active infinitive of pūteō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-E…
c: Le poisson commence à puer par la tête.
Tom a décidé de subir l'intervention.
L'intervention humaine sur la nature ne trouve pas ses limites.
Doğadaki insan müdahalesinin hiçbir sınırı yoktur.

priorité.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prioritātem, derived from Latin prior.

serrer.e: Inherited from Old French serrer, from Vulgar Latin *serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, crossbar”).

quoique.e: From quoi + que, replacing earlier que que.
c: Cela ne sert à rien d'essayer quoique ce soit.
Je n'ai jamais pu te cacher quoique ce soit.
Tom travaille comme croupier dans un casino.
Tom bir kumarhanede krupiye olarak çalışıyor.

ressource.e: From Latin resurgere (“to rise again, resurface”), itself from re- (“again”) + surgere (“to rise”), from sub- (“under”) + regere (“to direct”).
c: J'utilise Internet comme ressource pour mes recherches.
Araştırmam için İnternet'i bir kaynak olarak kullanıyorum.
Nous devons essayer de protéger l'environnement.

toast.e: Borrowed from English toast. Doublet of tôt.
c: J'ai mangé une toast au petit déjeuner.

bâton.e: Inherited from Old French baston, probably from a Vulgar Latin bastōnem, itself a modification of Late Latin bastum, or possibly noun use of the verb *bastāre, from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō).

citoyen.e: Inherited from Middle French citoyen, from Old French citoien, citeien, from earlier citeain, equivalent to cité + -ain (later confused with or influenced by the suffix -ien).

abattre.e: Inherited from Middle French abbatre, from Old French abatre, from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere.

habit.e: Inherited from Old French habit, abit, borrowed from Latin habitus.

otage.e: Inherited from Old French hostage. By surface analysis, hôte + -age.

interview.e: Borrowed from English interview. Doublet of entrevue.

héroïne.e: From Latin hērōina, from late (2nd century) Ancient Greek ἡρωΐνη (hērōḯnē), feminine to ἥρως (hḗrōs, “hero”) "hero, demigod". By surface analysis, héros + -ine.

opérer.e: Borrowed from Latin operārī (“to labor”). Doublet of œuvrer and ouvrer.

rupture.e: Borrowed from Latin ruptūra. Doublet of roture.

batterie.e: From Old French baterie, from batre (“to hit”).

enseigne.e: Inherited from Latin īnsignia, a neuter plural reinterpreted as a feminine singular. Doublet of insigne.

enseigner.e: Inherited from Middle French enseignier, from Old French enseignier, from Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (also found in Medieval Latin), from Latin signāre. Compare Italian insegnare, Spanish enseñar.

promener.e: From a metathesis of Middle French pourmener, Old French pourmener, pormener (based on numerous verbs beginning with the prefix pro-), itself from pour- and mener; alternatively and less likely corresponds to a Vulgar L…

écrivain.e: Inherited from Old French escrivain, from Vulgar Latin *scrībānem, from Latin scrība, with altered declension. Compare Occitan escrivan, Catalan escrivà, Italian scrivano, Spanish escribano.

complice.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin complex.

bâtard.e: Inherited from Middle French bâtard, from Old French bastard (“child of a nobleman by a woman other than his wife”), from Medieval Latin bastardus (“illegitimate child”), from Proto-Germanic *banstuz, *bunstuz (“a bond”…

torture.e: Inherited from Late Latin tortūra, from Latin tortus, from torqueō.

loyauté.e: Inherited from Middle French loyaulte, from Old French loiauté (whence English loyalty), leialté, possibly corresponding to Medieval Latin lēgālitās, lēgālitātem, from Latin lēgālis.

brigade.e: Inherited from Middle French brigade, from Italian brigata.

collège.e: Inherited from Middle French college, from Old French college, borrowed from Latin collēgium.

poumon.e: Inherited from Old French poumon, pulmun, inherited from Latin pulmōnem (“lung”), from Proto-Indo-European *pléwmō.

destruction.e: Inherited from Old French destrucion, borrowed from Latin dēstrūctiōnem.

charité.e: Inherited from Old French charité, carité, a borrowing from Latin cāritātem (“love, regard”), which see for more. Doublet of cherté.

considérer.e: Inherited from Middle French consyderer, from Old French considerer, borrowed from Latin cōnsīderāre (“to examine, look at, inspect; to consider; to investigate”).

girl.e: From English girl. Doublet of gow.

désirer.e: Inherited from Latin dēsīderāre (“long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”).

moderne.e: From Late Latin modernus (“recent, actual”), from the adverb modo (“recently, just now”).

mentionner.e: * Derived from mention + -er. Compare Italian menzionare, derived the same way. * Alternatively, the term could have been borrowed from Italian menzionare.

pétrole.e: From Medieval Latin petroleum, from petra (“rock”) + oleum (“oil”).

solitaire.e: Learned borrowing from Latin sōlitārius. In Middle and Old French there existed the words soltain, soutain, inherited from Vulgar Latin *sōlitānus, from Late Latin sōlitāneus.

arracher.e: By prefix substitution from Old French esrachier (see also the form arachier), from Latin ērādīcāre. Doublet of éradiquer, which was borrowed.

tendre.e: Inherited from Old French tendre, from Latin tenerum, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).

sincère.e: Inherited from Middle French sincere, borrowed from Latin sincērus.

issue.e: Inherited from Middle French issue, from Old French issue (“exit”), from issu, past participle of issir, eissir.

issu.e: Past participle of the Old French issir (displaced by Modern French sortir), inherited from Latin exeō.

saut.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin saltus. Cognate with Sicilian sautu.

timide.e: From Middle French timide, from Latin timidus.

chevalier.e: Inherited from Middle French chevalier, from Old French chevalier, from Late Latin caballārius, from Latin caballus. Doublet of cavalier.

ordure.e: Inherited from Old French ord (“filthy”), from Latin horridus (“horrid”), + -ure.

volontaire.e: Inherited from Middle French voluntaire, from late Old French voluntaire, borrowed from Latin voluntārius (“voluntary; volunteer”), from voluntās (“free will”), from volō, velle (“wish, intend”).

interrogatoire.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin interrogatōrium, from Late Latin interrogatōrius.

trahison.e: Inherited from Old French traïson, from trair, or from Latin traditiōnem. Equivalent to trahir + -ison. Doublet of tradition.

vomir.e: Inherited from Old French vomir, from Vulgar Latin *vomīre, from Latin vomere.

confirmer.e: From Middle French confermer, from Latin cōnfirmāre.

soucier.e: Inherited from Middle French soucyer, from Old French, inherited from Latin sollicitō. Doublet of solliciter.

cruel.e: Inherited from Old French cruel, from Latin crūdēlis; either remade based on the Latin or evolved from the Old French form crual, possibly from a Vulgar Latin form *crūdālis.

scandale.e: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum. Doublet of esclandre.

échantillon.e: From Old French eschandillon (“standard”), from Old French eschandiller (“to verify the measures of merchants”), — a primarily Lyonnais word, from Latin scandaculum (“ladder”), from Latin scandere (“to climb”).

christine.e: Borrowed from Latin Chrīstiāna, the name of an early martyr. Doublet of chrétienne.

funérailles.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin funerālia. See also funéral, funéraire.

césar.e: Inherited from Middle French Cæsar, borrowed from Latin Caesar. Doublet of tsar.

jouet.e: Inherited from Middle French jouet, corresponding to jouer + -et.

chaos.e: Borrowed from Latin chaos, from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos).

outil.e: Inherited from Middle French outil, from Old French ostil, ustil, from Vulgar Latin *usitilium, derived from Latin ūtēnsilia.

dessert.e: Inherited from Middle French dessert, from desservir (“disserve”), from dés- (“dis-”) + servir (“serve”).

veuve.e: Inherited from Old French vaüve, veve, vedve, from Vulgar Latin *viduva, from Latin vidua.

veuf.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.

es: contrario a/de lo que se anticiparía

contenir.e: Inherited from Old French contenir, borrowed from Latin continēre.

espagne.e: Inherited from Old French Espangne, Espaigne, from Latin Hispānia. The /s/ was preserved or reinstated under learned influence (instead of expected *Épagne).

altesse.e: Borrowed from Italian altezza or, less convincingly, from Spanish alteza. Doublet of hautesse, the inherited French equivalent.

net.e: From Old French net, inherited from Latin nitidus (“shiny”) through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *nittus. Doublet of nitide, a borrowing.

population.e: Borrowing from Late Latin populātiōnem from Latin populus (“people”).

mondial.e: Inherited from Middle French, originally referring to the worldly (material) as distinct from the spiritual. Compare Ecclesiastical Latin mundialis.

juillet.e: Modification of Old French juignet (“little June”), diminutive of juin (“June”), based on Old French juil, from Latin iūlius.

capacité.e: From Old French, from Latin capācitātem. By surface analysis, capace (“capacious”) + -ité (“-ity”).

ordonner.e: Inherited from Middle French ordonner, from Old French ordiner, borrowed from Latin ordināre. Spelling influenced by donner (“give”).

admirer.e: ), borrowed from Latin admīrārī. The restored ⟨d⟩ was silent at first, but came to be pronounced since at least the 18th century.

pasteur.e: Inherited from Middle French pasteur, from Old French pastur, pastor, an accusative form corresponding originally to nominative pastre (whence modern pâtre), from Latin pastor, pastōrem.

patrouille.e: From Old French patrouille, patouille (“a night-watch”, literally “a tramping about”), from patrouiller, patouiller, patoiller (“to paddle or pudder in water, dabble with the feet, begrime, besmear”), from patte, pate (…

patrouiller.e: From patouiller with the /ʁ/ taken after similar-sounding words such as vadrouiller.

sel.e: Inherited from Middle French sel, from Old French sel, from Latin salem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂l-.

conducteur.e: Learned borrowing from Latin conductorem, from condūcō (“lead, bring or draw together”), itself from con- (“with, together”) + dūcō (“lead, guide”). Or from Latin conductum (supine of condūcō) + -eur. Cf.

stable.e: Borrowed from Latin stabilis. Replaced Middle French, Old French estable, an earlier borrowing from the same Latin source.

panneau.e: Inherited from Old French panel, inherited from Vulgar Latin *pannellus. Doublet of panel.

tragédie.e: From Old French tragedie, a borrowing from Latin tragoedia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”), a reference to the goat-…

serveur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ser- Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *serwos Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *serweyéti Proto-Italic *serwijeti Proto-Italic *serwijit Proto-Italic *serwi…

marge.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin marginem, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs.

prière.e: Inherited from Old French priere, preiere, from Early Medieval Latin precāria, derived from Latin precem.

impôt.e: Inherited from Old French impost, borrowed from Latin impōsitus, albeit with syncope.

vendeur.e: From vendre + -eur, or from Old French *vendour, vendeor from Latin venditōrem.

combinaison.e: From the verb combiner + -aison, modeled after or borrowed from Late Latin combīnātiōnem.

poing.e: Inherited from Middle French poing (“fist”), from Old French poing (“hand”), from Latin pugnus, from Proto-Italic *pugnos, from Proto-Indo-European *puǵnos, *puḱnos, from *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).

chapitre.e: From Middle French chapitre, from Old French chapitre (also capitre, chapitle), an early borrowing from Late Latin capitulum (literally “little head”), diminutive of Latin caput (whence French chef).

four.e: Inherited from Middle French four, from Old French four, forz, forn, from Latin furnus, from Proto-Italic *fornos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰr̥-nós, from *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”).

rapporter.e: Inherited from Old French rapporter (attested since the mid-twelfth century), from Latin reportare.

écriture.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French escriture, inherited from Latin scrīptūra (“a writing, scripture”), from scrīptum, the supine of scrībō (“to write”). Compare Middle French scripture, a borrowing from Latin.

publicité.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūblicitātem, itself constructed from pūblicus (“public”) + -tās (noun-forming suffix).

cendre.e: Inherited from Middle French cendre, from Old French cendre, from Latin cinerem, from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust, ashes”).

motif.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin mōtīvus.

respiration.e: Learned borrowing from Latin respirātiō. By surface analysis, respirer + -ation.

quinze.e: Inherited from Middle French quinze, from Old French, from Latin quīndecim.

avril.e: Inherited from Old French avril, from Latin Aprīlis.

pipi.e: Child speak, formed by doubling the first element of pisser (“to piss”).

cran.e: Deverbal of créner (“to kern”), from crenedes (“notched”), from Vulgar Latin *crinare, probably of Celtic/Gaulish origin, from Proto-Celtic *krini-, from Proto-Indo-European *krey- (“to divide, separate”).

principe.e: Inherited from Old French principe, from Latin prīncipium.

essentiel.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin essentiālis.

brise.e: Origin obscure. Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from a Germanic language, but the exact source is unclear; possibly Frankish *brāþi (“steam, vapor”).

aimable.e: Inherited from Middle French aimable, amable, from Old French amable, from Latin amābilis. By surface analysis, aimer + -able. Doublet of amabile.

symbole.e: Borrowed from Latin symbolum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon).

endormir.e: From en- + dormir or Latin indormīre.

foncer.e: From Old French fons, fonz ( > French fond) + -er.

satellite.e: Borrowed from Latin satellitem (accusative singular of satelles).

rembourser.e: From re- + embourser, which is from em- + bourse + -er.

vallée.e: Inherited from Middle French valee, from Old French valee, from val + -ée, from Latin vallis. Cf. also Medieval Latin valleta.

franc.e: Inherited from Middle French franc, from Old French franc (“free, genuine, sincere”), from Late Latin Francus (“a Frank”).

couronne.e: Inherited from Old French corone, inherited from Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē).

plante.e: Inherited from Old French, inherited from Latin planta (“sole of the foot”), from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from *pleh₂- (“flat”).

planter.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin plantāre.

menu.e: Inherited from Middle French menu, from Old French menu, from Latin minūtus (“minute, tiny”). Doublet of minute.

légal.e: Borrowed from Latin lēgālis. Doublet of loyal.

bonté.e: Inherited from Old French bonté, bunté, from Latin bonitātem. By surface analysis, bon + -té. Doublet of bounty.

acier.e: Inherited from Old French acier, acer, from Late Latin aciārium, from Latin acies, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”).

subir.e: Inherited from Middle French subir, borrowed from Latin subīre (“approach”).

branche.e: Inherited from Old French branche, from Late Latin branca, possibly of Gaulish origin.

révéler.e: From Old French reveler, borrowed from Latin revēlāre.

producteur.e: Borrowed from Latin productor, from productus.

lame.e: Inherited from Latin lāmina, through the accusative lāminam. Doublet of lamine, a borrowing.

goutte.e: Inherited from Middle French goutte, from Old French gote, gute, goute, from Latin gutta. The second t was added back in Middle French to reflect the original Latin spelling.

rate.e: From Germanic, probably Dutch rate (literally “honeycomb”), as the cellular tissue of the spleen is said to resemble honeycomb, from Proto-Germanic *hrētō-, from Proto-Indo-European *kreh₁d-eh₂-.

ticket.e: English ticket, itself a borrowing from Middle French estiquet (thus a reborrowing).

chloé.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek χλόη (khlóē, “young green shoot”), an epithet of goddess Demeter

oser.e: Inherited from Old French oser, from Early Medieval Latin ausāre, frequentative from Latin audeō. Compare Occitan ausar.

dealer.e: Borrowed from English deal, suffixed with -er.

deuil.e: Alteration of Old French duel, plural dueus (possibly influenced by analogy to œil and its plural), which probably came from Late Latin dolus, a derivative of Latin dolor (“pain”), or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *doliu…

statue.e: From Old French statue, from Latin statua.

excellence.e: Learned borrowing from Latin excellentia. By surface analysis, exceller + -ence.

piquer.e: Inherited from Middle French picquer, from Old French piquer (“to pierce with the tip of a sword”) (cf.

basket.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English basketball.

pathétique.e: Borrowed from Latin pathēticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós).

ruiner.e: From ruine. Cf. also Latin ruīnāre. Compare Italian rovinare, Occitan arroïnar, Spanish ruinar, arruinar.

prime.e: From the feminine of Old French prim, prin, from Latin prīmus. Noun from English premium.

bloquer.e: Inherited from Old French bloquer, from Middle Dutch blok, from Old Dutch *blok, from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką.

bénir.e: Inherited from Old French beneïr, inherited from Latin benedīcere.

hélas.e: Inherited from Old French elas, variant of a las, from a (“ah”) + las, from Latin lassus (“weary”).

sec.e: Inherited from Old French sec, from Latin siccus (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.

éclater.e: Inherited from Old French esclater, of Germanic origin, from Old High German skleizan or Frankish *slītan, from Proto-Germanic *slītaną (“to tear apart”).

protocole.e: From Middle French protocolle, protocole (“document, record”), from Medieval Latin prōtocollum (“the first sheet of a volume (on which contents and errata were written)”), from Byzantine Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon,…

chatte.e: Inherited from Middle French chatte, from Old French chate, from Late Latin catta, feminine of cattus. By surface analysis, chat + -e.

vodka.e: Borrowed from Russian во́дка (vódka), diminutive of вода́ (vodá, “water”).

roue.e: Inherited from Old French ruee, from earlier rode, from Latin rota. The current form may have been influenced by rouer and rouelle. Doublet of rote, a borrowing from Medieval Latin.

boucle.e: Inherited from Old French boucle, bocle, from Latin buccula (“the cheek strap of a helmet”), diminutive of bucca.

mordre.e: Inherited from Old French mordre, from Vulgar Latin *mordĕre, from Latin mordēre.

délire.e: Learned borrowing from Latin dēlīrium. Not related to Turkish delirmek.

resto.e: Clipping of restaurant. The original spelling restau has been altered to resto under the influence of other colloquial nouns in -o.

trente.e: Inherited from Old French trente, from Latin trīgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *tri(d)ḱomt (“thirty”).

douloureux.e: Inherited from Middle French douloureux. By surface analysis, douleur + -eux.

tonne.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *temh₁-? Proto-Indo-European *tend- Proto-Indo-European *tondeh₂ Proto-Celtic *tondā Gaulishbor.?

demoiselle.e: Inherited from Old French damoisele, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, diminutive of Latin domina. Compare Spanish doncella and damisela, Italian donzella and damigella, Portuguese donzela. Doublet of donzelle.

relève.e: Deverbal from relever. See also relief.

relever.e: Inherited from Old French relever, from Latin relevāre, corresponding to re- + lever.

allumer.e: Inherited from Old French alumer, from Early Medieval Latin allūmināre. Compare Occitan alumar.

conflit.e: From Old French conflit (ca. 1200), a borrowing from Latin cōnflictus.

accomplir.e: Inherited from Middle French accomplir, from Old French acomplir, from Vulgar Latin *(ac)complīre, from Latin complēre.

pension.e: Inherited from Old French pension, panssion, borrowed from Latin pēnsiōnem (“payment, rent”), from pēnsus, the past participle of pendō (“weigh, pay”).

routine.e: From French route (“road, route”), and Old French -ine: a suffix for diminutive purpose.

chagrin.e: From chagriner, perhaps from Frankish *gram, akin to German Gram.

local.e: Borrowed from Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus.

appuyer.e: Inherited from Middle French apuyer, Old French apoiier, borrowed from Medieval Latin *appodiāre, from Latin podium. Compare Spanish apoyar, Portuguese apoiar, Italian appoggiare.

réduire.e: Inherited from Middle French reduire, from Old French reduire, an alteration or Gallicization of Latin redūcere (“reduce”), after conduire.

filé.e: From filer (“to turn into (a) thread(s)”), from Latin fīlāre, from fīlum (“thread”).

rite.e: Inherited from Middle French rite, rit m (first attested in 1479), borrowed from Latin ritus m (“rite”).

symptôme.e: From Middle French (sinthome, Bernard de Gordon). Borrowed from Latin symptōma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma).

feuille.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃-der. Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom? Proto-Indo-European *dʰelh₁-der. Proto-Indo-European *dʰolh₁yom?

candidat.e: Learned borrowing from Latin candidātus (“a person who is standing for public office”), from candidus (“candid, white”), in reference to Roman candidates wearing bleached white togas as a symbol of purity at a public fo…

soupir.e: Deverbal from soupirer (Old French sopir, sospir), or possibly from Latin suspirium.

cercueil.e: Alteration of Old French sarqueu, sarcou, from Latin sarcophagus. Doublet of sarcophage.

trône.e: Inherited from Middle French throne, from Old French trone, from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “a seat, chair”).

tarder.e: Inherited from Old French tarder, from Latin tardāre.

administration.e: From Old French administration, from Latin administrātiōnem.

juin.e: Inherited from Old French juin, from Latin iūnius.

fabrique.e: Borrowed from Latin fābrica. Doublet of forge.

obscurité.e: From Latin obscūritātem. By surface analysis, obscur (“dark”) + -ité (“-ity”).

colline.e: Borrowed from Italian collina, from Late Latin collina, from Latin collinus.

avoué.e: Inherited from Old French avoé (“protector, defensor”), from Latin advocātus. Doublet of avocat.

puits.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French puis, puiz, from Latin puteus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *paw- (“to strike”).

octobre.e: Inherited from Old French octobre, borrowed from Latin Octōbrem. Replaced the inherited Old French uitovre. Compare also the Old French form witembre from the Vulgar Latin variant octember.

aimée.e: From aimée (“beloved”), feminine singular past participle of aimer (“to love”); originally a nickname and also a variant of Latin Amāta.

république.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(H)reh₁-der. Proto-Indo-European *(H)reh₁ís Proto-Italic *reis Latin rēs Proto-Italic *poplosder. Old Latin poplusder.

testament.e: From Old French testament, from Latin testāmentum.

facture.e: Learned borrowing from Latin factūra. Compare the inherited Old French faiture.

basse.e: Borrowed from Italian basso; homophony with Etymology 1 led to reinterpretation as a feminine, specifically as an ellipsis of la voix basse (“the low voice”).

médaille.e: Etymology tree Latin mediālis Early Medieval Latin medālia Italian medagliabor. French médaille Borrowed from Italian medaglia. Doublet of maille.

texte.e: From Latin textus, perfect passive participle of texō (“weave”).

établir.e: Inherited from Old French establir, inherited from Latin stabilīre.

record.e: English record, itself from Old French record.

blé.e: Inherited from Middle French blé, from Old French blet, from Early Medieval Latin blādum, from Frankish *blād (“field produce”), from Proto-Germanic *blēduz (“flower, leaf”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“to bloom…

guerrier.e: From guerre + -ier. From Old French guerrer, guerreier.

entrain.e: Either a deverbal from entraîner (“to charm, enthuse”) or composed of en + train as a derivation from être en train (“to be in a good mood”).

suprême.e: Inherited from Middle French suprême, borrowed from Latin suprēmus.

décrire.e: Inherited from Old French descrivre, from Latin dēscrībere (“describe”).

enveloppe.e: Inherited from Middle French enveloppe, anveloppe, from Old French envelope (“that which envelops, a type of garment”), from envoloper, anveloper (“to wrap around, enfold, cover”).

dalle.e: Inherited from Middle French dalle (“sink, gullet”), a borrowing from Old Norse dæla (“a small dale, ship's drain or pump, a small bucket, a groove, trough, trench, eaves”), from Proto-Germanic *dalą (“valley”), cognate…

cadre.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwṓr Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr Latin quattuor ▲ Latin quadrus Latin quadrōbf.? Latin quadrus Proto-Indo-European *-om Proto-Italic *-om Latin -um Latin quadrum Italian quadrobor.

prétendre.e: Inherited from Middle French pretendre, from Old French pretendre, a borrowing from Latin praetendere.

gris.e: Derived from Old French or Old Occitan, both from Frankish *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz (“grey”). Akin to Old High German grīs (“grey”) (German greis) and Dutch grijs (“grey”). More at grizzle.

magicien.e: Inherited from Middle French magicien. By surface analysis, magique (“magic”) + -ien.

canard.e: Inherited from Middle French canard, from Old French canart, quanart (“duck”), from cane (“female duck", also "boat”), perhaps ultimately from the same imitative root as caner (“to cackle, prattle”) (although caner is a…

quantité.e: Inherited from Middle French quantité, from Old French quantite, from Latin quantitātem, possibly borrowed or semi-learned.

gymnastique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin gymnasticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek γυμναστικός (gumnastikós). By surface analysis, gymnaste + -ique.

punir.e: Inherited from Middle French punir, from Old French punir, from Latin pūnīre. May have been borrowed due to its late appearance.

hélicoptère.e: From Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “spiral”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”). Coined in 1861 by Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt.

dinde.e: , the Indies), the French called turkeys coq d'Inde, poule d'Inde (literally “hen from India”), etc. D'Inde was ultimately spelled dinde by (rebracketing).

mêler.e: Inherited from Middle French mesler, from Old French mesler, from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin miscēre.

anthony.e: Unadapted borrowing from English Anthony, from Latin Antōnius. Doublet of Antoine.

organe.e: Borrowed from Latin organum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “organ, instrument, tool”). Doublet of orgue, an older borrowing.

époux.e: Inherited from Old French espos, espus, from Latin spōnsus, whose meaning was "promised, engaged"; displaced in that sense by fiancé.

ingénieur.e: Modified, based on the verb ingénier, from Old French engigneor, itself from engin or from Medieval Latin ingeniātōrem or ingeniārius (“one who makes or uses an engine”), from Latin ingenium (“an engine”), from in (“in”…

pape.e: Inherited from Middle French pape, from Old French pape, from Ecclesiastical Latin papa, from early Byzantine Greek παπᾶς (papâs, “patriarch, bishop”), from late Ancient Greek πάπας (pápas).

pouce.e: Inherited from Old French pouce, pouz, peuce, from Latin pollicem.

faiblesse.e: Inherited from Old French feblesce. By surface analysis, faible + -esse.

libération.e: Borrowed from Latin līberātiōnem. See also livraison.

vaincre.e: Inherited from Old French veintre, later veincre, vencre, inherited from Latin vincere, from Proto-Italic *winkō, from Proto-Indo-European *wi-n-k-, nasal infix from *weyk- (“to overcome”).

chaussette.e: From chausse + -ette. Compare Occitan cauceta, Catalan calceta.

estimer.e: Etymology tree Old Latin aestumō Latin aestimōlbor. Old French estimer Middle French estimer French estimer From Middle French estimer, from Old French estimer, a learned borrowing from Latin aestimāre.

silencieux.e: Borrowed from Latin silentiōsus (adjective). Documented since 1527.

avertir.e: From Middle French advertir, from Old French avertir, from Latin advertō.

délit.e: Inherited from Old French delit, borrowed from Latin dēlīctum.

requin.e: From Middle French requin (1539), of uncertain origin. Several hypotheses have been advanced: * From requiem. ) may be influenced by this, it is probably a folk etymology.

détention.e: Borrowed from Latin detentiōnem. Equivalent to détenir (“to hold, to possess”) + -tion.

tumeur.e: Inherited from Old French tumour, from Latin tumor.

crainte.e: From craindre + -te. Attested since the 13th century; replaced Old French crieme.

panier.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin pānārium (“breadbasket”), from pānis (“bread”).

tracy.e: Tracy-sur-Loire: From Latin Draptiacus, Dractiacus, Traciacus ; from anthroponym Draccius. :Tracy-sur-Mer: From Latin Traceum ; from anthroponym Draccius or Thracius.

clara.e: From Italian Clara, Latin clāra. Latinate variant of Claire.

nièce.e: Inherited from Middle French niepce, Old French niece, from Late Latin neptia, from Latin neptis.

élu.e: Inherited from Middle French esleu, from Old French esleü.

élire.e: Inherited from Middle French eslire, from Old French eslire, from Vulgar Latin *exlegere, from Latin ēligere. Compare (obsolete) Spanish esleír, Italian scegliere.

sagesse.e: From sage + -esse, equivalent to Latin sapientia (“wisdom, science”).

douzaine.e: Inherited from Middle French douzaine, from Old French dozaine, from doze (“twelve”), from Vulgar Latin *dōdeci, from Latin duodecim. Equivalent to douze + -aine.

trouble.e: Deverbal from troubler or from Old French troble.

troubler.e: Inherited from Old French trobler, trubler, with metathesis from torbler, tourbler, turbler, from Vulgar Latin *turbulāre, itself either from Latin turbāre or from turbula, diminutive of turba.

connexion.e: From Latin cōnexiōnem. By surface analysis, connecter + -xion.

renverser.e: From re- + Old French enverser, the latter from Latin inversāre.

usage.e: From Middle French usage, from Old French usage. By surface analysis, user + -age. Compare Medieval Latin usagium.

sourd.e: Inherited from Middle French sourd, from Old French sourt, sord, surt, surz, from Latin surdus, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“ringing, whistling”).

communiquer.e: Borrowed from Latin commūnicāre. Doublet of communier.

saigner.e: Attested in Old French as saignier, from Latin sanguināre.

festival.e: English festival, from Old French festival.

linge.e: From a substantivation of Old French linge, from Latin līneus.

fragile.e: Learned borrowing from Latin fragilis. Doublet of frêle.

concevoir.e: Inherited from Old French concevoir, from Vulgar Latin *concipēre, from Latin concipere.

obéir.e: Inherited from Middle French obeir, from Old French obeir, borrowed from Latin oboedīre.

chant.e: Inherited from Old French chant, from Latin cantus.

curiosité.e: Borrowed from Latin cūriōsitātem. By surface analysis, curieux + -ité.

entraîneur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Old French en- French en- Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ-der.?

archives.e: Borrowed from Latin archīvum (with a change in gender), from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon).

demeure.e: Deverbal from demeurer. Akin to Italian dimora.

tissu.e: Inherited from Old French tissu, participle of tistre (modern tisser). Compare Italian tessuto.

résidence.e: Inherited from Middle French residence, from Old French residence, first known attestation 1260-1270, borrowed from Latin residentia.

débattre.e: Inherited from Middle French debatre, from Old French debatre. Equivalent to dé- + battre.

prostituée.e: Nominalized passive past participle of prostituer.

bracelet.e: From Middle French bracelet, from Old French bracelet, diminutive form of bras (“arm”).

confortable.e: From English comfortable, from earlier Middle English comfortable, itself from Old French confortable.

navette.e: From Latin nāvis (“ship”) + -ette (referring to the boat-like shape of a shuttle).

cervelle.e: Inherited from Middle French cervelle, from Old French cervele, from Latin cerebella, the plural of cerebellum (whence French cerveau) reinterpreted as a feminine singular.

baron.e: Inherited from Middle French baron, from Old French baron, from Latin barōnem.

jumeau.e: Inherited from Old French jumel, gemel (cf. also the less often used French dialectal form gémeau, as well as Gémeaux), from Latin gemellus, diminutive of geminus.

mystérieux.e: Inherited from Middle French mysterieux. By surface analysis, mystère (“mystery”) + -eux.

campus.e: Borrowed from Latin campus. Doublet of camp and the inherited champ.

augmenter.e: Borrowed from Late Latin augmentāre (“increase”), from Latin augmentum (“growth, increase”), from augeō (“increase”).

cash.e: Borrowed from English cash. Doublet of caisse.

vilain.e: Inherited from Old French vilain, vilein, villein, from Late Latin vīllānus (“farm worker”), from Latin vīlla. Not related to vil.

royal.e: Inherited from Middle French roial, from Old French roial, from earlier reial, real, from very early Old French (c. 880) regiel, from Latin rēgālis, from rēx (“king”) + -ālis. Equivalent to roi + -al.

exposition.e: Inherited from Old French esposicion, borrowed from Latin expositiōnem.

nid.e: Inherited from Old French nid, from Latin nīdus, from Proto-Italic *nizdos (“nest”), from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (“nest”).

viser.e: Inherited from Middle French viser, from Old French viser, from Late Latin vīsāre, from Latin vīsere, intensive of videō. Compare voir.

assiette.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assedita, past participle of *assedere, from Latin assidēre.

boum.e: Imitative. The spelling variant boom is borrowed from English.

atelier.e: , to hold a broken bone in place, splint”) + -ier (suffix denoting the location of an abode). ; board, plank”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis; axle”)) + -ula (diminutive suffix).

divin.e: Inherited from Old French divin, from Latin dīvīnus. Doublet of devin.

balader.e: Verb formed from ballade (“lyric poem”), referring to the constant movement of troubadours, jugglers, etc.

capital.e: Borrowed from Latin capitālis. Doublet of cheptel.

hémorragie.e: From Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “a violent bleeding”).

drap.e: From Late Latin drappum (“cloth”), first recorded in Frankish ordinances (The Capitularies of Charles the Great). More at drape.

novembre.e: Inherited from Old French novembre, from Latin novembrem.

quelconque.e: Inherited from Old French quelesquunques, a borrowing of Latin qualiscumque, matched to the Old French quel (“which”) + que (“what”) + onques (“ever”). See Italian qualunque, a similar formation.

opéra.e: Borrowed from Italian opera, from Latin opera. Doublet of œuvre and opus.

racheter.e: Inherited from Middle French racheter, from Old French rachater. By surface analysis, re- (“re-”) + acheter (“to buy”).

accrocher.e: From a- + croc + -er. Compare Franco-Provençal acrochiér, Italian accroccare.

quête.e: Inherited from Middle French queste, from Old French queste, from Latin quaesta, noun use of quaesita, feminine of quaesitus, past participle of quaerō.

inquiétude.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in- Proto-Indo-European *kʷyeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *kʷyéh₁tis Proto-Italic *kʷjētis Latin quiēs Proto-I…

grève.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grava (attested in Mediaeval Latin), of pre-Latin origin, possibly Gaulish *grawa, from Proto-Celtic *grāwā.

tennis.e: Borrowed from English tennis. The sense "sneaker" is a pseudo-anglicism derived from tennis shoe.

culotte.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-der.? Latin cūlus Old French cul Middle French cul French cul French -otte French culotte From cul m + -otte f. Equivalent to the feminine derivative of culot m.

oignon.e: Inherited from Middle French oingnon, from Old French oignon, from Latin ūniōnem.

tigre.e: Inherited from Middle French tigre, from Old French tigre, from Latin tigris.

foire.e: Inherited from Old French foire from a Vulgar Latin *fēria from the classical Latin noun fēriae.

chariot.e: Inherited from Old French chariot, from char or from charrier + -ot.

mannequin.e: Borrowed from Middle Dutch manneken, mannkijn.

aiguille.e: Inherited from Old French aguille, from Late Latin acūcula, diminutive of Latin acus (“needle”). Perhaps influenced phonetically by aiguiser. Compare Occitan agulha.

suisse.e: From Suisse. The meaning "guard" is a metonymic reference to the practice of hiring Swiss mercenaries to serve as guards at European courts.

fournir.e: From Old French furnir, fornir (whence also English furnish), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *frumjan (“to complete, execute”), from Proto-Germanic *frumjaną (“to further, promote”), from Proto-Indo-European *promo-…

légume.e: Borrowed from Latin legūmen (cf. older form lesgum); was once feminine and became masculine by the 17th century. Replaced the Old French leün, which was inherited from the same source.

sperme.e: Borrowed from Latin sperma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma).

évacuer.e: Inherited from Old French evacuer, a borrowing from Latin ēvacuāre.

gras.e: Inherited from Old French gras, from Late Latin grassus. Doublet of crasse.

poème.e: From Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma).

prêter.e: Inherited from Middle French preter, prester, from Old French prester, from Latin praestāre. Cognate with Italian prestare, Norman prêter, Portuguese prestar, Romanian presta, Spanish prestar.

confier.e: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin cōnfīdō, based on the existing French fier.

dégueulasse.e: From dégueuler (“to vomit”) + -asse. Compare English vomitrocious.

ligue.e: Inherited from Middle French ligue, from Italian lega, from the verb legare, from Latin ligō (“to tie”).

massacre.e: Inherited from Middle French massacre, from the verb massacrer.

massacrer.e: Inherited from Middle French massacrer, from Old French macecrer, macecler, probably from Vulgar Latin *matteuculāre, from *matteuca (whence French massue), from *mattea or Late Latin mattia, from Latin mateola (“hoe”).

muscle.e: Inherited from Middle French muscle, a borrowing from Latin mūsculus (“a muscle”, literally “little mouse”). See also the inherited doublet moule (“mussel, clam”).

veiller.e: Inherited from Middle French veiller, veigler, from Old French veillier, veiller, from Vulgar Latin *viglāre, contracted from Latin vigilāre. Compare the borrowed doublet vigiler.

anonyme.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “without name”), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma), Doric dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

fermeture.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin firmatūra. By surface analysis, fermer + -ure.

quasiment.e: From quasi + -ment. Cognate with Italian quasimente.

intervenir.e: Inherited from Middle French intervenir (attested since 1475), borrowed from Latin intervenīre (“intervene”). Compare also Old French entrevenir, which may have been inherited or a composition with venir.

automne.e: From Old French automne, a borrowing from Latin autumnus. The inherited equivalent was après août (literally “after August”).

accro.e: Clipping of accroché, past participle of accrocher.

horloge.e: Inherited from Middle French horloge, from Old French orloge, oriloge, from Latin horologium, from Ancient Greek.

vomi.e: Borrowed from Latin vomitus, or nominalisation of the past participle of vomir.

économie.e: Borrowed from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”).

colonne.e: Inherited from Middle French colomne, colonne, from Old French columne, colonne, from Latin columna. Doublet of colombe.

pétrin.e: Inherited from Old French pestrin, inherited from Latin pistrīnum.

pipe.e: From the Old French verb piper (“to squeak, chirp”), from Latin pipare (“to squeak”).

pirate.e: Inherited from Old French pirate, borrowed from Latin pīrāta.

frit.e: Inherited from Old French frit, from Latin frīctus.

peindre.e: Inherited from Middle French paindre, from Old French peindre, paindre, inherited from Latin pingere (“to paint”).

dé.e: Inherited from Old French dé, of obscure origin: perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *dadu, itself from Latin dātum, or alternatively of Arabic origin; cf أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād).

ancêtre.e: Inherited from Old French ancestre, ancessor, from nominative case of Latin antecessor. Doublet of antécesseur.

acide.e: Borrowed from Latin acidus (“acid”), from aceō (“to be sour”).

saisir.e: Inherited from Middle French saisir, from Old French saisir, seisir (whence English seize), from Early Medieval Latin sacīre (“lay claim to, take seisin”), from Frankish *sakjan (“to sue, litigate; accuse”).

fixer.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ-der. Proto-Italic *feigʷō Latin fīvō Latin fīgō Latin fixuslbor. Old French fix Middle French fixe Proto-Italic *-āzi ▲ Latin -ereinflu.

dignité.e: Inherited from Old French dignité, borrowed from Latin dignitātem. Compare the inherited Old French deintié.

élection.e: Inherited from Middle French election, borrowed from Latin ēlēctiōnem.

catastrophe.e: Borrowed from Latin catastropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ).

marteau.e: Inherited from Middle French marteau m, from a back-formation from Old French marteaus (ca.

jet.e: Inherited from Old French get, giet, from a Vulgar Latin *iectus, jectus, an alteration of Latin iactus (“a throwing, throw”).

volontiers.e: Inherited from Old French volentier, veluntiers, from Latin voluntārie (used as an adjective), derived from voluntārius. Compare with the etymologically related terms volontaire, volonté, vouloir.

saisi.e: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

trouille.e: From Old French troillier (“to grind”, from truil, troil (“grape press”)) or Dutch drol (“to go to stool”, “dejection”).

colin.e: From a medieval diminutive of Nicolas.

machin.e: Back-formation from machine, converted to a masculine noun.

christopher.e: Borrowed from English Christopher, as a variant of the standard French Christophe.

déterminer.e: Borrowed from Latin dētermināre (“to delimit; to confine; to define; to designate”).

ouvrier.e: Inherited from Old French ovrier, inherited from Latin operārius. Cf. also the doublet opéraire, a very rare and jargony term borrowed from the same Latin term.

pompe.e: From Middle French pompe, from Middle Dutch pompe (“device for raising water, pump”). Related to Middle Low German pumpe (“a pump”). More at pump.

marc.e: ), deverbal from marcher (“to trample, walk over”).

profit.e: Inherited from Old French profit, from Latin prōfectus.

tache.e: Inherited from Middle French tache, from Old French tache, taiche, taje (“mark, spot, stain”), from Vulgar Latin *tacca, *tecca, from Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌺𐌽𐍃 (taikns, “mark, sign”), from Proto-Germanic *taiknaz, *taikną (“s…

absent.e: Borrowed from Latin absentem. Compare the popular form ausent.

cinquième.e: Inherited from Middle French cinquiesme. Also cinq + -ième.

coke.e: Borrowed from English coke (“residue from roasting in a coal oven”).

antenne.e: Inherited from Middle French antenne, from Old French antaine, borrowed from Latin antemna or antenna.

satan.e: From Latin Satan, ultimately from Hebrew שָׂטָן (satán, “adversary, accuser”).

apercevoir.e: Inherited from Old French apercevoir (“to become aware of”), from percevoir.

guère.e: Inherited from Middle French guere(s), from Old French gaire(s), guaire(s) (“much”), from Frankish *waigaro (“much”), related to *waigr (“resistant”).

provoquer.e: Inherited from Middle French provoquer, from Old French provoker, provoquer, borrowed from Latin prōvocāre.

fleuve.e: ), according to the traditional view, a dissimilated form of fluive, fluie, a re-borrowing of Latin fluvius (“stream”).

recette.e: Inherited from Old French recete (also reçoite, receite, recepte), from Latin recepta, derived from recipere (“to receive”). The Old French form is phonetically regular (cf.

plaie.e: Inherited from Old French plaie, from Latin plāga (hence English plague).

cuire.e: Inherited from Middle French cuire, from Old French cuire, from Late Latin cocere, from Latin coquere.

leslie.e: Borrowed from English Leslie. By folk etymology confused with Liesel, Liesl, German pet forms of Elisabeth.

bénédiction.e: Borrowed from Latin benedictiōnem. Cf. the inherited Old French beneïson.

compassion.e: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin compassiō, from Latin compatior (“to suffer with”).

val.e: Inherited from Old French val, from Latin vallem.

duc.e: Inherited from Middle French duc, from Old French duc, borrowed from Latin ducem (“duke, commander”), from dūcere (“to lead”). Doublet of doge.

bidon.e: Inherited from Middle French bidon (“small portable container, sealed and made of wood or metal”), from Old Norse bida, *biða (“container, vessel”), from Proto-Germanic *bidōn, *bidjan (“tub, vessel, vat”), from Proto-I…

sobre.e: Inherited from Old French sobre, borrowed from Latin sobrius.

flamme.e: Previously flame, from Middle French flame, whence English flame, from Latin flamma.

anneau.e: Inherited from Middle French anneau, from Old French anel, from Latin ānellus, diminutive of ānus (“ring”).

canal.e: Borrowed from Latin canālis. Doublet of chenal.

exposé.e: Past participle of verb exposer (to expose).

violet.e: From Old French violet, a back-formation from violette (“violet (flower)”), from viole + -ette, from Latin viola.

péter.e: From pet + -er. Compare Catalan petar, borrowed into Spanish as petar.

évasion.e: Borrowed from Latin ēvāsiōnem, action noun from ēvādere.

discret.e: Inherited from Old French discret, borrowed from Latin discretus (“separate”).

petit-fils.e: Inherited from Middle French petit fils, petit filz.

délicat.e: Inherited from Middle French delicat, borrowed from Latin dēlicātus. Doublet of délié.

ère.e: ), a borrowing from Late Latin aera.

mariner.e: Originally "to pickle in brine or seawater", from marin (“of the sea”).

drame.e: Borrowed from Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “play, drama”, noun).

are.e: Learned formation from Latin area, a piece of level ground. Doublet of aire.

intense.e: Inherited from Middle French intense, from Old French intense, which was borrowed from Latin intēnsus.

août.e: Inherited from Old French aost, from Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Doublet of auguste.

assaut.e: Inherited from Old French assaut, asalt, from Vulgar Latin *assaltus, modification of Latin assultus.

survivant.e: Compare Spanish sobreviviente, Galician and Portuguese sobrevivente.

çà.e: From Middle French and Old French ça, from Vulgar Latin *ecce hāc. Compare Portuguese cá, Spanish acá. The grave accent now serves to distinguish it from ça (“that”).

mouche.e: Inherited from Middle French mousche, from Old French mousche, musche, from Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus- (“a fly”).

clef.e: Inherited from Middle French clef, from Old French clef, from Latin clāvis, from Proto-Italic *klāwis, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kleh₂w-. According to Bescherelle.

relecture.e: From Latin. By surface analysis, re- + lecture.

décembre.e: Inherited from Old French decembre, a borrowing from Latin decembrem.

douceur.e: Inherited from Old French dolçor, from Late Latin dulcōrem, from dulcis (“sweet”) + -or. By surface analysis, doux + -eur.

glisser.e: From Middle French glisser, from Old French glicier (“to slip, slide, glide”), from a merger of Old French glacier (“to slip, slide”) and Old French gliier, glier (“to slip, slide, glide”), from Frankish *glīdan (“to sl…

faîte.e: Inherited from Old French feste, from Frankish *first, from Proto-Germanic *firstiz. Compare Dutch vorst, German First, Old English first. The spelling was influenced by Latin fastīgium.

michel.e: Etymology tree Biblical Hebrew מִי (mí) Biblical Hebrew כַּ־ (ka-) Biblical Hebrew אֵל (él) Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mīḵāʾēl)bor. Koine Greek Μῐχᾱήλ (Mĭkhāḗl)bor. ”).

bougie.e: From Bougie, the French name for the Algerian town of Béjaïa بجاية, formerly known for exporting candle wax. Attested 1300 for "fine candle wax", and 1493 for "candle made from such wax".

relais.e: From Old French relaier (Modern French: relayer).
