longueur.e: Etymology tree French long Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *-ōs Proto-Italic *-ōs Latin -ōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French longueur From long + -eur.

thème.e: Inherited from Middle French theme, from Old French teme, tesme, a learned borrowing from Latin thema, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).

contenu.e: Past participle of contenir. Compare Italian contenuto, Catalan contingut, Spanish contenido, Portuguese conteúdo.

corée.e: Internationalism. See English entry for Korea for further etymology.

came.e: Borrowed from Dutch kam (“cog of a wheel; originally, comb”).

moustache.e: Borrowed from Neapolitan mustaccio (compare Italian mostaccio), from Early Medieval Latin mustācium, from Byzantine Greek μουστάκιον (moustákion), diminutive from Ancient Greek μύσταξ (mústax).

poésie.e: Inherited from Middle French poesie, from Late Latin poēsia, from earlier poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis).

garantie.e: From Middle French garantie, from Old French garantie, guarantie (“protection, defense”), from Old French garantir, guarantir (“to warrant, vouch for something”), from Old French garant, guarant, warant (“a warrant; war…

bacon.e: Unadapted borrowing from English bacon, from Middle English bacon (“meat from the back and sides of a pig”), from Old French bacon, bacun (“ham, strip of lard”), from Frankish *bakkō, from Proto-Germanic *bakō, *baką, *…

hôte.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis Proto-Indo-European *pótis Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstipotis Proto-Italic *hostipotis Latin hospes Old French oste Middle French hoste French hôte Inherited from Middle French…

conclusion.e: From Old French, from Latin conclūsiōnem, from the past participle stem of conclūdere (“conclude”).

pull.e: Pseudo-anglicism; clipping of pull-over, from English pullover.

voile.e: From an Old French voil, veil, from Latin vēlum, from Proto-Indo-European.

règne.e: Inherited from Middle French regne, from Old French regne, borrowed from Latin rēgnum.

régner.e: Inherited from Old French reignier, borrowed from Latin rēgnāre (“to govern”).

compliment.e: Borrowed from Italian complimento, itself a borrowing from Spanish cumplimiento, from Latin complēmentum. Doublet of complément.

grotte.e: Borrowed from Italian grotta, from Latin crypta. Doublet of crypte.

tristesse.e: First attested in Old French as tristesce, tristece. From triste + -esse, modeled after Latin trīstitia.

orchestre.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra). The word was feminine (like its etymon) until the 18th century.

génétique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γεννητικός (gennētikós).

planche.e: Inherited from Old French planche, from Vulgar Latin planca, contracted from palanca, from Latin phalanga, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx).

sorcier.e: Inherited from Old French sorcier, from Early Medieval Latin sortiārius, derived from Latin sortem.

lent.e: Inherited from Old French lent, from Latin lentus. Doublet of lento, taken from Italian.

louche.e: From Old French lousche, from Latin lusca, feminine of luscus (“one-eyed”) ( > Old French lois). Cognate in particular with Italian losco, with whom it shares the semantic shift to describe a shady individual.

biscuit.e: Inherited from Middle French biscuit, from Old French bescuit, from Early Medieval Latin biscoctus (literally “twice-baked”). Doublet of biscotte and biscotto.

archer.e: From Middle French and Old French archier, from Vulgar Latin *arcārius, from Classical Latin arcuārius, derived from Latin arcus (“bow”). Equivalent to arc + -er.

bazar.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *wes-der. Proto-Indo-European *kʷel-der. Middle Persian wʾčʾl Classical Persian بازارbor. French bazar First attested in c.

quarantaine.e: From quarante + -aine, the medical sense a calque of Italian quarantena.

graver.e: From Old French, from Frankish *graban, from Proto-Germanic *grabaną. Akin to English grave (“pit for burial”).

rebelle.e: Inherited from Old French rebelle, borrowed from Latin rebellis.

descente.e: Inherited from Old French descente, from descendre.

terreur.e: Inherited from Middle French terreur f, from Old French terreur f, itself borrowed from Latin terror m.

innocence.e: Inherited from Old French inocence, a borrowing from Latin innocentia.

janvier.e: Inherited from Old French janvier, from Latin Iānuārius.

cheville.e: Inherited from Old French cheville, from Vulgar Latin *cavicla, dissimilated and syncopated form of Classical Latin clāvicula, diminutive of clāvis (“key”). Doublet of clavicule, a borrowing.

ais.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin axis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”). Doublet of axe, a borrowing.

plomb.e: Etymology tree Latin plumbum Old French plom Middle French plom French plomb Inherited from Middle French plom, from Old French plom, from Latin plumbum.

décharger.e: Inherited from Old French deschargier, from Late Latin discarricāre, from carricō, from Latin carrus (“four-wheeled baggage wagon”).

épuisé.e: From the verb épuiser. Literally, “used up”.

gravité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin gravitās. Replaced the older inherited grieté, griéveté.

taupe.e: Inherited from Old French taupe, inherited from Latin talpa.

bétail.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French bestail, bestaille. By surface analysis, bête (“animal”) + -ail.

catholique.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek κᾰθόλου (kăthólou) Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Hellenic *-kos Ancient Greek -κός (-kós) Ancient Greek -ῐκός (-ĭkós) Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós)bor. Latin catholicusbor.

sacrifier.e: Borrowed from Latin sacrificāre (“sacrifice”), from sacer (“sacred”).

saluer.e: Inherited from Middle French saluer, from Old French saluer, earlier saluder, from Latin salūtāre.

inspiration.e: Inherited from Old French inspiration, borrowed from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem (nominative: īnspīrātiō), from Latin īnspīrātus (past participle of inspīrō).

majorité.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin maiōritās. By surface analysis, majeur + -ité.

blair.e: Shortening of blaireau, an old slang term for a nose.

coco.e: From Middle French coche, coco, from Italian cocco and Spanish coco, both from Portuguese coco.

jazz.e: Borrowed from English jazz. The compound jazband is attested in a 1918 copy of Le Matin.

noyer.e: From Vulgar Latin nucārius (“nut tree”) from Classical Latin nux. Compare Spanish noguera, Portuguese nogueira, Catalan noguera, Occitan noguièr. Equivalent to noix + -ier.

jacques.e: Etymology tree Biblical Hebrew עָקַב Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (yaʿăqōḇ)bor. Ancient Greek Ἰακώβ (Iakṓb) Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos)bor. Latin Iācōbusslbor.?

tordre.e: Inherited from Old French tordre, tortre, from Vulgar Latin *torcĕre, from Latin torquēre.

missile.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Latin missilis (“that may be thrown”) (as in English).

syndicat.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱómder.? Proto-Indo-European *sem-der.? Proto-Hellenic *ksún Ancient Greek σύν (sún) Ancient Greek σῠν- (sŭn-) Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-der.

tournoi.e: Inherited from Old French tornoi; morphologically, deverbal from tournoyer (“to turn around, spin”).

dénoncer.e: Inherited from Latin dēnūntiāre (“to announce, foretell”), via Old French denuncier or denuntier (“to denounce”).

fée.e: Inherited from Old French fae, from Vulgar Latin Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Catalan, Occitan, and Portuguese fada, Italian fata, Spanish hada.

fameux.e: Borrowed from Latin famōsus, from fama; cf. Old French fame.

ci.e: Inherited from Late Latin ecce hīc.

sirène.e: Borrowed from Latin sirēna, from Latin Sīrēn, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). Cf. also Old French sereine. Doublet of serin.

pat.e: Borrowed from Italian patta (“tie, draw”), influenced by mat (“mate”).

galaxie.e: From Old French galaxie, borrowed from Latin galaxiās, from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, “milky”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”).

statut.e: Inherited from Old French statut, from Late Latin statūtum (“a statute”), neuter singular of Latin statūtus, past participle of statuō (“to set up, establish”).

extrême.e: Inherited from Middle French extreme, extrême, borrowed from Latin extrēmus.

requête.e: From Middle French requeste, from Old French requeste, from Vulgar Latin *requaesita, from Latin requīsīta.

citron.e: From Latin citrus (“citron tree, thuja”), probably connected with Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, “cedar, juniper”).

identification.e: From the Late Latin verb identificare.

commentaire.e: From Middle French commentaire, from Latin commentārium.

unir.e: Inherited from Old French unir, borrowed from Latin ūnīre.

arnaquer.e: Believed to originally stem from a Picard cognate of arnacher or harnacher (“to dress up ridiculously”).

quai.e: Inherited from Old French cail, specifically from forms without the final l such as kay, kai. Doublet of age and haie.

maïs.e: Borrowed from Spanish maíz, from Taíno mahís.

cocktail.e: Borrowed from English cocktail, which is of unclear origin.

pêcher.e: Inherited from Old French peschier, from Latin piscārī.

pénible.e: Inherited from Middle French penible, from Old French peinible. By surface analysis, peine + -ible.

vain.e: Inherited from Old French vain, from Latin vānus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty”).

afghanistan.e: Ultimately from Classical Persian افغانستان (afġānistān), apparently through English Afghanistan.

oreiller.e: Inherited from Old French orillier. By surface analysis, oreille + -ier. Cf. also Medieval Latin auriculāre, substantivized form of Latin auriculāris. Doublet of auriculaire.

fontaine wallace.e: Literally, “Wallace fountain”, named after British aristocrat Sir Richard Wallace (1818–1890) who donated them during the Siege of Paris.

tactique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τακτικός (taktikós).

villa.e: Borrowed from Italian villa. Doublet of ville.

croiser.e: From croix + -er. Compare Spanish and Portuguese cruzar.

vitre.e: Borrowed from Latin vitrum. Doublet of verre. Compare Spanish vidrio and Catalan vidre.

apparaître.e: Inherited from Middle French apparoistre, from Old French aparoistre, from Late Latin appārēscere (“begin to appear”), from Latin appareō.

tonnerre.e: Inherited from Old French tuneire, from Latin tonitrus (“thunder”).

grange.e: Inherited from Middle French grange, from Old French grange, from Vulgar Latin *grānica, from Latin grānum (“grain”).

amateur.e: Learned borrowing from Latin amātōrem (“lover”), from amō (“to love”). Displaced Old French ameor, which was inherited from the same source but disappeared by the 15th century.

élite.e: Feminine of élit (“chosen, selected”), old past participle of verb élire (displaced in modern use by élu).

chantage.e: From (faire) chanter (“to blackmail; to force a confession”) + -age (verbal noun-forming suffix).

ralentir.e: From a now obsolete alentir, corresponding to a- (“toward”) + lent (“slow”) + -ir (“verbal suffix”).

solaire.e: Learned borrowing from Latin sōlāris, from sōl (“sun”).

comparer.e: Borrowed from Latin comparāre (“compare, match, place together, couple”).

banc.e: From Old High German banc, from Frankish and Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”). Doublet of banque.

engin.e: Inherited from Middle French engin m, from Old French engin m, from Latin ingenium n.

maillot.e: From Old French mailloel, from maille.

trajet.e: Borrowed from Italian tragetto, from Latin trāiectus, past participle from trāiciō (“transfer, pass through; transfix”).

peste.e: Learned borrowing from Latin pestis (“plague; pest”).

déconner.e: From dé- + con + -er, literally “to pull out of the cunt”.

confession.e: Inherited from Old French confession, from Latin cōnfessiōnem (“confession, acknowledgment, creed or avowal of one's faith”).

carnet.e: From a diminutive of Old French quaern, quaer. Equivalent to cahier + -et.

complot.e: Inherited from Middle French complot (“crowd-, plot”).

nier.e: Inherited from Old French noiier (stressed stem ni-), from Latin negāre. Reformed to avoid confusion with noyer.

dépôt.e: From Old French depost, from Latin dēpositum (“deposit”, noun), also the passive participle of dēpōnere (“to deposit”). Cognate with Spanish depósito.

nichon.e: From nicher (“nestle”) + -on (because the breasts nestle in the blouse, or perhaps because the infant nestles against the breast).

registre.e: Inherited from Middle French registre, from Medieval Latin registrum.

présentation.e: From Old French presentation, from Latin praesentātiōnem (“representation, exhibition”).

fabriquer.e: Learned borrowing from Latin fabricāre. Doublet of forger.

joint.e: From the past participle of the verb joindre (see § Etymology 1, above), or from Latin iūnctus.

onde.e: Inherited from Old French unde, onde, from Latin unda.

grippe.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb-der. Proto-Germanic *grīpaną Frankish *grīpander. Old French *gripper French gripper French grippe From gripper.

détresse.e: Inherited from Old French destresce, from Late Latin districtia, from the past participle of distringere.

hurler.e: Inherited from Old French hurler, from Vulgar Latin ūrulāre, from Latin ululāre, from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root. Doublet of hululer.

orage.e: Inherited from Old French orage m, from Vulgar Latin *aurāticum m, derived from Latin aura f (“wind, breeze”).

cavalier.e: Borrowed from Italian cavaliere, itself borrowed from Old Occitan cavalier, from Late Latin caballārius. Doublet of chevalier, which was inherited.

déchirer.e: Inherited from Middle French deschirer, from Old French descirer, from de- + escirer, from Frankish *skeran (“to shear, cut”), from Proto-Germanic *skeraną (“to shear, shave, cut”).

brosse.e: From Middle French brosse, from Old French broce, brosse, broisse (“brushwood, brush”), of unknown origin. Probably cognate with Catalan brossa and possibly with various other Romance words.

craquer.e: Inherited from Middle French craquer, from Middle Dutch kraken (“to crack, crackle”), from Old Dutch *krakōn, from Frankish *krakōn (“to crack, crackle, shriek”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerg- (“to crow, shout”).

difficulté.e: Inherited from Middle French difficulté, from Old French difficulté, a borrowing from Latin difficultās.

impatient.e: Borrowed from Latin impatientem. Morphologically analyzable as im- + patient.

guy.e: Inherited from Middle French Guy, from Old French Gui, from Old High German Wido, a short form of names beginning with the element Proto-Germanic *widuz (“wood”).

pyjama.e: English pyjama, from Urdu پایجامه (pāyjāma) / Hindi पैजामा (paijāmā), from Persian پایجامه (pâyjâma) / پاجامه (pâjâma, “leg garment”).

flèche.e: Inherited from Middle French fleche, from Old French fleche, from Vulgar Latin *fleccia, borrowed from Frankish *fliukkijā, from Proto-West Germanic *fleuk(k)ōn + *-jā.

hommage.e: From Old French homage, hommage. By surface analysis, homme + -age.

boxe.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from boxing, from English box (“blow”).

concierge.e: Probably from Vulgar Latin *cōnservius, from Latin cōnservus (“fellow-slave”).

vaisselle.e: Inherited from Old French vaissele, veissele, from Vulgar Latin vāscella, from the neuter plural of Late Latin vāscellum, diminutive of Latin vāsculum, diminutive of vās (“vessel”).

ris.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French ris (“reef”) for earlier *rifs (nom. sg. and acc. ), probably borrowed from Old Norse rif (“reef”). See English reef for more.

cuit.e: Inherited from Old French cuit, from Latin coctus, perfect passive participle of coquō (“cook, ripen”).

premièrement.e: Etymology tree French premier Proto-Indo-European *men- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *méntis Proto-Italic *mentis Latin mēns Latin mente Old French -ment Middle French -ment French -ment French première…

fracture.e: Inherited from Middle French fracture, from late Old French fracture, borrowed from Latin fractūra. Compare the inherited Old French fraiture, and the frainture (influenced by fraindre).

éléphant.e: Inherited from Middle French elephant, from Old French elefant, a borrowing from Latin elephantus, from Ancient Greek ἐλέφας, ἐλέφαντος (eléphas, eléphantos).

bouclier.e: Ellipsis of Old French escut boucler (“shield with a buckle”), with change of suffix. Morphologically, from boucle + -ier.

voyou.e: From voie (“way, street”) + -ou, from Latin via.

coiffure.e: From coiffer (“to cover the head, to give a haircut, style the hair”) + -ure.

barrière.e: Inherited from Old French barriere, from barre, from Vulgar Latin *barra, possibly from Frankish *bara, from Proto-Germanic *barō.

papillon.e: ), byform of paveillon, whence the modern doublet pavillon (“pavilion”). Both from Latin pāpiliōnem.

dramatique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δραματικός (dramatikós), from δρᾶμα (drâma, “drama, play”) (whence drame).

pourvoir.e: Inherited from Middle French pourveoir, from Old French porveoir (whence English purvey), from Latin prōvideō (whence English provide), from prō- + videō.

ras.e: From Old French rés (remodelled after raser), itself from Latin rāsus. Doublet of rez.

district.e: Learned borrowing from Latin districtus. Doublet of détroit.

grille.e: Inherited from Middle French grille, grisle, from Old French greille, graïlle, from earlier gradilie (end of 10th century), from Latin crāticula (or a Vulgar Latin graticula).

mâle.e: Inherited from Middle French masle, from Old French masle, from Vulgar Latin masclus, contracted form of Latin masculus.

ciao.e: Borrowed from Italian ciao (“hello, goodbye”), from Venetan ciao (“hello, goodbye; your (humble) servant”), from Venetan s-ciao (“servant, slave”) or s-ciavo (“servant, slave”), from Medieval Latin sclavus (“Slav, slave…

poète.e: Borrowed from Latin poēta, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs).

licence.e: Inherited from Old French licence, borrowed from Latin licentia.

col.e: Inherited from Old French col, from Latin collum (“neck”). Doublet of cou.

khan.e: From Middle French chan, from Old French chan, from Medieval Latin chānus, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.

transmission.e: Borrowed from Latin trānsmissiōnem, from transmittere.

gré.e: Inherited from Old French gré, from Latin grātum, from grātus (“agreeable”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese grado.

beau-père.e: Inherited from Middle French beau pere, beaupere, beau-père, biau pere. By surface analysis, beau- + père.

maîtriser.e: From maîtrise, which derives from maître.

solo.e: Borrowed from Italian solo. Doublet of seul.

toile.e: Inherited from Old French toile, earlier teile, from Latin tēla.

parrain.e: Inherited from Old French parrain, parrein, parrin, from Early Medieval Latin patrīnus (“godfather”), from Latin pater (“father”).

transmettre.e: Inherited from Middle French transmettre, borrowed from Latin trānsmittere (“to transmit”), based on French mettre. Appeared in Old French as the form trametre.

honorable.e: Inherited from Old French honorable, honurable, borrowed from Latin honōrābilis.

facteur.e: Borrowed from Latin factor. Compare Old French faitor, faitre.

claque.e: Deverbal from claquer (“to clap”). Noun 1 sense 5 developed as paying audience members to applaud started at the Paris Opera.

henri.e: Inherited from Old French Henri, of Germanic origin.

brandon.e: Inherited from Middle French brandon, from Old French brandon, from Frankish *brand (“burnt log; brand; cinder”) + -on.

onze.e: Inherited from Middle French unze, from Old French onze, from Latin ūndecim.

pâle.e: From Old French pale, palle, from Latin pallidus (“pale, pallid”). In Old French one would expect a syncopated *paut, *paude; the form pal(l)e requires a lack of syncope.

pacifique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin pācificus (“peace making”).

conte.e: Inherited from Middle French conte, from Old French conte, compte, derived from the verb conter, compter, or from Latin computus. See compte.

compagnon.e: Inherited from Old French compaignon, from Late Latin compāniōnem (literally “he with whom one shares one's bread”) (compare Italian compagnone, Spanish compañón), from com- (“with”) + pānis (“bread”), first attested in…

caravane.e: From Old French carvane, a borrowing from Persian کاروان (kârvân), from Middle Persian kʾlwʾn' (kārawān).

pharmacie.e: Inherited from Old French farmacie, borrowed from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”).

défiler.e: From dé- + filer, or file, for certain senses.

âgé.e: Inherited from Middle French aage, from the Old French aé, from Latin aetatem (accusative of aetas).

chanteur.e: Inherited from Old French chanteor (oblique form), from Latin cantōrem. By surface analysis, chanter + -eur. Compare also chantre, derived from the Latin nominative. Alternatively, from a Latin cantator, cantatorem.

rançon.e: Inherited from Old French rençon, raençon, inherited from Latin redemptiōnem. Doublet of rédemption.

bowling.e: Borrowed from English bowling. The sense "bowling alley" is a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English bowling alley.

us.e: Inherited from Old French us, from Latin ūsus.

affiche.e: Deverbal from afficher (“to put up, display”).

afficher.e: ], from Old French afichier (“to declare firmly”), equivalent to a- + ficher (“to fasten, fix, settle in”). More at fix.

loge.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ-der.? Proto-Germanic *laubą Proto-West Germanic *laub Proto-Germanic *-jô Proto-West Germanic *-jō Frankish *laubijābor. Early Medieval Latin laubiader.

loger.e: Inherited from Middle French logier, from Old French logier, from loge + -er.

rocher.e: Inherited from Old French rochier, from roche.

héritier.e: Inherited from Middle French heritier, from Old French eritier, from Latin hērēditārius. Doublet of héréditaire.

fusion.e: Inherited from Middle French fusion, from Old French fusion, a borrowing from Latin fūsiōnem. Doublet of foison.

traumatisme.e: Formed as: traumat(ique) + -isme, after the Ancient Greek τραυματισμός (traumatismós).

comtesse.e: From Middle French contese, contesse, from Old French contesce, contesse, cuntesse; equivalent to comte (“earl”) + -esse (“-ess”).

basé.e: Semantic loan from English based (see there for more).

défaite.e: From Middle French desfaicte, from Old French desfaite. Cognate with English defeat.

talon.e: From Old French talon (“heel, spur”). Cognate with Italian tallone.

haricot.e: (Sense 1) From Middle French haricot, a deverbal derivation of Old French harigoter (“to shred, slice up, slice into pieces”), from Frankish *hariōn (“to ruin, lay waste, ravage, plunder, destroy”), from Proto-Germanic…

escroc.e: Borrowed from Italian scrocco, from Old High German *scurgo (attested in Old High German fiurscurgo (“fire-maker, stoker”); modern German Schurke, schüren), from Old High German scurgen.

andré.e: From Latin Andreās, from Ancient Greek Ἀνδρέας (Andréas).

georges.e: From Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios).

blâmer.e: Inherited from Old French blasmer, from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre). Doublet of blasphémer, which was borrowed from Latin.

brouillard.e: From brouiller + -ard, restructuring of an older brouillas, derived from the same verb.

caleb.e: Borrowed from Late Latin Caleb, Calebus, from Koine Greek Χάλεβ (Kháleb), from Biblical Hebrew כָּלֵב (Kālēḇ), possibly related to כֶּלֶב (keleḇ, “dog”), referring to dogs’ unconditional devotion to their masters.

brut.e: Inherited from Middle French brut, from Old French brut, from Latin brūtus (“heavy, dull”).

cinquante.e: From Old French cinquante, from Latin cīnquāgintā.

trottoir.e: Etymology tree Middle French trotter French trotter Old French -eoir French -oir French trottoir From trotter + -oir.

voire.e: Inherited from Latin vēra, neuter plural of vērus (“true”). Related to vrai (“true”), from Latin vērāx.

encre.e: From Old French enque, from Late Latin encaustum, from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον (énkauston). Compare Italian inchiostro.

foudre.e: Inherited from Old French foudre, from Latin fulgura, nominative plural of fulgur, from Proto-Italic *folgos. Alternatively, from fulgere.

marchand.e: Inherited from Middle French marchand, from Old French marcheant, earlier marchedant, from Vulgar Latin *mercatantem, from the verb *mercatare, from Latin mercatus (“market”).

démocratie.e: Inherited from Middle French democratie, from Medieval Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā).

script.e: Borrowed from English script. Doublet of écrit.

loyal.e: Inherited from Old French loial (with various alternative forms: leial, leal, loyel) from Latin lēgālis. Equivalent to loi + -al. Doublet of légal.

sueur.e: Inherited from Old French suor, suur, from Latin sūdor, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.

battue.e: From Portuguese batuda or Italian battuta ("a beating"). See Latin battuo ("to beat").

plonger.e: From Old French plongier, from Vulgar Latin *plumbicāre, from Latin plumbum (“lead”).

vagin.e: Borrowed from Latin vāgīna. Compare the inherited doublet gaine. Compare also gouine, which may be borrowed from Breton gouin, itself ultimately borrowed from the Latin.

typique.e: From Latin typicus (“typical”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”).

alfred.e: From English Alfred, from Old English Ælfræd.

sucer.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sewg- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *séwgeti Proto-Italic *sougō Latin sūgō Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Italic *-tus Latin -tus Latin sūctus Proto-Indo-European *-…

allonger.e: Most likely from a- + long + -er, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from ad + Late Latin longāre, from Latin longus.

case.e: Borrowed from Latin casa, in the sense of "hut, cabin". The other senses are a semantic loan from Spanish casa. Doublet of chez, which was inherited.

domestique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin domesticus (“of the house, domestic; familiar; native”), from domus (“home, house; place of one's birth or residence, native country”).

veine.e: Inherited from Middle French vene, from Old French veine, from Latin vēna, of uncertain Proto-Indo-European origin.

honnêteté.e: From Old French honesté, from Latin honestātem, reshaped as if from honnête + -té starting from Middle French honesteté. Compare Spanish honestidad and Portuguese honestidade.

patrie.e: Borrowed from Latin patria, from pater (whence French père).

guider.e: g. Frankish *wītan, Proto-Germanic *wītaną, possibly through an Early Medieval Latin intermediary. Compare Italian guidare, Spanish guiar.

pan.e: Inherited from Old French pan, from Latin pannus. Doublet of pagne.

séparation.e: Borrowed from Latin sēparātiōnem. Cf. also inherited Old French sevraison.

caca.e: From Latin cacāre (“to defecate, to shit”).

désespoir.e: Inherited from Middle French desespoir. By surface analysis, dés- + espoir.

auberge.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan alberga (“camp, hut”), from Frankish *harjabergu, composed of the elements *harjaz (“army”) and *berganą (“to shelter, to protect”). Doublet of albergue.

zombi.e: Attested 1832, but the 1765 Encyclopédie (t. 11, p. v. nègre) already has zambys «dieux esprits des tribus africaines». Borrowed from Haitian Creole zonbi, from a Bantu language.

soie.e: Inherited from Middle French soye, from Old French soie, earlier seie, from Latin sēta, saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”).

chèvre.e: Inherited from Middle French chevre, from Old French chievre, from Latin capra, from caper.

hache.e: Etymology tree Frankish *happjābor. Vulgar Latin *happia Old French hache Middle French hache French hache Inherited from Middle French hache, from Old French hache, borrowed from Frankish *happjā (“axe, hatchet”).

fraude.e: ), a borrowing from Latin fraus, fraudem.

mont.e: Inherited from Old French mont, from Latin montem.

alien.e: Borrowed from English alien (“stranger, foreigner”), from Middle English alien, from Old French alien, from Latin aliēnus.

australie.e: Borrowed from English Australia. By surface analysis, Latin austrālis + -ie.

insulte.e: Inherited from Middle French insult m, probably borrowed from Medieval Latin insultus (“attack, assault”). By surface analysis, deverbal from insulter.

insulter.e: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsultāre. Morphologically, from insulte + -er.

farce.e: Inherited from Old French farse, from Medieval Latin farsa, from the feminine perfect passive participle from Latin farciō (“to stuff”). Doublet of far.

instrument.e: From Middle French instrument, from Old French instrument, from Latin īnstrūmentum.

gage.e: Inherited from Middle French gage, from Old French gage, guage, from Early Medieval Latin wadius (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), from Frankish *waddī.

précédent.e: Inherited from Old French precedent, borrowed from Latin praecedentem. Attested earlier than the verb précéder, which is possibly a back-formation.

âne.e: Etymology tree Latin asinus Old French asne Middle French asne French âne Inherited from Middle French asne, from Old French asne, from Latin asinus.

corruption.e: Inherited from Old French corruption, borrowed from Latin corruptiōnem.

épicerie.e: From épice (“spice”) + -erie, literally “spice shop”, as they originally sold spices.

déchet.e: Deverbal from déchoir. Compare typologically German Abfall; Czech odpad.

gratuitement.e: Inherited from Middle French gratuitement. By surface analysis, gratuit + -ment.

supermarché.e: Calque of English supermarket; by surface analysis super- + marché.

pleur.e: Inherited from Old French plor; deverbal from pleurer.

cracher.e: Inherited from Middle French cracher, from Old French crachier (“to eject from the mouth”), from Vulgar Latin *craccare, of imitative origin, possibly via Frankish *hrākijan or *hrakkjan; compare Old High German hrahhan…

rideau.e: Inherited from Middle French rideau, from Old French ridel (“a curtain", originally, "a plaited stuff”), perhaps from Old High German ridil (“a headband; ribbon”), from Proto-Germanic *wriþilaz, from *wrīþaną (“to twist…

février.e: Inherited from Old French fevrier, Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin Februārius.

repousser.e: From re- + pousser, or from Late Latin repulsāre.

surmonter.e: From Old French, corresponding to sur- + monter.

agneau.e: Inherited from Old French agnel, aignel, agniau, from Latin agnellus (according to the TLFi, an early borrowing), diminutive of agnus.

syndrome.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ).

parcours.e: From Vulgar Latin percursus, nominalised past participle of percurrere. Parcourir is a much later borrowing from percurrere.

parcourir.e: From par- + courir, based on Latin percurrere.

scolaire.e: Borrowed from Late Latin scholāris, from schola (“school”). Compare the doublet écolier.

raser.e: Inherited from Old French raser, from Vulgar Latin *rāsāre, a frequentative verb formed from Latin rāsus, past participle of rādō. Compare Italian rasare.

cheminée.e: From Old French cheminee, from Late Latin [camera] camīnāta, from Latin camīnus (“furnace”), from Ancient Greek κάμῑνος (kámīnos). Unrelated to cheminer or chemin although an influence is possible.

saoul.e: Inherited from Old French saül, saol, inherited from Latin satullus, diminutive of satur (“full”).

chiant.e: From the verb chier. The adjectival senses are from its derivative faire chier.

observation.e: Borrowed from Latin observātiōnem. By surface analysis, observer + -ation.

môme.e: 19th century, probably imitative of a child's first attempts at speech.

papi.e: From papa, analogically with mamie. Compare German Papi.

distraire.e: Borrowed from Latin distrahere, with conjugation based on French traire.

triple.e: Semi-learned term resulting from a modification, under the influence of the Latin etymology, of Old French treble, itself from Latin triplus.

regret.e: From Middle French regret, from Old French regret (“lamentation, complaint”), deverbal of regreter (“to lament”).

vulgaire.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wolgosder.? Proto-Italic *welgosder.? Latin vulgus Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.?

grain.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French grain, grein, from Latin grānum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.

grenier.e: Inherited from Middle French grenier, from Old French grenier, gernier, guernier, from Latin grānārium.

aîné.e: Inherited from Middle French aisné, from Old French aisné, contraction of ainz (“before”) + né (“born”).

char.e: Inherited from Old French char, from Latin carrus, a loan from Transalpine Gaulish. Doublet of car (“coach”), a borrowing from English.

aigle.e: Inherited from Middle French aigle, from Old French aigle, itself either borrowed from Old Occitan aigla or taken from Latin aquila, though not as a popular term. Cf.

matelas.e: From Old French materas, probably from Italian materasso (perhaps via Frankish), from Arabic مَطْرَح (maṭraḥ, “carpet, place where something is thrown”), from طَرَحَ (ṭaraḥa, “to throw”). Doublet of matras.

proie.e: Inherited from Old French proie, preie, from Latin praeda (probably via a Late Latin variant proeda or *prēda; the expected outcome of praeda would be *priée).

angoisse.e: Inherited from Old French angoisse, from Latin angustia.

marcel.e: From Latin Marcellus, diminutive of Marcus.

peggy.e: Borrowed from English Peggy, popular in the 1970s.

délai.e: Inherited from Middle French delai, from Old French delai, delaie (“delay”), from delaier, delayer, deslaier (“to put off, delay, offlet, drain”), from des- + laiier (“to leave”), partly from Frankish *lattjan (“to dela…

inscrire.e: Borrowed from Latin īnscribere, with conjugation partially based on écrire (cf. Middle French escrire).

cassie.e: From Occitan cacìo, from acacia. Doublet of acacia.

nègre.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *negʷ-? Latin nigrum Spanish negrobor. ▲ Latin nigrum Old Galician-Portuguese negro Portuguese negrobor.

vainqueur.e: Etymology tree French vaincre Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French vainqueur From vaincre + -eur.

araignée.e: Inherited from Old French areignee, extended form of araigne, from Latin arānea. Equivalent to now archaic ara(i)gne + -ée.

colonie.e: ), from Latin colōnia (“colony”), which see. Doublet of Cologne.

faillite.e: Borrowed from Italian fallita, influenced by failli, faillir. Doublet of faute.

égalité.e: From égal + -ité, or borrowed from Latin aequālitātem. Cf. also the variant forms equalité, esgalité (Middle French), igauté, and the inherited Old French form oelté.

honorer.e: Inherited from Old French honorer, borrowed from Latin honorāre.

mental.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin mentālis (“of the mind, mental”).

renard.e: Inherited from Middle French renard, from Old French renart, the name of the fox in the medieval Roman de Renart.

vœu.e: Inherited from Old French vuz, inherited from Latin vōtum. Doublet of vote, a borrowing from English.

françois.e: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin Franciscus (from Francia + -iscus). Doublet of Français.

mineur.e: Borrowed from Latin minor. Compare the inherited doublet moindre.

honoré.e: From Late Latin Honorātus, from honōrātus. Cognate with Italian Onorato.

isabelle.e: From Old Spanish Isabel in the 12th century, ultimately from Hebrew אֱלִישֶׁבַע (Elishéva, “my God is an oath”).

agresser.e: Initially from Latin aggressus, although the term fell out of use in the 16th century. When it re-entered modern French, likely derived from agressif, on the model of collectif/collecter, régressif/régresser.

colis.e: Borrowed from Italian colli, plural of collo.

grimper.e: Inherited from Middle French grimper, probably from a nasalisation of Middle French gripper, after Middle French ramper (“to crawl”) (see modern ramper), to which it is semantically related.

dessiner.e: Inherited from Middle French desseigner, borrowed from Italian disegnare, from Latin designāre. Doublet of désigner.

mouiller.e: Inherited from Old French moillier, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“soak”), a verb based on Latin mollis (“soft”). Compare Occitan molhar.

obsession.e: From Latin obsessiōnem (“a besieging”), from obsidere (“to besiege”); see obsess.

peser.e: Inherited from Middle French peser, from Old French peser, from Classical Latin pēnsāre, whence also the doublet penser 'think'.

purée.e: Inherited from Old French puree; feminine past participle of verb purer (“to make pure”), from Late Latin purare (same sense), from Classical Latin pūrus (“pure”).

invasion.e: Borrowed from Late Latin invāsiōnem, nominative of invāsiō.

messe.e: Inherited from Middle French messe, from Old French messe, from Late Latin missa, from Latin missum.

revoilà.e: From re- (“a repetition, a turn back”) + voilà (“there”).

vice.e: Inherited from Middle French vice, from Old French vice, borrowed from Latin vitium.

graisse.e: Inherited from Old French craisse, from Vulgar Latin *crassia, from Latin crassus. Compare Occitan graissa, Catalan greix.

opposer.e: Borrowed from Latin opponere, with conjugation based on poser.

arc.e: Inherited from Old French arc, from Latin arcus (“bow, arch”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo-.

taureau.e: Inherited from Old French torel, a derivation of tor, taur, from Latin taurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *táwros.

selle.e: Inherited from Middle French selle, from Old French sele, from Latin sella, from Proto-Italic *sedlā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.

banane.e: Borrowed from Portuguese banana, from a Niger-Congo language spoken in the Guinea region. See Portuguese banana for more information.

commune.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin communia, neuter plural of communis.

aspect.e: Borrowed from Latin aspectus. The grammatical sense is a semantic loan from Russian вид (vid).

thérapeute.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θεραπευτής (therapeutḗs, “attendant”).

désagréable.e: From dés- + agréable. Compare Catalan and Spanish desagradable, Italian sgradevole and Portuguese desagradável.

fédération.e: Learned borrowing from Latin foederātiōnem. By surface analysis, fédérer + -ation.

rein.e: Inherited from Middle French rein, from Old French rein, from the plural reins, from Latin rēnes < rēn.

fontaine.e: Inherited from Middle French fontaine, from Old French fontaine, from Late Latin fontāna, from substantivation of the adjective Latin fontānus, from fons.

favori.e: ), from Italian favorito, past participle of favorire (“to favour”).

religieux.e: Inherited from Middle French religieux, from Old French religieus, from Latin religiōsus.

ruine.e: Inherited from Middle French ruyne, from Old French ruine, borrowed from Latin ruīna.

publier.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *poplosder. Old Latin poplusder.

attentat.e: From Middle French attemptat. By surface analysis, attenter + -at.

balai.e: ), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *banatlo- (“broom plant”). It is uncertain whether the Celtic word passed into French through a Gaulish *balano- or rather through Middle Breton balain, balazn, from Old Breton balan.

distributeur.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin distribūtor. By surface analysis, Latin distribūtum (supine of distribuō) + -eur.

environs.e: By surface analysis, en- + viron + -s; see Old French viron for more.

florence.e: Etymology tree Latin flōrens Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -ia Latin Flōrentia Middle French Florence French Florence Inherited from Middle French Fl…

belle-mère.e: Inherited from Middle French belle-mere, belle-mère. By surface analysis, belle- + mère.

isolé.e: Borrowed from Italian isolato, past participle of isolare.

éthique.e: From Latin ethicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós).

if.e: Inherited from Middle French if, from Old French if, from northern Vulgar Latin *ivus (“yew tree”), from either Proto-Celtic *iwos or Proto-Germanic *īhwaz, both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyHw-.

borne.e: Inherited from Old French bontie, bodne, from Medieval Latin (Merovingian) bodina, butina (“limit, boundary”), a Celtic/Transalpine Gaulish borrowing, from Proto-Celtic *bonnicca (“boundary”), possibly from Proto-Indo-E…

coca.e: Apocope of Coca-Cola; ultimately the same as Etymology 2.

béton.e: Inherited from Old French betun, from Vulgar Latin *bittūmen, from Latin bitūmen. Doublet of bitume, a borrowing from Latin.

fumier.e: Inherited from Old French femier, from Vulgar Latin *femārium, from *femus, alteration of Latin fimus. Spelling influenced by fumer.

baraque.e: Borrowed from Valencian barraca, probably from Paleo-Hispanic.

tortue.e: Inherited from Middle French tortue, borrowed from Old Occitan tortuga, tartuga, from Late Latin tartarūcha, feminine form of tartarūchus, a mythological spirit of Greek origin, from Ancient Greek ταρταροῦχος (tartaroûk…

gâche.e: From Middle French gache (“a mason's tool for mixing, spatula, trowel”), from Old French gaiche (“oar, rowing”), derivative of gaschier (“to wash, soak”), from Old Frankish *waskan, *wascōn (“to wash, bathe”), from Prot…

conditionnel.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin conditiōnālis (“conditional”), from conditiō (“condition”).

soupçon.e: From the Old French sospeçon, inherited from the Latin suspectiōnem. Not a doublet of suspicion.

lessive.e: Inherited from Old French lissive, leissive, from Latin lixīva, noun use of the adjective lixīvus (“made into lye”), from the phrase [aqua] lixīva by ellipsis.

urine.e: Inherited from Middle French urine, from Old French orine (modified per the Latin word), from Latin urīna. Old French orine likely derived from a Vulgar Latin *aurīna, influenced by aurum (“gold”). Compare Italian orina.

dorénavant.e: Univerbation of Old French d'ore en avant (“from now forward”). Cognate with Portuguese doravante and Italian d'ora in avanti.

escorter.e: From escorte + -er, ultimately borrowed from Italian scortare.

draguer.e: From Middle French dragger (“to dredge”), equivalent to drague + -er.

outre.e: Borrowed from Latin uter. Originally masculine in French; feminine since the beginning of the 16th century.

diabolique.e: From Middle French diabolique, fron Late Latin diabolicus, from Koine Greek διαβολικός (diabolikós, “devilish”), from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “the Devil”).

mouton.e: Inherited from Middle French mouton, from Old French mouton, from Vulgar Latin moltō, from Gaulish *multon-, from Proto-Celtic *moltos.

justifier.e: Inherited from Old French justifier, borrowed from Late Latin iūstificāre.

rasoir.e: Inherited from Old French rasuir, from Late Latin rasōrium, from Latin rāsus (“shaved”). By surface analysis, raser + -oir.

sympathique.e: Inherited from Middle French sympathic, from sympathie, from Late Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia), from συν- (sun-, “with, together”) + πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

confirmation.e: From Old French confirmacion, from Latin cōnfirmātiōnem.

latin.e: Inherited from Middle French latin, from Old French latin, borrowed from Latin latīnus.

actif.e: Inherited from Old French actif, from Latin āctīvus.

confusion.e: Inherited from Middle French confusion, from Old French confusion, borrowed from Latin cōnfusiōnem, from verb confundo.

jupe.e: Inherited from Middle French jupe, from Old Italian giubba, from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba, “long garment”).

épargner.e: Inherited from Old French espargnier, from Vulgar Latin sparāniāre (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), from Frankish *sparanjan, from Proto-West Germanic *sparēn (compare English spare).

patate.e: Borrowed from Spanish patata (“potato”), from Taíno batata (“sweet potato”).

séquence.e: Borrowed from Late Latin sequentia, from Latin sequēns.

marina.e: Latin Marīna. A Latinate variant of the French Marine.

intrus.e: Learned borrowing from Latin intrūsus (“thrusted in”).

yoga.e: Borrowed from Sanskrit योग (yóga, “yoking, union”), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *yáwgas, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *yáwgas, from Proto-Indo-European *yéwg-o-s, from *yewg- (“to join”).

cape.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan capa, from Late Latin cappa (compare the inherited doublet chape; cf. also the Old Northern French variant cape).

troupeau.e: From Middle French trope, troupe, from Old French trope, trupe, of unknown origin, though likely related to Early Medieval Latin troppus (“herd”).

abeille.e: Etymology tree Latin apis Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Proto-Italic *-kelos Latin -cula Latin apiculader.

minus.e: Latin minus, ellipsis of minus habēns (literally “that has less, having less”). Compare Italian minus habens. Doublet of moins.

cam.e: From English cam, a shortening of camera.

manoir.e: From a substantivation of the Old French verb manoir, itself from Latin manēre (“stay; remain”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“stay; stand still”).

jambon.e: From Middle French jambon, from Old French gambon, gamboun, jaumbeun; equivalent to jambe (“leg”) + -on.

cérébral.e: A learned formation from the root of Latin cerebrum and the suffix -al.

tiers.e: Inherited from Old French tiers, from Latin tertius.

hypothèse.e: Inherited from Middle French hypothese, a learned borrowing from Late Latin hypothesis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument, supposition”, literally “a placing under”).

marron.e: Etymology tree Byzantine Greek μάραον (máraon)bor. Italian marronebor. French marron Borrowed from Italian marrone.

billard.e: Derived from bille (“log, tree trunk”) + -ard, the term billard ("little log") originally referring to the cue stick with which the game is played.

sauveur.e: Inherited from Old French salveor, sauveor, from Late Latin salvātōrem. By surface analysis, sauver + -eur.

séduire.e: Altered or Gallicized from Latin seducere, based on other verbs such as conduire, réduire, etc.

coiffeur.e: Etymology tree French coiffer Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French coiffeur From coiffer + -eur.

marais.e: Inherited from Middle French marais, from Old French mareis (“marsh”) (compare Medieval Latin maresc, maresch), from Frankish *marisk (“marsh, swamp”). Related to marécage.

armoire.e: Inherited from Old French armaire, aumaire, borrowed from Latin armārium, from arma (“weapons, tools”).

vertu.e: Inherited from Middle French vertu, from Old French vertu, from Latin virtūtem.

récolte.e: Borrowed from Italian ricolta (modern Italian raccolta).

récolter.e: From récolte (borrowed from Italian ricolta, feminine past participle of ricogliere) + -er.

touriste.e: Borrowed from English tourist. By surface analysis, tour + -iste.

éveiller.e: Inherited from Middle French esveiller, from Old French esveiller, esveillier, from Vulgar Latin *exviglāre < *exvigilāre, from Latin ēvigilāre.

balcon.e: Etymology tree Proto-Germanic *balkô Frankish *balkōbor. Medieval Latin balcōbor. Italian balconebor. French balcon Borrowed from Italian balcone.

trophée.e: Inherited from Middle French trophée, borrowed from Latin trophaeum, tropaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion, “monument of an enemy's defeat”), from neuter of τροπαῖος (tropaîos, “of defeat”), from τροπή (tropḗ,…

pincer.e: Inherited from Old French pincier, pincer (“to pinch”).

primaire.e: Borrowed from Latin prīmārius. Doublet of premier.

invention.e: Borrowed from Latin inventiōnem, from invenio.

gilet.e: From regional Italian gileccu (Calabria), gilecco (Genoa), gelecco (Naples), ggileccu (Sicily), etc.

paiement.e: From Middle French paiement. Morphologically, from payer + -ment.

coopération.e: Learned borrowing from Latin cooperātiō. By surface analysis, coopérer + -ation.

trajectoire.e: Borrowed from New Latin trājectōria f (“trajectory”) (used by Newton).

messager.e: Inherited from Old French messagier, from message.

frangin.e: Uncertain, possibly a diminutive of frère.

age.e: Ca. 1800, from a dialectal (southern Oïl or Franco-Provençal) form of haie, from Frankish *haggju. Cognate with English hedge, which see for more. Doublet of haie and quai.

rude.e: Inherited from Old French rude, a borrowing from Latin rudis (“unwrought”).

traquer.e: From Middle French trac, from Old French trac (“a track, trace, a beaten path, course”), from Middle Dutch treck, treke (“a drawing, draft, delineation, feature, train, procession, line or flourish with a pen, sketch”),…

insupportable.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin īnsupportābilis. Morphologically, from in- + supportable.

cargaison.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan cargueson, from cargar (cognate with French charger).

camille.e: (male): From Latin Camillus :(female): From Latin Camilla

authentique.e: From Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós).

raide.e: From Middle French roide, generalized from Old French roide f, inflected form of roit, reit, from Latin rigidus. Doublet of rigide.

via.e: Borrowed from Latin viā, the ablative of via (“road, way”), of uncertain origin, plausibly cognate with vehō (“convey”).

creux.e: Uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin crosuin, from Latin corrosum, or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *crosus, of Gaulish origin.

grec.e: Inherited from Middle French grec, borrowed from Latin graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós).

philosophie.e: Inherited from Old French philosophie, from Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φῐλοσοφῐ́ᾱ (phĭlosophĭ́ā); compare philosophe.

suspendre.e: Borrowed from Latin suspendere. Cf. also Old French souspendre, soupendre, which disappeared under the influence of the Latin.

obstacle.e: Borrowed from Latin obstāculum, from obstō.

peintre.e: Inherited from Middle French paintre, from Old French peintre, paintre, from the nominative case of Vulgar Latin *pinctor, from Classical Latin pictor (“painter”). Cf.

pourboire.e: Univerbation of pour boire, literally “for drinking”; compare German Trinkgeld.

comptoir.e: Inherited from Middle French comptoir, comtoir, contoir (also comptoer, contoer, comptouer, contouer), from compter, conter (“to count”) + -oir (“instrument suffix”) calquing earlier Medieval Latin computātōrium.

pelle.e: Inherited from Middle French pelle, from Old French pele, from Latin pāla (“shovel, spade”). Doublet of pale, which is of either dialectal or Occitan origin.

grenouille.e: Inherited from Middle French (g)renouille, from Old French (g)renoille, from Vulgar Latin *rānucula, diminutive from Latin rāna (“frog”).

violon.e: From viole + -on (diminutive suffix). Compare Italian violino.

montage.e: From monter (“to mount”) (from mont (“mount(ain)”), from Latin mons (“mountain”) + -age.

offenser.e: From offense + -er, from Latin offēnsāre (“to strike against”), replacing previous Middle French offendre.

rhume.e: Borrowed from Late Latin rheuma, from Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma).

claude.e: Borrowed from Latin Claudius m, Claudia f.

charbon.e: Inherited from Old French charbon, inherited from Latin carbōnem (“coal”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker (“to burn”). Doublet of carbone.

armure.e: Inherited from Middle French armure, from armure, armeüre, from Latin armātūra. Doublet of armature, a borrowing.

mat.e: Probably from Latin mattus, which is from madere; see Italian matto.

graine.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grāna, neuter plural of grānum reanalysed as a feminine. Compare grain.

berger.e: Inherited from Old French bergier, from Late Latin vervēcārius, from vervēx + -ārius. Compare Romanian berbecar, Piedmontese bërgé, Sardinian berbecarju, berbecàlgiu, berbegarzu.

assumer.e: Borrowed from Latin assūmere, from ad- + sūmō (“to take”).

beau-frère.e: Inherited from Middle French beau frere, beau-frere, beaufrere, beau-frère, beauffrère, biau frere. By surface analysis, beau- + frère.

jeanne.e: From Middle French Jehanne, from Latin Iohanna. Equivalent to Jean (“John”) + -e (feminine ending).

égo.e: Via English from Latin ego, as a translation of Sigmund Freud's Ich in German. Doublet of je.

donneur.e: From donner + -eur. Compare donateur, a borrowing from Latin donātor.

humide.e: Borrowed from Latin hūmidus, variant of ūmidus.

square.e: Borrowed from English square. Doublet of équerre.

alentours.e: From Old French a l'entor, reinterpreted as a noun, then as a plural noun.

voisinage.e: From voisin + -age. Displaced Old French visné.

guérison.e: From Middle French guerison, from Old French guarisun (“healing”, ca. 1100). By surface analysis, guérir + -ison.

paille.e: Inherited from Old French paille, from Latin palea, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”).

humble.e: From Old French, from Latin humilis (“low, slight, hence mean, humble”) (compare Greek χαμαλός (khamalós, “on the ground, low, trifling”)), from humus (“the earth, ground”), humi (“on the ground”).

distorsion.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin distorsiō, from Latin distortiō.

réclamer.e: Inherited from Old French reclamer, borrowed from Latin reclāmāre, from clāmō.

costaud.e: From côte (“side”), as in “a man with strong sides.”

ring.e: From English ring (sense 1) and Dutch ring (sense 2).

exposer.e: Inherited from Middle French exposer, borrowed from Latin expōnere, contaminated by and conjugated like French poser. Compare Old French espondre, which was inherited.

moine.e: Inherited from Middle French moine, metathesis from Old French monie, from Late Latin monicus, variant of monachus.

calendrier.e: Inherited from Old French calendier, kalendier (cf. also the early Middle French form chalendrier), from Latin calendārium. Doublet of calendaire.

litre.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin litra, from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra, “a Sicilian coin, a measure of weight”).

chimie.e: From Middle French chymie, borrowed from Latin chimia, from alchemia.

détente.e: Borrowed from Latin *detendita, as a feminine past participle of detendō (“to relax”).

limousine.e: From the name of the former French region Limousin, from Limoges. The naming of the car is sometimes attributed to Limoges-born engineer Charles Jeantaud.

tronche.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trunca, feminine form of truncus (“tree trunk”) (→ tronc).

vapeur.e: Inherited from Middle French vapeur, from Old French vapour, vapor, borrowed from Latin vapor m.

persuader.e: Inherited from Middle French persuader, from Latin persuādeō (“to persuade”).

carré.e: Inherited from Middle French quarré, from Old French quarré, from Latin quadrātus. Compare the borrowed doublet cadrat.

iris.e: Borrowed from Latin iris, Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris).

pigeon.e: Etymology tree Latin pīpiō Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.?

agenda.e: Borrowed from Latin agenda, substantive use of the neuter plural of agendus (“which ought to be done”), future passive participle (gerundive) of agō (“to do, act, make”).

recours.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin recursus, past participle of recurrō.

culot.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-der.? Latin cūlus Old French cul Middle French cul French cul Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Italic *-tosder.?

cycle.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Late Latin cyclus.

champignon.e: Inherited from Old French champegnuel, from Vulgar Latin *campāniolus (“grows in the field”), from Late Latin campāneus (“relating to fields”), from Latin campānia (“level country”).

musical.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin mūsicālis. By surface analysis, musique + -al.

collecte.e: Borrowed from Latin collēcta, from colligō. Compare cueillette, an inherited doublet.

inspection.e: Inherited from Old French inspeccion, borrowed from Latin īnspectiōnem (“examination, inspection”), from the verb īnspectō (“to inspect”), from spectō (“to observe, to watch”), frequentative of speciō (“to look at”).

perruque.e: Probably borrowed from western Lombard parrucca. Compare the phonetic changes of intervocalic -L- into -R- of Italian parlare and Sicilian parrari.

bonus.e: English bonus, from Latin bonus. Compare bon (“good”), a doublet inherited from the same Latin word.

achat.e: Inherited from Old French achat, deverbal from achater (compare modern French acheter).

mousse.e: Originally from a dialect south of the Loire, from Vulgar Latin *muttius (compare Occitan mos), of Gaulish origin, or alternatively from Latin mutilus (compare Italian mozzo).

chauffer.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱleh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *ḱl̥h₁éh₁yeti Proto-Italic *kalēō Latin caleō Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁k- Proto-Indo-European *-yét…

stage.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stagium, itself from Old French estage: ester + -age (whence modern French étage).

remords.e: From Old French remors, from Medieval Latin remorsus, from Latin remordeō (“to torment, to vex”, literally “to bite back”), from re- + mordeō (“to bite”). The d was added later by analogy with remordre.

hart.e: Inherited from Middle French hart, from Old French hart, hard, a borrowing from Frankish *heʀdā.

gelée.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gel- Latin gelū Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu.

ironie.e: Borrowed from Latin īrōnīa, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία (eirōneía).

plume.e: Inherited from Old French plume, from Latin plūma.

permanence.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin permanentia, from Latin permaneō (“to remain; last”).

comique.e: From Latin cōmicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós).

procéder.e: Inherited from Old French proceder, borrowed from Latin prōcēdere.

réflexion.e: Borrowed from Late Latin reflexiōnem. By surface analysis, refléter + -xion.

imposer.e: From Latin imponere; by surface analysis im- + poser. Cf. the Old French form emposer.

logiciel.e: From logique + -iel, by analogy with and opposition to matériel.

mèche.e: Inherited from Old French mesche, from Late Latin *micca or Vulgar Latin *mysca, alteration of Latin myxa (“sebesten tree”).

relâcher.e: Inherited from Old French relascher (cf. also Latin relaxō), corresponding to Modern French re- + lâcher.

guise.e: Inherited from Middle French guise, from Old French guisse, guise, vise (“guise, manner, way”), from Old Frankish *wīsa (“manner, way, fashion”), from Proto-Germanic *wīsǭ (“manner, way”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd…

confort.e: From Old French conforter, from Late Latin cōnfortāre (“strengthen greatly”), itself from Latin con- (“together”) + fortis (“strong”).

adapter.e: From Latin adaptare, from ad + aptare (“to fit”).

saucisse.e: Inherited from Old French saucice, from Late Latin [farta] salsīcia, ultimately from Latin sāl (“salt”).

bouquin.e: Inherited from Middle French boucquain (“old book of little esteem”), from a derivative of Middle Dutch boec (“book”).

substance.e: Borrowed from Latin substantia (“substance, essence”), from substāns, present active participle of substō (“exist”, literally “stand under”), from sub + stō (“stand”).

créateur.e: Inherited from Middle French createur, from Old French creatur, creator, borrowed from Latin creātōrem.

ivrogne.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ebrionia, from ēbrius (whence ivre).

river.e: From a Germanic source (compare Danish rive).

diversion.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diversiōnem, from Latin divertō (“to divert”); see divert.

pique-nique.e: From pique + nique, from piquer (“to pick”, verb) + nique (“small thing”).

hugo.e: From Old French Hugo, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *hugi (“thought, mind, spirit”).

romain.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin rōmānus.

fantasme.e: Learned borrowing from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma). Doublet of fantôme.

baleine.e: Inherited from Old French baleine, borrowed from Latin bālaena, from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina).

cogner.e: Inherited from Latin cuneāre, ultimately from cuneus (“wedge”).

fraternité.e: Inherited from Old French fraternité, borrowed from Latin frāternitātem, from frāter (“brother”).

imaginaire.e: Learned borrowing from Latin imāginārius, from imāgō (“image”).

torse.e: Borrowed from Italian torso, from Latin thyrsus. Doublet of thyrse.

cartel.e: Borrowed from Italian cartello, diminutive of carta, from Latin carta. Related to English card.

autel.e: Inherited from Old French autel, from a change of suffix from earlier alter, borrowed from Latin altāre (mostly attested in the plural form altāria).

bénéfice.e: Inherited from Old French benefice (attested since 1198), borrowed from Latin beneficium.

alias.e: Learned borrowing from Latin aliās (“at another time; elsewhere, under other circumstances, otherwise”).

perle.e: From Old French perle, from Medieval Latin perla, from Latin perula (“little pear”). Alternatively derived via unattested Medieval Latin *pernula from Latin perna (“haunch; a marine bivalve shaped like a leg of lamb”).

rime.e: Inherited from Middle French rime, from Old French rime, which see.

futé.e: Participle adjective of Middle French futer.

littérature.e: (circa 1120). From Latin litteratūra (“lettering, erudition”), from littera (“letter”), from Etruscan, from Ancient Greek διφθέρᾱ (diphthérā, “tablet”).

acheteur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Proto-Italic *ad- Latin ad- substratebor.?

express.e: Borrowed from English express, from French exprès, from Latin expressus.

seau.e: Etymology tree Latin situla Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Latin -la Latin sitella Proto-Indo-European *-ós Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-ós Proto-Indo-European…

enthousiasme.e: Inherited from Middle French enthousiasme, from Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós).

orteil.e: From Middle French and Old French orteil, variant of arteil (“toe”), from Latin articulus (“knuckle”). Doublet of article, of learned origin.

immigration.e: From Latin immigrō and modelled on émigration.

aérien.e: Inherited from Old French aerien, equivalent to a learned borrowing from Latin āēr with suffix -ien.

étiquette.e: Inherited from Middle French estiquette (“ticket, memorandum”), from Old French estiquette, from Old French estechier, estichier, estequier, estiquer (“to attach, stick”), (compare Picard estiquier (“to stick, pierce”))…

coton.e: Inherited from Old French cotoun, coton, from Italian cotone, from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun), variants of Arabic قُطْن (quṭn); see cotton for more.

crayon.e: Etymology tree Latin crēta French craie Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.? Latin -ō Frankishinflu.

bac.e: Inherited from Middle French bac, from Old French bas, bac- (“flat boat”), of obscure origin. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *baccu (“container”), from Latin bacar (“kind of wine glass”).

es: prueba de acceso a la universidad

paysan.e: Inherited from Old French païsan. By surface analysis, pays + -an. Related to païen.

réchauffer.e: From Old French reschauffer and its variants. By surface analysis, ré- + échauffer.

brique.e: Of Germanic origin, from Middle Low German bricke and Middle Dutch brike, related to breken (“to break”).

clôture.e: Inherited from Old French closture (see also closure), from Late Latin clausūra, from Latin clausus.

intégrité.e: Borrowed from Latin integritātem (“soundness, integrity”), from integer.

chrétien.e: Inherited from Old French chrestien or Christian, from Latin Christiānus, ultimately from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós). Doublet of crétin and Christian.

soulever.e: From sou- + lever, or Latin sublevāre. Compare Spanish solevar.

sapin.e: From Latin sappinus (“fir tree”), from a combination of Gaulish *sappos (“fir tree”) and Latin pinus (“pine tree”).

épidémie.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios). Cognate to Old French ypidime.

encourager.e: Inherited from Old French encoragier. By surface analysis, en- + courage + -er.

grenade.e: Substantive use of Old French grenate in pomme grenate (“pomegranate”), from dialectal northern Italian pom granat, from Medieval Latin pomum granatum (“seeded fruit”), from Latin grānātum.

fourgon.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *furicōnem, from *furicāre, from Latin furō (“to steal”).

entretenir.e: Inherited from Middle French entretenir, from Old French entretenir; equivalent to entre + tenir.

ballet.e: Borrowed from Italian balletto, diminutive form of ballo (“group dance”) (cognate with Old French bal), from Late Latin ballō (“to dance”). By surface analysis, bal + -et.

menton.e: Inherited from Old French menton, mentun, from Vulgar Latin *mentō (accusative *mentōnem), from Classical Latin mentum. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to project”).

prudence.e: From Latin prūdentia, contrasting from prōvidentia. See prudent, and compare providence.

luire.e: Inherited from Old French luire, variant of luisir, from Latin lūcēre. For the Old French change in verb class, cf. plaire, taire < plaisir, taisir. For the change of stressed -ē- after palatals, see placere > plaisir.

débris.e: From Old French debrisier, from des- + brisier (“to break”).

régiment.e: From Middle French regement, régiment, and its source, Late Latin regimentum (“direction for government; course of medical treatment”), from Latin regere (“rule”).

noce.e: Inherited from Old French noce, noces, from Vulgar Latin *noptiās, from Latin nuptiās.

racine.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds Proto-Italic *wrādīks Latin rādīx Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos Proto-Italic *-īnos Latin -īnusnom.

sûreté.e: From sûr + -eté, or modified from Old French seürté, from Latin secūritātem. Doublet of sécurité.

naze.e: Apocopic form of argot nazi or nasi (“syphilitic”), probably from dialectal nase (“snot”), from German Nase (“nose”).

bœuf.e: Inherited from Middle French bœuf, from Old French buef, boef, from Latin bovem (“ox”), from Proto-Italic *gʷōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (compare English cow).

composer.e: Inherited from Old French composer, from com- + poser, as an adaptation of Latin compōnere.

sonde.e: From Middle French, from Old French sonde (“sounding line”), from Old English sund- (“sounding”), as in sundġierd (“sounding-rod”), sundlīne (“sounding-line, lead”), sundrāp (“sounding-rope, lead”), from sund (“ocean, s…

pdg.e: Initialism of président directeur général m or présidente directrice générale f.

condamnation.e: From condamner + -ation, or borrowed from Latin condemnātiōnem.

soulager.e: Alteration of Old French suslegier (probably under the influence of solacier (“to solace”) and soulas) from Vulgar Latin *subleviāre, from Latin sublevāre (“to lift up, to raise; to lighten”), from sub- (“from under”) +…

distrait.e: From Old French destrait, past participle of destraire (modern distraire), from Latin distrahō (“to distract”).

vase.e: From Middle French, from Middle Dutch wase (“mud, silt, wet ground, clod of dirt, grass”), from *Old Dutch waso, from Proto-Germanic *wasô (“moisture, ground”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“moist, wet”).

torche.e: Inherited from Old French torche, from Vulgar Latin *torca, from torqua, Classical Latin torques, from the verb torqueō (“to twist; to turn”).

mécanique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”) (whence machi…

hourra.e: Of exclamatory origin, first attested 1694 as houzaye. Compare English huzzah, heeze (“to hoist”), hurrah.

ouragan.e: Etymology tree Taíno *hurakābor. Spanish huracánbor. French ouragan Ultimately from Taíno *hurakā (“hurricane”), via a Caribbean form with /-ɡ-/.

mou.e: Inherited from Old French mol, inherited from Latin mollem.

pic.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *piccus, from Latin pīcus.

haleine.e: Inherited from Old French aleine, deverbal from alener (“to breathe”), from Medieval Latin anhēlō by metathesis. The h appeared around the 16th century under the influence of Latin hālō (“to blow”).

catégorie.e: Inherited from Middle French categorie, from Late Latin catēgoria.

ruban.e: From a form of Middle Dutch ringhband, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz + *bandą, *bandiz (“band, fetter”).

buffet.e: Inherited from Middle French bufet (1150), from Old French bufet, of uncertain origin; possibly a Celtic borrowing. Compare Scottish Gaelic biadh (“food, sustenance”), buadha (“valuable, precious”).

embuscade.e: Inherited from Middle French embuscade, itself a borrowing from Italian imboscata.

vaccin.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-Europeander.? Latin vacca Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos Proto-Italic *-īnos Latin -īnus Latin vaccinusder.

migraine.e: From Late Latin hemicrania, from Ancient Greek ἡμικρανία (hēmikranía).

coude.e: Inherited from Old French code, cote, coute, cute, inherited from Latin cubitum, cubitus. Doublet of cubitus.

définition.e: Inherited from Middle French definition, ultimately from Latin dēfīnītiōnem.

reprocher.e: ] French reprocher Inherited from Old French reprochier, from Vulgar Latin *repropiāre, from prope (“nearby”). See also rapprocher.

sylvia.e: From Latin Silvia. A Latinate variant of Sylvie.

pâte.e: Inherited from Middle French paste, from Old French paste, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).

aspirine.e: Borrowed from German Aspirin, from acetylierte Spirsäure (“acetylated salicylic acid”). The second word comes from the name of the plant genus Spiraea.

recommander.e: From re- + commander, or ultimately from Latin re- + commandāre, commendāre.

sanctuaire.e: From Old French saintuaire, from Late Latin and Latin sanctuārium (“sacred place, shrine”), from Latin sanctus (“holy, sacred”).

richesse.e: Inherited from Old French richesce. By surface analysis, riche + -esse.

architecte.e: Inherited from Middle French architecte, from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”).

femelle.e: Inherited from Middle French femelle, from Old French femele, from Latin fēmella f.

pope.e: From colloquial Russian поп (pop) and Попъ (Pop), from Old Church Slavonic попъ (popŭ), from Byzantine Greek πάπας (pápas)

fouet.e: From Middle French fouet, diminutive in -et of Old French fou (“beech”), from Latin fagus. ɛ] was contracted to [wɛ] and this later developed regularly to [wa] (as it did in oi, oe).

artère.e: Inherited from Old French artere, artaire, borrowed from Latin artēria, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría).

apocalypse.e: From Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis).

chapelle.e: Inherited from Middle French chapelle, from Old French chapele, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin cappella, diminutive of cappa.

lécher.e: From Middle French lecher, from Old French lechier, from a Vulgar Latin *liccāre (compare Italian leccare), itself probably from Frankish *likkōn. See English lick for more.

cacahuète.e: Borrowed from Spanish cacahuete, from cacahuate (“peanut”), from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl (“cocoa bean”).

exemplaire.e: From Middle French exemplaire, Old French essamplaire, from Latin exemplāris. Related to exemple.

certitude.e: From Middle French certitude, borrowed from Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus (“sure”).

bec.e: Inherited from Old French bec, from Latin beccus (“beak”), from Gaulish *beccos, from Proto-Celtic *bekkos.

crevette.e: Borrowed from Norman crevette, attested in 1532, from earlier cravette, crabette.

hamburger.e: From English hamburger, from German Hamburger.

maternel.e: From Latin māternus, from māter (“mother”) with the suffix -el or from Medieval Latin māternālis.

gai.e: From Old French gai, from Old Occitan gai, from Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌴𐌹𐍃 (*gaheis, “impetuous”); or from Frankish *gāhi (“fast, sudden, impetuous”), Frankish *wāhi (“pretty”), both from Proto-Germanic *ganhuz (“lively, fast…

horizon.e: Borrowed from Latin horizōn, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).

grandeur.e: Inherited from Old French grandur. By surface analysis, grand + -eur.

judith.e: From Hebrew יְהוּדִית (Y'hudít, “woman from Judea, Jewess”).

éclat.e: Deverbal from éclater (“to burst”), from Middle French esclater (“to break, break violently”), from Old French esclater (“to separate from, sunder out”) (deverbal also in Old French esclat), from Frankish *slaitan (“to…

falaise.e: Inherited from Old French faleise, faloise, from Frankish *falisa, from Proto-Germanic *falisaz (“rock, cliff”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelis-, *pels- (“rock, cliff”). More at fell.

logement.e: Inherited from Middle French logement, loigement. By surface analysis, loger + -ment. Related to lodge, lobby, leaf.

clou.e: Inherited from Old French clou, from Latin clāvus, from Proto-Italic *klāwos, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u-.

brutal.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin brūtālis (“savage, stupid”), from brūtus (“dull, stupid”). See brut and -al.

trembler.e: Inherited from Middle French trembler, from Old French trambler, trembler, from Late Latin tremulāre, ultimately from Latin tremere (one of the sources of French craindre). Morphological doublet of trémuler.

initiative.e: From Medieval Latin *initiativus (“serving to initiate”), from Late Latin initiare (“to begin, Latin initiate”), from Latin initium (“beginning”), from ineo (“enter, begin”).

argument.e: Borrowed from Latin argūmentum, from arguō (“prove, argue”).

sirop.e: From Old French sirop, borrowed from Medieval Latin siroppus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “beverage”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”).

sublime.e: Inherited from Middle French sublime, borrowed from Latin sublimis.

économique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin oeconomicus. By surface analysis, économie + -ique.

nain.e: Inherited from Old French nain, from Latin nānus.

rampe.e: Back-formation from the Old French verb ramper (“to go up, climb, ascend”).

ramper.e: Inherited from Middle French ramper, from Old French ramper (“to crawl up, climb”), from Frankish *rampōn, *hrampōn, from *rampa, *hrampa (“hook, claw, talon”), from Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to shrink up, shrivel”).

écarter.e: According to the Trésor de la Langue Française, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *exquartāre, from classical Latin quartus.

nuque.e: Inherited from Middle French nuque, nuche, borrowed from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ).

récent.e: Borrowed from Latin recentem. Replaced the inherited Old French roisant, roisent, resant.

quotidien.e: Learned borrowing from Latin quotīdiānus, late spelling of Classical cottīdiānus, from cottīdiē (“daily”); cognate with English quotidian.

nouille.e: From early noudle, from German Nudel.

valet.e: Inherited from Old French vaslet, from Medieval Latin *vassellittus, diminutive of Late Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from Latin vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from…

paysage.e: From pays + -age. Cf. also Italian paesaggio, Catalan paisatge, Spanish paisaje, Portuguese paisagem, Romanian peisaj.

cure.e: Inherited from Middle French cure, from Old French cure, from Latin cūra, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).

fosse.e: Inherited from Middle French fosse, from Old French fosse, from Latin fossa.

lin.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin līnum.

rancune.e: From Middle French rancune, from Old French rancune, dissimilated from rancure, from Vulgar Latin *rancura, from Latin rancor.

dance.e: Borrowed from English dance. First attested in 1994. Doublet of danse.

autographe.e: Borrowed from Latin autographum, in turn from Ancient Greek αὐτόγραφον (autógraphon, “a writing in one’s own hand”). By surface analysis, auto- + -graphe.

dépense.e: Inherited from Middle French despense, from Late Latin dīspēnsa, feminine past participle of dīspendō, from Latin dis- + pendō.

paisible.e: Inherited from Old French peisible. By surface analysis, paix (“peace”) + -ible.

milo.e: Cognate to English Miles and Milo.

cuisinier.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coquīnārium, or a later formation corresponding to cuisine + -ier.

banlieue.e: Inherited from Old French banlieue, from Medieval Latin banleuca. Compare Middle High German banmile, modern German Bannmeile.

cuillère.e: Inherited from Old French cuilliere, from Latin cochleārium (“spoon”), from cochlear (“spoon”), from cochlea (“snail”). Compare Italian cucchiaio, Catalan cullera, Spanish cuchara.

imposteur.e: From Late Latin impostor < impositor, agent noun of Latin impōnō (“impose”).

commencement.e: From Old French comencement, corresponding to commencer (“to begin”) + -ment.

caserne.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan cazerna, from Latin quaterna (neuter plural of Latin quaternus). Doublet of cahier, inherited from Latin, and quaterne, a later borrowing.

effraie.e: From orfraie, under the influence of effrayer.

petite-fille.e: Inherited from Middle French petite-fille, from petite (“little, small”) + fille (“daughter”).

province.e: Borrowed from Latin prōvincia. Doublet of Provence.

mythe.e: From Latin mythos m, from Ancient Greek μῦθος m (mûthos).

muet.e: Inherited from Middle French mut, muet, from Old French mu, mut, mui, from Latin mūtus, of Proto-Indo-European origin.

camping.e: Borrowed from English camping. The sense "campsite" is a pseudo-anglicism.

yacht.e: Borrowed from English yacht, from Dutch jacht.

prophète.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per-der.? Proto-Indo-European *per-der.? Proto-Indo-European *pér Proto-Indo-European *-o Proto-Indo-European *próder.

obligation.e: Borrowed from Latin obligātiōnem, from the verb obligō (“tie together”).

perspective.e: Learned borrowing from Latin perspectīvus, from perspiciō

tomate.e: Borrowed from Spanish tomate, from Classical Nahuatl tomatl.

milan.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan milan, from Vulgar Latin *mīlānus, alteration of Latin mīlvinus, from mīlvus.

pelouse.e: Originally dialectal, a borrowing from Provençal or Occitan pelouso, pelos (“thickset”), from Latin pilosus. Doublet of pileux.

flûte.e: From Old French fleüte, from Old Occitan flaut. The contraction of the Old French hiatus created a long vowel in Middle French, which is indicated by the modern circumflex.

fiction.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin fictiōnem (accusative of fictiō).

spirituel.e: Borrowed from Late Latin spīrituālis, from Latin spiritus.

pré.e: Inherited from Old French pred, pré, from Latin prātum.

sente.e: Inherited from Latin sēmita. Compare sentier.

pois.e: Inherited from Old French pois, from earlier peis from Latin pisum, from Ancient Greek πίσος / πίσον (písos / píson).

infecter.e: From Latin īnfectus, perfect passive participle of inficiō (“dye, taint”).

croissance.e: From croiss- + -ance, corresponding to the rare Latin form crēscentia.

évanouir.e: Inherited from Old French esvanir, evanir, probably from a Vulgar Latin *exvānīre, later influenced from the Latin form ēvānuit (“vanished”) of ēvānescō, ēvānēscere.

quelquefois.e: Inherited from Middle French quelquefoys, equivalent to quelque (“some”) + fois (“time”). Compare Walloon kécfeye.

doyen.e: Inherited from Old French deien, from Late Latin decānus, from Latin decem.

griffe.e: Inherited from Middle French griffe, either deverbal from griffer, which see, or through an unattested Old French noun from Old High German grif, from Proto-Germanic *gripiz.
