pâques.e: Etymology tree Biblical Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésaḥ)bor. Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā)bor. Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha)bor.

laid.e: From Middle French laid (“hideous, ugly”), from Old French laid, leid (“unpleasant, horrible, odious”), from Vulgar Latin *laitus (“unpleasant, ugly”), from Frankish *laiþ (“unpleasant, obstinate, odious”), from Proto-G…

josé.e: An old French vernacular form of Joseph.

bouquet.e: Etymology tree Proto-Germanic *buskaz Frankish *buskbor. Early Medieval Latin boscus Old French boisder.

majeur.e: From Middle French majeur, a borrowing from Latin maior (“larger, greater”). Doublet of maire, major, and mayeur.

bassin.e: Inherited from Middle French bassin, from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinus /*baccinum, probably from Gaulish.

bonnet.e: Inherited from Middle French bonet, from Old French bonet (“material from which hats are made”), from Frankish *bunni (“that which is bound”), from Proto-Germanic *bundiją (“bundle”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (…

psychologie.e: From New Latin psychologia (coined by Marko Marulić from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + Latin -logia (“study of”)).

secouer.e: From Old French secorre or secourre, from Latin succutiō.

compréhension.e: Borrowed from Latin comprehēnsiōnem, from comprehendere (“to grasp”), from the prefix com- + prehendere (“to seize”).

semestre.e: From Latin semestris (“six months”), from sex (“six”) + mensis (“month”).

discrétion.e: Borrowed from Late Latin discretiōnem, from Latin discernō.

gaber.e: From Middle French, from Old French gaber (“to tell jokes”), from Old Norse gabba (“to mock”), from Proto-Germanic *gabbōną (“to mock, jest”), from Proto-Indo-European *ghabh- (“to be split, be forked, gape”).

médium.e: Borrowed from Latin medium. The sense of "person who contacts the dead" is probably a semantic loan from English medium. Doublet of mi-.

capsule.e: Borrowed from Latin capsula, diminutive of capsa (whence caisse).

éponge.e: Inherited from Middle French esponge, from Old French espoinge (cf. also variant espoigne), from Vulgar Latin *sponga, from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá).

percer.e: From Old French percier, from Vulgar Latin *pertusiāre, from Latin pertusus (“perforated”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-dʰh₁- (“to pierce, strike”). Compare Italian pertugiare.

adrénaline.e: Borrowed from English adrenaline. Genericized trademark.

ironique.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin īrōnicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós). By surface analysis, ironie + -ique.

avatar.e: From Hindustani अवतार / اوتار (avtār), from Sanskrit अवतार (avatāra, “descent of a deity from a heaven”), a compound of अव (ava, “off, away, down”) and the vṛddhi-stem of the root तरति (√tṝ, “to cross”).

sécher.e: Inherited from Old French secher, sechier, from Latin siccāre. By surface analysis, sec + -er.

thon.e: From Latin thunnus, thynnus (itself from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos)), possibly through the intermediate of Old Occitan ton.

choquer.e: Inherited from Middle French chocquer (“to clash in battle, shock, offend, hurt”), from Old French choquer (“to strike against”) and Picard chuquier, çuker (“to collide in battle, knock”), both of Germanic origin, possi…

toutefois.e: Inherited from Middle French toutesfoys, from the plurals toutes and fois. In Old French, the adverb was totesvoies (from voie (“way”)), closer to Italian tuttavia and Portuguese todavia.

loup-garou.e: Inherited from Old French leu garoul, a pleonastic compound of leu (“wolf”) + garoul (“werewolf”); the latter from garulf, from Frankish *werawulf. Equivalent to loup + -garou.

gilbert.e: From Old French Gislebert, from Proto-Germanic *Gīslaberhtaz, from *gīslaz (“pledge”) + *berhtaz (“bright, famous”).

réduction.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin reductiōnem.

deuxièmement.e: Etymology tree French deuxième Proto-Indo-European *men- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *méntis Proto-Italic *mentis Latin mēns Latin mente Old French -ment Middle French -ment French -ment French deuxièm…

anomalie.e: Ultimately a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνωμαλία (anōmalía).

alexis.e: From the Latin Alexius, a saint's name, from Ancient Greek Ἄλεξις (Álexis, “helper, defender”).

carbone.e: Learned borrowing from Latin carbōnem, coined by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789. Doublet of charbon.

chelsea.e: The name of the municipality is derived from the English toponym Chelsea, referring in this case to the town in Vermont (the former hometown of the first colonists).

fidélité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin fidēlitās. By surface analysis, fidèle + -ité.

politicien.e: From politique + -ien, calque of English politician.

triomphe.e: ), borrowed from Latin triumphus, which see.

acquérir.e: Inherited from Middle French acquerir, from Old French acquerir, aquerre, from Vulgar Latin *acquaerere, from Latin quaerere. Compare also quérir, conquérir.

soupirer.e: Inherited from Middle French souspirer, from Old French souspirer, from Latin suspīrāre, from sub- + spīrō.

trait.e: Inherited from Old French trait, from Latin tractus.

dépit.e: Inherited from Old French despit, inherited from Latin dēspectus.

vanter.e: Inherited from Old French vanter, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin vānitāre, from Latin vānus or vānitās. Compare Italian vantare.

chiot.e: ; alternative spelling (from reanalysis as chien + -ot) of Middle French chiau (1515), from Old French chael, from Latin catellus.

coque.e: Inherited from Old French coque (“shell”), from Latin coccum (“berry”).

pentagone.e: From Latin pentagonus, which came from πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos). Morphologically penta- + -gone.

forteresse.e: Inherited from Old French forteresce, from Medieval Latin. Morphologically, from fort (“strong”) + -eresse (“-ess”).

précision.e: First attested in 1380 as Middle French precision (“cutting off”), borrowed from Latin praecīsiōnem (“cutting off”).

conquérir.e: Inherited from Old French conquerre (under the influence of quérir), from Latin conquaerere, from conquirere.

tabasser.e: From tabac + -asser; see passer à tabac, taper.

conception.e: Inherited from Old French conception, concepcion, borrowed from Latin conceptiōnem (“comprehension, understanding”).

défunt.e: ), a borrowing from Latin (de vita) defunctus.

potion.e: Borrowed from Latin pōtiōnem. Doublet of poison, which was inherited.

rassurer.e: Inherited from Old French rasseürer, from re- + asseürer. By surface analysis, r- + assurer.

cuisse.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *koḱs- Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂ Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂ Proto-Italic *koksā Late Latin coxa Old French cuisse French cuisse Inherited from Old French cui…

geler.e: Inherited from Old French geler, from Latin gelāre.

toxique.e: Borrowed from Latin toxicus (“poisoned”), from toxicum (“poison”), from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón) [φάρμακον (phármakon)] ("poison for use on arrows"), from τοξικός (toxikós, “relating to arrows or archery”), from…

vieillard.e: Inherited from Old French vieillard, from vieil + -ard.

brun.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-? Proto-Germanic *brūnaz Frankish *brūnbor. Old French brun French brun From Middle French, from Old French brun (“polished, shiny, brown”).

approuver.e: Borrowed from Latin approbāre, approbō, adapted to French prouver. By surface analysis, a- + prouver.

infini.e: From Latin īnfīnītus (“boundless, unlimited, endless, infinite”), from in- + fīnītus (“finished, terminated, having been finished or terminated; limited, bounded, having been limited or bounded; finite”), perfect passiv…

bouchée.e: From bouche + -ée, possibly Vulgar Latin *buccata, from Latin bucca. Compare Italian boccata, Romanian bucată; cf. also Portuguese and Spanish bocado.

vérification.e: From Middle French verifficacion, veriffication, verificacion, vérificacion, verification, borrowed from Latin vērificātiō.

couvent.e: Inherited from Old French cuvent, covent, cuvenz, from Latin conventus. Doublet of convent.

réservation.e: Borrowed from Late Latin reservātiōnem, reservātiōnem, from Classical Latin reservātus, perfect passive participle of reservō.

diffusion.e: Borrowed from Latin diffusiōnem. By surface analysis, diffuser + -ion.

cross.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from cross country. -cross exists in English to refer to cross country, but only as a suffix.

greffe.e: Inherited from Old French groife, greife, from Latin graphium (“stylus”), later influenced by greffier (“clerk”).

exagérer.e: Learned borrowing from Latin exaggerō (“to exaggerate, amplify”).

nœud.e: Inherited from Old French neu, from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”). Doublet of knout.

hormone.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὁρμῶν (hormôn), present participle of ὁρμάω (hormáō, “to set in motion, to urge on”), from ὁρμή (hormḗ, “rapid motion forwards, onrush, onset, assault, impulse to do a thing, effort”…

porteur.e: Inherited from Old French portour, from Late Latin portātōrem, from Latin portō. By surface analysis, porter + -eur.

relier.e: From re- + lier, or from Latin religāre. Found in Old French as reloier.

appliquer.e: Borrowed from Latin applicāre. Eventually replaced the inherited Old French applier, aploier.

patricia.e: Borrowed from Latin Patricia, feminine of Patricius.

péril.e: Inherited from Old French peril, from Vulgar Latin *periclu(m), syncopated form of Latin perīculum.

semer.e: Inherited from Old French semer, from Latin sēmināre.

impatience.e: Inherited from Old French impacience, from Latin impatientia. Morphologically analyzable as impatient + -ence.

heurter.e: Inherited from Middle French heurter, from Old French hurter (“to ram into, strike, collide with”), from Frankish *hūrt (“a battering ram”), from Proto-Germanic *hrūtaną, *hreutaną (“to fall, beat”), from Proto-Indo-Eur…

toux.e: Inherited from Old French tous, tos, from Latin tussem, from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s- (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).

olive.e: Inherited from Old French olive, from Latin olīva.

trêve.e: Attested in Old French as trieve, treve, from Frankish *treuwu, from Proto-Germanic *trewwō (“fidelity; pledge”). Cognate with Dutch trouw, German Treue, English truce. More at true, truce.

hériter.e: Inherited from Old French eriter, from alteration of an earlier *hereter, from Latin hērēditāre.

visa.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *weyd- Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *widtós Proto-Italic *wissos Latin vīsus Latin visader.

têtu.e: Inherited from Old French testu, from teste (“head”) + -u. Morphologically, from tête + -u. Compare Catalan and Occitan testut and Walloon tiestou.

défaire.e: Inherited from Middle French desfaire, from Old French desfaire, from Early Medieval Latin disfacere. Synchronically dé- + faire.

épave.e: The substantivization of Old French espave, from Latin expavidus.

fréquenter.e: Borrowed from Latin frequentāre, infinitive of frequentō.

municipal.e: Etymology tree Latin mūniceps Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -iusnom.

cote.e: Inherited from Middle French quote, quotte, borrowed from Late Latin quota, from Latin quotus. Doublet of quota, an unadapted borrowing.

application.e: Inherited from Middle French application, from Old French aplicacion, from Latin applicātiōnem.

soumettre.e: Inherited from Old French suzmetre, from Latin submittere or summittere. Displaced the borrowed equivalent Middle French submettre. Equivalent to sous- + mettre.

déception.e: Borrowed from Late Latin dēceptiōnem, from dēcipiō, whence French décevoir.

défier.e: From dé- + fier, with influence of the Latin diffido.

meute.e: Inherited from Middle French meute, from muete, from Latin *movita, feminine substantivization of Latin *movitus, 'vulgar' perfect passive participle for moveō (“move”).

coq.e: Inherited from Middle French coq, from Old French coc, from Late Latin coccus, from Proto-West Germanic *kokk, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz. Cognate with English cock, Dutch kok, Danish kok, Icelandic kokkur.

anéantir.e: From a- + néant + -ir. Compare annihiler, a parallel formation.

fût.e: Inherited from Middle French fust, from Old French fust, from Latin fūstis.

mule.e: Inherited from Old French mule, from Latin mūla (“a she-mule, mule”), feminine of mūlus (“a mule”).

fourmi.e: Inherited from Old French furmi, from a Vulgar Latin *formīcus, from Latin formīca (cf. also the feminine Old French formie).

terrasse.e: From terre, probably influenced by Old Occitan terrassa.

cavalerie.e: Borrowed from Italian cavalleria. Compare Old French chevalerie.

climat.e: Inherited from Middle French climat, borrowed from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma).

corrompre.e: Inherited from Old French corrompre, borrowed from Latin corrumpere (based on rompre).

capture.e: Borrowed from Latin captūra (“catching, capture”), from captus, perfect passive participle of capiō (“capture, seize, take”).

extraire.e: Changed, based on the Latin root, from the original Old French estraire, from Vulgar Latin *extragere, from Latin extrahere.

sentence.e: Inherited from Old French sentence, itself borrowed from Latin sententia.

connasse.e: From con (“cunt”) + -asse (pejorative suffix). Compare Spanish coñazo.

sinistre.e: Borrowed from Latin sinister, whence also French senestre, an inherited doublet.

pauvreté.e: Inherited from Old French poverté (through the influence of pauvre), from Latin paupertātem.

plaider.e: Inherited from Middle French plaider, from Old French plaidier, from plait, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *placitare, from Latin placitum. Cognate with English plead.

épais.e: Etymology tree Latin spissus Old French espés Middle French espés French épais Inherited from Middle French espés, from Old French espés, from Latin spissus, from Proto-Indo-European *spidtos.

bourbon.e: The French Bourbon dynasty is named for the lordship of Bourbon l'Archambault.

brèche.e: Inherited from Middle French breche, bresche, from Old French breche, bresche (“a breach, an opening, crack”), from Frankish *breka (“a breach, break”), from Proto-Germanic *brekō (“a breaking, breach, fallow ground”),…

chaton.e: First attested in the 1530s in Middle French; by surface analysis, chat (“cat”) + -on (forming diminutives). Compare English catkin.

musulman.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Ottoman Turkish مسلمان (Müslüman, “Muslim”), from Persian مسلمان (mosalmân, “Muslim”), from Arabic مُسْلِم (muslim, “Muslim”).

harmonie.e: Learned borrowing from Latin harmonia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía).

hostile.e: Inherited from Middle French hostile, hostif (this form with a change of suffix), borrowed from Latin hostilis.

tremper.e: Inherited from Middle French tremper, a metathesis of Old French temprer, from Latin temperāre (“mix, moderate”). Doublet of tempérer, a borrowing.

intermédiaire.e: From intermède + -aire. Influenced in form by médiaire (“medial”).

prophétie.e: From Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía, “prophecy”).

activer.e: From actif, both from Latin activus.

hallucination.e: Borrowed from Latin hallūcinātiōnem. By surface analysis, halluciner + -ation.

sourcil.e: Inherited from Middle French sourcil, from Old French sourcil, sorcil, inherited from Latin supercilium.

clos.e: Past participle of clore. From Old French clos. Corresponds to Latin clausus.

dot.e: ), a borrowing from Latin dos. Doublet of dose.

montréal.e: Inherited from Middle French Montreal, from Mont Royal (“Mount Royal”), after the nearby mountain, Mont Royal, named by Jacques Cartier. It is uncertain how Royal became -real.

quarante.e: Inherited from Old French quarante, from Late Latin quarranta, from Vulgar Latin *quadrāntā, from Latin quadrāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥(d)ḱomt (“four-ten”).

froc.e: From Middle French frocq (“cloth made of coarse wool”), from Old French froc (compare Late Latin hroccus (“frock”)), from Frankish *hrokk (“robe, tunic”), from Proto-Germanic *hrukkaz (“robe, garment, cowl”), variant of…

berceau.e: From Old French berçuel (diminutive of bers) from Vulgar Latin berciolum diminutive of *bertium, from Gaulish *berta, from Proto-Celtic *bertā, variant of *bereti (“to carry”). Compare Old Irish bert (“bundle”).

chalet.e: Swiss French, from Franco-Provençal çhalè (“herdsman's hut in the mountains”), from Old Franco-Provençal chaslet, diminutive of chasel (“farmhouse”), from Late Latin casalis (“house-like, house-related”), from Latin cas…

envoler.e: From en (“from”) + voler. Unrelated to Latin involāre.

francine.e: Inherited from Old French Francine, from Franc + -ine. Today often associated with the given names France and Françoise.

harceler.e: Inherited from Middle French harceller, herseler. Equivalent to an extended form of herser (“to harrow”), from herse.

révélation.e: Borrowed from Late Latin revēlātiōnem, from Latin revēlātum.

servant.e: From Middle French, from Old French servant, a substantivized present participle of servir. Cf. also Latin serviens, and French sergent.

jadis.e: From Old French ja a dis (“there are days before”), from ja (“already”) + a (“has”) + plural of di (“day”).

étendre.e: Inherited from Middle French estendre, from Old French estendre, from Latin extendere.

pitoyable.e: From pitié + -able, phonologically altered after apitoyer.

répugnant.e: Inherited from Middle French repugnant, from Old French repugnant, borrowed from Latin repugnantem.

beignet.e: Inherited from Middle French bignet, from Old French bignet (“fried dough enveloping a food substance”), a diminutive of bigne, bugne, buyne (“lump, swelling”), from Frankish *bungjō (“lump, bump, swelling”), from Proto…

enfreindre.e: Inherited from Middle French, Old French enfraindre, from Vulgar Latin *īnfrangere, from Latin īnfringere.

flou.e: From Middle French flou, from Old French flou, flo (“soft, wilted, tired, exhausted”), from Old Frankish *hlāo (“lukewarm, tepid, mild”), from Proto-Germanic *hlēwaz (“warm, lukewarm”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlēw- (…

crédible.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin crēdibilis, from crēdō (“believe”). Compare croyable.

boulevard.e: Inherited from Middle French boulevard, bollevart, boulevars, bolevers, bollewerc (“rampart”), from Middle High German bolewerc, bolwerc (modern German Bollwerk) or Middle Dutch bolwerk (“bulwark, bastion”). g.

cire.e: Inherited from Middle French cire, from Old French cire, chiere, ciere, from Latin cēra.

gamme.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin gamma. Doublet of gamma.

détenir.e: Inherited from Old French detenir, borrowed from Latin detinēre, and adapted to the conjugation of tenir.

écharpe.e: Inherited from Middle French escharpe, escherpe, from Old French escharpe, escherpe, eskerpe, eschreppe, escreppe (“small bag, satchel”).

centime.e: From cent + -ime, on the model of décime.

librairie.e: Inherited from Middle French librairie, from Old French librairie, from Latin librāria (“library”), from liber (“book”). Sense “bookseller, bookshop” is from 16th century, and displaced “library” sense.

venise.e: Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Venetia.

foin.e: Inherited from Middle French foin, from Old French fein, from Latin fēnum, monophthongized variant of Latin faenum (“hay”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-no-, from *dʰeh₁(y)-.

absolu.e: Inherited from Middle French absolut, replaced earlier asolu (c. 1100), from Latin absolūtus (“unconditional”), perfect passive participle of absolvō (“loosen, free; complete”).

bulletin.e: From Old French bullette + diminutive suffix -in, or possibly a borrowing from Italian bollettino.

roche.e: Inherited from Old French roche, from Early Medieval Latin rocca, of uncertain origin. Doublet of roche. Compare Italian rocca, Spanish roca, as well as English rock, Dutch rots and Breton roc'h.

endurer.e: Inherited from Old French endurer, andurer, from Latin indūrāre. According to the TLFi, it was a borrowing (semi-learned), however it was attested as early as 1050. Doublet of indurer, a later borrowing.

intrusion.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from intrūdō.

évier.e: Inherited from Old French evier, ewer, inherited from Latin aquārium. Doublet of aquarium, a later borrowing.

similaire.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin similāris, extended from Latin similis (“like”).

vivres.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃- Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti Proto-Italic *gʷīwō Latin vivō Old French vivre Middle French…

tenant.e: Present participle of tenir. From Old French tenant; corresponding to Latin tenentem.

exclure.e: Borrowed from Latin exclūdere. Doublet of the inherited éclore.

moulin.e: Inherited from Middle French moulin, from Old French molin, from Late Latin molīnum, from the adjective molīnus, from Latin molō.

sonia.e: From Russian Со́ня (Sónja), pet form of Софи́я (Sofíja, “Sophie”).

fugitif.e: Inherited from Middle French fugitif, a borrowing from Latin fugitīvus. Supplanted the earlier Old French form fuitif.

plier.e: Inherited from Middle French plier, from Old French pleier, ploiier, from Latin plicāre.

raisin.e: Inherited from Old French raisin, from Late Latin racīmus, from Latin racēmus. Doublet of racème, a borrowing.

vicieux.e: Borrowed from Latin vitiōsus. See vice + -eux. Cf. also Old French voisos.

lard.e: Inherited from Old French lard, from Latin lārdum, lāridum (“bacon fat”).

procurer.e: Derived from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, administer”), from Latin prō- (“on behalf of”) + cūrō (“to care for”).

fanny.e: Borrowed from English Fanny, also used as a pet form of Stéphanie.

cliché.e: Past participle of clicher (“to stereotype, (originally) to copy”, literally “to click, clink”), from Middle French clicher, from Old French cliquer (“to click, clack, sound, resound”), of Germanic origin, related to Du…

trancher.e: Inherited from Old French trenchier. Compare Catalan trencar, Italian trinciare, and Spanish truncar.

moelle.e: Inherited from Middle French moelle, mouelle, from Old French moele, mëoule, moelle, muële, mëolle, mëule, inherited from Latin medulla. Doublet of médulla.

traque.e: From Old French trac, from Old Norse traðk (“track”). Related to tread.

asiatique.e: Borrowed from Latin āsiāticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιατικός (Asiatikós).

comble.e: Inherited from Old French cumble, inherited through a Vulgar Latin form *cumlu(s) from Latin cumulus. Doublet of cumulus, a borrowing.

courtoisie.e: Inherited from Old French cortoisie, from cortois (“courteous”). By surface analysis, courtois + -ie.

écureuil.e: Inherited from Middle French escureul, escuirel, escurel, from Old French escurel from Late Latin *scūriolus, diminutive of *scūrius, variant of Classical Latin sciūrus, from Ancient Greek σκίουρος (skíouros).

repère.e: Initially, a variant spelling of repaire; then linked to Latin reperiō (“to find”), which caused the etymological link between it and its doublet to be lost.

briquet.e: Specialised sense of Middle French briquet (“piece, morsel”), from brique.

achever.e: Inherited from Middle French achever, from Old French achever, from Vulgar Latin *accapāre. Compare English achieve.

disposer.e: Borrowed from Latin dispōnere, and influenced by French poser.

tricher.e: Inherited from Middle French tricher, from Old French tricher, trichier (“to defraud, conceal, cheat”), of disputed origin.

franchise.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French franchise (“freedom, privileged liberty”), from franc (“free”) + -ise (from Latin -itia).

teint.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin tinctus.

hanche.e: From Old French, from Proto-Germanic *hanka. Replaced Latin coxa (“hip”), which was retained in French as cuisse (“thigh”). Compare English haunch.

bulle.e: Borrowed from Middle French bulle, from Old French bulle, borrowed from Latin bulla. Doublet of the inherited boule.

jouir.e: Inherited from Middle French jouir, jouïr, iouyr, from Old French joïr, from Vulgar Latin *gaudīre (*gaudiō), from Latin gaudēre. Doublet of gaudir, which was a borrowing.

cordon.e: Inherited from Old French. By surface analysis, corde (“rope”) + -on (diminutive suffix).

tailleur.e: Etymology tree Latin tālea Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu.

ficelle.e: Probably from Vulgar Latin filicella, from Latin fīlum ("thread").

saumon.e: From Latin salmō, potentially from Gaulish salmō.

jade.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-der. Proto-Italic *olnos Old Latin olle Latin ille Latin illa Old French la Middle French la French la French l' Proto-Indo-European *welH-der.

distribuer.e: From Middle French distribuer, from Old French destribueir, from Latin distribuō.

convenable.e: From convenir + -able. Compare typologically Russian подходя́щий (podxodjáščij) (< подходи́ть (podxodítʹ), под- (pod-) + ходи́ть (xodítʹ)).

orgueil.e: Inherited from Middle French orgueil, from Old French orgoil, from Vulgar Latin *orgollium, borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *uʀgōllju, from Proto-Germanic *uzgōljō.

jeep.e: Borrowed from English jeep. Genericized trademark.

artillerie.e: ”), from artillier (“to equip, provide with contraptions”), alteration of atiller (“to arrange, adjust, put on clothes or, especially, pieces of armour”) (influenced by art), itself from a Vulgar Latin *apticlāre < *apt…

attraction.e: From Old French attraction, from Latin attractiōnem.

gymnase.e: From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion). Compare Catalan gimnàs, Italian ginnasio, Portuguese ginásio, Spanish gimnasio.

permanent.e: From Middle French permanant, permanent, from Latin permanentem (accusative of permanēns).

amendement.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- Proto-Indo-European *mend-der.

cuivre.e: Inherited from Old French cuivre, quivre, queivre, coivre, from Latin Cyprium, cupreum (aes) (compare cuprum) from Ancient Greek Κῠ́προς (Kŭ́pros, “Cyprus”).

peigne.e: Inherited from Old French peigne, from Latin pectinem.

plombier.e: From plomb + -ier or from Old French plummier, from Latin plumbārius.

piler.e: Inherited from Latin pīlāre (“to ram down”), from pīla (“column”).

baigner.e: Inherited from Old French baignier, from Vulgar Latin *baneare, Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum, and probably later influenced by the related French bain.

investisseur.e: From investiss(ant) (stem of the present participle of investir) + -eur.

marquis.e: From Old French marchis, from the same origin as marcher.

duchesse.e: Inherited from Old French duchesse. By surface analysis, duc (“duke”) + -esse (“-ess”).

clin.e: Inherited from Middle French clin, related to the verb cligner.

précaution.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin praecautiō, from praecaveō.

ail.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin allium.

session.e: Inherited from Old French session, borrowed from Latin sessiōnem.

contribution.e: Learned borrowing from Latin contribūtiō. By surface analysis, contribuer + -tion.

itinéraire.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin itinerārium, from Late Latin itinerārius.

maniaque.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). By surface analysis, manie + -aque.

étrangler.e: Inherited from Old French estrangler, inherited from Latin strangulāre. Doublet of stranguler.

exploiter.e: Inherited from Old French esploitier (with /k/ reinserted per the Latin etymon), from earlier espleitier, from Vulgar Latin *explicitāre, a frequentative of Latin explicāre. Morphologically a doublet of expliciter.

dom.e: Borrowing from Italian don or older dom, from Latin dominus (“master”). Cognate with English don.

répandre.e: From re- + épandre. Compare Romanian răspândire.

devise.e: From Old French devise (“division, separation; heraldic band, emblem”), from deviser. The financial sense is a semantic loan from German Devise. Compare divisa in the other Romance languages.

manifeste.e: From Old French, from Latin manifestus.

manifester.e: From Old French, from Latin manifestus.

design.e: Borrowed from English design. Doublet of dessein.

moutarde.e: From Old French moustarde, from moust (“must”) (modern moût), from Latin mustum.

métaphore.e: Learned borrowing from Latin metaphora, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá).

bâtir.e: From Middle French bastir, from Old French bastir, from Vulgar Latin *bastīre (“to build, construct; weave, sew”), borrowed from Frankish *bastijan (“to sew, weave”).

pavillon.e: Inherited from Middle French pavillon, from Old French paveilun, inherited from Latin pāpiliōnem. Doublet of papillon.

cafétéria.e: From Italian caffetteria. Doublet of cafetière.

globe.e: Inherited from Middle French globe, borrowed from Latin globus.

lente.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lenditem, alteration of Late Latin lendinem, itself an alteration of Classical Latin lendem.

arche.e: Inherited from Old French arche, borrowed from Late Latin arca, from Latin arcus.

éclairer.e: Inherited from Old French esclairer, from Vulgar Latin *exclāriō, *exclāriāre, from Latin exclārāre, from ex- + clārō.

module.e: Learned borrowing from Latin modulus. Doublet of moule.

ignorance.e: Inherited from Old French ignorance, borrowed from Latin ignōrantia.

cogne.e: Deverbative of cogner (“to thwack, strike”) (for Noun 2, in reference to police aggression)

ambitieux.e: Inherited from Old French ambitios, borrowed from Latin ambitiōsus.

morsure.e: Inherited from Middle French morsure, from Old French morsure, from Early Medieval Latin morsūra; equivalent to mors + -ure.

sermon.e: Inherited from Old French sermon, from Latin sermōnem.

alaska.e: Borrowed from English Alaska, ultimately from Aleut alaxsxaq.

grèce.e: Inherited from Old French Grece, from Latin Graecia

hospitalité.e: From Old French hospitalité (ca. 1200), a borrowing from Latin hospitālitās. It remained a learned word and therefore did not undergo the regular muting of preconsonantal /s/ (as in hôpital).

coût.e: Inherited from Middle French coust, from Old French cust, equivalent to a deverbal from coûter.

faucon.e: Inherited from Middle French faulcon, from Old French falcun (“falcon”), from Late Latin falcōnem, accusative form of falcō (“falcon”), probably of Germanic origin.

detroit.e: Borrowed from English Detroit, from French Détroit, from détroit.

fibre.e: Inherited from Old French fibre, borrowed from Latin fibra.

rail.e: Borrowed from English rail. Doublet of règle, reille, rigole, and rille.

croyable.e: From croy- (a stem of the verb croire) + -able.

cerf.e: Inherited from Middle French cerf, from Latin cervus.

parasite.e: Borrowed from Latin parasītus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos).

dôme.e: Inherited from Middle French dosme, from (Old Provençal) Old Occitan doma, borrowed from Late Latin dōma (“roof, housetop”), from Koine Greek δῶμα (dôma, “roof, housetop”) previously meaning "house".

porte-bonheur.e: From porter bonheur (“to carry luck, to bring luck”).

invincible.e: Inherited from Middle French invincible, from Latin invincibilis (“unconquerable”).

bouc.e: Inherited from Middle French bouc (“male goat”), from Old French buc (“male goat”), from Latin buccus, perhaps from the confluence of Frankish *bukk (“male goat”) (compare Old Dutch buck (“male goat”)), from Proto-Germa…

frein.e: Inherited from Old French frein, from Latin frēnum n. Cognate with Portuguese freio and Spanish freno. Cf. the borrowed freiner.

limonade.e: From limon (“lemon”) + -ade. Compare Italian limonata, Spanish limonada, Venetan łimonada.

aire.e: Inherited from Old French aire, eire, from Latin ārea. Doublet of are and area, which were learned borrowings.

suture.e: Learned borrowing from Latin sūtūra (“suture”). Compare couture.

thèse.e: Learned borrowing from Latin thesis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θέσις (thésis).

farine.e: Inherited from Old French farine, from Latin farīna.

enseignement.e: From Old French enseignement. By surface analysis, enseigner (“to educate; to teach”) + -ment.

naïf.e: Inherited from Old French naïf, inherited from Latin nātīvus. Doublet of natif. Semantical shift from "original; natural; simple" to "simple-minded".

sorcellerie.e: By dissimilation from Old French sorcererie (whence also the haplological form sorcerie), from sorcier + -erie.

envoi.e: From earlier envei, envoy; from the verb envoyer (“to send”).

hawaï.e: Ultimately from Hawaiian Hawaiʻi, from Hawaiki, from Proto-Nuclear Polynesian *Sawaiki.

notion.e: Borrowed from Latin nōtiōnem (accusative singular nōtiōnem).

contourner.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *contornāre, from cum and tornāre. Also con- + tourner.

rabbin.e: From Ecclesiastical Latin rabbinus, from Koine Greek ῥαββί (rhabbí), from post-biblical Hebrew רַבִּי (rabbī, “my master”).

terrestre.e: Inherited from Old French terrestre, borrowed from Latin terrestris.

phare.e: Borrowed from Latin pharus, itself from Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros).

phares.e: Borrowed from Latin Pharae, from Ancient Greek Φαραί (Pharaí).

homard.e: ), probably via Middle Low German hummer from Old Norse humarr (“lobster”), from Proto-Germanic *humaraz. A direct borrowing from Scandinavian is less likely regarding the late attestation.

terminal.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin terminālis, from Latin terminus.

toubib.e: From 19th-century military slang, borrowed from Algerian Arabic طبيب (ṭbīb), from Arabic طَبِيب (ṭabīb, “doctor”).

initiale.e: * (noun sense 1): Ellipsis of lettre initiale. * (noun sense 2): Ellipsis of consonne initiale.

poney.e: Borrowed from English poney (now pony), apparently from Middle French poulenet (“little foal”), ultimately from Late Latin pullānus (“young of an animal”).

négro.e: Borrowed from Spanish negro, first attested in 1845. Doublet of nègre, borrowed earlier from Spanish.

drague.e: From Middle English dragge, from Old Norse draga (“that which is dragged, dragged load”), from Proto-Germanic *dragǭ (“sledge, sled”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to haul, pull”). Cognate with English dray.

obligatoire.e: Borrowed from Late Latin obligātōrius, from obligō (whence French obliger).

grade.e: Borrowed from Latin gradus. Compare degré. Doublet of gradus.

effondrer.e: Inherited from Old French esfondrer, from Vulgar Latin *exfunderare, from fundus (“fond”). Compare Catalan esfondrar.

gorille.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin Gorilla, from Ancient Greek Γόριλλαι (Górillai).

neutre.e: Inherited from Old French neutre, from Latin neuter.

abandon.e: From Old French (mettre) a bandon (“to deliver”, literally “to place in someone's power”).

cadet.e: Borrowed from Occitan capdet, from Late Latin capitellum (“small head”). Doublet of chapiteau, cadeau, and caudillo.

présidence.e: From président + -ence, or a borrowing from Medieval Latin praesidentia. See also préséance.

people.e: Since 2000, named after People, an American weekly magazine that specializes in celebrity news, human-interest stories, and gossip. That word itself is derived from Old French peuple, thus making it a reborrowing.

veau.e: Inherited from Old French veel, vedel, inherited from Latin vitellus. Doublet of vitellus.

châtiment.e: Inherited from Old French chastiement, from the verb chastier (whence Modern French châtier), from Latin castīgō.

voyageur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- Proto-Italic *wiā Latin via Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos Proto-Italic *-ātos Latin -ātus Proto-Indo…

adolescent.e: Learned borrowing from Latin adolēscentem, present participle of adolēscō.

apprêter.e: Inherited from Old French aprester, corresponding to a- + prêt + -er.

coutume.e: From Middle French coustume, from Old French coustume, from Latin cōnsuētūdinem. Doublet of consuétude and costume.

capote.e: Ultimately from Latin caput (“head”), with the diminutive French suffix -ote. Piecewise doublet of capot.

cruauté.e: First attested in Old French, corresponding to cruel + -té. Possibly from an unattested Vulgar Latin *crūdālitās, crūdālitātem (from Latin crūdēlitātem).

banal.e: From ban + -al, related to Medieval Latin bannālis, from bannus.

sieur.e: From the oblique case of Old French sire (see also French sire), from Vulgar Latin *seior (“lord, elder”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”) (whence also seigneur, from the accusative form), from senex (“old”).

mélodie.e: From Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā).

égypte.e: Inherited from Middle French Egypte, from Old French Egypte, borrowed from Latin Aegyptus, from Ancient Greek Αἴγυπτος (Aíguptos).

surf.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from surfing. Note that the English noun surf only refers to an instance of surfing, and not the activity itself.

wagon.e: Borrowed from English wagon, from Middle Dutch wagen.

ketchup.e: Borrowed from English ketchup, from Malay kicap, from Hokkien 膎汁 (kê-chiap).

ramon.e: Diminutive of Old French raim (“branch”). Compare rameau.

immobile.e: Inherited from Old French immobile, from Latin immōbilis. Morphologically analyzable as im- + mobile. Doublet of immeuble.

coéquipier.e: From co- + équipier (“player in a team”).

vermine.e: Inherited from Old French vermine, from verm + -ine, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *verminum, from Latin vermis (“worm”).

ôter.e: From Middle French, from Old French oster, from Latin obstō.

orphelin.e: From Old French orfelin, by dissimilation from orfenin, diminutive of orfene, from ecclesiastical Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós).

médoc.e: From Latin (Pagus) Medullicus (“country of the Medulli”), the local Celtic/Gaulish tribe who had inhabited the area.

mécanisme.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin mechanismus, from Ancient Greek μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine”).

martial.e: Learned borrowing from Latin martiālis (“of Mars, the Roman god of war”).

fonder.e: Inherited from Old French fonder and its variants, from Latin fundāre.

antibiotique.e: From anti- + biotique. Coined in 1889 by French mycologist Jean Paul Vuillemin.

masculin.e: Inherited from Old French masculin, borrowed from Latin masculīnus.

insensible.e: Inherited from Old French insensible, from Late Latin īnsēnsibilis.

laine.e: Inherited from Middle French laine, from Old French lainne, lein, from Latin lāna.

détour.e: From Old French destour, deverbal from destourner.

palace.e: Borrowed from English palace, itself from Old French palais. Doublet of palais.

céleste.e: Inherited from Middle French celeste, from Old French celeste, borrowed from Latin caelestis.

pieu.e: Inherited from Middle French pieu, a backformation from Old French peus, pex, nominative singular and oblique plural of pel, from Latin pālus (“post, stake”), from Proto-Italic *pākslos, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-…

schéma.e: Borrowed from Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”).

élan.e: Deverbal from élancer (“to throw oneself at”).

roux.e: Inherited from Old French ros, from Latin russus.

tentation.e: From Old French, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin tentātiōnem.

seize.e: Inherited from Middle French seze, from Old French seize, seze, from Latin sēdecim.

pédale.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ped- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *pṓds Proto-Italic *pets Latin pēs Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.?

gratter.e: Inherited from Middle French gratter, from Old French gratter, grater, borrowed from Frankish *kratton, from Proto-Germanic *krattōną, from Proto-Indo-European *gred-, see also Albanian gërresë (“rasp, scraper”), German…

prédire.e: Inherited from Middle French predire, borrowed from Latin praedīcere.

jacuzzi.e: Borrowed from English jacuzzi. Genericized trademark.

impeccable.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin impeccābilis, from peccāre (whence pécher).

cerise.e: Inherited from Old French cerise, from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), u…

entrepreneur.e: Inherited from Middle French entrepreneur, from entreprendre (“to undertake”) + -eur.

occupation.e: Learned borrowing from Latin occupātiō, occupātiōnem. By surface analysis, occuper + -ation.

crabe.e: From a Norman dialect (compare Jèrriais crabe), partly from Old Norse krabbi and partly from Middle Dutch crabbe, both from Proto-Germanic *krabbô. Cognate with Old English crabba (“crab; crayfish”). More at crab.

lie.e: Inherited from Old French lie, from Early Medieval Latin lias (“lees, dregs”) (descent via winemaking common in monasteries), from Gaulish *ligyā, *legyā (“silt, sediment”) (compare Welsh llai, Old Breton leh (“deposit,…

caoutchouc.e: Borrowed from Spanish cauchuc (an early variant of caucho), from Quechua kawchu. The final -c was formerly variably pronounced or silent, but is now always silent.

injustice.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin injūstitia, from iniustus (“unjust”).

lueur.e: Inherited from Middle French luour, lueur, from Old French lueur, luur, from Vulgar Latin *lūcōrem, from Latin lūceō. Compare Italian lucore, Romanian lucoare, Catalan llugor, Occitan lugor.

stagiaire.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stagiārius, from stagium + -ārius. By surface analysis, stage + -aire.

triangle.e: Borrowed from Latin triangulum. By surface analysis, tri- + angle.

provisoire.e: From Latin prōvideō (“to foresee; to provide”) (supine stem prōvīs-) + -oire (suffix forming adjectives).

immortel.e: Borrowed from Latin immortālis. By surface analysis, im- + mortel.

frotter.e: From Middle French frotter, from Old French froter (“to stroke, wipe, rub”), of uncertain origin. Generally assumed to be from Latin frictāre, frequentative of fricāre through its past participle frictus (“rubbed”).

rive.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin rīpa, from Proto-Indo-European *rey- (“to cut, tear, scratch”).

duo.e: Borrowed from Italian duo. Doublet of deux.

compréhensible.e: Inherited from Middle French comprehensible, borrowed from Latin comprehēnsibilis.

pêcheur.e: Inherited from Middle French pescheur, ultimately from Latin piscātōrem. By surface analysis, pêcher + -eur.

cavale.e: Borrowed from Occitan cavala or Italian cavalla, from Latin caballa.

collaboration.e: From collaborer + -tion, from Late Latin collaboratio, from Latin com- (“with”) + labōrō (“work”).

parlement.e: Inherited from Old French parlement, from Middle English parlement.

ivresse.e: First attested in Old French. By surface analysis, ivre + -esse.

obscur.e: Inherited from Middle French obscur, from Old French oscur, from Latin obscurus. The -b- through learned relatinisation in Middle French.

vitrine.e: From verrine, remodelled after its etymon, Latin vitrum (“glass”). By surface analysis, vitre (“pane of glass”) + -ine.

rebours.e: From Vulgar Latin *rebursus, alteration of reburrus (“with bristing hair”) by analogy with reversus.

bouffon.e: Inherited from Middle French boufon, from Italian buffone.

hui.e: Inherited from Old French hui, from Latin hodiē, from hōc (“this”) + diē. Cognate with Occitan uòi, uèi, Catalan hui and avui, Galician hoxe, Spanish hoy, Portuguese hoje and Italian oggi.

relaxer.e: Borrowed from Latin relaxāre. Cognate with Spanish relajar. See also Old French relaisser and Modern French relâcher.

complication.e: Learned borrowing from Latin complicātiō. By surface analysis, compliquer + -ation.

carotte.e: Borrowed from Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτόν (kărōtón).

navigation.e: ], from Latin nāvigātiōnem (“sailing, navigation”), from nāvigātus, perfect passive participle of nāvigō (“sail”). By surface analysis, naviguer + -tion.

seringue.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin syringa, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, syrinx”).

biologie.e: As a French word, coined by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1802. Possibly formed as bio- + -logie. Possibly borrowed from German Biologie or New Latin biologia.

dortoir.e: Inherited from Old French dortour, from Latin dormītōrium (“dormitory”). Doublet of dormitoire, a borrowing.

émeute.e: From the old past participle of émouvoir (“to move emotionally”), influenced by meute (“pack (of hounds)”).

box.e: Borrowed from English box. Doublet of boîte.

volcan.e: Probably borrowed through Italian vulcano and Spanish volcán, from Latin Vulcānus (“Vulcan”).

sélection.e: Learned borrowing from Latin sēlēctiō (“the act of choosing out, selection”), from sēligō (“to choose out, select”), from sē- (“apart”) + legō (“gather, select”).

poussin.e: Inherited from Late Latin pullicēnus. Compare Italian pulcino.

squelette.e: From Middle French scelette, a learned borrowing from Latin sceletus, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós, “dried up, withered, dried body, parched, mummy”).

recommandation.e: From the verb recommander with the suffix -ation.

inclus.e: Borrowed from Latin inclūsus. Doublet of the inherited enclos.

inclure.e: Borrowed from Latin inclūdere, with conjugation modeled on clore; compare the inherited doublet enclore.

vieillir.e: From vieux, vieil (“old”) + -ir. Compare Catalan envellir, Spanish envejecer, Portuguese envelhecer.

malle.e: Inherited from Middle French malle, from Old French male (“leather bag, leather or wooden travel-case”), from Frankish *malha (“leather bag”), from Proto-Germanic *malhō (“leather bag”), from Proto-Indo-European *molko-…

peluche.e: From Old French peluchier (“to peel; pluck”).

interprétation.e: Learned borrowing from Latin interpretātiō. By surface analysis, interpréter + -ation.

évêque.e: Inherited from Old French evesque, inherited from Late Latin episcopus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos).

écouler.e: From é- + couler, or possibly from Vulgar Latin *excolāre, from Latin cōlāre. Compare Italian scolare, Portuguese escoar, Spanish escolar, Sicilian sculari.

consacrer.e: Inherited from Old French consecrer, cunsecrer, borrowed from Latin cōnsecrāre, and altered under the influence of sacrer.

andouille.e: Inherited from Old French andoille, from Early Medieval Latin inductilis, from Latin indūcō (“cover, overlay”).

parce que.e: Inherited from Old French par cel que (literally “by this that”). Cognates with Catalan perquè; Italian perché; Portuguese and Spanish porque.

agiter.e: From Latin agitāre (“to disturb, agitate, toss about”).

gaspiller.e: Inherited from Middle French gaspiller (“to waste”), of uncertain origin.

noyau.e: Inherited from Middle French noyau, backformed from Old French noiaus, plural of noial, a variant of Old French noel, from either Early Medieval Latin nōdellus (“buckle”), diminutive of nōdus (“knot”), or Late Latin nuc…

déshabiller.e: From Middle French desabiller. By surface analysis, dés- + habiller.

admirable.e: Inherited from Middle French admirable, borrowed from Latin admirābilis.

pleinement.e: Inherited from Middle French plainement. By surface analysis, plein (“full”) + -ment.

haler.e: From Middle French haler, from Old French haler (“to pull, haul”), from Frankish *halōn (“to haul, drag, fetch”) (also Old Dutch *halōn), from Proto-Germanic *halōną, *halēną, *hulōną (“to call, fetch, summon”), a confl…

caleçon.e: Borrowed from Italian calzone, with an excrescent schwa (cf. the form calçon, attested in the sixteenth century). Doublet of chausson, an inherited form.

taxe.e: From the verb taxer. Cf. also Medieval Latin taxa.

trousse.e: Inherited from Old French trousse, trosse, torse. Equivalent to deverbal formation from trousser.

solde.e: Borrowed, with influence from the second etymology, from Italian saldo, from saldare.

punch.e: Borrowed from English punch, from Hindi पाँच (pā̃c, “five”)/Urdu پانچ (pānc). Doublet of cinq.

faculté.e: Learned borrowing from Latin facultās. Doublet of facilité.

pôle.e: Inherited from Middle French pole, from Old French pole, from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos).

expulser.e: Borrowed from Latin expulsāre. Compare pousser, the inherited simplex.

ignoble.e: Inherited from Middle French ignoble, borrowed from Latin ignōbilis, from in- (“not”) + gnōbilis, later nōbilis (“noble”).

offerte.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin offerta.

croyance.e: Inherited from Old French croiance, one of the variants of creance, from Late Latin crēdentia, from Latin crēdēns. Possibly a doublet of créance.

flatter.e: Inherited from Middle French flatter (“to flatter, to caress with the flat of the hand”), from Old French flater (“to deceive by concealing the truth, to stroke with the palm of the hand”), from Frankish *flat (“palm, f…

amer.e: Inherited from Old French amer, from Latin amārus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃mós (“bitter, raw”).

bouchon.e: Inherited from Middle French bouchon (“bundle of hemp or foliage, oakum”), from bousche (“handful of straw, bundle of twigs”), from Vulgar Latin bosca (“brush, bundle of branches”), from Frankish *bosc (“bush”), from Pr…

fournisseur.e: From fourniss(ant) (stem of the present participle of fournir) + -eur.

convaincant.e: Respelling of convainquant, the present participle of convaincre.

lourdes.e: A corruption or misreading of Medieval Latin Lorus, a name belonging to a Moorish Christian convert with an unknown etymology and meaning.

néant.e: Probably from Latin ne gentem ("no person, no one"), or ne entem (“not existing”). Compare Italian niente.

nevada.e: Borrowed from English Nevada, from Spanish nevada (“snow-covered”)

lézard.e: Inherited from Middle French lezart, from Old French lezart, lesard, laisarde, lajjsarde, from Latin lacertus. Compare English lizard.

poivre.e: Etymology tree Indo-Aryanbor. Ancient Greek πέπερῐ (péperĭ)bor. Latin piper Old French peivre French poivre Inherited from Old French peivre, peivere, from Latin piper.

emparer.e: Borrowed from Occitan emparar, from Vulgar Latin *imparāre (the native form would be *emperer). Compare Italian imparare (“to learn”).

concurrent.e: Inherited from Latin concurrentem, present active participle of concurrō (“happen at the same time”), from con- (“with”) + currō (“run”).

lointain.e: Inherited from Old French loingtien, from Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longē. Compare Italian lontano.

massif.e: Inherited from Old French massiz (with the suffix replaced by -if), from Vulgar Latin *massīcius, from Latin massa.

envahir.e: From Old French envaïr, from Vulgar Latin *invādīre, from Latin invādere.

anxiété.e: Borrowed from Latin anxietātem. By surface analysis, anxieux + -té.

flirter.e: Borrowed from English flirt. Forms with -eu- may have arisen by influence of fleur (“flower”).

gonfler.e: Inherited from Latin cōnflāre. Compare Italian gonfiare.

orgasme.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀργασμός (orgasmós, “excitement, swelling”).

transformation.e: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin trānsfōrmātiōnem, from Latin trānsfōrmō.

vip.e: Borrowed from English VIP (“very important person”).

tornade.e: Ultimately, a borrowing from Spanish tornado.

karaté.e: Borrowed from Japanese 空(から)手(て) (karate), from 唐(から)手(て) (karate), from Okinawan 唐手(とぅーでぃー) (tūdī).

autobus.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew Proto-Indo-European *tó- Proto-Hellenic *autós Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewder.

considération.e: Inherited from Old French consideracion, from Latin cōnsīderātiōnem.

fossé.e: Inherited from Middle French fossé, from Old French fossé, from Late Latin fossātum, from Latin fossō.

régulier.e: Inherited from Old French reguler, borrowed from Late Latin regulāris.

hystérique.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós), from ὑστέρα (hustéra).

comparaison.e: ), a borrowing from Latin comparātiō(nem). By surface analysis, comparer + -aison.

bi.e: From bisexuel, or possibly directly from English bi.

évoluer.e: Back-formation from évolution. Cf. also Latin ēvolvō.

ragoût.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus Proto-Italic *gustus Latin gustus Middle French goûtder. Middle French ragoûterder.

sentimental.e: English sentimental. By surface analysis, sentiment + -al.

romance.e: Borrowed from Spanish romance, itself probably a borrowing from either Old French romanz or Old Occitan romans, meaning a narrative work in the vernacular speech, from Vulgar Latin *romanĭce (“in a Roman manner”), compa…

débuter.e: Inherited from Middle French, from dé- + but (“mark, goal”), from Old French but (“aim, goal, end, target”), of Germanic origin, either via Old French butte (“mound, knoll, target”) from Frankish *but (“stump, log”), or…

renforcer.e: From r- (variant of re-) + Old French enforcier.

omelette.e: Inherited from Old French amelette, derived by metathesis from older alemette, itself an alteration of alemelle (“blade”), probably rebracketed from la (definite article, "the") lemelle (“blade”), diminutive of lame or…

marathon.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Μαραθών (Marathṓn).

cahier.e: Inherited from Old French quaer, quaïer, from Latin quaternus. Doublet of caserne, from Old Occitan, and quaterne, a later borrowing from Latin. See also the old diminutive carnet.

messire.e: From Old French mes (“my”) + sire (“sire”). This was the nominative (and vocative) form in Old French, the oblique form gave rise to monsieur.

toutou.e: Reduplication of a sound-symbolic syllable to-, denoting a small and probably cute object. Appeared in the 17th century with the sense of "favorite", then evolved into "a docile person".

poignard.e: Alteration of Old French poignal, poignel, from Vulgar Latin *pugnāle(m), from Latin pugnus (“fist”) (whence French poing), in the manner of manuālis.

agitation.e: Borrowed from Latin agitātiōnem. By surface analysis, agiter + -ation.

es: escalamiento de paredones / paramentos rocosos / pétreos
escalamiento de paredes / faces rocosas / pétreas

implication.e: Learned borrowing from Latin implicātiō. By surface analysis, impliquer + -ation.

virginité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin virginitās. First known attestation 881 in The Sequence of Saint Eulalia.

étagère.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan estagiera (modern Occitan estatgiera).

ohé.e: Inherited from Old French, from ô and hé. Probably influenced by Latin ohe (same meaning).

crêpe.e: Substantivisation of Old French crespe, from Latin crispus, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.

poteau.e: Inherited from Middle French postiau, poteaul, from post, from Old French post, from Latin postis.

étincelle.e: Inherited from Old French estencele, from Vulgar Latin *stincilla, a metathesis of Latin scintilla.

smoking.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English smoking jacket.

treize.e: Inherited from Middle French treize, from Old French treize, treze, from Latin trēdecim.

mêlée.e: Inherited from Old French meslee, older meslede, from the feminine past participle of early Medieval Latin misculō, derived from Latin misceō. By surface analysis, mêl- + -ée.

compteur.e: From compter (“to count”) + -eur (“-er”). Doublet of conteur. Compare comptoir.

gel.e: Inherited from Latin gelū, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). For the sense of "gel", compare English gel; compare gélatine.

delà.e: By surface analysis, de + là. Compare Italian di là.

exil.e: Altered, based on Latin, from the Old French form eissil, essil, exill, itself a semi-learned term from Latin exilium, exsilium.

vital.e: Inherited from Old French vital, from Latin vītālis (“of life, life-giving”).

tribord.e: From earlier tribort, from Middle French estribord (also destrebort), from Old French estribord, a Germanic loanword, probably from Old English stēorbord or Middle Dutch stuurboort.

ascension.e: Inherited from Old French ascension, borrowed from Latin ascēnsiōnem.

axe.e: Borrowed from Latin axis. Compare the inherited doublet ais.

majordome.e: Borrowed from Italian maggiordomo, from Late Latin maior domūs (“steward”), from Latin maior (“main, principal”) + genitive singular of domus (“household”).

moniteur.e: From Latin monitor; in the sense of 'computer screen', calqued after English monitor.

vocation.e: Inherited from Old French vocation, borrowed from Latin vocātiōnem.

banquet.e: Inherited from Middle French banquet, from Italian banchetto (“light repast between meals, snack eaten on a small bench”, literally “a small bench”), from banco (“bench”), from Lombardic bank (“bench”) / Lombardic panch…

allusion.e: Borrowed from Latin allūsiōnem (“frolicking”), from allūdō (“to frolic”).

madeleine.e: From earlier gâteau à la Madeleine, after the given name Madeleine (“Magdalene”), of uncertain reference: see more above.

composition.e: Inherited from Old French composicion, borrowed from Latin compositiōnem.

barque.e: Inherited from Middle French barque, probably borrowed from Italian barca or a Medieval Latin equivalent, from Late Latin barca. Doublet of barge.

divertissement.e: From divertir (“to amuse; to entertain”) + -ment, from Latin divertere (“to separate; move away”).

songe.e: Inherited from Old French songe, from Latin somnium. Compare Italian sogno, Spanish sueño and Portuguese sonho.

réviser.e: Borrowed from Latin revisere, based on French re- + viser, or a learned formation stemming from Latin revisus. Compare Spanish revisar.

étroit.e: Inherited from Old French estroit, inherited from Latin strictus. Doublet of strict. Compare also étreint. Compare Spanish estrecho and Portuguese estreito.

ostie.e: Variant of hostie. Compare Spanish hostia, which is similarly used as an interjection.

diplomatique.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin diplomaticus.

vaurien.e: Univerbation of vaut rien. Compare German Taugenichts or Dutch deugniet.

seuil.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *solium, a blend of Latin solum (“flat ground”) + solea (“flat object, sandal”). Compare Italian soglia.

robinet.e: Diminutive form of robin (“sheep”), because early taps were often in the shape of a sheep's head.

trappe.e: From Middle French trappe, from Old French trape (“trap, snare”), from Old Frankish *trappā (“trap, snare”), from Proto-Germanic *trap-, *tramp- (“to step”), from Proto-Indo-European *dremb- (“to run”).

marionnette.e: From a diminutive of mariole, from the name Marie (“Mary”).

console.e: Probably a shortened from consolateur, denoting the same architectural element, ultimately from consoler (“to console, to comfort”).

coureur.e: Inherited from Middle French coureur. By surface analysis, courir + -eur.

consommation.e: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnsummātiō. By surface analysis, consommer + -ation.

préciser.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-i Proto-Indo-European *préh₂i?

descendant.e: Borrowed from Latin dēscendentem, the present participle of dēscendere, itself from dē + scandere (“climb, ascend”).

baptême.e: Inherited from Middle French baptesme, from Old French batesme, bapteme, baptesme (earlier batesma), a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin baptisma, from Ancient Greek βάπτισμα (báptisma), and Late Latin ba…

disciple.e: Inherited from Old French deciple, borrowed from Latin discipulus.

graal.e: From Medieval Latin gradālis (“dish”), of unknown origin.

passe-temps.e: Inherited from Middle French passetemps. By surface analysis, passe (“pass”) + temps (“time”).

oie.e: Inherited from Old French oie, from earlier oe, oue, from Vulgar Latin auca, contraction of *avica, from Latin avis (“bird”).

clore.e: From Middle French clore, from Old French clore, from Latin claudere. Now largely replaced by fermer because of interference with clouer (“to nail”) in certain conjugated forms.

manuscrit.e: 1594, from Medieval Latin manuscriptum (“writing by hand”), from Latin manu (ablative of manus (“hand”)) + scriptus (past participle of scribere (“to write”)), calqued from a word of Germanic origin.

chauve-souris.e: Used as early as the 8th century in Gallic Late Latin calva sōrex (“bald mouse”); the first element ("bald") may originally be an alteration of Vulgar Latin *cawa (“crow, tawny owl”).

tambour.e: Borrowed from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr) or Persian تبیر (tabir, “drum”), related to Armenian տաւիղ (tawiġ), English tabla.

accessoire.e: From Medieval Latin accessorius, as in the phrase accessorium sequitur principale (“the accessory follows the principal”). Possibly influenced by accidens (“falling down, something unfortunate happening”).

fessée.e: From past participle of fesser (“to spank”), originally "to strike"; the verb was influenced in both form and sense by the unrelated fesse (“buttock”).

corne.e: Inherited from Old French corne, from Vulgar Latin *corna (taken as a feminine singular), from Classical Latin cornua, plural of cornū (whence cor).

tombeau.e: Inherited from Middle French tumbeau, from Old French tumbel, tombel, diminutive of tumbe, from Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos). By surface analysis, tombe + -eau.

interpol.e: Abbreviation of (Organisation) Inter(nationale de la) Pol(ice criminelle).

prototype.e: Borrowed from Latin prōtotypus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πρωτότυπος (prōtótupos).

infidèle.e: Learned borrowing from Latin īnfidēlis. By surface analysis, in- + fidèle.

ruisseau.e: From Old French ruissel, from Vulgar Latin *rivuscellum (“brook, stream”), from Latin *rīvusculum (“creek, rivulet”) + -ellum (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from rīvus (“rivulet”) + -usculum (“-cule: forming diminutive…

réjouir.e: Inherited from Old French resjoir, from r- + esjoir, corresponding to Modern French r- + *éjouir. It is not a doublet of rejouir / re-jouir (“to orgasm again”), which is derived from re- + jouir.

numérique.e: From Latin numerus (whence nombre) + -ique. Use in electronics is a semantic loan from English digital, which has also been directly borrowed into French.

chancelier.e: From Old French chancelier, cancelier, from inherited from Late Latin cancellārius, from Latin cancellus.

brouhaha.e: Disputed. Possibly by assimilation from Hebrew בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא (barúkh habá, “blessed (be) who comes”), a collocation occurring in Psalm 118:26 and an interjection meaning “welcome” in Modern Hebrew.

costa.e: Borrowed from Occitan Costa, from Latin costa.

bull.e: Clipping of bulldozer, from American English bulldozer.

naples.e: Inherited from Middle French Napples, from Italian Napoli, from Latin Neāpolis, from Ancient Greek Νεᾱ́πολῐς (Neā́polĭs), from νέᾱ (néā, “new”) + πόλῐς (pólĭs, “city”).

galère.e: From Catalan galera, from Medieval Latin galēra, alternative form of galea, from Byzantine Greek γάλεα (gálea). Compare galée, from Old French, directly from Latin galea.

efficacité.e: Borrowed from Latin efficācitātem. Morphologically, from efficace + -ité.

éclaircir.e: From Late Latin *exclaricire, from Latin claricare.

avant-hier.e: From avant (“before”) + hier (“yesterday”). See also Italian avantieri.

crucial.e: From a root of Latin crux (“cross”). The sense of "crucial" is a semantic loan from English crucial.

cynique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin cynicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós).

raid.e: Borrowed from English raid, from Scots raid. Doublet of rade from Middle English.

pin.e: Inherited from Old French pin, from Latin pīnus, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *poi- (“sap, juice”).

clope.e: Unknown. Compare Dutch klop (“a knock, bump, butt”).

écurie.e: Inherited from Middle French escuyrie, from Old French esquierie, escurie, thus ultimately from the root of écuyer.

fondateur.e: Borrowed from Latin fundātōrem. Compare fondeur.

ancre.e: From Old French ancre, from Latin ancora (“anchor”).

marbre.e: Inherited from Old French marbre, from Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros).

entente.e: From the verb entendre, from Middle French entendre and Old French entendre, from Latin intendere (“to turn one’s attention, to strain”).

caillou.e: Borrowed from Norman caillou, from Old French caillou, kailleu, caillo, caliou, cailloun, calloun, related to Judeo-Old French chailos, chaillous and Old French chaille (“small stone, pebble”), of uncertain origin.

corbeau.e: Inherited from Middle French corbeau m, from Old French corbel m, itself either a diminutive of corp m (“raven”), or from a Late Latin corbellus, corvellus m, from Latin corvus m (Vulgar Latin variant *corbus m).

trac.e: From Old French trac (“track”), of uncertain origin.

pencher.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pendicāre, from Latin pendere (“hang”). Compare pendre.

fraise.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰreh₂ǵ-der.? Proto-Indo-European *sróh₂gsder.? Proto-Italic *frāgom Latin frāga French *fraige French fraise Earlier *fraige, from Latin frāga, plural of frāgum.

querelle.e: From Old French querele, from Latin querella (“complaint”), from queror (“to lament, to complain”).

coquille.e: From a combination of Vulgar Latin *conchilia (from Latin conchylium) with coccum.

habile.e: ), a borrowing from Latin habilis (“suitable, apt”).

émetteur.e: From émett(ant) (stem of the present participle of émettre) + -eur.

global.e: From globe (“globe”) + -al, from Latin globus (“globe, sphere”).

pudding.e: Borrowed from English pudding. Doublet of boudin.

négligence.e: Borrowed from Latin negligentia, variant of neglegentia.

aquarium.e: Borrowed from Latin aquārium. Doublet of évier.

éprouver.e: Inherited from Middle French esprouver, Old French esprover, from prover < Latin probāre. Equivalent to é- + prouver.

entrailles.e: From the plural of Old French entraille, from Early Medieval Latin intrālia (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), from Latin interanea, from interaneus, from inter. Compare Spanish entraña.

fourrer.e: Inherited from Old French, corresponding to feurre + -er.

aviation.e: Coined by French journalist Guillaume Joseph Gabriel La Landelle in 1863 together with aviateur; from Latin avis (“bird”) + -ation.

fragment.e: Learned borrowing from Latin fragmentum (“a fragment, remnant”).

étang.e: Derived from the Old French verb estanchier, through an earlier form estanc. Unrelated to Latin stāgnum (“pond”), which influenced the change in spelling from ⟨c⟩ to ⟨g⟩.

distinguer.e: From Middle French distinguer, a 14th-century borrowing from Latin distinguere.

locataire.e: Ultimately from Latin locus (“place”) + -aire, literally “locatee”, a person to which a place is rented. Compare Italian locatario.

dynamique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós).

flacon.e: Inherited from Middle French flascon, from Late Latin flascō. Doublet of fiasco and flasque.

érection.e: Inherited from Middle French erection, borrowed from Latin ērectiōnem.

coquin.e: From Middle French coquin, from Old French coquin, of obscure origin.

crotte.e: Attested since the late 12th century as crotes de chievres (“goat droppings”); probably from Old Dutch *krotta, deduced from Rhine Franconian krotz (“poorly molded brick; thick earthclod; shriveled fruit; remnant”), wit…

couture.e: Inherited from Old French costure, from Vulgar Latin *cōnsutūra, from Latin cōnsūtus, from cōnsuō.

boulet.e: From Middle French boulet, corresponding to boule + -et.

jogging.e: Borrowed from English jogging. The sense "jogging pants" is a pseudo-anglicism.

quatorze.e: Inherited from Old French quatorze, from Latin quattuordecim.

canot.e: From Middle French canot (“little boat”, also “dugout”), partly continuing (in diminutive form) Old French cane (“boat, ship”), from Middle Low German kane (“boat”), from Old Saxon *kano, from Proto-West Germanic *kanō,…

perquisition.e: From Late Latin perquisitionem, from Latin perquirō.

plâtre.e: Inherited from Middle French plâtre, plastre, from Old French plastre (first attested ca.

coriace.e: Borrowed from Late Latin coriāceus (“leathery”), a derivative of corium (→ French cuir (“leather”)). Doublet of cuirasse.

pet.e: Inherited from Middle French pet, from Old French pet, from Latin pēditum.

mature.e: Inherited from Middle French mature, borrowed from Latin mātūrus. Doublet of mûr.

dubois.e: From du (“of the”) + bois (“wood”), referring to a dweller in or near a small wood.

autrui.e: Inherited from Old French autrui, from Vulgar Latin *alterui, alteration (after cui) of Latin alterī, dative singular of alter. Compare Italian altrui.

mutation.e: Inherited from Middle French mutation, from Old French mutacion, borrowed from Latin mutātiōnem.

créatif.e: Formed from the root of Latin creatus and the suffix -if, or borrowed from Late Latin creativus.

esthétique.e: Borrowed from New Latin aesthēticus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek αἰσθητικός (aisthētikós).

contrôleur.e: From Old French contrerollour, contreroulour. By surface analysis, contrôler + -eur.

s: se prendre les pieds dans le tapis

rené.e: From Latin Renātus, name of a legendary 5th century French saint, from renātus (“reborn”), with identical meaning in French (rené).

sédatif.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sedātīvus, from sedō.

naviguer.e: ), a borrowing from Latin navigāre. Doublet of nager (“to swim”).

en: fly by the seat of one's pants

opérateur.e: Borrowed from Latin operātōrem. Cf. also ouvreur (“worker in glassmaking or papermaking”), possibly an inherited doublet.

chargeur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- Proto-Indo-European *-ós Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós Proto-Celtic *karros Gaulish *karrosbor.

tendresse.e: From tendre + -esse. Compare Occitan and Catalan tendresa, Italian tenerezza, Aromanian tinireatsã, Old Sicilian tinirizza, Romanian tinerețe, Spanish and Portuguese terneza.

séoul.e: Borrowed from Korean 서울 (Seoul). Note that it predates the standard romanization Seoul in Korean.

tyran.e: Inherited from Middle French tyran, borrowed from Latin tyrannus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos). Replaced Old French tirant.

gramme.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek γράμμα (grámma, “a small weight”).

désigner.e: Borrowed from Latin dēsignāre, dēsignō. Doublet of dessiner.

automobile.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew Proto-Indo-European *tó- Proto-Hellenic *autós Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewder.

coursier.e: From course + -ier. Appeared in Old French as corsier, and in Medieval Latin cursārius.

chronique.e: Borrowed from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).

furax.e: From furieux + -ax. The Latin word is unrelated.

pion.e: Inherited from Old French peon, from Late Latin pedōnem, derived from Latin ped- (“foot”). Doublet of péon, which was borrowed from Spanish peón.

ingrédient.e: From Middle French ingredient, from Latin ingredientem, present participle of ingredior (“to go or enter into or onto”).

annulation.e: Borrowed from Latin annūlātiōnem. By surface analysis, annuler + -ation.

circuler.e: Borrowed from Late Latin circulāre, post-Augustan form of circulor. Compare cercler, possibly an inherited doublet.

coudre.e: Inherited from Old French coudre, cosdre, from Vulgar Latin *cōsere, from Latin cōnsuere. The original Old French infinitive was *co(u)sre, where -d- was inserted as a gliding sound.

protéine.e: From Ancient Greek πρωτεῖος (prōteîos, “of the first quality”) + -ine. Coined 1838 by Dutch chemist Gerardus Johannes Mulder.

nausée.e: Borrowed from Latin nausea, nausia, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “seasickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).

nice.e: Inherited from Old French nice, inherited from Latin nescius.

haut-parleur.e: From haut + parleur, a calque of English loudspeaker.

pente.e: From Vulgar Latin *pendita, nominalized feminine of *penditus, Vulgar Latin perfect participle (compare Classical Latin pēnsus) of pendere (“to hang”).

annuel.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin annuālis, from Latin annus (“year”).

parallèle.e: Inherited from Middle French parallèle, borrowed from Latin parallēlus.

nonne.e: Inherited from Old French none, nominative singular of nonain, from Late Latin nonna. Compare German Nonne.

comète.e: Inherited from Middle French comète, from Old French comete, from Latin comēta, from Ancient Greek κομήτης (komḗtēs, “long-haired”).

flanc.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French flanc, from Frankish *hlanku. Cognate with Italian fianco.

scandaleux.e: Borrowed from Latin scandalōsus. By surface analysis, scandale + -eux.

monastère.e: Borrowed from Latin monastērium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermit's cell”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”). Doublet of moutier (Old French mostier).

coussin.e: From Middle French, from later Old French coissin, from Vulgar Latin coxīnus (“seat pad”), derived from Latin coxa (“hip, thigh”) with the suffix possibly after Latin pulvīnus (“pillow”).

fureur.e: Inherited from Middle French fureur, from Old French furor, borrowed from Latin furor.

délivrer.e: Inherited from Late Latin dēlīberāre, dēlīberō (“to set free”) (unrelated to the Classical Latin dēlīberō (“to weigh, to ponder”), which was borrowed in French as délibérer). By surface analysis, dé- + livrer.

hygiène.e: From Ancient Greek ὑγιεινή (hugieinḗ) τέχνη (tékhnē) (art of health), from ὑγιεινός (hugieinós, “of health, good for the health, wholesome, sound, healthy”), from ὑγιής (hugiḗs, “healthy, sound”).

sentier.e: Inherited from Old French sentier, from Early Medieval Latin sēmitārius, derived from Latin sēmita (whence sente).

traiteur.e: Etymology tree French traiter Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French traiteur From traiter + -eur.

caramel.e: Borrowed from Spanish caramelo, derived from Portuguese caramelo, probably derived from Late Latin calamellus, and therefore doublet of the inherited chalumeau.

tampon.e: Nasalized variant of tapon, from Frankish *tappō, from Proto-Germanic *tappô (“plug, tap”), cognate with Dutch tappe, German Zapfen, Old English tæppa, English tap.

vocal.e: Inherited from Old French vocal, borrowed from Latin vōcālis. Doublet of voyelle.

pyramide.e: Learned borrowing from Latin pȳramis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís).

branler.e: Inherited from Middle French bransler, from Old French bransler (“to shake (a sword at), move”), a contracted form of brandeler (“to wobble”), from Vulgar Latin *brandus (“firebrand, flaming sword, sword”), ultimately f…

chope.e: From Alemannic German (Alsatian) Schoppe, which is related to German schoppen (“to tuck”). Compare modern German Schoppen.

porche.e: Inherited from Old French porche, inherited from Latin porticus. Doublet of portique.

fléau.e: Inherited from Old French flaiel, flael, flayau, inherited from Latin flagellum.

catalogue.e: Borrowed from Late Latin catalogus, itself from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “an enrollment, a register, a list, catalogue”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, to tell at length or in order, to make a list”),…

belle-fille.e: Inherited from Middle French belle-fille. By surface analysis, belle- + fille.

cobra.e: Borrowed from Portuguese cobra, from Latin colubra. Doublet of couleuvre.

milice.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Latin mīlitia (“military, military service”), from mīles (“soldier”).

agonie.e: Borrowed from Latin agōnia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía).

buisson.e: Inherited from Middle French buisson, from Old French buison, buisson, boissun (“stand of wild shrubs”), diminutive of Old French bois, bosc (“area planted with trees”), from Frankish *bosk, *busk (“bush”), from Proto-G…

sanglot.e: Inherited from Old French sangloit, singlot, from Vulgar Latin *singluttus, a blend of gluttīre (“to swallow”) + Latin singultus (“a hiccup”). Compare Catalan sanglot, Italian singhiozzo, and Occitan sanglòt.

dialogue.e: Inherited from Middle French dialogue, from Late Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos, “conversation, discourse”), from διά (diá, “through, inter”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, discourse”), from δι…

benne.e: Inherited from Latin benna, from Gaulish bennā.

motion.e: Inherited from Old French motion, mocion, borrowed from Latin mōtiōnem, noun of action from perfect passive participle mōtus (“having been moved”), from verb movēre (“move”), + noun of action suffix -iō.

clandestin.e: Learned borrowing from Latin clandestīnus (“secret, concealed”).

peupler.e: From peuple + -er. Compare Catalan, Spanish, and Occitan poblar, Portuguese povoar, Italian popolare.

glorieux.e: From Middle French glorieux, from Old French glorious, from Latin gloriosus.

tablette.e: From Old French tablete, diminutive of table.

venin.e: Inherited from Middle French venin, from Old French venim, from Vulgar Latin *venīmen, from Early Medieval Latin venīnum, from Classical Latin venēnum.

capot.e: Inherited from Old French capote (“hooded cloak”), diminutive of cape, from Late Latin cappa. Piecewise doublet of capote.

maréchal.e: From Middle French mareschal, from Old French mareschal, marescal, from Medieval Latin mariscalcus, from Frankish *marhskalk, from *marh (from Proto-Germanic *marhaz (“horse”)) + *skalk (from Proto-Germanic *skalkaz (“s…

tic.e: Onomatopoeic; originally of horses in the 17th century. Compare Italian ticchio with a similar meaning.

diviser.e: Alteration, based on the Latin etymology, of Old French deviser, itself from a Vulgar Latin *devisāre < *divisāre, from Latin dīvīsum, supine of dīvidō (“to divide”). Compare deviser.

tracteur.e: Formed from Latin tractus (“traho”) + the suffix -eur.

sceller.e: Inherited from Middle French sceller, from Old French seeler, from Vulgar Latin *sigellāre, from Latin sigillāre (“to seal”), from sigillum (“seal”). See sceau.

tousser.e: Inherited from Old French toussir with change of conjugation class, from Latin tussīre.

pureté.e: Alteration of Old French purté, inherited from Late Latin pūritātem, from Latin pūrus (“pure”) + -tās (noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, pur + -eté.

mosquée.e: Borrowed from Italian moschea, ultimately from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, literally “place of prostration”).

croûte.e: Inherited from Middle French crouste, from Old French croste, cruste, from Latin crusta (“hard outer covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).

prévisible.e: From the verb prévoir, from pré- + visible.

hameçon.e: Inherited from Old French ameçon, a derivative of Old French aim, from Latin hāmus (“hook”).

saboter.e: From sabot (“clog”) + -er, because mill workers would throw their wooden clogs into the machinery to make it halt or break down.

revers.e: Inherited from Old French revers, from Latin reversus.

divan.e: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish دیوان (dîvân), from Persian دیوان (divân).

citrouille.e: Diminutive of Old French citre, from Latin citrus. Compare Italian cetriolo.

poêle.e: Inherited from Old French poil, inherited from Latin pēnsilis. Spelling influenced by Etymology 2.

dinosaure.e: Borrowed from English dinosaur. Coined by paleontologist Richard Owen in 1842.

gendre.e: From Old French gendre, inherited from Latin gener.

intimider.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intimidāre (“to make afraid”), from timidus (“afraid, timid”).

crapaud.e: Inherited from Middle French crapaud, from Old French crapaut, crapot (“frog, toad”), from Frankish *krappō, *krappa (“hook, claw”) (because of a toad's hooked feet) + -aud. Compare Catalan gripau, Occitan grapaut.
