curry.e: Borrowed into Middle French from multiple sources including English curry, all ultimately derived from Tamil கறி (kaṟi).

avorter.e: Inherited from Latin abortāre (“to bring forth prematurely”).

firme.e: Borrowed from English firm (“commercial undertaking, corporate name”) and/or German Firma (“business, business name, signature”), both from Italian firma (“signature”), from firmare (“to sign”), from Latin firmō (“to ma…

requérir.e: Inherited from Middle French requerir, from Old French requerre (with a conjugation change as with quérir), from Latin requirere.

caverne.e: Inherited from Middle French caverne, from Old French caverne, borrowed from Latin caverna.

moralité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin mōrālitātem. By surface analysis, moral + -ité.

hosto.e: Borrowed from a regional language of France, ultimately from Latin hospitālis. Doublet of hôtel. First documented as soldiers' slang in 1915.

carnaval.e: Either from Italian carnevale, from Medieval Latin carnelevale, from caro (“flesh”) + levo (“to lighten, to raise”), or directly from Medieval Latin.

diabète.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek διαβήτης (diabḗtēs, “passing through”).

gain.e: Inherited from Middle French gain, from Old French gaaing, deverbal from the verb gaaignier (“to earn, gain, seize, conquer by force”) (whence Modern French gagner).

démoniaque.e: Inherited from Old French demoniaque, a borrowing from Late Latin daemoniacus.

velours.e: Inherited from Old French velor, an alteration of velos, either from velu (“hairy”) + -os (“-ous”), or a borrowing from Old Occitan velos; either way, from Latin villus.

pertinent.e: Inherited from Old French pertinent (first attested circa 1300), borrowed from Latin pertinēns, pertinentem.

caviar.e: Borrowed from Italian caviaro or Ottoman Turkish خاویار (havyar), from Persian خاویار (xâvyâr).

songer.e: Inherited from Middle French songer, from Old French songier, from Latin somniāre.

broche.e: Inherited from Old French broche, from Vulgar Latin brocca (“spike”), feminine substantive of Classical Latin broccus (“pointy-toothed or prominent-toothed”), ultimately from Gaulish, compare Old Irish brog (“awl”).

racaille.e: Inherited from Old French rascaille (“outcast, rabble”), perhaps from rasque (“mud, filth, scab, dregs”), from Vulgar Latin *rasicō (“to scrape”). Cognate with English rascal.

cliver.e: 16th century, from Dutch klieven, of Germanic origin. More at English cleave.

crédibilité.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin credibilitātem, from Latin credibilis. By surface analysis, crédible + -ité.

brin.e: Unknown origin; possibly of Gaulish origin (compare Catalan bri, Spanish brenca (“fiber”), brinza (“blade of grass, filament”)), from Proto-Celtic *brinikā, from *brinos (“filament, fiber”) (compare Breton broenenn, Wel…

enceint.e: Inherited from Old French enceinte, from Latin incīnctus, past participle of incingō. Compare Italian incinto, Spanish encinto.

subtil.e: ), itself inherited from Latin subtīlis. til/. The modern /y/ is of semi-learned origin.

imprimer.e: Borrowed from Latin imprimere. Doublet of empreindre, which was inherited. Unrelated to primer.

ultra.e: From Latin ultrā. Doublet of outre.

klingon.e: From the TV series Star Trek.

carnage.e: Inherited from Middle French carnage, itself probably from a Norman or Picard (Old Northern French) variant of Old French charnage, itself from char (see also chair (“flesh”)), or from a Medieval Latin carnāticum (“slau…

attentif.e: Inherited from Old French attentif, derived from Latin attentus, with the suffix -if.

recrue.e: Inherited from Old French recreü, past participle of recreistre (from re- + creistre, whence French croître).

claquer.e: Inherited from Middle French claquer, from Old French claquer, clacquer (“to clack, clap, clatter”), from Middle Dutch klacken (“to clack, crack, whack, shake”), from Old Dutch *klakon, from Proto-Germanic *klakōną (“to…

brume.e: Inherited from Old French brume, borrowed from Latin brūma (“winter”), possibly through the intermediate of Old Occitan bruma.

verrou.e: Backformation from Middle French verroux, from the nominative-singular/accusative-plural of Old French veroil, from Vulgar Latin *verruculum, from Latin vericulum, diminutive of verū.

siffler.e: Inherited from Old French sifler (later orthographically influenced by souffler), from Vulgar Latin *sīfilāre, probably an Osco-Umbrian influenced variant of Latin sībilāre (compare Spanish chiflar, Friulian sivilâ).

cascade.e: Borrowed from Italian cascata, from cascare (“to fall”).

psychotique.e: From psychose, on the model of névrose–névrotique.

nécessiter.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin necessitāre (“to oblige, compel”), from Classical Latin necessitās (“necessity, compulsion”) (whence nécessité). According to the Trésor de la langue française, attested by the 14th century.

pou.e: Inherited from Old French pouil, peouil, püil, from Late Latin peduclus < peduculus, variant of Latin pēdīculus, from pēdis, from Proto-Indo-European *pezd-.

vernis.e: Inherited from Old French vernis, verniz, borrowed from Medieval Latin vernīx (accusative singular vernīcem), from veronīx, from Byzantine Greek βερενίκη, βερονίκη (bereníkē, beroníkē, “resin amber”), from Ancient Greek…

grotesque.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek κρύπτω (krúptō) Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ)bor. Latin crypta Italian grotta Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-iskbor.

repaire.e: Deverbal from repairer. Doublet of repère.

baba.e: Borrowed from Polish baba, introduced in France in the eighteenth century at the court of Stanisław Leszczyński, king of Poland, duke of Lorraine and father-in-law of Louis XV.

forge.e: Inherited from Old French forge, from earlier faverge, inherited from Latin fābrica. Doublet of fabrique, which was borrowed.

fa.e: Borrowed from Occitan Fan, from Latin fanum.

dominique.e: Borrowed from Late Latin Dominicus, derived from Dominus (“Lord”).

tsar.e: From Russian царь (carʹ), from Old East Slavic цьсарь (cĭsarĭ), from Proto-Slavic *cěsařь, from a Germanic language, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar. Doublet of César.

camelot.e: Inherited from Middle French Camalot, from Old French Camaalot.

rogne.e: Inherited from Old French roigne, from Latin arānea (“spider's web”), possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *ronea or *aronea, influenced by rodō (“gnaw”). Compare Italian rogna.

grill.e: Clipping of grill-room, from English grill room.

revendre.e: Inherited from Old French revendre, from Latin revēndere, from re- (“re-: again, back”) + vēndere (“to sell”). Equivalent to re- + vendre.

maine.e: From Old French Cemaine, from Latin *Cenomania, from the name of the Gaulish Cenomani tribe of Gallia Celtica. The word was rebracketed as ce (“this”) + Maine, and the ce- was lost by the 12th century.

étalon.e: Inherited from Old French estalon, from Frankish *stallo, from *stall (“stable”) where the horses were kept. More at English stall.

manège.e: Borrowed from Italian maneggio, deverbal of maneggiare (cognate with French manier).

strict.e: Borrowed from Latin strictus, perfect participle of stringere (“to draw tight, bind, contract”). Doublet of étroit.

lanceur.e: Etymology tree French lancer Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French lanceur From lancer + -eur.

crèche.e: From Middle French cresche, from Old French creche, cresche (“manger, feeding trough”), from Late Latin cripia (“feeding trough”), from Frankish *krippija, *kribbija (“crib”), from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ (“crib”), from…

confondre.e: Inherited from Old French confondre, borrowed from Latin cōnfundere.

carreau.e: Inherited from Old French quarel, from Vulgar Latin *quadrellus from Classical Latin quadrus. Compare Italian quadrello, Spanish cuadrillo.

interviewer.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Indo-European *-tér Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥tér Proto-Italic *n̥ter Latin inter Latin inter-der.

mathématiques.e: Learned borrowing from Latin mathēmaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “fond of learning”).

mathématique.e: Inherited from Middle French mathematique, from Latin mathematicus.

raoul.e: From Germanic, first attested in Old French as Raol.

maestro.e: Borrowed from Italian maestro, from Latin magistrum. Doublet of magister, borrowed from Latin, maître, inherited from Latin, and master, borrowed from English.

ampleur.e: Etymology tree French ample Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *-ōs Proto-Italic *-ōs Latin -ōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French ampleur From ample (adjective) + -…

savant.e: Old present participle of the verb savoir (modern: sachant).

imitation.e: From Middle French imitation, from Old French imitacion, from Latin imitātiōnem.

antique.e: Inherited from Old French antique, from antic, borrowed from Latin antīquus.

écosse.e: Inherited from Middle French Escosse, from Old French Escoce, Escouce, from Latin Scōtia. The Old French variant with ou is the expected one.

gracier.e: From Medieval Latin grātiō, from Latin grātia. By surface analysis, grâce + -er.

réveillon.e: From réveill-, the stem of réveiller (“to wake up”) + -on.

facilité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin facilitās (“ease, easiness”). By surface analysis, facile + -ité. Doublet of faculté.

façade.e: Borrowed from Italian facciata, a derivation of faccia (“front”), from Latin facies (“face”).

golfe.e: Borrowed from Italian golfo, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos). Doublet of gouffre.

remédier.e: Borrowed from Latin remediāre. See also remède.

clause.e: From Old French clause, borrowed from Medieval Latin clausa.

tarif.e: From Italian tariffa or Spanish tarifa, from Ottoman Turkish تعرفه (ta'rife), from Persian تعرفه (ta'refe), from Arabic تَعْرِفَة (taʕrifa).

hanter.e: From Middle French hanter, from Old French hanter (“to frequent, abide in one place”), from Old English hāmettan (“to bring home; provide a home for; house”) or/and Old Norse heimta (“to bring home”); both from Proto-Ge…

porte-parole.e: From porter + parole. First attested in 1552 as Middle French porteparolle.

secourir.e: Inherited from Middle French secourir, from an alteration of Old French sucurre, secorre (based on courir), from Latin succurrere.

résurrection.e: Inherited from Old French resurrection, borrowed from Late Latin resurrēctiōnem.

caresser.e: Borrowed from Italian carezzare. Morphologically, from caresse + -er.

lucille.e: Borrowed from Latin Lūcilla, feminine diminutive form of Lūcius.

momie.e: From Latin mumia, from Arabic مُومْيَاء (mūmyāʔ).

sultan.e: Inherited from Middle French sultan (“ruler of a Muslim state”), from Ottoman Turkish سلطان. See English sultan for more.

gazon.e: Inherited from Middle French gazon, from Old French gason, wason (“piece of ground covered with grass, turf”), from Frankish *wasō (“ground, turf”).

cueillir.e: Inherited from Old French coillir, formed analogically, with the verbal suffix -ir, from cueil, stressed conjugated form of the original cueudre, cueildre, cueldre, from Latin colligere (“collect”), from con- (“with, to…

vertébral.e: Learned borrowing from Latin vertebrālis. By surface analysis, vertèbre + -al.

allergie.e: Borrowed from German Allergie, coinage crafted using Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”).

bikini.e: Named after the place name Bikini, from Bikini, the name of the atoll where the United States tested nuclear weapons in July 1946; it was reckoned that the bathing suit would cause as much excitement as an atom bomb.

rival.e: Borrowed from Latin rīvālis (literally “person using the same stream as another”), from rīvus (“small stream, brook”). Unrelated to rive.

tailler.e: Etymology tree Latin tālea Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu.

interrupteur.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin interruptor, from Latin interrumpō (whence interrompre).

clavier.e: Formed from the root of Latin clāvis (whence French clef), with the suffix -ier. Cf. also Medieval Latin clāvārius.

prescrire.e: ), borrowed from Latin praescrībere with adaptation to inherited écrire.

thorax.e: From Latin thōrax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).

artificiel.e: Borrowed from Latin artificiālis. By surface analysis, artifice + -iel.

thoracique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θωρακικός (thōrakikós), from θώραξ (thṓrax) (whence thorax).

paroisse.e: From Old French, from Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”).

obsèques.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin obsequiae, alteration of Latin exsequiae.

pellicule.e: Borrowed from Latin pellicula (“small skin or hide”).

dégoûter.e: From Old French desgouster (“to put off one's appetite”), from des- (“dis-”) + gouster, goster (“to taste”), from Latin gustāre (“to taste”), or rather derived from dégoût, from goût.

lorraine.e: Inherited from Old French Loherraine, from Medieval Latin Lotharingia, Lothringia; compare Lothringia, German Lothringen.

lentille.e: Inherited from Old French lentille, from Vulgar Latin *lenticla, from syncopation of Latin lenticula. The "lens" meaning is because early lenses resembled lentils.

combler.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin cumulāre. Doublet of the borrowing cumuler.

justine.e: From Latin Iustina, name of early saints, feminine of Iustinus, derivative of Iustus, from iustus (“just”). The feminine equivalent of Justin.

asthme.e: From Latin āsthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma).

hymne.e: Inherited from Middle French hymne, hynne, from Old French ymne m or f, from Latin hymnus m, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος m (húmnos).

érotique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin erōticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós, “related to love”), from ἔρως (érōs, “sexual love”).

famine.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French famine, formed from the root of Latin famēs (“hunger”) with the suffix -ine.

abîmer.e: From abime, abîme, from Late Latin *abyssimus < Latin abyssus (“abyss”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos, “bottomless pit”).

melon.e: Inherited from Old French melon, from Late Latin mēlōnem, shortening of Latin mēlopepō, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn, “melon”). More at English melon.

conquête.e: From Middle French conqueste, from Old French conqueste, cunqueste, from a Vulgar Latin *conquista, from the feminine of Latin conquisitus. Compare the masculine form conquêt.

aviser.e: Inherited from Old French aviser, from avis.

cartouche.e: Borrowed from Italian cartuccia, a diminutive of carta, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs).

obus.e: Borrowed from German Haubitze, from Czech houfnice (“catapult”).

succession.e: Borrowed from Latin successiōnem (accusative singular successiōnem).

dauphin.e: Inherited from Old French dalphin, from Latin delphinus.

hercule.e: Inherited from Middle French Hercule, from Latin Herculēs, from Ancient Greek Ἡρακλῆς (Hēraklês).

offensive.e: First attested 1417; formed from offense, from Latin offēnsare (“to strike against”).

kgb.e: Borrowed from Russian КГБ (KGB), through phonetic spelling of Komitét Gosudárstvennoj Bezopásnosti and acronymization.

morse.e: From Russian морж (morž), from Northern Sami.

frire.e: Inherited from Old French frire, from Latin frīgere, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.

chameau.e: Inherited from Middle French chameau, from Old French chamel, inherited from Vulgar Latin *camellus, a variant of Classical Latin camēlus (which would have yielded *chamoil).

abîme.e: Inherited from Old French abisme, from a Late Latin *abīsmus (or similar; compare Spanish, Portuguese abismo), a formally unclear alteration of Latin abyssus (“bottomless pit”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos).

rejet.e: Compare with rejeter (verb) and English reject (verb and noun).

prescription.e: Inherited from Old French prescripcion, itself borrowed from Latin praescrīptiō.

exploit.e: Deverbal from exploiter. Corresponds with Old French espleit; cf. Latin explicitus.

chêne.e: Inherited from Middle French chesne, from Old French chesne, chaisne, chasne, from Vulgar Latin *cassanus (attested in Medieval Latin as casnus), probably from Gaulish kassanos.

violette.e: From violette (“violet”). Cognate with English Violet.

gaufre.e: From Middle French gaufre, from Old French walfre, from Frankish *wāfilu, *wāfilā or Middle Dutch wafele, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wēbilǭ, *wēbilō, possibly related to Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to braid, weave…

négligé.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *-kʷe Proto-Indo-European *nékʷe Proto-Italic *nekʷe Latin neque Latin nec Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *léǵeti Proto…

négliger.e: Etymology tree Latin nec Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *léǵeti Proto-Italic *legō Latin lego Latin negligere French négliger Inherited from Latin negligere.

natal.e: Borrowed from Latin nātālis. Doublet of Noël.

fez.e: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish فس (fes). Mentioned as bonnet de fez in 1664. By the 19th century the word fez alone stood for the hat.

master.e: Borrowed from English master. Doublet of maestro, borrowed from Italian, magister, borrowed from Latin, and maître, inherited from Latin.

ingrid.e: From Swedish, Norwegian and Danish Ingrid, from Old Norse Ingiríðr.

apaiser.e: Inherited from Old French apaisier, from paiz, pais (“peace”).

guillaume.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French Guillaume, Willame, from Frankish *Willahelm (“William”, literally “will-helmet”), from Proto-Germanic *Wiljahelmaz. Cognate with Old High German Willahelm (“William”).

contraint.e: Conjugated form of the verb contraindre (“to constrain”). From Middle French constraint, from Old French constraint, contraint, corresponding to Latin cōnstrictus (through a Vulgar Latin form *constrinctus).

frisson.e: Inherited from Late Latin *frīctiōnem, from Latin frīgeō (“to be cold”). Unrelated to the Classical Latin frictiō, borrowed as French friction.

barbare.e: From Medieval Latin barbarinus (“Berber, pagan, Saracen, barbarian”), from Latin barbaria (“foreign country”).

pare-brise.e: From parer + brise. Compare Spanish parabrisas, Italian parabrezza, Portuguese para-brisa.

margot.e: Diminutive of Marguerite (the French equivalent of English Margaret) + -ot (a diminutive suffix used with names).

ouïe.e: Deverbal of ouïr, corresponding to Latin audīta < audītus. Compare Occitan ausida, Catalan oïda, Spanish oído, Portuguese ouvido, Italian udito, Romansh udida, Friulian uldide.

matériau.e: Analogical levelling of matériaux, the plural form of Old French matérial.

compenser.e: Borrowed from Latin compēnsāre, from com- (“together”) + pensō (“to weigh”).

louisiane.e: From Louis + -iane. Named for king Louis XIV of France.

torpille.e: From obsolete torpin with change of suffix.

castor.e: Inherited from Middle French castor, from Old French castor, borrowed from Latin castor, itself from Ancient Greek κάστωρ (kástōr).

méprendre.e: From Old French mesprendre. Compare to English misapprehend. Corresponding to mé- + prendre.

cube.e: Borrowed from Latin cubus, from Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos).

rédemption.e: Learned borrowing from Latin redemptiōnem. Doublet of rançon.

label.e: Borrowed from English label, itself from Old French label, lambel (“fringe, strip”), 1899.

garant.e: Inherited from Middle French garant, from Old French garant, garand, guarant, a borrowing from Frankish *warand, from Frankish *warjan (“to authorise, warrant”). Cognate with Old High German werento (“guarantor”).

déplaire.e: From dé- + plaire, after Latin displicere.

expirer.e: Learned borrowing from Latin exspīrō (“to expire”).

catch.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from English catch-as-catch-can (a style of wrestling now known as catch wrestling). Doublet of chasser (“to hunt”).

faisable.e: Inherited from Old French fesable. By surface analysis, faire + -able.

errant.e: From Old French errant, from Latin errantem.

errer.e: From Old French errer, from Latin errāre.

fiasco.e: Borrowed from Italian fiasco. Doublet of flacon and flasque.

amnésie.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía, “forgetfulness”).

crête.e: Inherited from Old French creste, from Latin crista.

hypnose.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).

suspense.e: Nominalisation of the feminine form of suspens.

ballade.e: Inherited from Old French balade, from Provençal balada (“song for dancing”), from balar (“to dance”), from Late Latin ballare, borrowed from, or related to, Ancient Greek βαλλίζω (ballízō). Doublet of ballée.

plate-forme.e: Inherited from Middle French plateforme, corresponding to plate (“flat”) + forme (“form”).

punaise.e: From the feminine of punais (“having a foul odor”), from Vulgar Latin *pūtināsius, from Latin puteō + nāsus, based on nāriputēns.

vinaigre.e: Inherited from Middle French vinaigre, from Old French vinaigre. By surface analysis, vin + aigre. Compare Catalan and Occitan vinagre.

tempérament.e: Inherited from Middle French tempérament, borrowed from Latin temperāmentum. By surface analysis, tempérer + -ment.

immortalité.e: Borrowed from Latin immortālitātem. By surface analysis, in- + mortalité or immortel + -ité.

dague.e: From Old French (13th century), from either Old Occitan or Italian daga. The Catholicum Armoricum glosses Breton dac as French dague, Latin pugio, adding ou c'est badelaire (Du Cange).

gilles.e: Inherited from Old French, from an alteration of Latin Aegīdius.

démocrate.e: Back-formation from démocratie, based on aristocratie > aristocrate.

cosmos.e: From Latin cosmos, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos).

marjorie.e: Variant of Marguerite. From English Marjorie.

pancarte.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pancharta.

patriote.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin patriōta (“fellow countryman”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs, “of the same country”).

poire.e: Inherited from Old French peire, from Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, considered as a feminine singular.

souverain.e: Inherited from Old French soverain, from Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super. Compare Italian sovrano; Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish soberano.

dorer.e: Inherited from Old French dorer, inherited from Late Latin deaurāre, from Latin aurāre.

roc.e: ), ultimately from Latin rocca, hence doublet of roche.

excentrique.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin excentricus, from ex- (“away”) + centrum (“the centre”) + -icus. By surface analysis, ex- + centre + -ique.

lamentable.e: Learned borrowing from Latin lāmentābilis (“full of sorrow, mournful; deplorable”), from lāmentor (“lament”), from lāmenta (“wailing, weeping”).

viole.e: ], probably from Old Occitan viola (modern Occitan viula), from Medieval Latin *vitula (“stringed instrument”). Compare Italian viola.

délinquant.e: Present participle of délinquer, or borrowed from Latin delinquentem.

imprudent.e: Learned borrowing from Latin imprūdens. Morphologically analyzable as im- + prudent.

hormis.e: Originally as hors mis, as a past participle of mettre hors (“put outside; exclude”).

épice.e: Inherited from Old French espice, an old (12th century) borrowing from Latin speciēs, which in Late Latin meant "spice", "foodstuff", "commodity", "drug". Doublet of espèce.

nourrice.e: Inherited from Middle French nourrisse, nourrice, from Old French nurrice, from Late Latin nūtrīcia, feminine of Latin nūtrīcius.

organique.e: Borrowed from Latin organicus. By surface analysis, organe + -ique.

brebis.e: Inherited from Old French berbis, berbiz, from Vulgar Latin *berbicem, from Late Latin berbēcem, from Latin vervēx (“wether”).

intestin.e: ), learned borrowing from Latin intestīnum n.

galant.e: Present participle of Old French galer, from Frankish *wala (“well”), from Proto-Germanic *wela, from Proto-Indo-European *wel(h₁)- (“to choose, wish”).

prospérité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin prosperitās. By surface analysis, prospère + -ité.

wisconsin.e: From English Wisconsin, itself a borrowing from French Ouisconsin.

essuyer.e: Inherited from Old French essuier, from Latin exsūcāre.

interruption.e: Inherited from Old French interrupcion, borrowed from Latin interruptiō.

prairie.e: Inherited from Old French praerie, from Vulgar Latin *prataria, from Latin prātum (“meadow”) + -aria. See also pré and -erie.

impérial.e: Learned borrowing from Latin imperiālis, from imperium (whence French empire).

estelle.e: Adapted borrowing of Occitan estela (“star”), from Latin stēlla (“star”). Doublet of étoile.

vanité.e: Inherited from Middle French vanité, from Old French, borrowed from Latin vānitātem.

agriculture.e: From agri- + culture, or borrowed from Latin agricultūra.

colombe.e: Inherited from Old French colombe, from Latin columba. Cf. also the masculine Old French form colomb, coulon.

mûr.e: Inherited from Middle French meur, from Old French meur, from Latin mātūrus. Doublet of mature.

mare.e: From Middle French mare, from Old French mare, from Old Norse marr (“lake, sea, pool”), from Proto-Germanic *mari (“lake, sea”), from Proto-Indo-European *móri. Doublet of mer inherited from Latin.

biche.e: Inherited from Middle French biche, from Old French biche (“doe, female deer”) and bisse (“wild animal”), of uncertain origin and relation.

moule.e: Inherited from Old French modle, an old (11th century) borrowing from Latin modulus (“measure”) (compare Catalan motlle). Doublet of module, a more recent borrowing.

digital.e: Borrowed from Latin digitālis. Doublet of dé. Use in electronics is a literal borrowing from English, through a misinterpretation of the English word digit.

immonde.e: From Latin immundus (“unclean”). Compare Italian immondo, Spanish inmundo and Portuguese imundo.

restauration.e: Borrowed from Late Latin restaurātiōnem. By surface analysis, restaurer + -ation.

meneur.e: Etymology tree Latin mīna Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu.

guet.e: Deverbal from guetter, or masculine form of guette. Compare the original Old French gué.

manœuvre.e: From Old French manovre, from Medieval Latin manū opera (“handiwork”), a calque of Proto-West Germanic *handuwerk. Equivalent to main (“hand”) + œuvre (“work”).

ridiculiser.e: From ridicule + -iser, attested since 1675. Displaced older ridiculer and ridiculariser.

timbre.e: Inherited from Old French timbre, via Byzantine Greek, from Ancient Greek τύμπανον (túmpanon, “drum”). Less likely a direct descendant of Latin tympanum. Doublet of tympan.

gerber.e: From Middle French gerber, from gerbe (“sheaf”), from Old French jarbe, garbe (“sheaf, ear of grain, wreath”), borrowed from Frankish *garbā (“sheaf”).

inconvénient.e: From in- + convénient, or from Middle French inconvenient, borrowed from Latin inconvenientem.

puanteur.e: From Middle French. By surface analysis, puant + -eur.

bave.e: From Old French beve (altered based on baver), from Vulgar Latin root *baba, of imitative origin. Compare Spanish baba, Portuguese baba.

opium.e: From Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion).

apprenti.e: Inherited from Middle French apprentis, from Vulgar Latin *apprenditīcius, from the past participle of Latin apprehendere.

hésitation.e: Borrowed from Latin haesitātiōnem. By surface analysis, hésiter + -ation.

sincérité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin sincēritās. By surface analysis, sincère + -ité.

précipité.e: Borrowed from New Latin praecipitātum. By surface analysis, précipiter + -é (result suffix).

lyon.e: From Latin Lugdūnum, from Gaulish *Lugudūnon (“fort of Lug”), from the Celtic deity Lugus, from Proto-Celtic *Lugus.

intensité.e: From intense + -ité. Cf. also Medieval Latin intensitas.

investigation.e: From Old French investigacion, from Latin investigātiōnem.

arroser.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrōsāre, from Latin rōs (“dew”).

serge.e: Inherited from Middle French sarge, from Old French sarge, from Vulgar Latin *sarica, from Latin sērica, ultimately from the Ancient Greek σηρῐκός (sērĭkós, “silken”).

ronger.e: From Old French rongier, from a crossing of rungier (from Latin rūmigāre (“chew”)) with influence from a Vulgar Latin *rodicāre, itself from Latin rōdō (“to gnaw”).

courbe.e: From Vulgar Latin *curbus, from Latin curvus.

pétition.e: Inherited from Old French peticiun, borrowed from Latin petitiōnem.

croc.e: Inherited from Middle French croc, from Old French croc, croke (“curved instrument, hook”), from Frankish *krōk (“hook”) or from Old Norse krókr (“hook, bend, bight”), both from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“hook”), from Pro…

alain.e: First attested in Old French, from Old Breton Alan.

manie.e: Borrowed from Latin mania or Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).

manier.e: From Old French manier, Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manizāre. Compare Italian maneggiare, whence French manège.

forfait.e: From Old French forfait, past participle of forfaire, from for(t) (variant of Old French fuer, fur) and faire.

tao.e: Borrowed from Mandarin 道 (Dào, literally “The Way”).

alabama.e: Borrowed from English Alabama, itself likely from Alabama Albaamaha.

cannelle.e: Diminutive of canne (“reed”); from Old French canele, kanele

challenge.e: Borrowed from English challenge, from Old French chalonge, from Latin calumnia. Doublet of calomnie.

paralysie.e: Borrowed from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”).

gomme.e: Borrowed from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (“acanthus resin, gum”).

turquie.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Turcia, Turchia; alternatively from turc + -ie.

souche.e: Inherited from Middle French souche, from Old French çoche, from Vulgar Latin *tsucca, from Gaulish *tsukka, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“stock; stump”). Cognate with Catalan and Spanish soca, Sicilian zuccu.

diarrhée.e: Inherited from the Middle French diarrie. By surface analysis, dia- + -rrhée.

constater.e: From constat, borrowed from Latin cōnstat, the third-person singular present active indicative of cōnstō. Compare also coûter.

radical.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin rādīcālis.

loisir.e: Inherited from Old French loisir, from Latin licēre, infinitive of licet. The final -ir < Latin -ēre is regular and results from the palatalization of the preceding -c- to *[d͡zʲ], as in gésir, moisir, plaisir.

épingle.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *spingula, a cross between Late Latin spīnula and spīcula. Cognate with Neapolitan spingula.

huître.e: From Old French uistre, oistre, from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon).

médiocre.e: Learned borrowing from Latin mediocris, from medius (“middle, central”).

bruxelles.e: Of Germanic origin, composed from *brōk (“marsh”) + *sali (“building, room”).

répliquer.e: Borrowed from Latin replicāre. See also replier.

dicton.e: Renaissance borrowing of Latin dictum, with francisation of the ending. Doublet of dit.

garde-robe.e: Ellipsis of armoire garde-robe, from garder (“to keep safe”) + robe (“dress”).

gifle.e: Inherited from Middle French gifle, from Old French giffe, *gifle, *gifre, from Old Dutch *kifel, from Frankish *kebr, from Proto-Germanic *kebrą.

démence.e: Borrowed from Latin dēmentia, from dēmēns.

bourre.e: Inherited from Old French boure, borre, from Late Latin burra (“coarse fabric or material”).

vocabulaire.e: Borrowed from Late Latin vocābulārium, from Latin vocabulum.

rivage.e: Inherited from Old French rivage, from Late Latin rīpāticum. Equivalent to by surface analysis, rive + -age.

contrainte.e: From the feminine of contraint; Middle French constrainte.

cheeseburger.e: Unadapted borrowing from American English cheeseburger.

rubrique.e: Inherited from Middle French rubrique, from Old French rubrique, from Latin rubrīca (“red ochre”) the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”).

cathédrale.e: Borrowed from Late Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρᾱ (kathédrā, “seat”).

confronter.e: From Middle French confronter, borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre.

démontrer.e: Inherited from Middle French demonstrer, from Old French demonstrer, demoustrer, from Latin dēmōnstrāre.

capuche.e: From cape + -uche, or borrowed from Italian cappuccio. Compare capuce.

couronner.e: Inherited from Old French coroner, from Latin corōnāre. By surface analysis, couronne + -er.

comparaître.e: Formed from paraître, apparaître based on Old French comparoir, from Latin comparere.

rédaction.e: Learned borrowing from Latin redactiō, from redigō (whence rédiger).

anévrisme.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνεύρυσμα (aneúrusma).

martyr.e: Inherited from Old French martire, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur), later form of μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).

laurent.e: From Old French Lorenz, from Latin Laurentius.

sushi.e: Unadapted borrowing from Japanese 寿司 (sushi).

roupie.e: From Portuguese rupia, from Sanskrit रूप्य (rūpya, “silver coin”).

infanterie.e: Borrowed from Italian infanteria and fanteria, from infante (“child”) (cognate with French enfant).

intègre.e: Learned borrowing from Latin integer. Doublet of entier.

recueillir.e: Inherited from Old French recoillir, from Latin recolligere, see re-, cueillir.

popularité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin populāritās. By surface analysis, populaire + -ité.

crocodile.e: Derived from Old French cocodril, inherited from Latin crocodīlus with metathesis, later respelled to match the Latin form. Compare English crocodile, itself respelled from Middle English cocodrill.

défaillance.e: From Middle French defaillance, equivalent to défaillir (“to faint”) + -ance.

gibier.e: Inherited from Old French gibiez, with change of suffix, and that from Frankish *gabaiti (“to hunt with falcons”), from *ga- + *bītan (“to bite”).

stratégique.e: From Ancient Greek στρατηγικός (stratēgikós). By surface analysis, stratégie + -ique.

rayer.e: From raie + -er. Found in Old French as roier. Cf. however also Old French raier, rayer, possibly from Latin radiāre.

éclipse.e: From Latin eclīpsis (“eclipse”), from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “eclipse”), from ἐκλείπω (ekleípō, “to abandon”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and λείπω (leípō, “to leave behind”).

donjon.e: From Old French donjon, from Vulgar Latin *dominiōnem.

jean-pierre.e: Jean + Pierre. Literally, “John-Peter”. * (surname): Most prevalent in Martinique.

récupération.e: Inherited from Middle French recuperation, recuperacion, borrowed from Latin recuperātiō. Morphologically, from récupérer + -ation.

danemark.e: A modification of Middle French Danemarche (from Old French Danemarche, Old French Denemarche) after Danish Danmark.

vessie.e: Inherited from Middle French vessie, from Old French vessie, from Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca.

stabilité.e: Borrowed from Latin stabilitātem, see stable, -ité.

user.e: Inherited from Old French user, from Early Medieval Latin ūsāre, frequentative from Latin ūtī. Cognate with Italian usare, Spanish usar.

tan.e: From Middle French tan, from Old French tan, from Latin tannum (“oak bark”), from Gaulish *tannos (“oak”), from Proto-Celtic *tannos (“green oak”).

africain.e: Inherited from Middle French african, africain, from Latin africānus. By surface analysis, Afrique + -ain.

répit.e: Inherited from Old French respit, inherited from Latin respectus. Doublet of respect.

coyote.e: Borrowed from Spanish coyote, from a Nahuan language, from Proto-Nahuan *koyoo-tl.

blaireau.e: Inherited from Middle French blereau, blariau, from Old French blarel, from blair. * Possibly from Frankish *blari (“sporting a white blaze on the forehead”) (compare *blasā).

pie.e: Inherited from Old French pie, from Latin pīca (“magpie”), feminine of pīcus (“woodpecker”).

transpirer.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspirāre, from Latin trāns + spiro.

labeur.e: Inherited from Old French labor, borrowed from Latin labōrem.

injecter.e: Borrowed from Latin iniectāre, injectāre, from iniectus, injectus.

philosophe.e: Inherited from Middle French philosophe, from Latin philosophus, from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos).

porcelaine.e: From Old French (1298 AD) pourcelaine (“cowrie, cockle, or similar univalve seashell; the polished material of these shells”). By metaphorical extension, also fine china, which had a similar appearance.

leroy.e: From le (“the”) + roi (“king”). From Middle French roy (“king”).

astuce.e: From Old French astuce (first attested in 1267/68), a semi-learned borrowing from Latin astūtia.

caractéristique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χαρακτηριστικός (kharaktēristikós).

denis.e: Inherited from Latin Dionȳsius, borrowed from Ancient Greek Διονύσιος (Dionúsios).

douane.e: Attested in Old French in 1281 as dohanne with the meaning “building where the rights of entry and exit of goods are earned” (Angevin Archives of Naples).

kidnappeur.e: From English kidnapper, reanalyzed in French as kidnapper (verb) + -eur (suffix forming agent nouns).

vis-à-vis.e: From Old French vis + à + vis, vis m being an obsolete word for “face”, replaced in Modern French by visage m.

stupidité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin stupiditās. By surface analysis, stupide + -ité.

insignifiant.e: Literally, “which has no signification”, from in- + signifier + -ant.

maint.e: Inherited from Middle French maint, from Old French maint, meint (“many”), from Frankish *managiþu (“a large quantity, a great many”), from Proto-Germanic *managiþō (“large quantity, multitude”), from Proto-Indo-Europea…

matrice.e: Inherited from Old French matrice, borrowed from Latin mātrīcem. Supplanted the older inherited forms marriz, marris.

émettre.e: From Middle French emettre, formed after Latin ēmittere. By surface analysis, é- + mettre.

corvée.e: Inherited from Late Latin conrogāta [opera], from the feminine past participle of Latin conrogō.

tonneau.e: Inherited from Middle French tonnel, from Old French tonel. By surface analysis, tonne + -eau.

impératrice.e: Borrowed from Latin imperātrīcem. Compare Old French empereriz.

bâbord.e: From Dutch bakboord (from bak (“rear”) + boord (“board”)), because the pilot was formerly located on the starboard and turned his back to the other side.

compatible.e: Inherited from Middle French compatible, from Medieval Latin compatibilis.

addiction.e: Ultimately from Latin addictiōnem; probably through English addiction.

partiel.e: Borrowed from Latin partiālis. Doublet of partial.

carrefour.e: From Old French quarrefourc, from Latin quadrifurcus, from quadri- < quattuor + furca.

hue.e: Onomatopoeic. Compare German hü, hüa, Dutch ju.

méditation.e: Learned borrowing from Latin meditātiō. By surface analysis, méditer + -ation.

compatriote.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin compatriota, itself likely a calque of Ancient Greek συμπατριώτης (sumpatriṓtēs). By surface analysis, com- + patriote.

chandelle.e: Inherited from Old French chandele, chandeile, chandoile, from Latin candēla (with a change of suffix to -elle, from Latin -ella). Doublet of candela.

crosse.e: Inherited from Middle French crosse, from Old French crosse (“shepherd's staff”), from a Germanic language, likely Frankish *krukkju, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *krukjō (“staff, crutch”).

humilité.e: Borrowed from Latin humilitātem, from humilis (whence French humble) + -tās.

soixante.e: Inherited from Old French soissante, seixante, from Latin sexāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”).

contribuer.e: From Old French contribuir, borrowed from Latin contribuō.

pékin.e: Borrowed from Mandarin 北京 (Běijīng), specifically the Nanking court dialect from before the modern palatalization of [k] to [t͡ɕ]. Doublet of Beijing.

panda.e: Of unclear ultimate origin but probably from the second element of nigálya-pónya, a form recorded by Brian Houghton Hodgson and possibly ultimately derived from regional Tibetan ཕོ་ཉ (pho nya), whose usual meaning is “m…

pupille.e: ), a borrowing from Latin pupillus, pupilla.

oculaire.e: Borrowed from Latin oculāris, from oculus (whence œil).

poulette.e: Inherited from Old French. By surface analysis, poule + -ette (diminutive suffix).

couillon.e: Inherited from Middle French couillon, from Old French coillon (“testicle”), from Late Latin cōleōnem, derived from Latin cōleus (“sack, bag; scrotum”). By surface analysis, couille + -on. Compare Occitan colhon.

lambert.e: From Old French Lambert, from Proto-West Germanic *Landaberht, from *land (“land”) + *berht (“bright”).

plane.e: From Old French plane, from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos), from πλατύς (platús, “wide, broad”).

molle.e: Borrowed from translingual Molle, and later through French who have travelled South America from Spanish and as well Quechua directly, which backcrossed its meaning to the specific species used by the Incas.

orléans.e: Inherited from Old French Orliens, from Latin Aurelianum. Doublet of Aurélien.

stationnement.e: From stationner + -ment. The word has been in use in French for a long time.

dynastie.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dewh₂-der. Proto-Hellenic *dunamai Ancient Greek δύναμαι (dúnamai) Ancient Greek -άζω (-ázō)influ. Proto-Indo-European *-tósder.

portugais.e: From Portuguese português, replacing earlier Portugalois.

prospère.e: Borrowed from Latin prosperus, prosper. Cf. also the Anglo-Norman form prospre.

senior.e: Borrowed from Latin senior. Doublet of sire, seigneur, and sieur.

chercheur.e: Inherited from Old French cercheor. By surface analysis, chercher (“to search”) + -eur.

belgique.e: Originally an adjective, borrowed from Latin Belgicus; morphologically, from Belge + -ique. Noun use arose by ellipsis of province belgique.

poétique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin poēticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ποιητικός (poiētikós).

autriche.e: From Middle French Aust(e)riche, Ost(e)riche, from Old French Ostriche (ca. 1200), from Middle High German Ōsterīche, from Old High German Ōstarrīhhi (literally “eastern realm”).

gâter.e: Inherited from Middle French gaster, from Old French gaster, guaster, which see for more.

vogue.e: Inherited from Middle French vogue (“wave, course of success”), from Old French vogue (“a rowing”), from voguer (“to row, sway, set sail”), from Old Saxon wogōn (“to sway, rock”), var.

macho.e: Borrowed from Spanish macho, from Latin masculus. Doublet of mâle. :* c. 1952 :* c.

maquette.e: From Italian macchietta (“speck, little spot”), diminutive of macchia (“spot”), ultimately from Latin macula (“spot, stain”).

hypothèque.e: Borrowed from Latin hypothēca (“pledge given as surety for a loan”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē).

fat.e: From Old Occitan fat, from Latin fatuus.

lobe.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Ancient Greek λοβός (lobós).

convertir.e: From Old French convertir, from Latin convertō.

québec.e: Borrowed from Algonquin kepék (“(it) narrows”), originally referred to the area around Quebec City where the Saint Lawrence River narrows to a cliff-lined gap.

moustique.e: Borrowed from Spanish mosquito, diminutive of mosca, from Latin musca, whence also the French doublet mouche (“a fly”). The metathesis of /k/ and /t/ might have been due to influence of tique (“a tick”).

nombril.e: Inherited from Middle French nombril, from Old French nonbril, from Vulgar Latin *umbilīculus (compare Occitan embonilh), from Latin umbilīcus. e. a rebracketing).

calorie.e: 1845, formed from Latin calor + -ie. Cf. also French chaleur.

trébucher.e: Inherited from Middle French trebucher, from Old French trebuchier (“to overthrow, topple”), from tres- + *buchier, from Old French buc (“trunk of the body”), from Old Frankish *būk (“belly, trunk, torso”), from Proto-G…

brièvement.e: From Old French briefment (Marie de France, 13th century).

sofa.e: Ultimately from Arabic صُفَّة (ṣuffa, “a long seat made of stone or brick”), from Aramaic צפא (ṣipā’, “mat”)/Classical Syriac ܨܦܬܐ. The word may have entered French via Turkish sofa.

dixième.e: Inherited from Middle French dixiesme. By surface analysis, dix + -ième.

gémir.e: Inherited from Old French gemir, borrowed from Latin gemere. Doublet of geindre, the properly native form.

sceptique.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *spéḱyeti Proto-Hellenic *sképt͏̌omai Ancient Greek σκέπτομαι (sképtomai) Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Hellenic *-kos Ancient G…

lunaire.e: Inherited from Middle French lunaire, from Latin lūnāris.

rubis.e: Inherited from Old French rubi, rubin, borrowed from Medieval Latin rubinus, from Latin rubeus.

abominable.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin abōminābilis (“abominable, detestable”).

inculpation.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin inculpātiō. By surface analysis, inculper + -ation.

contredire.e: Inherited from Old French contredire, borrowed from Latin contrādīcere, from contrā (“against”) + dīcō (“to speak”). By surface analysis, contre- + dire.

étui.e: Inherited from Middle French étui, from Old French estui (“case, sheath”), of uncertain origin.

croisade.e: Inherited from Middle French croisade (15th century), as it were crois + the suffix -ade.

dictionnaire.e: Inherited from Middle French dictionnaire, borrowed from Medieval Latin dictiōnārium (“dictionary”), derived from Latin dictiō (“saying, speaking”) + -ārium.

eagle.e: Borrowed from English eagle. Doublet of aigle.

virilité.e: Borrowed from Latin virilitātem. By surface analysis, viril + -ité.

niquer.e: From faire la nique, nique + -er (verb suffix).

hydrogène.e: From hydro- + -gène. Coined by French nobleman and chemist Antoine Lavoisier in 1783.

huitième.e: Inherited from Old French huictiesme. By surface analysis, huit + -ième.

romaine.e: Feminine of romain ("Roman") from Latin romanus.

ovni.e: Acronym of objet volant non identifié, a calque of English unidentified flying object.

chœur.e: Inherited from Middle French cuer, quer, a semi-learned adaptation or borrowing (from different stages in time) from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós). Doublet of chorus.

contracter.e: A learned word created from the root of Latin contractus.

chaperon.e: From Old French, from chape (“head covering”) as the women who acted as chaperones wore head coverings. Equivalent to chape + -eron. More at English cap, cape.

forum.e: * Most meanings: Learned borrowing from Latin forum. * Internet: Borrowed from English forum.

cygne.e: Inherited from Old French cisne, cine, from Late Latin cicinus, from Latin cycnus (“swan”), from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos).

orgie.e: Borrowed from Latin orgia, a neuter plural reinterpreted as a feminine singular; itself from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia).

tempe.e: From Vulgar Latin *tempula, from Latin tempora, originally an accusative plural form of tempus.

skate.e: Pseudo-anglicism, the first sense derived from English skateboard, and the second from English skateboarding. Note that the English noun skate only refers to an instance of skateboarding, and not the activity itself.

couvercle.e: Inherited from Old French covercle, from Latin cooperculum.

exquis.e: Inherited from Old French esquis, past participle of esquerre, from Latin exquirere with a change in conjugation. /k/ was originally lost and later reinserted per the Latin etymon.

mâcher.e: From Middle French mascher, from Old French mascher, inherited from Latin masticāre. Doublet of mastiquer.

enchaîner.e: From en- + chaîne + -er. Possibly also corresponds to Vulgar Latin *incatēnāre, from Latin catēnāre. Compare Italian incatenare; Catalan, Occitan, and Catalan encadenar; and Portuguese encadear.

piment.e: Inherited from Latin pigmentum. In Old French, piment (also pimenc) had meant 'balsam, fragrant spice'. Certain modern senses represent semantic loans from Spanish pimiento. Doublet of pigment, a borrowing from Latin.

microbe.e: From Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “life”).

continu.e: Inherited from Old French continu, borrowed from Latin continuus.

simuler.e: Learned borrowing from Latin simulāre (“to imitate, to feign”). Doublet of sembler.

sachet.e: From sac + -et, with palatalization of c.

bernadette.e: Diminutive of Bernarde, the feminine form of Bernard. Established as a given name due to Saint Bernadette of Lourdes (baptized Bernarde).

aboyer.e: From Middle French abayer, from Old French abaier, abayer, abaüer, probably of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Latin baubari, Italian abbaiare.

vigueur.e: Inherited from Old French vigur, borrowed from Latin vigorem.

consolation.e: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnsōlātiō. Morphologically, from consoler + -ation.

osaka.e: Borrowed from Japanese 大(おお)阪(さか) (Ōsaka, literally “large hill”).

orthographe.e: Borrowed from Latin orthographia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρθογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (orthogrăphĭ́ā).

mire.e: Borrowed from Italian mira, from Latin mīrō (“to wonder at”).

soutif.e: Clipping of soutien-gorge with an otherwise unknown suffix.

vrille.e: Inherited from Old French verille, ve(d)ille, from Vulgar Latin *vĭtīcula, from Late Latin vītīcula, from Classical Latin vītĭcula.

gouverner.e: Inherited from Old French governer, guverner, from Latin gubernāre, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, govern”).

récompenser.e: Borrowed from Late Latin recompēnsāre, from Latin re + compenso.

refrain.e: Alteration of Old French refrait, past participle of the verb refraindre (based on the verb's infinitive), itself from Vulgar Latin *refrangere, from Latin refringere.

trame.e: Inherited from Old French traime (altered to conform with the verb tramer), from Latin trāma.

maturité.e: Borrowed from Latin mātūritātem. Doublet of mûreté, a now-rare inherited form. By surface analysis, mature + -ité.

littéraire.e: Learned borrowing from Latin litterārius, from littera (whence lettre).

pépin.e: Inherited from Old French pepin, and according to Etymonline, probably from a root like Vulgar Latin *pép(p)-, an expressive creation used to convey smallness.

blocage.e: Inherited from Middle French bloccage. By surface analysis, bloquer + -age.

capitole.e: Learned borrowing from Latin Capitolium. Doublet of capitoul and Chapteuil.

paragraphe.e: Borrowed from Latin paragraphus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos). Doublet of paraphe.

extorsion.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin extortiō.

abbé.e: Inherited from Old French abé, borrowed from Latin abbātem, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶ (abbâ), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Compare English abbot.

éclaire.e: (13th century) Deverbal without suffix of éclaircir, because this plant was reputed to brighten the view.

aléatoire.e: Borrowed from Latin āleātōrius (“relating to a gamester”).

purger.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥ Proto-Italic *pūr? Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu.

dax.e: Borrowed from Occitan Dacs, from Latin Aquae Tarbellicae.

plie.e: Inherited from Late Latin platessa. Cognate with Italian platessa.

ardoise.e: From vernacular Late Latin of Northern France like Vulgar Latin *ardēsia, possibly from Gaulish artuā or Gaulish root *ard(u)- (“high, in altitude”), found also in Ardu-enna (the Ardennes), a region where slate has been…

extension.e: Inherited from Old French estension, borrowed from Latin extentiōnem.

paternité.e: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin paternitātem (“paternity, fatherhood”), from paternus (“relating to a father, paternal”) + -itās, from pater (“father”).

européen.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek Εὐρώπᾱ (Eurṓpā) Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Ancient Greek -ῐος (-ĭos) Ancient Greek Εὐρωπαῖος (Eurōpaîos)bor.

vautour.e: Inherited from Old French voltur, voutour, from Classical Latin vulturem. Compare Old Italian avvoltore, Catalan and Occitan voltor.

vipère.e: ], from Old French vipre, directly borrowed from Latin vīpera. Displaced an earlier Old French doublet guivre (cf. also French vouivre) and its Old Northern French equivalent wivre.

cabaret.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kh₂em-der. Proto-Indo-Iranian *kmáratider. Proto-Iranian *kamarāder. Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára)bor. Latin camerader. Old Northern French cambereteder.

carrosse.e: Borrowed from Italian carrozza. An older form carroche was borrowed from the older Italian carroccia.

intellectuel.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin intellēctuālis. Morphologically, from intellect + -uel. Cognate to English intellectual.

sanglier.e: Inherited from Old French sengler, from Vulgar Latin *singlāris, inherited from Latin singulāris (porcus) (literally “solitary pig”), with later substitution of the suffix -ier for -er.

vielle.e: Compare Old Occitan viola (modern Occitan viula). Possibly ultimately from Medieval Latin vitula. Compare also Catalan, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish viola, Spanish vihuela.

insu.e: Inherited from Middle French adjective insceu (“unknown”), corresponding to in- + su.

ravisseur.e: From raviss(ant) (stem of the present participle of ravir) + -eur.

thune.e: Of unclear origin; perhaps from Tunes, an obsolete form of Tunis. The semantic development went from "alms" to "five-franc coin" to "money".

radeau.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan radel, a diminutive of rat, itself from Latin ratis (“raft”).

paume.e: From Middle French paulme, from Old French paume, palme, from Latin palma, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂. Doublet of palme (“palm leaf”).

discrimination.e: Borrowed from Latin discrimīnātiōnem. By surface analysis, discriminer + -ation.

saveur.e: Inherited from Old French savor, savour, inherited from Latin sapōrem (“taste, flavour”).

clarté.e: Inherited from Middle French clarté f, inherited from Old French clarté f, borrowed from Latin clāritātem f.

casserole.e: Inherited from Middle French casserolle. By surface analysis, casse (“container, recipient”) + -erole (diminutive suffix), a form of -ole lengthened with -er-.

troll.e: From Swedish troll, from Old Norse troll, from Proto-Germanic *truzlą, from Proto-Indo-European *dreh₂-.

alchimie.e: From Old French alkimie, borrowed from Medieval Latin alchēmia.

quadrant.e: Borrowed from Latin quadrantem (“fourth part of something, quarter”).

pulsion.e: Borrowed from Latin pulsiōnem, from pulsus.

baril.e: Inherited from Middle French baril, from Old French baril, bareil (“barrel”), of uncertain origin.

sarcastique.e: Coined after sarcasme. The Modern Greek word σαρκαστικός (sarkastikós) is a borrowing from French.

tech.e: Borrowed from Catalan Tec. Attested on the Cassini map (1740s).

gaston.e: First recorded for medieval French aristocracy, of disputed origin, possibly from Germanic gast "guest".

ulysse.e: Borrowed from Latin Ulyssēs. The Roman name is commonly used for the Greek character, perhaps because a Greek-derived name would be rendered identically to Odyssée (“Odyssey”).

créativité.e: Calque of English creativity, from créatif + -ité.

paddy.e: Borrowed from English paddy, from Malay padi.

cosmique.e: From Ancient Greek via Latin - see cosmic.

charrette.e: From Middle French charrete, from Old French charrete; from char + -ete (diminutive).

grande-bretagne.e: Inherited from Old French Grant Bretaigne, itself a calque of Latin Britannia Maior.

fade.e: From Vulgar Latin *fatidus, blend of Latin fatuus and vapidus.

considérable.e: From the verbe considérer with the suffix -able.

originaire.e: From the Latin orīginārius. Equivalent to origine + -aire.

lotus.e: Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

lutin.e: Inherited from Middle French luitin (“mischievous demon”), a variation (with change of suffix) of older luiton, luitun (“marine monster”), itself an alteration (probably after Old French luitier (“to fight”)) of Old Fre…

rêne.e: Inherited from Old French resne, redne, from Early Medieval Latin retina, ultimately from Latin retinere (“hold back, restrain”).

laveur.e: From laver + -eur. Cf. also Latin lavator. Compare Spanish lavador, Italian lavatore.

bille.e: Inherited from Middle French bille, from Old French bille (“small ball”), from Medieval Latin billia, from Frankish *bikkil (“ossicle, a die, talus”).

chevet.e: Inherited from Old French chevez, from Latin capitium.

merveilleusement.e: From merveilleuse + -ment, compare Old French merveillusement.

charlatan.e: From Middle French charlatan, from Old Italian ciarlatano. Pejorative meaning first recorded 1668.

maquiller.e: Inherited from Middle French macquiller (“to work, do”): * partly from Old French *makier (“to build, make”), from Frankish *makjan, *makōn or Old Dutch macōn (“to make, do”), both from Proto-West Germanic *makōn (“to b…

ouvrage.e: From Old French ovraige, ovrage, from Vulgar Latin *operāticum, from Latin opera. Cognate to Bourguignon ovraige.

charabia.e: Attested since at least 1838, originally to denote the incomprehensible talk of Auvergnats. The further etymology is uncertain. It's believed to possibly mimick a perceived Auvergnat pronunciation of /s/ as /ʃ/.

sanglant.e: Inherited from Late Latin sanguilentus, alternative form of sanguinolentus (whence sanguinolent).

devin.e: Inherited from Old French devin, inherited from Latin dīvīnus (“prophetic”). Doublet of divin.

courtier.e: From Old French courre (“to run”) (compare Modern French courir) + -etier.

murmurer.e: Inherited from Old French murmurer, borrowed from Latin murmurāre.

croissant.e: Present participle of the verb croître (“to increase, to grow”). From Old French croisant, from earlier creissant, from Latin crēscentem, present active participle of crēscō (“to augment”).

schtroumpf.e: Coined by Peyo, probably from German Strumpf (“stocking, sock”), which is not semantically related, but peculiar and “funny sounding” to the French ear because of the unfamiliar combinations of consonants.

astrid.e: Borrowed from modern Scandinavian (Swedish, Norwegian, Danish) Astrid.

baptiste.e: Inherited from Old French baptiste, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptista, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs).

lustre.e: Borrowed from Latin lūstrum (“purification celebrated every few years; a period of five or four years”).

communion.e: Inherited from Old French comunion, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin communiōnem, from Latin communis.

pilier.e: With a change of suffix, from Old French piler, from Vulgar Latin *pilāre, from Latin pila.

sabot.e: Inherited from Middle French savate (“old shoe”), of unknown origin.

pécheur.e: Inherited from Old French pecheor, inherited from Latin peccātōrem. By surface analysis, pécher + -eur.

superficiel.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin superficiālis. By surface analysis, superficie + -el.

aggraver.e: Learned borrowing from Latin aggravāre. By surface analysis, a- + grave + -er.

mémorable.e: Inherited from Middle French mémorable, itself borrowed from Latin memorābilis.

alphabet.e: Borrowed from Late Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha) (Α,α) and βῆτα (bêta) (Β,β) (the first two letters of the Greek alphabet), from Phoenician aleph 𐤀 (ʾ, “ox”) and beth 𐤁…

illico.e: Borrowed from Latin īlicō (“on the spot”), from in + ablative of locus (“place”).

surgir.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Italic *supo Latin sub Latin sub- Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *h₃réǵeti Proto-Italic *regō Latin regō Latin subrigō Latin surri…

distinction.e: Inherited from Old French distinction (attested from the 12th century), borrowed from Latin distinctiōnem.

sweat.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English sweatshirt.

camouflage.e: Etymology tree French camoufler Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos Proto-Italic *-ātos Latin -ātus Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos La…

énergétique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐνεργητικός (energētikós).

crasse.e: Feminine of the Old French adjective cras, from Latin crassus. Doublet of gras.

domination.e: From Latin dominātiōnem (“rule, dominion”), from dominor (“domineer; rule”).

alexandra.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀλεξάνδρα (Alexándra). Feminine form of Alexandre.

vieillesse.e: From Middle French vieillesse. By surface analysis, vieil + -esse. Compare Catalan vellesa, Spanish vejez, Italian vecchiaia.

thermique.e: From Ancient Greek θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) with suffix -ique.

boche.e: Either directly from tête de boche (“stubbornhead”), perhaps derived from caboche (“head”); or shortened from alboche, an alternation of allemand (“German”) influenced by tête de boche or the element -boche in rigolboch…

prolonger.e: Borrowed from Latin prolongāre. Cf. also Old French porloignier.

marguerite.e: From Latin margarīta (“pearl”), from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs).

coupon.e: From couper + -on. Compare Italian tagliando (“coupon, voucher”) from tagliare (“to cut”) for a similar semantic shift.

baptiser.e: Inherited from Middle French baptiser, from Old French baptisier, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptīzāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτῑ́ζω (baptī́zō, “to immerse, to baptize”).

blanchir.e: Inherited from Old French blanchir, from Vulgar Latin *blancīre, a verb based on Frankish *blank.

meuble.e: e. real estate). Doublet of mobile.

far.e: Probably to be linked to Late Latin farsus (past participle of farciō (“to cram, stuff”)), whence French farce (“stuffing”) and Old French fars (“stuffed”), perhaps with influence from Latin far (“farro, emmer wheat”),…

barge.e: Variant of barje, clipping of barjot, verlan form of jobard.

psychique.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ψυχικός (psukhikós, “of or relating to life or the soul”).

mûre.e: From an alteration of Old French meure, from Vulgar Latin *mōra, from Latin mōrum, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).

licencier.e: From Middle French licencier, licensier, licentier, borrowed from Medieval Latin licentiō.

cholestérol.e: From cholestérine, from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ, “gall, bile”) + στερεός (stereós, “firm, solid”); coined in 1816 by Michel Eugène Chevreul.

confisquer.e: From Latin cōnfiscāre (“declare property of the fisc”).

avide.e: Borrowed from Latin avidus (“greedy; eager; hungry”), from aveō (“wish, desire, long for, crave”).

elfe.e: Borrowed from Swedish älf, from Old Norse alfr, compare Old English ælf. Originated from Indo-European Proto-Indo-European *h₂elbʰós (“brilliant, shining white”) via Proto-Germanic *albiz (“elf”).

arabie.e: From Latin Arabia; alternatively from arabe + -ie.

plouc.e: Borrowed from Breton plouk, from Breton ploue. First attested in c. 1880s.

athènes.e: Learned borrowing from Latin Athēnae, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀθῆναι (Athênai).

clique.e: From Old French cliquer, of imitative origin.

fissure.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin fissūra.

bijouterie.e: From bijou (“piece of jewelry”) + -erie, with intrusive -t-.

chausser.e: Inherited from Old French chaucier, inherited from Latin calceāre.

nostalgie.e: Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “a return home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain, suffering”) as a calque of German Heimweh.

tchoque.e: Possibly imitative of the bird's call.

thorne.e: The municipality is named after the English market town of Thorne.

nouveauté.e: Inherited from Old French novelté. By surface analysis, nouveau + -té.

épeler.e: Inherited from Old French espeler, from earlier espelir, from Frankish *spellôn, from Proto-Germanic *spellōną. Compare English spell and Dutch spellen.

douille.e: Inherited from Middle French douille, from Old French doile, doelle (“the hollow part of a tool where the handle is fixed”), from Frankish *dollī, *dullī (“hollow tube, pipe”), from Proto-Germanic *dulją (“pipe”), from…

sarcasme.e: Borrowed from Late Latin sarcasmus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós).

judicieux.e: A scholarly, and adjectival, derivation ultimately based upon Latin iudicō.

pollution.e: Learned borrowing from Latin pollūtiō. By surface analysis, polluer + -tion.

climatique.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κλιματικός (klimatikós), from κλῐ́μᾰ, κλῐ́μᾰτος (klĭ́mă, klĭ́mătos). By surface analysis, climat + -ique.

fertilité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin fertilitās. By surface analysis, fertile + -ité.

paupière.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *palpetra, variant of Latin palpebra.

canular.e: Originally student slang, from pseudo-Latin canularium, from canula, 1913.

cadenas.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan cadenat, from Late Latin catēnātum, derived from Latin catēna (“chain”). Doublet of chaîné.

sponsor.e: Borrowed from English sponsor, from Latin spōnsor.

hic.e: From Latin hic est quaestio (“here is the question”).

sicile.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek Σῐ́κελος (Sĭ́kelos) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-i-eh₂ Proto-Hellenic *-íā Ancient Greek -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā) Ancient Greek Σικελία (Sikelía)der.

osseux.e: From os + -eux, or Late Latin ossuōsus, from Latin os.

lacs.e: Inherited from Middle French lacs, respelling (after related lacer, lacet) of older laz, las, from Old French laz, las, lais, lace, from Latin laqueus.

éloge.e: Borrowed from Latin ēlogium, later influenced by confusion with eulogia (“eulogy”).

dessein.e: Deverbal of Middle French desseigner (see dessiner). Doublet of dessin and design.

inestimable.e: Etymology tree Middle French in- Old Latin aestumō Latin aestimōlbor.

combustion.e: Inherited from Middle French combustion, from Old French combustion, from Latin combustiōnem.

préoccupation.e: Borrowed from Latin praeoccupātiōnem, composed of prae- and occupātiō.

râler.e: From earlier raller, from Middle French rasler (“to haggle, bargain for”). Doublet of racler.

sphère.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphēra. Replaced Old French espere, from the same Latin source.

sosie.e: From the Latin name Sosia. Compare Italian sosia, Spanish sosias and Portuguese sósia.

espérance.e: From espérer + -ance (Middle French and Old French esperance), or possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns. Compare Italian speranza, Spanish esperanza, Catalan esperança.

régional.e: From région + -al. See also Latin regiōnālis.

ain.e: Named after the River Ain, from Medieval Latin Hinnis, from earlier Igneus, of pre-Roman, probably Celtic, origin; perhaps Proto-Celtic *inn, itself likely related to the river River Inn (Latin Aenus), both related to *…

compréhensif.e: Borrowed from Late Latin comprehēnsīvus, from Latin comprehendō.

bowman.e: The name of the municipality is derived from the English surname Bowman. The municipality is named after early inhabitant and landowner Baxter Bowman.

démocratique.e: Inherited from Middle French democratique (“relating to democracy, democratic”), learned borrowing from Late Latin democraticus (“relating to democracy, democratic; democrat”), from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐκός (dēmokrătĭ…

décret.e: Inherited from Old French decré, decret, borrowed from Latin dēcrētum.

neuvième.e: Inherited from Old French neufyesme. By surface analysis, neuf + -ième.

piètre.e: Inherited from Old French piestre, peestre, paëstre, inherited from Latin pedestrem. Doublet of pédestre and perhaps pitre.

brusque.e: Borrowed from Italian brusco. Doublet of brusc.

bordeaux.e: Inherited from Middle French Bordeaulx, from Occitan Bordèu, from Old Occitan Bordel, from Latin Burdigala, from a Proto-Celtic root.

water.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of water-closet.

perche.e: Inherited from Old French perche, from Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē).

guichet.e: Inherited from Old French, a diminutive of Old Norse vík (“bay”). Compare English wicket, ultimately from the same source through Old Northern French and/or Anglo-Norman.

malpoli.e: From mal- + poli. The noun is the adjective used substantively.

fugue.e: Ca. 1600, borrowed in the musical sense from Italian fuga, itself a borrowing from Latin fuga. Doublet of fougue (from the inherited Italian cognate). ) may be a new borrowing from the Italian.

initial.e: Inherited from Middle French initial, from Latin initiālis, from initium (“a going in, entrance”).

sérénité.e: From sérène + -ité or borrowed from Latin serēnitātem.

infaillible.e: Borrowed from Late Latin īnfallibilis. By surface analysis, in- + faillible.

rain.e: From Middle French rain, from Old Dutch *rein, *rēn, from Proto-West Germanic *rain (“raised land, baulk, ridge”), from Proto-Germanic *rainaz, *rainō (“baulk, ridge”).

index.e: From Latin index (“pointer, indicator”), from indicō (“point out, show”).

épique.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós), from ἔπος (épos, “word”).

renifler.e: From re- + nifler (“to irritate, annoy”), from the same Germanic root as Italian niffo, niffa (“snout”); related to German Low German Niff (“nose, mouth, bill”), Dutch neb (“nose, beak”), English neb (“nose, beak, face”…

paroi.e: Inherited from Old French paroi, parei, pareit, from Late Latin parētem, from Latin parietem m.

compatir.e: Borrowed from Latin compati, and adapted as a fourth-conjugation French verb, as with the related pâtir.

grandement.e: Regularisation of Old French granment. By surface analysis, grand + -ment.

délégation.e: From déléguer + -ation, or borrowed from Latin delegātiōnem, from delego.

crampe.e: From a Middle French crampe, from Old French crampe, cranpe (“muscular contraction, cramp”), of Germanic origin, either from Frankish *krampō or from Middle Dutch crampe (“cramp”); both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *k…

durable.e: Learned borrowing from Latin dūrābilis. Morphologically, from durer + -able.

molécule.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin mōlēcula (“molecule”), diminutive of Latin moles (“(a) mass”). See mole.

précoce.e: 17th century, borrowed from Latin praecox. Doublet of abricot.

sortilège.e: Inherited from Old French, from Medieval Latin sortilegium, from Latin sortilegus (“sorcerer, diviner”), from sors (“sort”) + legere (“choose”).

novice.e: Inherited from Middle French novice, from Old French novice, borrowed from Late Latin novīcius, novīcia (“one who has newly entered a monastery or a convent”), from Latin novīcius, novītius (“new, newly arrived”), from…

polaire.e: Inherited from Middle French polaire, from Medieval Latin polāris (“relating to poles”), from Latin polus (“pole or end of an axis”), from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “sky, pivot or axis of a sphere”), from Proto-Indo-E…

pieux.e: Inherited from Middle French pieux, from Old French piu(s) (later changed on the basis of adjectives ending in -eux), from Latin pius.

poilu.e: From poil + -u; compare Spanish peludo. The figurative sense entered the language through French military slang.

hibou.e: Ultimately imitative. Possibly from or influenced by a descendant of Proto-West Germanic *hūō. Compare Old High German hūwo, ūvo, (h)ūwila and, as a borrowing into Romance, Catalan òbila, òliba.

rabais.e: Deverbal from rabaisser. Akin to Italian ribasso.

auxiliaire.e: Borrowed from Latin auxiliāris, from auxilium (“help”).

ravin.e: From ravine or raviner, from Old French ravine, from Latin rapīna.

carcasse.e: Unknown. Perhaps related to Old French charcois.

huissier.e: Inherited from Old French ussier, from uis (“door”) + -ier (suffix denoting occupation), or inherited from Latin ostiārius. Doublet of ostiaire.

mendiant.e: From the present participle of mendier, corresponding to Latin mendīcantem. Compare English mendicant, Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese mendicante.

euphémisme.e: From Late Latin euphemismos (“euphemism”), from Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός (euphēmismós), from εὐφημίζω (euphēmízō), from εὔφημος (eúphēmos, “uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (eû,…

élaborer.e: Borrowed from Latin ēlabōrāre. Cognate with Italian elaborare, Spanish elaborar.

atome.e: Inherited from Middle French athome, borrowed from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos).

amos.e: The city is named after Alice Gouin (né Amos; 1868–1940), the wife of prime minister of Québec Lomer Gouin (1861–1929).

fainéant.e: From feignant, the present participle of feindre (“to fake, to feign”), remotivated by folk etymology in fait (“does”) + néant (“nothing”).

mayonnaise.e: Possibly named after the city Maó, Minorca, whence the recipe was brought back to France.

déborder.e: From dé- + bord + -er. Cognate with Catalan and Spanish desbordar.

draper.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French draper (“to drape", also, "to full cloth”), from drap (“cloth, drabcloth”), from Late Latin drappus, drapus (“drabcloth, kerchief”), a word first recorded in the Capitularie…

brandir.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French brandir.

ulcère.e: Learned borrowing from Latin ulcus, ulceris.

pantin.e: Alteration of Middle French pantine, from pan (“piece of fabric”) + suffix -ine.

syrie.e: Inherited from Middle French Syrie, from Latin Syria, from Ancient Greek Συρία (Suría).

bled.e: Borrowed from Algerian Arabic, from Arabic بِلَاد (bilād).

glacier.e: Borrowed from Franco-Provençal gllaciér. First attested in 1757. Cognate with German Gletscher.

gênes.e: From Latin Genua, whence also Italian Genova.

jument.e: From Old French jument, from Latin iūmentum.

gendarme.e: Singular extracted from plural gendarmes, which arose as a re-spelling of gens d'armes (“people of arms", "armed people”).

hostilité.e: Inherited from Middle French hostilité (attested from 1353), borrowed from Latin hostilitātem.

cupidité.e: Borrowed from Latin cupiditātem. Compare the inherited Old French coveitié. Compare also convoitise, convoiter, from related inherited roots.

berry.e: Inherited from Latin Biturigum, genitive plural of Bituriges, the name of a Celtic tribe. The municipality is named after the Régiment de Berry.

pantoufle.e: Inherited from Middle French pantofle, pantophle, pantouffle, pantoufle, pantouphle, of unclear origin, often considered to be from Italian pantofola.

inondation.e: From Old French inundacion, from Latin inundātiōnem.

trinquer.e: Inherited from Middle French trinquer (ca. 1400), from Middle High German trinken, from Old High German trinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan, from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną. Cognate with English drink.

pendule.e: Clipping of Middle French funependule, a borrowing from Latin funependulus, from the ablative of funis + pendulus.

décapiter.e: Borrowed from Late Latin dēcapitāre, literally, “to de-head”.

variété.e: Inherited from Middle French varieté, borrowed from Latin varietātem.

expérimental.e: Inherited from Middle French experimental, borrowed from Latin experīmentālis.

extrémité.e: Etymology tree Latin extrēmus Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Proto-Italic *-tāts Latin -tās Latin extrēmitāsbor.

accessible.e: Borrowed from Late Latin accessibilis (“accessible”), from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”).

islande.e: Borrowed from Icelandic Ísland, from Old Norse íss (“ice”) + land (“land, country”).

nique.e: Inherited from Middle French nique, from Old French nic, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *hnukēn, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hnukāną (“to be bent, wrinkle”), similar to Swedish nyck (“whim, fancy”).

péri.e: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پری (peri), from Persian پری (pari).

périr.e: Inherited from Middle French perir, from Old French perir, from Latin perīre.

indication.e: From Latin indicātiōnem. By surface analysis, indiquer + -ation.

coroner.e: Borrowed from English coroner. First attested in 1624.

interrogation.e: Borrowed from Latin interrogātiōnem. By surface analysis, interroger + -ation.

perplexe.e: Borrowed from Latin perplexus, composed by per- + plexus, past participle of the verb plectere.

pénitence.e: Borrowed from Latin paenitentia. Compare the inherited Old French peneance, penance.

cannabis.e: Borrowed from Latin cannabis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). Doublet of chanvre.

galactique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin galacticus (“milky”), from Ancient Greek γαλακτικός (galaktikós).

hamster.e: Borrowed from German Hamster and ultimately of Balto-Slavic origin.

brouiller.e: Inherited from Middle French brouiller, from Old French brouiller, from Vulgar Latin *brodiculāre, from *brodicāre (compare Lombard brodigar (“to soil, pollute”)), from Late Latin brodium (“broth, stew, mixture”), from…

lavabo.e: Borrowed from Latin lavābō (“I will wash”), first-person singular future active indicative of lavō, lavāre (“wash, bathe”, verb).

assembler.e: Inherited from Old French asembler, from Latin assimulāre. See also assimiler, a borrowed doublet.

synthétique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συνθετικός (sunthetikós).

barbu.e: Inherited from Old French barbu, from Vulgar Latin *barbūtus (“bearded”). By surface analysis, barbe (“beard”) + -u.

cobaye.e: Learned borrowing from taxonomic name Cavia cobaya.

jaguar.e: From Portuguese jaguar, from Old Tupi îagûara.

orge.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin hordeum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰr̥sdeyom (“bristly”).

commandeur.e: Inherited from Middle French commandeur, from Old French comandeor. By surface analysis, commander + -eur.

ventilateur.e: Borrowed from English ventilator, calque of Latin ventilātōrem. By surface analysis, ventiler + -ateur.

déraper.e: Inherited from Middle French dialectal déraper (“to tear at”), from Occitan derapar, derrabar (“to tear, uproot”), from de- + rapar (“to seize, remove”), from Gothic *𐍂𐌰𐍀𐍉𐌽 (*rapōn, “to snatch, steal”), from Proto-…

déserter.e: Borrowed from Late Latin dēsertāre, from Latin dēsertus.

noirceur.e: Etymology tree French noir Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *-ōs Proto-Italic *-ōs Latin -ōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French noirceur From noir + -eur.

fondement.e: From Old French fondement, from Latin fundamentum.

amertume.e: Inherited from Latin amāritūdinem. Equivalent to amer + -tume.

ration.e: Learned borrowing from Latin ratiō. Doublet of raison, which was inherited.

aigu.e: Inherited from Middle French aigu, agu, from Old French agu, from Latin acūtus (“sharp”); related to English acute.

assignation.e: From Old French assignacion, from Latin assīgnātiō.

astéroïde.e: Borrowed from English asteroid, itself a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀστεροειδής (asteroeidḗs).

parchemin.e: Inherited from Old French parchemin, from Vulgar Latin *pergamīnus, from Late Latin pergamēna.

paries.e: Borrowed from Occitan Paries. Most prevalent in Pyrénées-Atlantiques department. Possibly related to Pariès.

purgatoire.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūrgātōrium (“cleansing”). By surface analysis, purger + -atoire.

avoine.e: From Old French aveine, from Latin avēna (“oats”).

fracas.e: Probably an independent derivation from fracasser, from Italian fracassare. Alternatively directly borrowed from Italian fracasso, from the same verb.

universel.e: Inherited from Old French universal, a borrowing from Latin ūniversālis.

élémentaire.e: Learned borrowing from Latin elementarius. By surface analysis, élément + -aire.

milord.e: Borrowed from English my Lord. See also milady.
