traceur.e: Etymology tree French tracer Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -(ā)tōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French traceur From tracer + -eur.

boucan.e: From obsolete verb boucaner (“to imitate the sound of the goat”), from bouc (“goat”). Compare with Italian baccano.

biographie.e: From bio- + -graphie, from Latin biographia, from Ancient Greek βιογραφία (biographía), composed by βίος (bíos, “life”) + γράφω (gráphō, “write”).

inhumain.e: Learned borrowing from Latin inhūmānus. By surface analysis, in- + humain.

gland.e: Inherited from Old French glant, from Latin glandem.

hypocrisie.e: Inherited from Middle French ypocrisye, from Late Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “acting on the stage, pretense”).

redresser.e: From Old French redrecier. By surface analysis, re- + dresser.

illustre.e: From Latin illustris (“bright, shining, brilliant, lustrous; clear, lucid; illustrious, distinguished, famous”), from illūstrō (“to illustrate”).

frousse.e: From onomatopoeic frou- (see frou-frou), elongated by an "s" to show the fear caused by a sudden noise.

omettre.e: Inherited from Middle French, borrowed or adapted from Latin omittere, based on French mettre.

rapidité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin rapiditās. By surface analysis, rapide + -ité.

naval.e: Inherited from Middle French naval, from nāvālis (“of ships”), from nāvis (“ship”) (whence nef).

bougre.e: From Old French bogre (“heretic”) (1172), also bogresse (“person who indulges in unnatural debauchery”) (1260), from Late Latin Bulgarus (“Bulgarian”), from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ).

glacial.e: Learned borrowing from Latin glaciālis. Morphologically, from glace + -ial.

modestie.e: Borrowed from Latin modestia. Morphologically, from modeste + -ie.

diva.e: From Italian, from Latin, the feminine form of dīvus (“divine one; deified mortal”).

chaudière.e: Inherited from Old French chaudiere, from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”).

ivoire.e: From Old French, from Latin eboreus, from ebur.

puceau.e: From Old French pucel, from the feminine pucele.

brancard.e: From branc, masculine form of branche (“branch”), with noun suffix -ard.

croquer.e: From Middle French croquer, crocquer, from Old French crokier (“to slap, hit, strike”), probably a variant of the same verb represented by Modern French craquer (“to break, crack, crunch”). More at craquer.

iceberg.e: Borrowed from English iceberg, from Dutch ijsberg (literally “ice mountain”).

étable.e: Inherited from Middle French estable, from Old French estable, from Latin stab(u)la pl.

élargir.e: From Middle French eslargir. By surface analysis, é- + large + -ir.

livrée.e: From Old French livree. Cognate with English livery.

musculaire.e: From Latin musculus + -aire, or borrowed from Medieval Latin or New Latin muscularis.

sacoche.e: Borrowed from Italian saccoccia, from sacco.

maritime.e: Inherited from Middle French maritime, borrowed from Latin maritimus (“of the sea”), from mare (“sea”). Doublet of Maremme.

seigneurie.e: From Middle French, from Old French signorie. Equivalent to seigneur + -ie.

prévision.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin praevisiō, from praevideō.

désarmer.e: From Middle French desarmer, from Old French desarmer. By surface analysis, dés- + armer.

déduire.e: Borrowed from Latin dēdūcere, on the model of conduire (from condūcere).

variole.e: From Middle French (plural variolez attested), borrowed from Occitan variola or directly from Medieval Latin variola, itself derived from Latin varius.

fiesta.e: Borrowed from Spanish fiesta. Originally Parisian slang. Doublet of fête.

tourmente.e: Inherited from Latin tormenta, plural of tormentum.

réconciliation.e: Learned borrowing from Latin reconciliātiō. By surface analysis, réconcilier + -ation.

copenhague.e: Ultimately from Danish København, from Old Danish Køpmannæhafn.

azote.e: From Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + ζωή (zōḗ, “life”), coined by Antoine Lavoisier.

sot.e: Inherited from Middle French sot, from Old French sot, from Medieval Latin sottus (“foolish”), of uncertain ultimate origin. Possibly an expressive interjection, similar to modern zut! ”).

boiteux.e: From Old French boistous or from boiter, from Old French botter, débotter (“dislocate”).

coûteux.e: From coût + -eux. Compare Italian and Spanish costoso.

camping-car.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from camping + car. Compare Japanese キャンピングカー.

véto.e: Learned borrowing from Latin vetō (“to oppose”).

offrande.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin offerenda, from Latin offerendus (literally “to be offered”), gerundive of offerō (“to offer”). Compare Catalan ofrena, Occitan and Romansh ufrenda, Portuguese oferenda, Spanish ofrenda.

renouveler.e: From Old French renouveler. Equivalent to re- + nouvel + -er.

savourer.e: Inherited from Old French savourer, from savour. Compare with the noun saveur.

es: ni le viene ni le va

narcotique.e: Inherited from Old French narcotique, borrowed from Medieval Latin narcōticus.

propulsion.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsiōnem, from Latin propulsus.

rossignol.e: From Old Occitan rossinhol (cf. Catalan rossinyol), from Vulgar Latin *lusciniolus, masculine diminutive of Latin luscinia (“nightingale”).

déluge.e: Inherited from Old French deluge, borrowed from Latin dīluvium.

forain.e: Inherited from Old French forain, from Vulgar Latin *forānus (“outsider”), from Latin forīs (“outside”). Assimilated to foire (“fair”) (which is from Latin fēria) through folk etymology.

freiner.e: (1907) From Latin frenare. Equivalent to frein + -er. Cf. also Old French frener, from Latin freno, frenare.

kiosque.e: Borrowed from Italian chiosco, from Ottoman Turkish كوشك (köşk), from Classical Persian کوشْک (kōšk, “palace, portico”), from Middle Persian kwšk' (kōšk).

jargon.e: Inherited from Old French jargon, gargun ("cheeping of birds"), from a root *garg expressing the sound of the throat or referring to it. See gargouille, gargariser, gargoter.

provocation.e: Borrowed from Late Latin provocātiōnem, from Latin provocō.

courtois.e: Inherited from Old French cortois, from Old French cort (whence Modern French cour) and -ois. Compare Czech zdvořilý, German höflich.

wyoming.e: From Munsee xwé:wamənk (literally “at the big river flat”).

dégoût.e: From Middle French desgoust, equivalent to a deverbal from dégoûter.

prostate.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one who stands before”).

cannes.e: Inherited from Old French Canua, possibly related to cane (“reed”). Or, possibly from a pre-Indo-European substrate toponym *kan ("tall, height").

mangeur.e: Etymology tree Latin mandūcō Latin mandūcāre Old French mangier Old French mengier Middle French manger French manger French -eur French mangeur From manger + -eur.

prêteur.e: Inherited from Middle French presteur. By surface analysis, prêter + -eur.

hospice.e: Inherited from Old French hospise, borrowed from Latin hospitium.

larbin.e: Perhaps from an alteration of habin (“dog”), with agglutination of definite article.

pornographie.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πορνογράφος (pornográphos).

philippines.e: Philippe + -ine + -s, a calque of Spanish Filipinas, using the pet form of Filipe (“Philip”) (French: Philippe), named after the King of Spain, Philip II.

berner.e: Inherited from Old French bren (“bran, excrement”), with metathesis (circa 1480s), having first had the meaning of "vanner le blé" or the scatological meaning of "fouiller d'excréments" present in Rabelais' writings.

banquette.e: Borrowed from Italian banchetta, diminutive of banca (“bench”).

sandale.e: ], from Ecclesiastical Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion), diminutive of σάνδαλον (sándalon, “sandal”).

encens.e: Inherited from Old French encens, borrowed from Late Latin incēnsum, from Latin incendō.

latte.e: Inherited from Middle French latte, from Old French latte, late, from a Germanic source, probably Frankish *lattu. See also German Latte, Dutch lat, and English lath and lattice.

poutre.e: From Old French poutre, probably from apocope of an earlier *poutrelle, from a Vulgar Latin *pultrella < pulitrella from the feminine of Latin pullitrum, ultimately from pullus (“colt, youngling”).

esquiver.e: Inherited from Middle French esquiver (“to escape”), from Spanish esquivar (“to avoid, reject, elude”), itself from Old French eschiver from Proto-West Germanic *skiuhan, if not formed from esquivo.

félicité.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin fēlīcitās.

minorité.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin minoritās. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English minority. By surface analysis, mineur + -ité.

transparent.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārentem (“transparent”), present participle of transpareō, from Latin trāns + pareō.

repentir.e: Inherited from Middle French repentir, from Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, from Late Latin paenitīre, from Classical Latin paenitēre. Compare English repent.

consommer.e: Derived from Latin cōnsummāre (“to sum up, amount to, finish”), conflated with consumer, from Latin cōnsumere (“to devour, waste, use up”).

portugal.e: Borrowed from Portuguese Portugal, from Latin Portus Cale.

héberger.e: Inherited from Old French herbergier, from Old High German heribergan, from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu (“army camp, shelter”). Related to German beherbergen, English harbour.

garnison.e: Inherited from Middle French garnison, from Old French garnison. By surface analysis, garnir (“to protect”) + -ison.

épine.e: Inherited from Middle French espine, from Old French espine, from Latin spīna, from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp point”).

hépatite.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin hēpatītis, from hēpar (“liver”) + -ītis (suffix denoting diseases characterized by inflammation).

prestation.e: From Latin praestātiōnem, from the verb praestare, from prae (“in front of”) + stare (“to stand”).

escale.e: Borrowed from Italian scala, from Latin scāla. Doublet of échelle, which was inherited.

cramer.e: Borrowed from Occitan cramar, cremar, from Latin cremō. Doublet of crémer.

tenace.e: Learned borrowing from Latin tenāx. Compare inherited Old French tenais.

tyrannie.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin tyrannia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τυραννία (turannía). By surface analysis, tyran + -ie.

clouer.e: From clou (“nail”), or alternatively from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus. Compare Italian chiavare, Catalan clavar.

merle.e: Inherited from Latin merula, the word for the male blackbird being mostly female until the 16th century. Probable influence of the Late Latin masculine form merulus.

saturation.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin saturātiō. By surface analysis, saturer + -ation.

picoler.e: Derived from pic(c)olo, from Italian piccolo.

sécheresse.e: Inherited from Old French secherece, from Vulgar Latin *siccāricia, from Latin siccus (“dry”). By surface analysis, sèche + -eresse.

initiation.e: Inherited from Middle French initiation, borrowed from Latin initiātiō. Morphologically, from initier + -ation.

archevêque.e: Inherited from Old French archevesque, from Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “first, chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”), from ἐπισκοπέω (episkopé…

mœurs.e: Inherited from Latin mōrēs (“ways, character, morals”), the plural of mōs.

trier.e: From Middle French trier, from Old French trier (“to choose, pick out or separate from others, sift, cull”), of uncertain origin. Cognate with Occitan triar. More at English try.

soute.e: From Old Occitan sota, originally a preposition, from Late Latin subtus (“under”).

projeter.e: From Latin prōicere (“to throw forth; to cast out”), from prō- + iacere. By surface analysis, pro- + jeter.

flan.e: Inherited from Old French flaon, from Late Latin fladō (“flat cake”), from Frankish *flaþō (“flat cake”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂t- (“broad, flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to spread out, be broad, be…

orgue.e: Borrowed from Latin organum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon). Doublet of organe, a later borrowing.

donation.e: From Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiōnem.

cerf-volant.e: From cerf (“deer”) + volant (“flying”, present participle of voler, "to fly"), because it is winged, with mandibles that resemble a deer's antlers.

crypte.e: Borrowed from Latin crypta, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ). Doublet of grotte, a borrowing from Italian.

fœtus.e: Learned borrowing from Latin fētus. This spelling is originally a hypercorrection (which already arises in Latin, where foetus is also found), but is today almost the only one in use.

terminus.e: Borrowed from English terminus, from Latin terminus. Doublet of terme.

intégration.e: Learned borrowing from Latin integrātiō. By surface analysis, intégrer + -ation.

pommade.e: Borrowed from Italian pomata, from pomo (“apple”), as such ointments were originally made from apples, from Latin pōmum.

mayo.e: The municipality is named after County Mayo in Ireland (derived from Irish via English).

rôder.e: Borrowed from Old Occitan rodar, from Latin rotāre. Doublet of rouer.

tige.e: Etymology tree substrate? Latin tībia Old French tige French tige Inherited from Old French tige, from Latin tībia. Doublet of tibia (“shin”), which was borrowed.

ukraine.e: Borrowed from Ukrainian Украї́на (Ukrajína) or Russian Украи́на (Ukraína), from Old East Slavic оукраина (ukraina).

extradition.e: Formed in French from Latin ex- (“out of”) + trāditiō (“handing over”).

procuration.e: Inherited from Middle French procuration, from Old French procuracion, from Latin prōcūrātiōnem; by surface analysis, procurer + -ation.

vêtu.e: Inherited from Middle French and Old French vestu.

potable.e: Borrowed from Late Latin pōtābilis, from Latin potō.

céline.e: From Latin Coelīna or Caelīna, name of a fifth century saint, derivative of the Roman gens name Caelius, from caelum (“heaven”). Also a short form of Marceline, a feminine diminutive form of Marcel.

biais.e: Probably borrowed from Old Occitan biais (“oblique direction”), of uncertain origin.

mesquin.e: Borrowed from Italian meschino or Spanish mezquino, both from Arabic مِسْكِين (miskīn).

dépouiller.e: Inherited from Middle French dépouiller, despouiller, from Old French despoillier, from Latin dēspoliāre. Compare Catalan despullar, Romanian despuia.

cratère.e: Borrowed from Latin crātēr, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κρατήρ (kratḗr).

médiatique.e: From média, itself from the Latin media, the nominative plural of medium.

minuteur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mey- Proto-Indo-European *-néwti Proto-Indo-European *minéwti Proto-Italic *minuō Latin minuō Latin minūtabor. Old French minute French minute Proto-Italic *-āzi ▲ Latin -ereinflu.

densité.e: Inherited from Middle French densité, from Old French dempsité, borrowed from Latin dēnsitātem.

restriction.e: Inherited from Middle French restriction, from Old French restriction, borrowed from Late Latin restrictiōnem, from Latin restringō.

occident.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin occidentem.

combustible.e: Etymology tree Latin combustus Middle French combust Middle French -ible Middle French combustible French combustible Inherited from Middle French combustible, from combust (past participle of comburir) + -ible.

hébreu.e: From Old French Ebreu, borrowed from Latin hebraeus.

hideux.e: From Middle French hideux, from Old French hideus, hydus, hisdos (“that which inspires terror”), from hide, hede, hisda (“horror, fear”), from Proto-West Germanic *agisiþu (“horror, terror”), from Proto-West Germanic *a…

t: hız ve gürültü ile yere çalma

bobine.e: Probably from Latin balbus because of the noise it made.

fast-food.e: Borrowed from English fast food. The sense "fast food restaurant" is a pseudo-anglicism.

charpentier.e: From Old French charpantier, carpentier, from Late Latin carpentārius (“carpenter”), from Latin carpentārius (“wagon-maker, carriage-maker”).

vandalisme.e: From vandale + -isme, coined by Henri Grégoire in 1794.

altercation.e: From Middle French altercacion, altercation, from Old French altercation, borrowed from Latin altercātiōnem.

arctique.e: Inherited from Old French arctique, borrowed from Latin arcticus.

antarctique.e: Inherited from Old French antartique, from Latin antarcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀνταρκτικός (antarktikós).

portion.e: Borrowed from Latin portionem (accusative singular of portio).

piller.e: Inherited from Middle French piller, from Old French pillier, derived from Latin pilleus.

couronnement.e: Inherited from Old French coronement. By surface analysis, couronner + -ment.

agricole.e: Borrowed from Latin agricola. Equivalent to agri- + -cole.

fumeur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-mós Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós Proto-Italic *θūmos Proto-Italic *fūmos Latin fūmus Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-Europ…

rhétorique.e: Learned borrowing from Latin rhētoricus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós).

martyre.e: Borrowed from Latin martyrium, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μαρτύριον (martúrion).

percevoir.e: Inherited from Old French percevoir, perceveir, from Vulgar Latin *percipēre, variant form of Classical Latin percipĕre (“to seize, to observe”).

dominion.e: From Middle French dominion, from Latin dominium, with the ending reinterpreted as French -on.

funéraire.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin fūnerārius, from Latin funus.

inaccessible.e: Borrowed from Late Latin inaccessibilis. By surface analysis, in- + accessible.

bombarder.e: From bombarde + -er, from Middle French bombarde, ultimately from Latin bombus.

soprano.e: Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superanus, from Latin super. Doublet of the inherited souverain.

détection.e: Learned borrowing from Latin dētēctiōnem. By surface analysis, détecter + -tion.

body.e: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of English bodysuit.

puéril.e: Borrowed from Latin puerīlis, from puer (“boy, child”).

lavande.e: From Middle French lavande (ca. 1300), ultimately from Medieval Latin lavendula. The French form is said to derive from Italian lavanda, though the latter is attested significantly later.

lunatique.e: Inherited from Old French lunatique, borrowed from Late Latin lūnāticus (“moonstruck”), derived from Latin lūna (“moon”). Replaced the older lunage.

lièvre.e: Inherited from Middle French lievre, from Old French lievre, from Latin leporem.

génocide.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁os Proto-Hellenic *génos Ancient Greek γένος (génos) Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-Europe…

trèfle.e: Inherited from Old French tresfle, from Vulgar Latin *trifolum, from Latin trifolium, calque of Ancient Greek τρίφυλλον (tríphullon). Or taken from the Greek itself. Compare Old French trefeuil.

globule.e: Learned borrowing from Latin globulus. By surface analysis, globe + -ule.

conformément.e: From conforme + -ment. An acute accent is added to the e of conforme to help the pronunciation.

corail.e: From Latin corallium (“coral”), from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion, “coral”).

chochotte.e: Perhaps from chouchoute, feminine equivalent of chouchou (“darling”).

conjurer.e: From Old French conjurer, from Latin coniūrō.

riposte.e: Borrowed from Italian risposta, from the verb rispondere (“to respond”).

phénix.e: ), a borrowing from Latin phoenix. Both the spelling and pronunciation have been relatinized.

démodé.e: From démoder (“to go out of fashion”).

harnais.e: From Old French hernois (“equipment for battle”) et al. from a Germanic root.

aval.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Latin ad Old French a French à Proto-Indo-European *welH-? Latin vallis Old French val French val French aval From à + val.

apéritif.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin aperītīvus (“opening”, adjective).

tanière.e: Inherited from Middle French taisnere, tesniere, derived from Old French taisson (“badger”), from Late Latin taxōnem, itself of Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *þahsuz (compare German Dachs (“badger”)).

contrefaçon.e: Based on the verb contrefaire. Composed of contre- + façon (the latter taken as a noun counterpart to faire).

pègre.e: Uncertain, perhaps related to Latin picāre (“to smear with pitch”).

chronologie.e: From chrono- + -logie, from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) and λόγος (lógos, “word”).

flaque.e: Borrowed from Picard flaque or Norman flaque, from Old Northern French flaque. Compare Old French flache (adjective).

flocon.e: From floc, derived from Latin floccus, + -on.

pochette.e: ], from Old French pochete (“small purse, small bag”), diminutive (with suffix -ete) of puche (“purse, bag”), from Frankish *pokō (“pouch, bag”), from Proto-Germanic *puhô (“bag, pouch”).

charitable.e: From Old French charitable, from charité.

parcelle.e: Inherited from Old French parcelle, from Late Latin particella, diminutive of Latin particula. More-or-less a doublet of particule.

cheng.e: Borrowed from Chinese 程 (chéng)/成 (chéng), etc.

muriel.e: Borrowed from English Muriel, anglicized form of Scottish Gaelic Muireall, from muir (“sea”), from Old Irish muir, from Proto-Celtic *mori, from Proto-Indo-European *móri; + geal (“white, bright”), from Old Irish gel, f…

semence.e: Inherited from Old French semance, semence, from Late Latin sementia, plural of sementium, neuter form derived from Latin sēmentis, itself derived from sēmen (“seed”).

indifférence.e: Borrowed from Latin indifferentia. By surface analysis, indifférent + -ence.

pourchasser.e: From Middle French, from Old French porchacier, from por- + chacier, from Late Latin captiāre (“to capture”), from Latin captāre.

symphonie.e: Borrowed from Latin symphōnia, from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). Doublet of chifonie.

ravoir.e: From Middle French ravoir: equivalent to re- + avoir.

mijoter.e: Borrowed from a western dialectal form like migeotter (“to ripen”), from Old French migoe, murjoe (“provision of food”), probably from a Frankish *mūsgauda, of which the first element would be *mūs (“mouse”).

relire.e: Inherited from Middle French relire, from Old French relire. Equivalent to re- + lire.

vaillant.e: Old present participle of the verb valoir (compare the modern form valant): from Old French vaillant, from Latin valentem.

incompréhensible.e: From in- + compréhensible, or from Middle French incomprehensible.

titrer.e: Inherited from Old French titler, from title, titil, from Latin titulus.

sage-femme.e: From Middle French sage-femme, from Old French sage-femme. By surface analysis, sage (“wise”) + femme (“woman”).

cor.e: Inherited from Old French cor, corn, from Latin cornū, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer-.

incliner.e: Learned borrowing from Latin inclīnāre (“incline, tilt”). Supplanted the inherited Old French encliner.

négligent.e: Borrowed from Latin negligentem, variant of neglegens.

dictature.e: Borrowed from Latin dictātūra, from dictō.

acquisition.e: Inherited from Old French acquisicion, borrowed from Latin acquisītiōnem.

rougir.e: From Old French rogir, from roge + -ir. By surface analysis, rouge + -ir.

carpe.e: From Late Latin carpa, probably from a language of eastern Europe.

pétale.e: From Ancient Greek πέταλον (pétalon), from πέταλος (pétalos, “broad, flat”).

tribal.e: From tribu + -al, possibly influenced by English tribal.

vannes.e: The Roman name was Latin Veneti, a Gaulish/Celtic tribe whose name likely shares a Proto-Indo-European origin with other similar sounding tribes, from Proto-Celtic *wenyā (“kindred, family”), from Proto-Indo-European *w…

érable.e: Inherited from Old French airable, from older arable, from Gallic Vulgar Latin or Late Latin acerābulus, from Latin acer (“maple”) + Gaulish *aballo- (“apple-tree”).

ambulant.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₂énts? Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰíder. Proto-Italic *amβi- Latin ambi- Proto-Indo-European *h₂elh₂-der.

puberté.e: Learned borrowing from Latin pūbertātem. By surface analysis, pubère + -té.

cuve.e: Inherited from Old French cuve, from Latin cūpa. Doublet of coupe, which came through a Late Latin intermediary variant.

armand.e: Cognate to English Herman and German Hermann, possibly also to German Hartmann.

bâche.e: Uncertain; perhaps a shortened form of Old French baschoe, from Latin bascauda (“woven vessel”); more at English basket.

fiole.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek φιάλη (phiálē)der. Latin phiala Late Latin fiolabor.

abriter.e: Inherited from Middle French, derivative of abri, from Old French abri (“a place where one is sheltered from the elements or harm”), from abrier (“to cover”).

justesse.e: Formed from juste + -esse; cf. also Latin iūstitia. Compare Italian giustezza, Spanish and Portuguese justeza, Catalan and Occitan justesa, Galician and Asturian xusteza, Friulian justece. Doublet of justice.

cadence.e: Inherited from Middle French cadence, borrowed from Italian cadenza. Doublet of chance.

agace.e: Inherited from Middle French agace, from Old French agace (“magpie”), from Frankish *agattjā or Old High German agaza (“magpie”), ultimately perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”).

ardent.e: Inherited from Old French ardent, borrowed from Latin ardentem.

soufre.e: Inherited from Middle French soufre, from Old French sulfre, soffre, from Latin sulfur, sulphur, sulphure, from Proto-Indo-European *swelplos, from the root *swel- (“to burn, smoulder”).

gaga.e: Reduplication of the base of gâteux (“senile”)

pinceau.e: From Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin *penicellus, alteration of Latin pēnicillum.

récréation.e: Borrowed from Latin recreātiōnem. By surface analysis, récréer + -ation. In the education sense compare Spanish recreo and Italian ricreazione.

sénile.e: Inherited from Old French senile, borrowed from Latin senīlis (“relating to old age”), from Latin senex (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”).

abstinence.e: Inherited from Middle French abstinence, from Old French abstinence, borrowed from Latin abstinentia.

miniature.e: Borrowed from Italian miniatura. Unrelated to minuscule.

boulanger.e: Inherited from Middle French boulanger, from Old French boulanger, bolengier (“baker”), from Picard Old French boulenc (“bun-maker, bread-maker”), of Germanic origin, from Low Frankish *bollā (“bun”) + -enc (“-ing”), fr…

bagel.e: Borrowed from English bagel, from Yiddish בייגל (beygl); ultimately from Middle High German bouc, boug- (“ring, bracelet”), from Old High German boug (“ring”), from Proto-Germanic *baug- (“ring”) plus *-il (noun suffix).

tonic.e: Borrowed from English tonic, from tonic water.

ronfler.e: Inherited from Middle French ronfler, from Old French ronfler, an expressive word of onomatopoetic origin. Compare Piedmontese romfé, Lombard romfà, Emilian romfè.

infidélité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin īnfidēlitās. By surface analysis, infidèle + -ité.

enclos.e: Past participle of the verb enclore. Corresponds to Latin inclūsus. Doublet of inclus.

yves.e: Unclear still today, either short form of Germanic or Celtic compound names beginning with iv- "yew" - see Proto-Germanic *īhwaz (“yew”) and Proto-Celtic *iwos (“yew”), both from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyHw- (“yew”).

truand.e: From Transalpine Gaulish *truganto. Cognate to English truant, Irish trogán, Welsh tru.

pionnier.e: Inherited from Middle French pionnier, from Old French peonier (“infantryman”), from peon (“footman”) (modern French pion), from Latin pedōnem.

risée.e: From ris + -ée, from the verb rire.

gobelet.e: From Old French gobel, from Old Occitan gobel (“to swallow up”), from Gaulish *gobbos, from Proto-Celtic *gobbos (“muzzle, snout, beak”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵoph₃o- (“eat”).

mousquetaire.e: Inherited from Middle French. By surface analysis, mousquet + -aire.

bambou.e: Borrowed from Portuguese bambu, from Malay bambu, from Kannada ಬಮ್ಬು (bambu).

léguer.e: Borrowed from Latin lēgāre, from lex (“law”) (whence loi).

entamer.e: From Provençal entamenar, from Latin intaminare, from Latin in- + tangere + -are.

gitan.e: Borrowed from Spanish gitano, itself derived from apheresis of older egiptano (“Egyptian”), from the mistaken belief that gypsies originated from Egypt.

truite.e: From Old French, from Late Latin tructa, possibly from Ancient Greek τρώκτης (trṓktēs).

clavicule.e: Borrowed from Latin clāvicula. Doublet of cheville, which was inherited.

gadget.e: Borrowed from English gadget, itself of French origin.

télépathie.e: From télé- + -pathie, on the model of English telepathy.

anecdote.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνέκδοτος (anékdotos, “unpublished”). Compare inédit.

diffamation.e: Inherited from Old French diffamacion, borrowed from Latin diffāmātiōnem, from diffāmō (“to spread an unfavorable report; to defame, malign, decry”), from dis- + fāma (“report, opinion, reputation”).

truie.e: Inherited from Late Latin troia. Cognate with Italian troia, Occitan truèja, Catalan truja, Walloon troye.

odorat.e: Borrowed from Latin odōrātus. Compare Italian odorato.

tiède.e: ), from Old French *tiede, from earlier *tebde, itself by regular syncope from Latin tepidus. The attested Old French tieve, teve reflects an eastern dialect form without syncope. Doublet of tépide, a borrowing.

coopératif.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin cooperātīvus.

éradiquer.e: Borrowed from Latin ērādicāre. Doublet of arracher, which was inherited.

formel.e: Learned borrowing from Latin formālis, from forma (“form”) (whence forme).

rouille.e: Inherited from Old French reoïlle, from Vulgar Latin *robicla, from syncopation of Latin *robicula, a diminutive of Latin rōbīgō (“rust”) + -cula (from -culus (suffix forming diminutives)).

flair.e: Deverbal from flairer, from Latin flagrare (“to blow”). Cognate to Portuguese cheiro.

saccager.e: From Italian saccheggiare, from sacco, from Latin saccus.

qualification.e: Inherited from Middle French qualification, from Medieval Latin quālificātiō.

infernal.e: Etymology tree Latin īnferna Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālis Latin īnfernālislbor.

diamètre.e: From Latin, from Ancient Greek, analyzable as dia- + -mètre.

croiseur.e: Doublet of croix, crux, and cruiser.

nudité.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin nūditās, from nūdus (whence nu).

beau-fils.e: Inherited from Middle French beau filz. By surface analysis, beau- + fils.

galilée.e: Inherited from Middle French Galilee, from Latin Galilaea, from Ancient Greek Γαλιλαία (Galilaía), from Hebrew הגליל (hagalil).

acolyte.e: Inherited from Old French acolyt, from Ecclesiastical Latin acolytus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, attendant”).

pastèque.e: Borrowed from Portuguese pateca, from Arabic بَطِّيخَة (baṭṭīḵa, “melon, watermelon”).

obséder.e: Learned borrowing from Latin obsideō, obsidēre.

ramoner.e: Inherited from Old French ramoner, ramon (“broom”) + -er.

géographie.e: Borrowed from Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).

hand.e: Clipping of handball. Compare foot from football.

paternel.e: From the stem of the Latin paternus and the suffix -el.

cidre.e: From Old French sidre, from Latin sicera, from Ancient Greek σῑ́κερᾰ (sī́keră), from Hebrew שֵׁכָר (šēḵār), from Proto-Semitic *šikar- (“alcoholic drink”).

ogre.e: Inherited from Old French ogre, itself probably an alteration, with influence from words like bougre, of an earlier form *orc, from Latin Orcus (“the underworld; the god Pluto”), with metathesis.

soucoupe.e: Calque of Italian sottocoppa, from sous (“under”) + coupe.

pinte.e: From Vulgar Latin *pincta (“mark used to indicate level on vessels”), from Latin pictus (“painted”), from Latin pingō (“paint”, verb).

lucratif.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French lucratif, from Latin lucrātīvus (“profitable”).

gourde.e: Inherited from Old French coorde, cohourde, with later voicing of initial c-, from Latin cucurbita. Doublet of courge (from the form cohourge). Compare English gourd.

coalition.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin coalitiōnem, from Latin coalitus (“fellowship, communion”).

matraque.e: From dialectal Arabic مَطْرَق (maṭraq). See Aramaic מטרקא (mṭrqʾ) for more.

épaisseur.e: Etymology tree Latin spissus Old French espés Middle French espés French épais Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *-ōs Proto-Italic *-ōs Latin -ōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur Fr…

soudoyer.e: From Old French soldoier, from solde.

confidence.e: Borrowed from Latin cōnfīdentia. Doublet of confiance.

canette.e: Inherited from Middle French kanete (“vase, pitcher for serving beer”), a diminutive (with suffix -ette) of Medieval Latin cana, canna (“can, jug, vessel”), from Frankish *kanna (“jug, pitcher, can”), from Proto-Germani…

grimer.e: From Middle French grime (“mask”) + -er, from Old French grime, from Frankish *grīmo, from Proto-Germanic *grīmô.

guérisseur.e: From guériss(ant) (stem of the present participle of guérir) + -eur. Inherited from Middle French gariseur.

cil.e: Inherited from Old French cil, from Latin cilium.

atrocité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin atrōcitās. By surface analysis, atroce + -ité.

appendicite.e: Borrowed from English appendicitis. Morphologically, from appendice + -ite.

héréditaire.e: Borrowed from Latin hereditārius. Doublet of héritier.

singer.e: In at least the ape sense, from singe (“monkey”).

orthodoxe.e: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin orthodoxus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “right”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”).

impératif.e: Inherited from Old French imperatif, borrowed from Latin imperātīvus.

fraction.e: Inherited from Old French fraction, borrowed from Latin fractiō.

avalanche.e: Borrowed from Franco-Provençal avalançhe (Savoy), blend of aval (“downhill”) and standard lavençhe, from Vulgar Latin *labanka (compare Occitan lavanca, Italian valanga), alteration of Late Latin lābīna (“landslide”) (c…

corvette.e: From Middle Dutch korf, korver (“a kind of ship”), or Middle Low German korf (“a kind of ship and basket”), + -ette.

moineau.e: Inherited from Old French moinel, equivalent to moine (because of its plumage) + -eau.

préméditation.e: Learned borrowing from Latin praemeditātiō. Morphologically, from préméditer + -ation.

préjudice.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin praeiūdicium (“previous judgment or damage”), from prae- (“before”) + iūdicium (“judgment”).

dicter.e: Borrowed from Latin dictāre. Compare Old French ditier.

compote.e: Inherited from Old French composte, compost, from Latin compostus, syncopated variant of compositus. Doublet of compost and composite.

coiffe.e: Inherited from Middle French coiffe, from Late Latin cofia, from Old High German *kuffia, *kuphia (“little cap”), diminutive of Old High German kuffa, kupha (“hood, cap”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuppu (“round object,…

gourmand.e: From Middle French gourmant (“glutton”), originally an adjectival form, from Old French, where it had the sense of trencherman, but of uncertain ultimate origin.

paradoxe.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin paradoxum, from Latin paradoxa (“things contrary to expectation”), from Ancient Greek παράδοξα (parádoxa).

réincarnation.e: From ré- + incarnation or from réincarner + -ation.

négociateur.e: From négocier + -ateur, or borrowed from Latin negōtiātōrem (“merchant, banker”).

lsd.e: Borrowed from German LSD, initialism of Lysergsäure-diethylamid.

jupon.e: Inherited from Middle French jupon. By surface analysis, jupe + -on.

grimace.e: Inherited from Middle French grimace, from Old French grimace, grimuche (“a contorted or wry face, grotesque countenance”), from grime (“mask”) + -ace (pejorative suffix; from Latin -āceus), from Old Frankish *grīma, *g…

adverse.e: Learned borrowing from Latin adversus (“against, opposite”).

engendrer.e: Inherited from Middle French engendrer, from Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerāre.

pourpre.e: Inherited from Old French, from Latin purpura, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra).

potence.e: Inherited from Old French, borrowed from Latin potentia.

papoter.e: From Old French papier (“to murmur”) (from the onomatopoeic root "papp-", occurring in Latin pappare (“to eat”), having to do with movement of the lips) + -oter.

spontané.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin spontāneus.

cruiser.e: Borrowed from English cruiser. Doublet of croiseur, croix, and crux.

antre.e: Borrowed from Latin antrum, from Ancient Greek ἄντρον (ántron).

enflure.e: Inherited from Middle French enfleure, see enfler + -ure.

fente.e: Attested since the 14th century. Either from Vulgar Latin *findita, feminine of *finditus, as an alternate past participle of Latin findō (normally fissus), or a later formation. Either way equivalent to fendre + -te.

python.e: Unadapted borrowing from English Python, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn).

méduse.e: From Méduse (“Medusa (Greek mythology)”), from Latin Medusa, from Ancient Greek Μέδουσα (Médousa), from μέδω (médō, “rule over”).

régent.e: Borrowed from Latin regente, singular ablative of regēns.

apogée.e: Borrowed from Latin apogaeum, from Ancient Greek ἀπόγειον (apógeion, “away from Earth”), from ἀπό (apó, “away”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

augure.e: Borrowed from Latin augurium. Doublet of heur.

rigide.e: Borrowed from Latin rigidus. Compare the inherited doublets roide and raide.

délicatesse.e: From Middle French delicatesse, equivalent to délicat + -esse, probably modelled on Italian delicatezza.

fatigant.e: Respelling of fatiguant, the present participle of fatiguer.

oral.e: Borrowed from Latin ōrālis, from ōs (“mouth”).

hebdomadaire.e: From Latin hebdomadārius, from Latin hebdomas (English hebdomad), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “seven, group of seven”).

verger.e: Inherited from Middle French vergier, from Old French vergier, from Vulgar Latin *virdiariu, syncopated form of Latin viridiārium, variant of viridārium, from viridis.

efforcer.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, ultimately from Latin fortis (“strong”).

pénétration.e: Learned borrowing from Latin penetrātiō. Synchronically, from pénétrer + -ation.

contretemps.e: From contre- + temps, by calque of Italian contrattempo.

convalescence.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin convalēscentia (“regaining of health”), from Latin convalēscō (“regain health, grow strong”).

incurable.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin incūrābilis. By surface analysis, in- + curable.

proportion.e: Inherited from Old French proportion, borrowed from Latin prōportiōnem.

rhinocéros.e: Borrowed from Latin rhīnocerōs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ῥινόκερως (rhinókerōs).

ardeur.e: Inherited from Old French ardour, ardor, ardur, borrowed from Latin ardorem (according to the TLFi etymological dictionary).

holocauste.e: Inherited from Middle French holocauste, from Old French olocauste, learned borrowing from Late Latin holocaustum, from the neuter form of Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos), from ὅλος (hólos, “whole”) + καυστός (ka…

déployer.e: Inherited from Middle French desployer, from Old French desploier, desploiier, itself from a compound of des- and ploiier, or possibly from Late Latin displicāre, or from Latin dēplicāre (“to unfold”).

adoptif.e: Borrowed from Latin adoptīvus, from adoptō (“to adopt”, literally “to choose for oneself”).

caisson.e: From Old Occitan caisson, from caissa. By surface analysis, caisse + -on.

myrtille.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin myrtillus.

pèlerin.e: Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin pelegrīnus m, a dissimilated form of Classical Latin peregrīnus m. Doublet of pérégrin m, a borrowing.

terril.e: From terre + -is, with spelling change reportedly reflecting Belgian colloquial pronunciation.

goudron.e: Inherited from Middle French goutren, from Old French catran, from Medieval Latin catarannus, from Arabic قَطْرَان (qaṭrān). Form influenced by Middle French goutte (see French goutte).

bouée.e: Partly from Middle Dutch boeye (“life buoy”); and partly continuing Middle French boue(e) (“a flotation signalling danger”), from Old French boue, buie (“a piece of wood or cork floating above an anchor to indicate wher…

purifier.e: Loaned from Latin pūrificāre, from pūrus (“pure; clean”).

bélier.e: From a change of suffix from Old French belin, probably ultimately of Dutch origin, cf. belhamel.

phoque.e: Etymology tree Pre-Greekbor.? Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē)bor. Latin phōcabor.

spéculation.e: First attested circa 1350, borrowed from Late Latin speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor.

joyau.e: Backformed from Old French joyaus, plural of joyal, variant of jouel, from Latin iocale.

anguille.e: ), from Latin anguīlla. The ⟨ll⟩ was originally pronounced /l/ (still found, alongside /ʎ/, until the 17th century).

miséricordieux.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin misericordiōsus . By surface analysis, miséricorde + -eux.

rescousse.e: Inherited from Old French rescusse, nominalised past participle of rescourre, from Latin excutere (“to shake off, drive out”).

apparent.e: Inherited from Old French aparent, aparant, borrowed from Latin appārentem.

erre.e: Possibly a descendant of Latin itinerem (“path”), or alternatively derived from errer (“to wander”).

tatiana.e: Borrowed from Russian Татья́на (Tatʹjána), from Latin Tatiana.

récré.e: Clipping of récréation. Compare Spanish recreo and Italian ricreazione.

pancréas.e: Borrowed from Latin pancreas, from Ancient Greek πάγκρεας (pánkreas).

impuissance.e: From in- + puissance (or possibly from impuissant + -ance).

trique.e: Variant of estrique, from Frankish *strīkan (“to strike”).

gingembre.e: Etymology tree Old Tamil 𑀇𑀜𑁆𑀘𑀺 (iñci) Proto-Dravidian *wēr Old Tamil 𑀯𑁂𑀭𑁆 (vēr) Old Tamil 𑀇𑀜𑁆𑀘𑀺𑀯𑁂𑀭𑁆 (iñcivēr)bor. Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀲𑀺𑀁𑀕𑀺𑀯𑁂𑀭 (siṃgivera)der.

verset.e: Inherited from Old French verset. By surface analysis, vers + -et.

bercail.e: Inherited from Old French bercal, from Vulgar Latin *berbicale, from *berbīx, from Latin vervex (“wether; castrated ram”).

gibbon.e: Brought to Europe from French India by Joseph François Dupleix, probably from an English folk etymology (compare English Gibbon) with an Aslian root.

latex.e: Borrowed from New Latin latex (“clear fluid which is part of a humour or bodily fluid”), a later use of Latin latex (“water; liquid, fluid”).

conversion.e: Learned borrowing from Latin conversiō, from convertō.

prothèse.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πρόσθεσις (prósthesis), where the prefix was confused with pro-.

navigateur.e: Learned borrowing from Latin nāvigātor. By surface analysis, naviguer + -ateur.

somnambule.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin somnambulus (“sleepwalker”), from Latin somnus (“sleep”) + ambulō (“to walk”).

ovale.e: Etymology tree Latin ovō Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālis Medieval Latin ovālisbor. French ovale Borrowed from Medieval Latin ovālis.

absurdité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin absurditās. By surface analysis, absurde + -ité.

ras-le-bol.e: From en avoir ras le bol (“to have had it up to here”, literally “to have a shaven arse (lit. bowl) of it”).

civière.e: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *cibaria, from Latin cibus.

gogo.e: Name of a character in Frédérick Lemaître’s play “Robert Macaire”, ultimately sound-symbolic. Compare gogue.

angélique.e: Borrowed from Latin angelicus, from angelus (“angel”).

supériorité.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin superioritātem, from Latin superior. By surface analysis, supérieur + -ité.

bascule.e: From earlier bacule, which folk etymology altered to bassecule under the influence of basse, feminine of bas (“low”).

basculer.e: Inherited from Old French baculer, from bas + cul + -er. The modern form (with the s pronounced) has been altered under influence of the noun bascule (“seesaw”).

nébuleuse.e: Feminine nominalization of nébuleux (adjective), attested from the 17th century.

doter.e: Borrowed from Latin dōtāre. Doublet of douer.

cathéter.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr, “surgical instrument for emptying the bladder”), from καθίημι (kathíēmi, “to descend, let down”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, suffix forming masculine nouns from verbs) (from Proto-Indo-E…

greffier.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin graphiārius (“scribe, secretary”), from graphium (“stylus”). Compare greffe (“clerk's office”).

bienfaiteur.e: From bienfait + -eur, modeled on Late Latin benefactōrem (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin benefaciō (“benefit someone”), from bene (“good”) + faciō (“do, make”).

significatif.e: Inherited from Middle French significatif, borrowed from Latin significātivus.

recouvrer.e: Inherited from Middle French recouvrer, from Old French recovrer, inherited from Latin recuperāre. Doublet of récupérer, which was borrowed from Latin.

voyeur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *weyd- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Indo-European *widéh₁yeti Proto-Italic *widēō Latin videō Old French veoir Middle Fren…

virgule.e: Borrowed from Latin virgula, diminutive of virga (“rod, branch”).

corbeille.e: Inherited from Middle French corbeille, from Old French corbeille, corbeil, corbele, curbeyle, from Late Latin corbicula, diminutive of Latin corbis (“basket”), probably from Frankish *korb, from Proto-Germanic *kurbaz,…

voûte.e: Inherited from Old French volte, from Vulgar Latin *volta < *volvita or *volŭta, for Latin volūta, from the feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Compare Italian volta; cf.

poulain.e: Inherited from Old French poulain, polain (“baby animal”), from a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin pullāmen, from Latin pullus (“animal young”).

raie.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *pr̥ḱéh₂ Proto-Celtic *ɸrikā Gaulish *ricābor.?

interminable.e: Borrowed from Latin interminābilis. By surface analysis, in- + terminer + -able.

vison.e: Inherited from Old French vison, of uncertain origin. Perhaps borrowed from a Germanic source such as Frankish *wisulā (compare Old High German wisula (“weasel”).

carotide.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek καρωτίς (karōtís), from κάρος (káros, “stupor”).

mulhouse.e: Borrowed from Alemannic German Milhüsa or its source Middle High German Mülnhūsen, from Old High German Mulinhūson; compare German Mülhausen (literally “mill house”).

exaucer.e: Originally a variant spelling of exhausser, from Old French exalcier, from Latin ex- + Vulgar Latin *altiāre, modelled after Classical Latin exaltāre (“raise, extol”).

théorique.e: Borrowed from Latin theōricus, from Ancient Greek θεωρικός (theōrikós). By surface analysis, théorie + -ique.

affût.e: Inherited from Old French affeul, aful (“cannon support”).

niche.e: Inherited from Middle French niche, from Old French niche, deverbal of nichier (“make a nest”), from an unattested verb *nīdicāre, from Latin nīdus (“nest”).

auguste.e: Borrowed from Latin augustus. Doublet of août, which was inherited.

aisément.e: Inherited from Middle French aiseement. By surface analysis, aisé + -ment.

décourager.e: From Middle French descourager (from whence English discourage), from Old French descouragier, from des- and corage.

adepte.e: Borrowed from Latin adeptus, the past participle of adipīscor (“to attain”).

mât.e: Inherited from Middle French mast, from Old French mast, from Early Medieval Latin mastus, from Frankish *mast, from Proto-Germanic *mastaz.

faisceau.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fascellus, diminutive of Latin fascis (“bundle”).

désirée.e: Literally, “desired”. French form of Latin Desideria, feminine form of the saint's name Desiderius (modern French Didier).

terrier.e: Inherited from Old French, from Medieval Latin terrārius (“of earth”) from Latin terra (“earth”); or equivalent to terre + -ier. Most terrier breeds were developed to hunt vermin both over and under the ground.

tourtereau.e: Inherited from Latin turturellus (or turturillus), both diminutives of turtur (“turtle (archaic), turtle dove, turtledove”).

morue.e: From Old French morlue, a compound of Breton mor (“sea”) + Old French lus (“pike”). Cognate with the specific name in Gadus morhua.

guette.e: From guetter or from Old French guaite f, from Medieval Latin wacta f, from Frankish *wahta f.

marmite.e: In Middle French (attested 1388) used in the sense of an earthen or metal cooking-pot; later (17th century) also of bombs or grenades from their resemblance to iron cooking-pots. g. a cooking-pan or a plate). e.

rincer.e: Inherited from Middle French rincer (“to rinse”), from Old French rincer, raïncier (“to rinse, cleanse”). Of contested origin.

leblanc.e: From le blanc, originating as a nickname for a light-skinned man.

indestructible.e: Borrowed from Latin indestructibilis. By surface analysis, in- + destructible.

indemnité.e: Learned borrowing from Latin indemnitās, from indemnis (whence indemne).

ressentiment.e: From ressentir + -ment, verbal root re- + sentir from Old French sentir from Latin sentiō, sentīre (“to feel”).

soudan.e: Borrowed from Arabic سُودَان (sūdān, “black people”, plural of أَسْوَد (ʔaswad)).

gronder.e: From Latin grundīre (“to grunt”), a form of grunnīre.

oseille.e: From Old French oisele, from Latin acidula.

sanctifier.e: ), relatinized form of Old French saintefier, itself either borrowed or inherited from Latin sānctificāre.

biblique.e: From Latin biblicus (“biblical”). By surface analysis, Bible + -ique.

relique.e: Inherited from Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae (“relics”).

escargot.e: From Occitan escargol, alteration of caragol, metathesis of cagaròl, see there for more. Doublet of cagouille.

affront.e: From Old French afront. Synchronically analysable as a deverbal from affronter.

ténébreux.e: First known attestation circa 1100 as tenebrus. Borrowed from Latin tenebrōsus.

normandie.e: Inherited from Old French Normendie, from normant + -ie.

algérie.e: Etymology tree Arabic جَزَائِر بَنِي مَزْغَنَّى (jazāʔir banī mazḡannā)ellip. Arabic الْجَزَائِر (al-jazāʔir)bor.

abbaye.e: Inherited from Middle French abbaïe, from Old French abaïe, from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbatia.

vertueux.e: From vertu + -eux. Cf. also Late Latin virtuōsus. Piecewise doublet of virtuose.

vendetta.e: Borrowed from Italian vendetta, from Latin vindicta. Doublet of vindicte, borrowed from Latin.

colo.e: Clipping of colonie (see colonie de vacances).

entorse.e: Substantivization of Old French entors, passive past participle of the verb entordre.

lama.e: From Spanish llama, from Quechua llama.

échéance.e: From past participle of échoir + -ance, possibly, but less likely, corresponding to a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *excadentia, from *excadens from *excadere, from Latin cadere (“fall”). Compare Italian scadenza.

whiskey.e: Borrowed from English whisky, whiskey, from Irish uisce beatha, Scottish Gaelic uisge-beatha (literally “water of life”).

buste.e: Etymology tree Latin būstum Italian bustobor. French buste Borrowed from Italian busto, from Latin būstum.

tardif.e: Inherited from Old French tardif, from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus.

précéder.e: First known attestation in Middle French as preceder, which is a borrowing from Latin praecedō.

stratagème.e: Inherited from Middle French stratageme, from Old French stratageme, a borrowing from Latin strategema, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (stratḗgēma).

suzuki.e: Borrowed from Japanese Suzuki (Suzuki), from Japanese すずき (Suzuki, “surname”) or Japanese スズキ (Suzuki, “automaker”); from Japanese 鈴木 (Suzuki) (automaker from the surname).

surplus.e: Inherited from Middle French surplus, from Old French sorplus. Equivalent to sur- + plus.

géométrie.e: From géo- + -métrie, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρία (geōmetría, “geometry, land-survey”), from γεωμετρέω (geōmetréō, “to practice or to profess geometry, to measure, to survey land”), from γαία (gaía, “earth, land, countr…

podium.e: Borrowed from Latin podium. Doublet of puy.

dégustation.e: Borrowed from Latin degustātiōnem, from degusto.

aligner.e: Inherited from Middle French aligner, from Old French alignier, from a- + lignier, from Latin lineāre (from linea (“line”)). Equivalent to a- + ligne + -er.

câlisse.e: Quebec eye-dialect spelling of calice (“chalice”). As with other sacres, the semantic shift occurred due to the surrounding taboos on blasphemy in predominantly Catholic Quebec.

rosée.e: Inherited from Old French rosee, rousee, rosede, from a Vulgar Latin *rōsāta (“dew, mist”), from Latin rōs (“dew, moisture”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rṓs.

carabine.e: 1611, alternative spelling charabine late 16th century, from carabin. The meaning "mistress of one of the carabins" is recorded in the dictionary of Guérin (1892).

baume.e: Inherited from Old French basme, from Latin balsamum, a borrowing from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon).

frontal.e: From front + -al; see also Medieval Latin frontalis, from Latin frōns, as well as fronteau and frontail.

cagoule.e: Inherited from Old French cogole, from Latin cucūlla.

radioactif.e: Coined by Pierre Curie and Marie Curie in 1898 from radio- + actif.

amande.e: Inherited from Old French almande, from Vulgar Latin *amend(u)la, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē). Doublet of amygdale and mandorle.

lugubre.e: Learned borrowing from Latin lūgubris (“mournful; gloomy”).

glande.e: Inherited from Old French glandre, from Medical Latin glandula, from glāns, glāndem.

buckingham.e: The district is named after the English town of Buckingham.

mogo.e: Borrowed from a Mande language with a noun meaning “man”.

teinture.e: Inherited from Middle French teinture, from Old French tainture, from Latin tinctūra, from tinctus the perfect passive participle of tingō.

envahisseur.e: From envahiss(ant) (stem of the present participle of envahir) + -eur.

alternatif.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin alternativus, from alternatus, perfect participle of alterno, from Classical Latin alter (“other”).

suceur.e: Etymology tree Latin sūctus Proto-Indo-European *-yetider. Latin -iō Latin *sūctiāre Old French sucer Middle French sucer French sucer French -eur French suceur From sucer + -eur.

lamar.e: From a placename in Normandy, which was derived from Old French la mare (“the pool”).

manigance.e: Origin unknown; the first element is ultimately identical with Latin manus (“hand”).

geneviève.e: From Medieval Latin Genovefa. * Possibly from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, family”) + *wībą (“woman, wife”).

mouette.e: From Middle French mouette, from Old French moette, diminutive of Old French maoe (Anglo-Norman mave, mauve), from Old English mǣw (“seagull”), from Proto-Germanic *maiwaz (“seagull”). Compare mauvis. More at mew.

chimpanzé.e: Borrowed from an unspecified Bantu language.

brasserie.e: From brasser (“to brew”) + -erie, from Old French bracer, from brace (“malt”), from Proto-Celtic *mrakis.

diversité.e: From Middle French diversité, from Old French diversité, from Latin dīversitātem.

calvaire.e: Figurative use of Calvaire, apparently not before the 18th century.

autruche.e: Inherited from Old French ostruce, according to the TLFi, from Vulgar Latin *austrūthiō, from Latin avis (“bird”) + strūthiō (“ostrich”), from Ancient Greek στρουθίων (strouthíōn).

restreint.e: Borrowed or adapted from Latin restrictus, modeled after étreint.

commenter.e: From Latin commentum, from comminisci (“to invent”).

abaisser.e: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French abaissier, from a (“to, towards”) + baissier (“to lower”). See Modern French à, baisser.

abstenir.e: Inherited from Old French abstenir, borrowed from Latin abstinēre (with conjugation adapted to French tenir), from abs + teneō.

récepteur.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re- substratebor.?

accélération.e: Learned borrowing from Latin accelerātiō. By surface analysis, accélérer + -ation.

circulaire.e: Borrowed from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus.

chasteté.e: Inherited from Middle French chasteté, from Old French, a semi-learned adaptation of Latin castitātem. By surface analysis, chaste + -té.

fraser.e: Inherited from Middle French fraser, fraiser, from Old French fraser, from Vulgar Latin *frēsāre, from the Late Latin term (faba) frēsa (“ground bean”), from frēsus (“crushed”), from the verb frendō (“to crush, gnash”).

fraîcheur.e: Etymology tree French frais Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *-ōs Proto-Italic *-ōs Latin -ōrem Old French -or Middle French -eur French -eur French fraîcheur From frais + -eur.

cacao.e: Borrowed from Spanish cacao, ultimately from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl.

athée.e: From Latin atheos, from Ancient Greek ἄθεος (átheos).

commodore.e: Borrowed from Dutch kommandeur, from Middle French commandeur; from Latin commendare, from com- + mandare, from mandō (“to order, command”).

nacelle.e: Inherited from Old French nacele (“small boat”), from Late Latin navicella, diminutive of Latin navis (“boat”). Doublet of navicelle.

frite.e: Ellipsis of patate frite (“fried potato”) or pomme frite (itself an ellipsis of pomme de terre frite); feminine of frit, the past participle of frire (“to fry”).

arès.e: Borrowed from Latin Arēs, from Ancient Greek Ἄρης (Árēs).

glousser.e: From Vulgar Latin *clociare, from Latin glocire.

thérapeutique.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θεραπευτικός (therapeutikós, “attentive, helpful, obliging, curative”). By surface analysis, thérapeute + -ique.

miaou.e: From earlier miault, myault, of onomatopoeic origin.

shooter.e: From English shoot + -er. First attested in 1900.

prêtresse.e: Inherited from Middle French prestresse. By surface analysis, prêtre (“priest”) + -esse (“-ess”).

tesla.e: Named after Serbian-American inventor Nikola Tesla.

nurse.e: Borrowed from English nurse, itself derived from Old French norrice. Doublet of nourrice.

appréhender.e: Borrowed from Latin apprehendere. Doublet of apprendre, which was inherited.

caméléon.e: Learned borrowing from Latin chamaeleōn, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek χᾰμαιλέων (khămailéōn).

masturbation.e: Inherited from Middle French, borrowed from New Latin masturbātiōnem. By surface analysis, masturber + -ation.

intriguer.e: Borrowed from Italian intrigare. Doublet of intriquer.

conservatoire.e: From conserver + -(at)oire (adjective-forming suffix), a learned formation built on the supine stem cōnservāt- of Latin cōnservāre, like the noun conservation. Corresponds to the Medieval Latin adjective cōnservātōrius.

libéral.e: Inherited from Old French liberal, from Latin līberālis (“befitting a freeman”), from līber (“free”).

boomer.e: Unadapted borrowing from English boomer, a clipping of baby boomer; mainly through the expression OK, boomer.

édifice.e: Borrowed from Latin aedificium, from aedificō (“to build”) (whence édifier).

aumônier.e: From Old French aumosnier, itself inherited from Late Latin eleemosynārius.

indistinct.e: Learned borrowing from Latin indistīnctus. By surface analysis, in- + distinct.

visibilité.e: Borrowed from Latin visibilitātem, from visibilis (“visible”). By surface analysis, visible + -ité.

dévier.e: Borrowed from Latin dēviāre. Compare the Old French desvoier (with a different prefix), whence French dévoyer.

bise.e: From Germanic, from Frankish *bîsi (“covered with clouds”), related to *bisa (“wind from the northeast”), from Proto-Germanic *bī̆s- (“to storm ahead”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂- (“to be afraid, fear”), see also…

benoît.e: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin Benedictus, from benedictus (“blessed; well spoken of”), from Latin benedicō. Cf. benoît. Compare Occitan Beneset, Catalan Benet, Italian Benedetto, Spanish Benito, Portuguese Bento.

orchidée.e: Borrowed from New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis).

ramer.e: Inherited from Middle French ramer, from Old French ramer, from Old French raim, rain, reimes, from Latin rēmus.

désoler.e: Borrowed from Latin dēsōlāre, from dē- + sōlus + -ō. Cognate with English desolate, Italian desolare, Portuguese desolar, Romanian dezolare, and Spanish desolar.

chenille.e: Inherited from Latin canīcula (“little dog”) (because of a caterpillar's head). Doublet of canicule.

dojo.e: From Japanese 道場 (dōjō, “place of the way”).

store.e: From Latin storea (“mat”), via regional Italian stora (modern Italian stuoia).

amender.e: From Old French amender, from Latin ēmendāre (“to free from faults, correct, improve, remedy, amend, revise, cure”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mendum (“fault”).

bûche.e: Inherited from Middle French busche, from Old French busche (“piece of wood to be burned”), from Vulgar Latin *busca, from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz. More at bush.

tourment.e: Inherited from Middle French tourment, torment, from Old French torment, from Latin tormentum. Related to tordre.

déserteur.e: Learned borrowing from Latin desertor. By surface analysis, déserter + -eur.

incarcérer.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin incarcerāre, incarcerō.

rab.e: Clipping of rabiot (“(originally fishermen and military cant) excess, remainder; (earlier) (1831) excess of fish remaining after rations had been imparted to the mates, (1859) soup soldiers often left over in their mess…

discréditer.e: From dis- + crédit + -er, perhaps from earlier désaccréditer.

canton.e: Inherited from Middle French canton, from Old French canton (from the 1240s), from Old Occitan canton (“corner; canton”) (recorded before 1218), adopted in Occitan from North Italian (Gallo-Italic, early Lombard) canton…

prestigieux.e: Learned borrowing from Late Latin praestīgiōsus. By surface analysis, prestige + -(i)eux.

charte.e: Inherited from Middle French charte, chartre, from Old French chartre, charte, from Latin chartula, diminutive of charta, with loss of the second -r- by dissimilation (or alternatively through influence from Latin chart…

enchanter.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Proto-Indo-European *keh₂n- Proto-Indo-European *kh₂néti Proto-Italic *kanō Latin canō Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Italic *-tos L…

juron.e: Etymology tree French jurer Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.? Latin -ō Frankishinflu. Old French -on Middle French -on French -on French juron From jurer + -on.

tourte.e: Ultimately from Latin turtur (“turtle, turtle dove, turtledove”). Compare tourterelle.

popotin.e: From a reduplication of po, from pot (“butt”).. From the 19th century.

larissa.e: Borrowed from English Larissa in the 20th century.

carpenter.e: Borrowed from English Carpenter, from Latin carpentarius. Doublet of Charpentier.

moisson.e: Inherited from Old French messon, meissun, from Latin messiōnem.

peureux.e: Inherited from Old French peoros, from Vulgar Latin *pavōrōsum, derived from Latin pavōrem (“fear”, noun). By surface analysis, peur + -eux.

terrifier.e: Loaned from Vulgar Latin *terrificare, from Latin terrārī + faciō, facere (“make”).

gouvernail.e: Inherited from Old French governail, from Latin gubernāculum. By surface analysis, gouverner + -ail.

flasque.e: Inherited from Latin flaccus, with spelling pronunciation of non-etymological s. Doublet of flache.

sororité.e: From Renaissance Latin sorōritās, from Latin soror (“sister”), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. Akin to Spanish sororidad, Portuguese sororidade, English sorority.

carapace.e: Borrowed from Spanish carapacho (“carapace, shell”), of uncertain origin.

talisman.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁- Proto-Hellenic *kʷélos Ancient Greek τέλος (télos) Proto-Indo-European *-yoh₂ Proto-Hellenic *-yō Ancient Greek *-ϳω (*-jō) Ancient Greek τελέω (teléō) Proto-Indo-European *-m…

hélice.e: Learned borrowing from Latin helix, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix).

pif.e: Possibly onomatopoeic. Compare however Central Franconian Pief, Peif (“stovepipe; flute”), akin to Dutch pijp, German Pfeife.

latitude.e: From Latin lātitūdō (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”), from older stlātus.

pieuvre.e: From Guernsey Norman pieuvre (introduced or popularised by Victor Hugo ca. 1866; cf. also Old Northern French puerve).

synonyme.e: From syn- + -onyme, from Late Latin synonymon, from Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”), composed by σύν (sún, “with”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “…

safari.e: Borrowed from Swahili safari (“journey”), from Arabic سَفَر (safar).

vignoble.e: Inherited from Old French vignoble (also latinised as vinoblium).

kangourou.e: Borrowed from English kangaroo; ultimately from Guugu Yimidhirr gangurru.

minutieux.e: Borrowed from New Latin minūtiōsus. Equivalent to minutie + -eux.

accordéon.e: Borrowed from German Akkordeon, from Akkord (“harmony”), itself from French accord, from Old French acorder, based on Italian accordare (“to tune”).

indes.e: From Latin India or from Latin Indus.

épiler.e: From Latin pilus (“hair”) prefixed with é-.

stase.e: Borrowed from New Latin stasis, derived from Ancient Greek στᾰ́σῐς (stắsĭs).

versailles.e: Uncertain, but possibly from Latin versus (“slope”) or versor (“to dwell”), both from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn around”).

partition.e: Inherited from Old French particion, from Latin partītiōnem. By surface analysis, partir + -tion.

célibat.e: Borrowed from Latin caelibātus, from caelebs.

primordial.e: Learned borrowing from Latin prīmōrdiālis (“of the beginning”).

suspicion.e: Learned borrowing from Latin suspiciō. Compare soupçon, derived from a related formation but not an actual doublet.

succomber.e: From Old French, borrowed from Latin succumbere.

éther.e: From Latin aethēr (“upper air, ether”), from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “air; ether”).

nakamura.e: Borrowed from Japanese 中村 (Nakamura) or 仲村 (Nakamura).

hutte.e: Inherited from Middle French hutte, from Old French hute (“hut”), from Middle High German hütte, from Old High German hutta (“hut”), from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ (“hut, shelter”), from *hūdijaną (“to conceal”), related to…

maudire.e: Inherited from Middle French maudire, mauldire, from Old French maudire, maldire, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin maledīcere (“to slander, curse”). Equivalent to mal + dire. Cf.

expiration.e: Inherited from Middle French expiration, borrowed from Latin exspīrātiōnem.

logistique.e: From Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós, “practiced in arithmetic, rational”), from λόγος (lógos). Sense of “logistic function” by Pierre François Verhulst (1845).

extincteur.e: Borrowed from Latin exstinctor. See éteindre + -teur.

vengeur.e: Inherited from Old French vengeor, vengeour, vengedur. By surface analysis, venger + -eur. Possibly corresponding to Late Latin vindicātōrem, from Latin vindicō. Compare Spanish vengador.

lutz.e: From the surname of Austrian skater Alois Lutz who invented the jump.

dissoudre.e: Inherited from Middle French dissoudre, from Old French dissoudre, from Latin dissolvo, from solvo, from luo

cocon.e: From Occitan coucoun (“cocoon”), derived from coco (“shell”).

renier.e: From Vulgar Latin *renegāre, from Latin re- + negāre. Compare Italian rinnegare and Spanish renegar.

verbe.e: Learned borrowing from Latin verbum. Doublet of verve.

prune.e: Inherited from Old French prune, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon).

péage.e: Via Provençal pezatge, from Medieval Latin pedāticum (found in medieval charters), from Latin pedem (“foot”). Alternatively a very old derivation of Old French pied (cf. the medieval forms paage, peage).

appli.e: Clipping of application, probably a calque of English app.

compression.e: First known attestation 1314, borrowed from Latin compressiōnem.

sanguinaire.e: Learned borrowing from Latin sanguinārius, from sanguis (whence French sang).

manchot.e: Inherited from Old French manc (itself from Latin mancus) + -ot.

arsenic.e: Learned borrowing from Latin arsenicum, from Late/Byzantine Greek ἀρσενικόν (arsenikón, “yellow arsenic”), from Classical Syriac ܙܪܢܝܟܐ (zarnīḵā), from Middle Persian *zarnīk, from Old Median *zaraniyakā, ultimately fro…
